    New in 0.4.51: 3D graphics, partitions and a disk installer

    Small software, built from the ground up.

    Xlabs makes low-level software with as little in the way as possible: Minimal-OS, an operating system for x86_64, and everything around it — an SDK, a 3D library, a TLS library, a desktop and a window manager. And a studio that builds apps for it in your browser.

    Open Run Studio Minimal-OS on GitHub
    Minimal-OS terminal

    About

    We write C and assembly, keep the codebase readable, and publish everything as open source under GPL-3.0. Each piece is small enough to read in an afternoon.

    Flagship

    Minimal-OS

    An operating system written in C and Assembly for x86_64 processors. It boots from an ISO on BIOS and UEFI machines, runs in QEMU and on real PCs, and can install itself onto a disk. Add the MOSdesk package and it boots to a desktop.

    Read the docsDownload an ISO

    What's new in 0.4.51

    GPU and 3D

    A 3D pipeline in the kernel

    The FGPU command processor draws depth-tested, lit and textured triangles, runs FGSL shaders, and places surfaces in VRAM. Drivers for NVIDIA Pascal and Turing cards and QEMU report VRAM and page flip; drawing on NVIDIA cards themselves is under way.

     FarcadeGL

    3D for every app

    A header-only library with command buffers, vertex layouts, textures, blending and GLSL-style shaders. fglcube and MOSdesk's Cube app show it off.

     Storage

    Partitions and big disks

    MBR and GPT tables with part, MinimaFS volumes up to 16 TiB, several mounted drives, and an NVMe driver next to AHCI.

     Installer

    Install to a disk

    install sata1 in the terminal, or the Installer app in MOSdesk, writes a disk that boots by itself on BIOS and UEFI PCs.

     Real hardware

    Ready for real PCs

    More than 1 GiB of RAM, UEFI boot with a GOP framebuffer, USB 3 (xHCI) and PS/2 keyboards and mice, and write-combining video memory.

     MOSdesk

    More apps

    Golf, Snake, Paint, a calculator, a clock, a text editor, the Installer and a FarcadeGL cube, plus user accounts with their own folders.

    How the pieces fit

    1. Your appA .run bundle: one PIE executable plus its resources, written in C or C++.
    2. SDKwindow.h, easyui.h, farcadegl.h, net.h and friends — thin wrappers over int 0x80.
    3. MOSdesk · mosWMA user-space desktop. mosWM owns the framebuffer and composites every window.
    4. Minimal-OSScheduler, MinimaFS, drivers, TCP/IP, the FGPU 3D pipeline, and the window and input syscalls apps rely on.
    5. MinimaSSLLinked into the kernel for TLS 1.3, and shipped as 0:/etc/minimaSSL.slib.

    What Minimal-OS does today

    Runs on several cores

    SMP with per-CPU run queues, a three-level scheduler, threads and a services manager.

    Runs your programs

    Ring-3 .run programs with a heap, files, packages and a validated syscall boundary.

    Talks to hardware

    Framebuffer and GPU adapters, USB 1.1 and USB 3 input, PS/2, AC'97 audio, AHCI and NVMe disks.

    Gets online

    Ethernet, ARP, IPv4, UDP, DHCP, DNS, TCP, and a TLS 1.3 client behind wget.

    Has a desktop

    MOSdesk and mosWM: windows, a taskbar, a file browser, themes and sign-in.

    Installs software

    .mpkg archives with LZSS compression, and the dlr package client.

    Draws in 3D

    A kernel 3D pipeline with shaders, used through FarcadeGL from any window or full-screen app.

    Manages disks

    MBR and GPT partitions, MinimaFS volumes up to 16 TiB, several drives at once.

    Installs itself

    One command, or the MOSdesk Installer, makes a disk that boots on BIOS and UEFI.

    Build And Debugging

    On this pagePrerequisitesMake TargetsResource RebuildsHTTPS TestCI And Interactive TestsLogs And DiagnosticsDebugging Rules

    Prerequisites

    The documented Debian/Ubuntu dependencies include GCC/binutils tooling, NASM, GRUB tools, xorriso, make, and QEMU. The repository's build_gccbinutils.sh creates the cross-toolchain expected by the Makefile at $HOME/cross/bin/x86_64-elf-gcc and x86_64-elf-ld.

    Create a QEMU disk image before running the full storage workflow:

    fallocate -l 256M sata256.img

    Make Targets

    make build-x86_64
make run
make minimaSSL-slib
make clean

    build-x86_64 compiles enabled modules, kernel implementation files, minimaSSL crypto sources, resource packages, and embedded package objects. It links dist/x86_64/kernel.bin, copies it to the ISO input tree, and creates dist/x86_64/kernel.iso.

    run builds first, then starts QEMU with the ISO, serial console, USB keyboard, AHCI disk, RTL8139 networking, and audio devices.

    minimaSSL-slib builds the SDK library and copies the result to the distribution build. The install1 rule then copies it into src/resources/install1 before building the embedded package.

    clean removes kernel and distribution output, Minimal-OS-SDK/build, minimaSSL bundles, and package objects. It also deletes every *.run file under the repository, including any hand-authored bundles; preserve any such files before running it. It does not remove source resources or the disk image. See Build Targets for details.

    Resource Rebuilds

    Resource directories are packaged into install1, install2, and install3:

    src/resources/install1 -> 0:/etc
src/resources/install2 -> 0:/programs
src/resources/install3 -> 0:/services

    Files added to install2/install3 are included as package prerequisites, so a changed program or service causes the corresponding embedded package to rebuild. Run make clean when removing a generated file should also remove its stale package object.

    HTTPS Test

    Run the focused TLS integration test:

    bash tools/debug/https_test.sh

    The script:

    1. builds the kernel;
    2. creates a temporary self-signed certificate;
    3. starts openssl s_server -tls1_3 on the host;
    4. starts QEMU with user-mode networking;
    5. sends n at the disk prompt;
    6. runs dhcp;
    7. runs wget https://10.0.2.2:8443/;
    8. checks for handshake and download completion.

    The test intentionally uses an IP address and defers certificate verification. It validates the TLS record/key schedule and HTTP exchange, not public CA trust.

    The crypto known-answer test is:

    gcc -std=c11 -I Minimal-OS-SDK/libraries/minimaSSL/include \
  tools/debug/mssl_tls_gcm_kat.c \
  Minimal-OS-SDK/libraries/minimaSSL/src/tls_gcm.c \
  -o /tmp/mssl_tls_gcm_kat
/tmp/mssl_tls_gcm_kat

    CI And Interactive Tests

    make ci-test
make ci-interact

    ci_test.sh is intended for automated checks. ci_interact.sh drives the terminal over serial and waits for command-specific success patterns. When a pattern fails, inspect its serial output and the generated QEMU log.

    Logs And Diagnostics

    Useful output sources include:

    • serial terminal output for initialization, commands, services, and TLS;
    • tools/debug/https_test.log for the HTTPS test guest console;
    • tools/debug/https_server.log for OpenSSL trace output;
    • qemu.log for QEMU guest errors and interrupts.

    OpenSSL's bad record mac means it rejected an authenticated TLS record before it could decode the encrypted inner message. Compare it with the guest's TLS stage message; the server-side error is often the primary failure and the guest receive error is a follow-on alert/close.

    Debugging Rules

    Build the smallest focused test after a change. Preserve existing user changes in a dirty worktree. Avoid using generated logs as source-of-truth code. For kernel crashes, inspect process creation, allocator state, interrupt state, serial output, and the last subsystem initialization message in that order.

    Boot And Kernel

    On this pageBoot ChainStartup OrderSIMD State (SSE, AVX, AVX-512)MemoryProcesses And ThreadsScheduling And SMPSyscall BoundaryKernel Interfaces

    Boot Chain

    GRUB loads the Multiboot2 kernel from the ISO. The boot entry is split between src/impl/boot/main.asm and src/impl/boot/main64.asm:

    1. Save the Multiboot information pointer.
    2. Verify the Multiboot signature, CPUID, and x86_64 long-mode support.
    3. Build initial PML4, PDPT, and page-directory tables.
    4. Enable PAE, long mode, NX, and paging.
    5. Load the 64-bit GDT and jump to long_mode_start.
    6. Pass the Multiboot information address to kernel_main().

    The initial low-memory map uses 2 MiB pages. PML4 slot 511 is reserved for a high MMIO address range. Later device mappings are made by src/impl/kernel/mmio.c. The Multiboot memory-map tag is parsed by multiboot2parse.c to determine the available RAM reported to the allocator and system information commands.

    The GRUB menu provides three entries: Minimal-OS for normal startup, Minimal-OS Memory Tester x64 for a standalone pattern test of free PMM pages, and Minimal-OS (No Disk) to boot without probing or mounting storage. The memory test reserves only free PMM pages and halts after reporting PASS or FAIL.

    Startup Order

    kernel_main() in src/impl/kernel/main.c performs the high-level startup:

    • serial output, BSP/SMP state, GDT, and command registration;
    • memory and startup routines;
    • PCI enumeration;
    • USB and graphics driver-manager registration;
    • network driver registration (RTL8139, RTL8168), Ethernet/IP/UDP/TCP setup, and network syscall state;
    • time and random seeding;
    • audio and AHCI storage-driver registration;
    • AP startup, interrupts, kernel background processes, and the terminal.

    The terminal owns the disk interaction. In normal mode it probes and mounts the disk and starts services; no-disk mode skips that path and still starts the terminal and keyboard tasks.

    RamFS mode (GRUB entry "Minimal-OS (RamFS)", kernel option ramfs or ramfs=<MiB>) runs the whole system from RAM, which makes it safe for testing on a real PC. Real disks (AHCI, NVMe) are never probed, so nothing reads or writes them. Instead a zeroed RAM disk, ram0 (64 MiB by default, less if memory is short, at least 16 MiB), is formatted as 0:, the system files are unpacked into it as format would, and startup goes on as usual (services, desktop). Every change is lost at the next boot. A boot module named mosfirmware (an .mpkg) is unpacked into 0:/firmware (by format and install too); make gpu-setup puts one on the ISO with NVIDIA's firmware files (see gpu.md), and the test VM uses it the same way.

    The kernel option serial-echo copies everything the terminal prints to COM1, so a headless VM's serial log contains command output as well as the kernel's own messages (tools/hyperv/mosvm.sh boots with it).

    SIMD State (SSE, AVX, AVX-512)

    The kernel is compiled without AVX; only user programs use the wide registers. cpu_simd_init_bsp() (src/impl/cpu_simd.c) runs first thing in kernel_main, before the IDT is loaded, and every AP runs cpu_simd_init_ap() at the top of ap_entry_c, before it can take an interrupt. When CPUID reports XSAVE and AVX they set CR4.OSXSAVE and XCR0 to x87|SSE|AVX, plus opmask, ZMM_Hi256 and Hi16_ZMM when the CPU has AVX-512F. The save area size is CPUID.(0xD,0).EBX for that XCR0, rounded up to 64 bytes (AVX2: 832, AVX-512: 2752). Without XSAVE or AVX, or with the noavx boot flag, nothing changes: CR4.OSFXSR only, fxsave64, 512 bytes.

    Nothing in context_switch.asm touches SIMD registers. Every kernel entry (the exception stub in idt_isr.asm, the IRQ stubs in idt_.asm, int 0x80 in syscall_isr.asm) saves the interrupted code's state in a 64-byte aligned area on the kernel stack and restores it before iretq, through the SIMD_SAVE/SIMD_RESTORE macros in src/impl/simd_save.inc. A context switch happens inside a timer IRQ or a blocking syscall, deeper than one of those stubs, so a sleeping process's state is already on its own kernel stack and comes back when it unwinds. The macros pick fxsave64 or xsave64 (header zeroed first, EDX:EAX = simd_xcr0) from the global simd_use_xsave, which is final before interrupts are first enabled, so one kernel runs on both kinds of CPU. xsaveopt is not used: its init/modified tracking is tied to the linear address of the last xrstor, and stack addresses are reused between processes.

    Kernel stacks grew because of this. Entries nest: a syscall, a timer IRQ while it sleeps, a page fault in the kernel, each with up to ~2.7 KiB of state plus its frame. At 16 KiB that left about 7 KiB for C code (14 KiB before), so a process kernel stack is now KERNEL_STACK_SIZE = 32 KiB, AP boot stacks are 32 KiB, and the per-CPU TSS stack (the double fault IST stack) is 16 KiB instead of 4 KiB. The boot CPU's stack is 256 KiB. A new process starts with whatever the previous code left in the registers (not cleared: a leak, not corruption).

    SYS_SYSINFO returns the SYS_CPU_* feature mask (SYS_SYSINFO_CPU_FEATURES) and the enabled XCR0 (SYS_SYSINFO_XCR0); the AVX-family bits are set only when the state is enabled, so a set bit means usable.

    Boot flag noavx keeps the SSE-only behaviour (a fallback for hardware trouble). It goes on the multiboot command line like ramfs; the GRUB entry "Minimal-OS (RamFS, noavx)" sets it. tools/debug/ci_os0.sh can boot it (see testing.md).

    Memory

    The physical memory manager (src/impl/pmm.c) allocates 4 KiB pages. The heap allocator (src/impl/kernel/allocator.c) provides variable-size allocations for kernel structures, file buffers, process objects, and driver state.

    Use page allocation for DMA-aligned or page-owned memory. Use alloc() or alloc_unzeroed() for ordinary objects. Large structures such as directory descriptors are deliberately heap allocated because kernel stacks are small.

    At boot the kernel takes the largest free block of RAM below 4 GiB. The heap gets the lower half and the page pool the upper half (at least 64 MiB). The kernel reaches all of it through an identity mapping of the first 4 GiB, which every process shares.

    Program memory above 4 GiB is managed by src/impl/proc/uvm.c: a sorted list of mapped areas per program, with a protection each. A page gets a frame from the page pool on its first use, in the page-fault handler, and reads as zero until written. SYS_VM maps, unmaps, protects and decommits such areas. Kernel code copies into or out of another program's memory with uvm_copy_in() and uvm_copy_out(), which work through the frames whatever page tables are loaded.

    Shared areas. A uvm_shm_t (uvm.h) is a reference-counted run of zeroed, physically contiguous frames from the low page pool that can be mapped into several spaces with uvm_map_shm(), each with its own protection (read-only for the window manager) and always NX. The creator holds one reference and every mapping (a uvm_area_t with shm set) holds one; the frames return to the pool when the last goes, so uvm_unmap, uvm_release_all and uvm_destroy of one space never free frames another space still maps. Their page-table entries carry the software bit PTE_SHARED, which release_frame, free_tables and uvm_protect/the fault path respect (the bit is kept, the frame is not freed). The pages are filled in at creation under the space lock, before the area is visible (no demand-zero). A shared area is never split: uvm_unmap and uvm_protect must cover it whole (otherwise SYS_ERR_INVAL and that area stays as it is; other areas in the range are still handled), uvm_protect may not grant more than the mapping started with or add execute, and uvm_decommit on one is refused with SYS_ERR_INVAL. Unmapping clears the entries, shoots down the TLBs of every CPU that has the space loaded (tlb.h) and only then drops the reference. The kernel writes into the frames through uvm_shm_base() (identity map). The window manager uses this for window frames (see User programs).

    Processes And Threads

    Kernel processes are created with createProcess(name, entry). A process entry must either loop, call sleep(), or terminate through process_exit()/kill(); returning from a raw kernel entry is not a normal completion mechanism.

    User .run programs are loaded as user processes. The loader maps the image, the main stack and the argument block into the new program's address space, then enters ring 3 through the process trampoline. See user programs.

    Kernel threads (thread_create()) are lightweight wrappers around kernel processes. thread_join() polls for process termination while yielding through sleep().

    User threads (SYS_THREAD)

    A user thread is a process_t whose mem_owner points at its program: it has its own kernel stack and registers but shares the owner's page tables, uvm space and SYS_HEAP allocation list. Threads of one program run in parallel on different CPUs (OS-3). The boot flag threads1cpu restores the old behaviour (every thread on its owner's CPU, no affinity), smpthreads forces multicore on; multicore is the default.

    • Placement. A new thread goes to the least loaded CPU its affinity allows (running processes count as load), is woken on the CPU it last ran on, and the periodic rebalance may move queued threads like any process. A CPU that receives work while idle is sent a reschedule IPI (vector 0x35) so it does not wait for its next tick.
    • Affinity and priority. SYS_THREAD_SET_AFFINITY/GET_AFFINITY (mask of CPUs, 0 = any) and SYS_THREAD_SET_PRIORITY/GET_PRIORITY, plus SYS_THREAD_GET_CPU and SYS_THREAD_INFO. The CPU count is SYS_SYSINFO_CORE_COUNT. Priority is the MLFQ floor (sched_prio): level 0 (default) starts interactive, 1 never above normal, 2 background only. Affinity is enforced when a thread is queued, woken or dispatched (scheduler_cpu_allowed()); a running thread outside its mask is kicked by an IPI and leaves at once.
    • TLB shootdown (tlb.c, vector 0x34). Each uvm_space_t keeps a mask of CPUs that may have its page tables loaded; switch_to() sets a CPU's bit before the CR3 load and clears the old space's bit (interrupts are off, and no user memory is touched in between). uvm_unmap/protect/decommit, the page-table pruning in uvm_unmap and the SYS_HEAP user-access changes call tlb_shootdown() while holding the space (or heap) lock: the sender flushes itself, posts one request (a single global slot under a lock), IPIs the CPUs in the mask and waits for each to flush (invlpg per page up to 48 pages, else a CR3 reload) and acknowledge. Frames and page-table pages are collected during the walk and handed back to the page pool only after the flush. A CPU spinning on any kernel spinlock, the space lock or the request slot services a pending request for itself (tlb_poll()), so two CPUs shooting at each other cannot deadlock. A CPU with interrupts off in a long system call acknowledges when it returns to user mode or opens a window: frames are therefore never freed under a system call that is still using them. Making a page more accessible needs no shootdown: a stale entry produces a spurious protection fault that uvm_handle_fault() (SYS_VM memory) and proc_heap_stale_fault() (SYS_HEAP memory) recognise, repair with invlpg and retry.
    • Exit and crash. Whoever calls exit (owner) or crashes (any thread) claims the program's end with group_dying; a second crasher just stops. The group's other threads are marked dead under their run queue's lock (scheduler_mark_dead: state change and dequeue as one step, the same lock the dispatcher pops and starts processes under) and the CPUs running them get a reschedule IPI; the scheduler tick also leaves a dead process. The owner waits (answering shootdowns) until none of its threads has on_cpu set before it unmaps its memory, and the reaper never frees a process that is on_cpu, current anywhere or in a deferred-reap slot.
    • Audited shared state. user_heap_allocations and the SYS_HEAP page-table writes: heap_lock (new). Thread creation versus exit: group_dying and the thread count are checked under the scheduler lock, and a thread created PAUSED is started with a compare-and-swap so a kill in between wins. cwd/env: g_cwd_lock. stdio sinks: per-sink busy flag. Futex queues: per-bucket spinlocks (waker and waiter on different CPUs; the woken thread is queued on its own CPU's run queue and the dispatcher skips a process another CPU is still switching away from). FS base: per CPU cache in the scheduler, reloaded on every switch to a user thread. in_syscall: only its own thread writes it and the fault handler reads it on that thread's CPU. Page faults: two CPUs faulting on one page both take the space lock; the second finds the frame in place. thread_count: scheduler lock.

    Scheduling And SMP

    Each online CPU owns a run queue with three levels:

    • interactive: terminal input and short blocking work;
    • normal: ordinary processes;
    • background: CPU-heavy or lower-priority work.

    A process that consumes its quantum is demoted. A process that blocks is promoted on wake. Periodic boosting prevents starvation, and periodic rebalancing moves queued processes between CPUs when the load difference is large enough.

    Run-queue locks are SMP-safe spinlocks. cli only disables interrupts on the current CPU; it is not a replacement for an atomic lock shared by CPUs.

    process_t contains fields consumed by context-switch assembly. Fields before the documented ABI boundary must not move without updating the assembly and verification code.

    Syscall Boundary

    User code invokes int 0x80. The syscall ISR saves registers into the packed syscall_regs_t layout, and syscall_dispatch() validates the requested operation and user pointers before calling a subsystem implementation.

    The user privilege table is separate from the syscall number table. For example, a user program may use TCP and filesystem calls, while DHCP remains a privileged operation because it changes the machine-wide network configuration. See user SDK syscalls for the complete user-facing API.

    Kernel Interfaces

    Public kernel contracts live in src/intf:

    • x86_64/proc.h and x86_64/scheduler.h define process/scheduler state.
    • x86_64/allocator.h and x86_64/pmm.h define memory allocation.
    • x86_64/minimafs.h defines filesystem objects and operations.
    • x86_64/syscall.h defines the syscall ABI structures and constants.
    • subsystem manager headers define driver registration and lifecycle methods.

    Implementations can grow internal structures, but shared headers and assembly offset contracts must remain synchronized.

    Hardware And Drivers

    On this pageDriver Manager PatternPCI And MMIOGraphicsUSBNetworkAudioStorageAdding A Driver

    Driver Manager Pattern

    Hardware support is registered during kernel startup through manager APIs. A manager selects an available driver, initializes it, and exposes a stable subsystem interface to the rest of the kernel. This keeps device-specific code out of terminal commands and protocol implementations.

    Relevant interfaces are in src/intf/x86_64 and implementations are in src/modules:

    • network_manager.h / network drivers;
    • gpu_manager.h / framebuffer drivers;
    • usb_manager.h / host-controller and device drivers;
    • audio manager interfaces;
    • storage manager and AHCI interfaces.

    A missing device is normally a supported degraded state. Graphics can continue headless, USB can fall back to PS/2, and audio can report that no compatible controller exists.

    PCI And MMIO

    PCI enumeration discovers devices by bus, device, and function. Driver code reads vendor/device IDs and maps BARs through the kernel MMIO allocator rather than using arbitrary virtual addresses.

    Enabling a device for a driver (pci_enable_io_busmaster) also brings it to full power (D0) if the firmware or a previous OS left it in a sleep state; until then its registers read as all ones.

    The MMIO subsystem reserves a high virtual range, creates page-table entries, and maps device registers or framebuffer memory. Device mappings must remain page aligned and should use the mapping helpers rather than direct identity assumptions.

    Graphics

    The display itself still comes from the linear framebuffer the bootloader set up (VBE on BIOS, GOP on UEFI); the Bochs/VBE driver can also set modes on QEMU's 1234:1111 device. Framebuffers are mapped write-combining (PAT entry 1), which makes pixel writes to a real graphics card much faster.

    On top of that, gpucore.c turns each display-class PCI device into a GPU adapter with video memory: total VRAM, the PCI BAR that is the CPU's window onto it, where the visible framebuffer sits in VRAM, and a VRAM allocator for the rest. Drivers:

    DriverDevicesWhat it knows
    gpu_nvidia.cNVIDIA, tuned for GTX 10 (Pascal) and RTX 20 / GTX 16 (Turing)chip and board name, VRAM size from the memory controller, BAR1 window, temperature
    gpu_bochs.cQEMU/Bochs standard VGAVRAM size, page flipping
    gpu_generic.ceverything elsethe framebuffer's BAR as VRAM window

    Drawing commands go through the FGPU command processor (SYS_GPU, fgpu.c), whose current backend renders 3D on the CPU. See GPU and 3D.

    USB

    UHCI and OHCI (USB 1.1) and xHCI (USB 3, every recent PC) controllers are driven. Directly attached HID boot keyboards and mice work on all three; hubs, EHCI, and USB storage are not supported yet. On xHCI the kernel takes the controller over from the firmware (legacy hand-off) and polls its event ring from the timer interrupt.

    PS/2 keyboards work too: the 8042 controller is initialised at boot and its scan codes are converted to the same HID reports, so layouts and key repeat behave the same as with USB.

    User programs use SYS_USB wrappers for initialization, polling, keyboard presence, key translation, and keyboard metadata.

    Network

    Network drivers register with the network manager, which uses the first one whose card is present: RTL8139 (rtl8139.c, QEMU's default) and RTL8111/8168 (rtl8168.c, PCI Express gigabit, 10ec:8168/10ec:8161). Both are polled from the PIT tick. See Networking.

    Audio

    Audio drivers register with the audio manager, which uses the first one whose hardware is present: Intel HD Audio (hda_driver.c, any PCI class 04:03 controller and its codecs), then AC'97 (ac97_driver.c). Both are polled from the PIT tick: they refill the DMA buffers the card has played with samples pulled from the mixer. The HD Audio driver walks each codec from its speaker, line-out and headphone pins to a DAC, and resamples when the codec cannot play a file's rate.

    The kernelaudio process decodes .adi files ahead of the card. Playback is controlled by the terminal's play, pause, stop, volume and seek commands, and by programs through SYS_AUDIO (Playing audio). Programs that make their own sound (games) use SYS_AUDIO_STREAM: up to 8 streams, each with its own rate and channel count, are resampled to the card's rate and mixed on top of the file player in the mixer (audio_streams.c). A stream's queue is filled by its program and drained by the driver's refill without a lock, and is closed when its program exits. make run QEMU_SOUND=hda boots QEMU with an HD Audio card instead of AC'97.

    If no compatible audio controller is present, initialization reports that state and the rest of the system continues.

    Storage

    Disks are block devices (blockdev.c): every SATA disk on every AHCI controller (sata0, sata1, ...) and every NVMe namespace (nvme0, ...). MBR and GPT partitions become child devices (sata0p1, nvme0p2). MinimaFS works on any block device, so a volume can be a whole disk (the original layout) or a partition. See Storage and packages.

    The filesystem uses a DMA bounce buffer for block I/O; the NVMe driver builds PRP lists and is polled.

    Adding A Driver

    A new driver normally needs:

    1. a hardware-facing interface structure and callbacks;
    2. a manager registration call during kernel_main();
    3. PCI/device detection and resource mapping;
    4. an implementation under src/modules or the relevant subsystem;
    5. a fallback behavior when the device is absent;
    6. build configuration in config.mk if the module is optional.

    Keep interrupt handlers short, protect shared state with the appropriate local interrupt and SMP locking rules, and expose only subsystem-level operations to commands and user syscalls.

    Playing audio (audio.h)

    Plays .adi files through the sound card the kernel found: Intel HD Audio or AC97, and lets programs play sound they make themselves through audio streams (below), mixed together with the file. There is one file player for the whole system. Opening a file replaces whatever was playing, including a file started with the terminal's play command. MOSdesk's Player app (0:/programs/mos_player.run) uses this API.

    Every call returns SYS_SUCCESS (0) or a negative SYS_ERR_* value.

    Functionssyscall_audio_status_t
    CallDoes
    mos_audio_open(path)Loads a file and starts playing it. SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND if it does not exist, SYS_ERR_INVAL if it is not a playable .adi, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if there is no sound card
    mos_audio_pause()Pauses
    mos_audio_resume()Continues; after the end it plays the file again from the start
    mos_audio_stop()Stops and unloads the file
    mos_audio_seek(ms)Jumps to a position in milliseconds
    mos_audio_volume(v)Sets the volume, 0-100. Opening a file resets it to the file's Globalvol
    mos_audio_status(&st)Fills a syscall_audio_status_t; works with nothing loaded

    syscall_audio_status_t

    FieldMeaning
    stateSYSCALL_AUDIO_IDLE (nothing loaded), _PLAYING, _PAUSED, _ENDED
    position_ms, duration_msWhere playback is and how long the file is
    sample_rate, channelsFrom the file's header
    volume0-100
    format"IMA-ADPCM" or "PCM16"
    driver"Intel HD Audio", "AC97", or "" when there is no sound card
    pathThe file that is loaded
    #include "audio.h"

int main(void) {
    if (mos_audio_open("0:/music.adi") != SYS_SUCCESS) return 1;
    syscall_audio_status_t st;
    do {
        mos_sleep(500);
        mos_audio_status(&st);
    } while (st.state == SYSCALL_AUDIO_PLAYING);
    return 0;
}

    Playback runs in the kernel, so it keeps going after the program exits. Call mos_audio_stop() first if it should not.

    Audio streams: sound a program makes

    For games, synthesizers and anything else that makes its own sound. A program opens a stream and keeps writing 16-bit samples into it; the kernel mixes up to 8 streams (from any programs) and the file player together, converting each stream's rate to the sound card's.

    CallDoes
    mos_audio_stream_open(rate, channels)Opens a stream: 8000-96000 Hz, 1 (mono) or 2 (stereo) channels. Returns a handle (1 or more), or SYS_ERR_BUSY when all 8 are taken, SYS_ERR_GENERIC with no sound card, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a bad rate or channel count
    mos_audio_stream_write(h, samples, frames)Queues frames frames (a frame is one sample per channel, stereo interleaved left, right). Returns how many it took: fewer when the queue is full, never blocks
    mos_audio_stream_queued(h)Frames still waiting to be played
    mos_audio_stream_query(h, &info)Fills a syscall_audio_stream_t: queued, capacity (16384 frames), mix_rate (the card's rate), underruns (times the stream ran dry while open)
    mos_audio_stream_set_volume(h, v)0-100, default 100
    mos_audio_stream_close(h)Closes it; what is still queued is dropped

    A stream belongs to the program that opened it and is closed when that program exits. The file player's volume does not affect streams, and opening or stopping a file does not touch them.

    Keep a little queued - 50-100 ms is a good amount - and top it up regularly: too little and the sound breaks up when the program is slow for a moment, too much and it lags behind the picture.

    #include "audio.h"

/* One second of a 440 Hz square wave. */
int main(void) {
    int h = mos_audio_stream_open(22050, 1);
    if (h < 0) return 1;
    static int16_t buf[22050];
    for (int i = 0; i < 22050; i++) buf[i] = (i / 25) % 2 ? 6000 : -6000;
    uint32_t done = 0;
    while (done < 22050) {
        long n = mos_audio_stream_write(h, buf + done, 22050 - done);
        if (n > 0) done += (uint32_t)n;
        else mos_sleep(20);
    }
    while (mos_audio_stream_queued(h) > 0) mos_sleep(20);
    mos_audio_stream_close(h);
    return 0;
}

    Doom's sound effects (programs/doom/sound.c) are a fuller example: up to 16 sounds mixed in the program into one stereo stream.

    Making .adi files

    python3 tools/audioconverter/wavtoadi.py --format IADPCM song.wav song.adi

    Takes 16-bit mono or stereo WAV. Rates from 8 to 48 kHz play as they are; the HD Audio driver resamples when the codec lacks the file's rate.

    Images (.img) and videos (.vid)

    Minimal-OS has its own picture and video formats, in Minimal-OS-SDK/include/mosmedia.h (plain C, no libc, so they run in programs, in mosWM and on the build PC).

    An .img is a raster picture (lossless RGB or RGBA) or a vector picture: paths filled and stroked with solid colors and gradients, drawn again at whatever size is asked for, so icons and logos stay sharp from 16 px to 1024 px and can be tinted with the theme's color (see Vector images).

    A .vid file uses one of three codecs, the way an .adi file is PCM16 or ADPCM:

    On this pageIn the terminalOn web pagesMaking filesHow the tiles codec worksHow the motion codec worksThe H.264 codecVector images.img layout (raster, version 1).vid layoutIn programsHardware decoding
    CodecForHow
    tilesscreen recordings, drawings, animation, gameslossless (or near-lossless with --loss), keeps transparency; only changed tiles are stored
    motioncamera footage, filmslossy and built like H.264: motion vectors, a transform, a range coder. RGB only; tens of times smaller on camera footage
    h264video that comes from, or goes to, the rest of the worldH.264 (AVC), Constrained Baseline profile: the codec of most video on the web. Smaller than motion at the same quality; encoded by x264 on the build PC

    Every player reads all three: the Video app, Mxplorer and the Python player (which uses ffmpeg for h264).

    .img.vid
    WhatA picture, 8-bit RGB or RGBA (transparency, like PNG), or a vector picture (shapes, any size)Frames in 32-bit ARGB8888 (including transparency), a frame rate and an .adi soundtrack
    CompressionRaster: lossless, about PNG's size, faster to decode. Vector: a few hundred bytes for an icontiles: lossless, only changed tiles are stored; motion: lossy, like H.264; h264: H.264 itself
    Opens withPhotos (0:/programs/mos_photos.run), and as a wallpaper in SettingsVideo (0:/programs/mos_video.run)
    In the terminalimg 0:/users/me/Pictures/cat.imgvideo 0:/users/me/Videos/clip.vid
    In Mxplorer<img src="cat.img">, or open the file's address<video src="clip.vid" controls>, or open the file's address
    Make onemosmedia img picture.png out.img, mosmedia vimg icon.svg icon.img (vector)mosmedia vid movie.mp4 out.vid (motion), mosmedia vid screen.mkv out.vid --codec tiles, mosmedia vid movie.mp4 out.vid --codec h264

    In the terminal

    The MOSdesk terminal opens pictures and videos in their apps:

    video 0:/users/me/Videos/clip.vid     # also: vid
img ~/Pictures/cat.img                # also: image, photo

    Relative paths are inside the current folder.

    On web pages

    Mxplorer shows .img pictures in <img> and plays .vid videos in <video>, with sound. It picks files by their extension, so other pictures (PNG, JPEG) still show a placeholder. A vector .img is shown at its natural size, like any other:

    <img src="logo.img" alt="Logo" width="200">
<video src="clip.vid" controls autoplay muted loop poster="still.img"></video>
<video controls><source src="clip.vid"></video>

    A video's sound plays from a file, so a downloaded video is written to 0:/data/mxplorer-video.vid the first time it plays with sound. Downloads are limited to 32 MiB; local files (0:/... in the address bar, or run Mxplorer 0:/path/page.html) have no limit, and local videos are read as they play. Pages from the network cannot use local files.

    Making files

    make build/tools/mosmedia builds the converter for the build PC (Linux or macOS), and make build/tools/mosmedia.exe the same tool for Windows (with MinGW-w64; on Windows, ffmpeg and ffprobe must be in PATH). It uses ffmpeg for everything it reads and writes, and codes the soundtrack itself (IMA ADPCM, the same bytes as tools/audioconverter/wavtoadi.py).

    Encoding uses every CPU core: each frame's macroblocks are decided on several threads as a wavefront (each row two macroblocks behind the one above), then written in order, so the file is byte-for-byte the same with any number of threads. ffmpeg decodes the input on its own, a few frames ahead, with the GPU's video decoder when there is one (NVDEC, VA-API, Quick Sync, D3D11/DXVA2 on Windows; -hwaccel auto). The encoding itself runs on the CPU.

    For viewing and debugging .img, .vid, and .adi files on Linux or Windows, see the Python player in tools/media.

    Small sample files are included: sample.img is a 320x180 RGBA gradient with transparent corners, sample.vid is a 2-second, 12 fps color test video (tiles codec), and sample-motion.vid and sample-h264.vid are the same video in the motion and h264 codecs. Open either in the Python player, for example:

    python tools/media/mosplayer.py docs/examples/sample.img
python tools/media/mosplayer.py docs/examples/sample.vid
    build/tools/mosmedia img logo.png logo.img        # any picture ffmpeg reads; keeps transparency
build/tools/mosmedia png logo.img logo.png        # and back
build/tools/mosmedia vimg logo.svg logo.img       # SVG -> vector .img (no ffmpeg needed)
build/tools/mosmedia png logo.img big.png --size 1024   # a vector .img drawn at 1024 px
build/tools/mosmedia vid film.mp4 film.vid --width 640 --q 26   # motion codec
build/tools/mosmedia vid screen.mkv screen.vid --codec tiles      # lossless
build/tools/mosmedia vid film.mp4 film.vid --codec h264 --width 640   # H.264 (needs ffmpeg with libx264)
build/tools/mosmedia unvid clip.vid check.mp4     # to look at the result (check.raw: exact pixels)
build/tools/mosmedia info clip.vid

    The picture codec and the tiles codec preserve all 8 bits per color channel. .img files may store opaque pictures as RGB or pictures with transparency as RGBA; tiles .vid files may store RGB or RGBA frames (the mosmedia vid converter writes RGBA and preserves any source alpha channel). Motion .vid files are RGB. The converter writes motion unless --codec tiles is given; programs using mvid_writer_* get tiles unless they set codec.

    vid options:

    OptionMeaning
    --codec motion / --codec tiles / --codec h264the codec (default motion; use tiles for screen recordings, drawings and anything with transparency)
    --q Nmotion: quality, 0 (best) to 51 (smallest), default 26; 6 steps double or halve the quantizer step. h264: x264's quality setting (-crf), the same scale
    --loss Ntiles: each colour may end up to N away from the source (alpha stays exact); 0, lossless, is the default
    --fastquicker, a little larger (motion: about 25% quicker and 3% larger; tiles: delta frames only use the last frame; h264: x264's veryfast preset instead of medium)
    --threads Nmotion: encoder threads (default: one per CPU core)
    --no-hwacceldecode the input on the CPU only
    --width Nscale (keeping the shape)
    --fps Nthe frame rate (the source's, at most 60)
    --key Na keyframe every N frames (default every 2 seconds)
    --no-audiodrop the sound

    What to expect, on a 3-minute camera clip at 200x112 (PSNR against the source; the original MP4 is 854x480 at 0.74 Mbit/s; measured with the first version of the encoder):

    EncodingPicture dataPSNR
    tiles, lossless131 MBexact
    tiles, --loss 875 MB39 dB
    motion, --q 2213.2 MB36.4 dB
    motion, --q 268.6 MB34.2 dB
    motion, --q 305.3 MB32.1 dB
    x264 -crf 23, for comparison3.9 MB33.4 dB

    So motion is around 20 times smaller than tiles on footage like this, and about 1.7 times the size of x264 at the same quality. Its sharp colour edges are limited by 4:2:0 colour (half-resolution colour, like nearly all video): lossless x264 in 4:2:0 reaches 38 dB on the same clip. The soundtrack (IMA ADPCM, 44.1 kHz stereo) adds 2.6 MB a minute either way. Decoding a 480p motion video takes under 10 ms a frame on one core of the build PC. Encoding 480p takes about 40 ms a frame on one core (about 30 ms with --fast) and scales with the cores. MinimaFS files stop at 4 GiB.

    How the tiles codec works

    A picture is cut into 64x64 tiles. Each tile is compressed on its own, so tiles can be decoded in any order or in parallel. Inside a tile:

    1. Each row picks a filter: the row as it is, minus the row above (in the same tile), or in a video minus the same row of the previous frame. The encoder tries each and keeps the smallest.
    2. The filtered values (per channel, modulo 256) are coded with QOI's operations: a run of the previous value, one of 64 recently seen values, a small difference, or the value written out. Runs carry on into the next row.

    Without a filter a row is coded against opaque black, so an opaque picture never spends bits on alpha.

    How the motion codec works

    The code is in Minimal-OS-SDK/include/mosmedia_motion.h. All of it is integer arithmetic, so every decoder (C or Python) shows exactly the pixels the encoder used as its reference.

    1. Colour. Each frame becomes YCbCr 4:2:0 (full range, BT.601): Y per pixel, Cb and Cr per 2x2 pixels. The coded size is rounded up to 16 by repeating the last column and row.
    2. Macroblocks. The picture is cut into 16x16 macroblocks (with 8x8 of each colour plane), coded left to right, top to bottom.
    3. Prediction. In a keyframe each 4x4 luma block is predicted from the pixels above and to its left (DC, vertical, horizontal or TrueMotion: left + above - corner), and each 8x8 colour block the same way. In other frames a macroblock is either *skipped* (moved by the predicted vector, nothing else stored), *moved* by a vector in quarter pixels from the last frame (bilinear, edges repeated) plus a residual, or predicted like a keyframe block. The predicted vector is the median of the left, above and above-right macroblocks' vectors.
    4. Transform. The residual goes through H.264's 4x4 integer transform and quantizer. QP (0-51) picks the step size; colour uses H.264's lower colour QP above 29. Keyframes use QP - 2.
    5. Deblocking. After a frame is decoded, a filter smooths 4x4 block edges whose two sides differ by less than the QP allows: first all vertical edges, then all horizontal ones. The filtered frame is the next frame's reference.
    6. Entropy coding. Everything is coded with a binary range coder (LZMA's: 11-bit probabilities, adapting by 1/32 a bit). Probabilities start at 1/2 in every frame. Coefficients are coded like CABAC: a coded-block flag, then a significance flag and a last flag for each position in zigzag order, then the levels from the last one back, as "more than 1", an adaptive unary part and Exp-Golomb for the rest, then the sign.

    The encoder searches motion with candidate vectors (zero, the predicted one, the neighbours' and the same macroblock's in the last frame), then a shrinking square pattern down to quarter pixels. For each macroblock it compares skip, moved and intra by distortion plus lambda times estimated bits (lambda as in H.264's reference encoder). If a frame does not fit its buffer, the encoder raises QP for that frame.

    The bitstream is exactly what mmc_decode_frame reads; for each macroblock:

    • P frames: skip (context: skipped neighbours), and if not skipped intra (context: intra neighbours);
    • intra: 16 luma modes in raster order (a flag "not the most probable mode", which is the smaller of the left and above block's modes, then the remaining mode in 1 or 2 bits), the colour mode (2 bits), the 16 luma blocks, then 4 Cb and 4 Cr blocks;
    • moved: the vector minus the predicted one (x then y: zero flag, sign, unary/Exp-Golomb size), then the 16 luma, 4 Cb and 4 Cr blocks;
    • each block: a coded flag (context: whether the left and above blocks have coefficients) and its coefficients.

    The H.264 codec

    Minimal-OS-SDK/include/mosmedia_h264.h is an H.264 decoder written for Minimal-OS: plain C without libc, so it runs in programs and in mosWM like the other codecs. Videos made elsewhere are almost always H.264, so this is the codec to carry them in, and the first piece a web video player needs.

    What it decodes: the Constrained Baseline profile.

    PartState
    I and P frames, several slices per pictureyes
    CAVLC entropy codingyes
    Intra prediction: 4x4 (9 modes), 16x16, colour, I_PCM; constrained intra predictionyes
    Inter prediction: 16x16 down to 4x4 blocks, quarter-pixel motion (6-tap filter), up to 16 reference frames, reference list reordering and memory management commandsyes
    In-loop deblocking filter, with per-slice offsetsyes
    4:2:0, 8 bits, progressive, cropping to any size; BT.601 and BT.709, full and limited rangeyes
    CABAC, B frames, the 8x8 transform (Main and High profile)no - refused with a message, not garbled
    Interlaced video, slice groups (FMO/ASO), weighted prediction, 4:2:2 / 4:4:4, more than 8 bitsno

    Main and High profile are what most downloaded films and the higher resolutions of video sites use, so they are the next step for this decoder (CABAC and B frames first). mosmedia vid --codec h264 always writes Constrained Baseline, so every .vid it makes plays.

    It is exact. H.264 defines the decoded pictures bit for bit. make test-h264 (tools/media/h264_check.sh, needs ffmpeg with libx264) lets x264 encode 23 test videos with very different settings - all block sizes, 1 to 16 reference frames, several slices, the best and the worst quality, deblocking off and at its extremes, constrained intra, noise, odd sizes from 16x16 to 1280x720 - and compares every byte of every frame with ffmpeg's decoder. make test-host checks the sample file against a checksum made the same way, seeks in it, and decodes 400 damaged copies, which must fail cleanly. Parts no test stream uses yet: I_PCM blocks, long-term reference frames and the memory management commands (x264 does not emit them in this profile).

    Speed. 854x480 decodes in about 4 ms a frame on one core of the build PC, without any SIMD.

    In a .vid. A frame is the 4-byte frame header (bit 0 of the first byte: keyframe) and one access unit in Annex B form (NAL units behind 00 00 01 start codes). A keyframe is an IDR picture and carries its parameter sets (SPS, PPS), so decoding can start at any keyframe. There are no B frames, so frames are stored in the order they are shown. The converter writes full-range BT.601 colour, like the motion codec, which lets the same colour conversion - on the CPU or on the graphics card - serve both; streams from elsewhere are converted by their own matrix and range.

    In programs. mvid_open / mvid_decode handle it like the other codecs. The decoder on its own:

    #include "mosmedia_h264.h"

h264_t d;
h264_init(&d, malloc, largest_access_unit);
if (h264_decode(&d, unit, unit_size))                   // one frame's NAL units
    h264_to_argb(&d, pixels, h264_width(&d), h264_height(&d), stride);
else if (h264_error(&d)[0]) puts(h264_error(&d));       // e.g. "CABAC (Main and High profile) is not supported"
h264_free(&d, free);

    Recording (mvid_writer_frame) stays tiles or motion: there is no H.264 encoder in the OS. mvid_writer_h264_frame stores frames something else encoded.

    What a web video player still needs. Sites deliver H.264 inside MP4 (or fragmented MP4 over DASH/HLS) with AAC sound, usually in Main or High profile. This decoder is the video half for the Baseline streams; an MP4 demuxer, an AAC decoder and the missing profiles are separate work.

    Vector images

    A vector .img (version 2) has no pixels. It holds a view box and a list of shapes, each a path with a fill and/or a stroke, and is rasterized when it is shown. mimg_decode draws it at its natural size (the view box rounded up), so Photos, Mxplorer and mosWM show vector files with no change; programs that want a crisp icon at the size they need call mimg_render.

    Make one from an SVG on the build PC (no ffmpeg needed):

    build/tools/mosmedia vimg icon.svg icon.img            # prints the shape count and size
build/tools/mosmedia vimg logo.svg logo.img --shift 8  # coordinate precision (default: from the size)
build/tools/mosmedia png icon.img icon.png --size 256  # look at it: 256 px on the longer side
build/tools/mosmedia png icon.img tinted.png --color 2255cc   # RRGGBB or AARRGGBB for "current color"
build/tools/mosmedia info icon.img                     # view box, paints, shapes, tintable or not

    docs/examples has sample-icon.svg (an envelope, 188 bytes as an .img, tintable) and sample-logo.svg (gradients, strokes, 839 bytes) to convert and try.

    What the converter reads

    <svg viewBox width height> (the view box is the natural size; without one the width and height are), <g>, <a>, <switch>, <use href> with x and y (also of <symbol>), <path d> with every command (relative ones, S, T, and arcs A/a turned into cubics), <rect rx ry>, <circle>, <ellipse>, <line>, <polyline>, <polygon>; transform (matrix, translate, scale, rotate, skewX, skewY); fill, stroke, stroke-width, stroke-linecap, stroke-linejoin, stroke-miterlimit, opacity, fill-opacity, stroke-opacity, fill-rule, color, display, visibility, as attributes and in style="" (a style wins), all inherited down the tree the way SVG inherits them; colors as #rgb, #rgba, #rrggbb, #rrggbbaa, rgb(), rgba(), hsl(), about 60 names, transparent, none and currentColor; and <linearGradient> / <radialGradient> referenced as url(#id) (with a fallback color), with <stop>s, href inheritance, gradientUnits (both), gradientTransform and spreadMethod.

    What it cannot draw is skipped with a warning and the rest is converted: text, images, filters, masks, clip paths, patterns, markers, <style> sheets (class selectors), stroke-dasharray (the line is drawn solid) and gradients with more than 8 stops (8 of them are used). Notes:

    • currentColor becomes a current color paint, which takes the color the program passes to mimg_render_ex; if the drawing sets the color property itself it is that fixed color instead.
    • Transforms are applied to the coordinates. A shape with a stroke under a transform that is not a similarity (a non-uniform scale or a skew) keeps its transform so the stroke bends like the SVG's.
    • opacity on a group multiplies into the opacity of each shape below it (SVG would composite the group at once, which differs only where shapes of one group overlap).
    • A gradient in objectBoundingBox units is turned into one in the shape's own coordinates, so the same gradient on two shapes is two paints.

    Layout (version 2)

    All numbers are little-endian. Header, 24 bytes like the raster header:

    OffsetSizeField
    04MIMG
    41version, 2 (raster files stay 1, so a reader that only knows version 1 refuses vector files)
    51channels, 4
    61shift, 0 to 12: coordinates are integers in 1/2^shift of a drawing unit (the converter picks about 14 bits for the view box: 1/512 unit for a 24-unit icon, 1/32 for a 256-unit logo)
    71flags: bit 0 set when some paint is "current color" (a tintable icon); the rest 0
    84natural width, 1 to 16384 (the view box rounded up)
    124natural height
    164payload size in bytes
    204reserved, 0

    The payload follows. A *varint* is LEB128 (7 bits at a time, low first, at most 5 bytes); an *svarint* is a varint of the zigzag value (v << 1) ^ (v >> 31); *fixed* is an svarint in the units above.

    FieldEncoding
    view boxsvarint x, svarint y (fixed), varint width, varint height (fixed, above 0)
    countsu16 paints (at most 1024), u16 shapes (at most 65535)
    paintsthat many paints
    shapesthat many shapes; the payload ends right after the last

    A paint starts with a byte: bits 0-1 the type (0 solid, 1 current color, 2 linear gradient, 3 radial gradient), bits 2-3 the spread (0 pad, 1 reflect, 2 repeat), bit 4 "has a matrix", bits 5-7 zero.

    TypeWhat follows
    solidu32 0xAARRGGBB
    current coloru8 alpha (multiplies the caller's alpha)
    gradientu8 stop count (1 to 8), each stop a u8 offset (0 to 255) and a u32 0xAARRGGBB; then f32 geometry: linear x1 y1 x2 y2, radial cx cy r fx fy (a focal point outside the circle is moved onto it)
    matrix (bit 4)f32 a b c d e f, from gradient space to the shape's path coordinates (x' = a x + c y + e, y' = b x + d y + f)

    Gradients are interpolated in sRGB without premultiplying. A gradient with no extent (equal end points, radius 0) paints its last stop. Stops whose offsets decrease are raised to the previous offset.

    A shape:

    FieldEncoding
    flagsu8: bit 0 fill, bit 1 stroke, bit 2 even-odd fill rule (else nonzero), bit 3 transform; bits 4-7 zero
    fillwith bit 0: varint paint index, u8 opacity (0 to 255)
    strokewith bit 1: varint paint index, varint width (fixed), u8 cap + join << 2 (caps 0 butt, 1 round, 2 square; joins 0 miter, 1 round, 2 bevel), u8 miter limit in 1/8 (at least 1.0), u8 opacity
    transformwith bit 3: f32 a b c d e f from path coordinates to drawing units (applied to the stroke too)
    pathruns: u8 op + (count - 1) << 3, then count groups of coordinates; ends with a 0 byte

    Path operations (coordinates are svarint fixed, relative to the current point; a quadratic's and a cubic's control points too):

    opMeaningCoordinates
    1movedx dy
    2linedx dy
    3quadratic curvecontrol dx dy, end dx dy
    4cubic curvecontrol 1 dx dy, control 2 dx dy, end dx dy
    5closenone; the current point returns to the subpath's start
    6horizontal linedx
    7vertical linedy

    A path begins with a move; a drawing operation after a close starts a new subpath where the last one began. Fills close open subpaths implicitly. The file is checked as a whole before any drawing: bad counts, indexes, unknown bits, runs that leave the payload or a payload that does not end exactly where the last shape ends are rejected.

    How it is drawn

    Curves are split into line segments by how far they bend at the target size (within 0.02 px); strokes are made from one convex polygon per segment, join and cap, all wound the same way (a join beyond the miter limit is a bevel; a zero-length subpath with round or square caps is a dot); and the segments are accumulated in a float buffer as exact signed area per pixel, the method of font-rs and stb_truetype. A pixel's coverage is its running sum along the row: nonzero is min(|sum|, 1), even-odd a triangle wave of |sum|. Edges are anti-aliased exactly (a half-covered pixel has alpha 127 or 128); where several edges of one shape cross a pixel the fill rules are approximated as in FreeType and AGG. Gradients are evaluated per pixel through a 256-entry table. Shapes composite in order with source-over into the non-premultiplied 0xAARRGGBB buffer.

    A picture is drawn into the rectangle it is given keeping its aspect ratio, centered (MIMG_FIT_CONTAIN); MIMG_FIT_STRETCH and MIMG_FIT_COVER are options of mimg_render_ex. Speed on one core of a modern PC (-O2, see make bench-vimg): the 24-unit sample icon takes 12 us at 16 px, 18 us at 32, 33 us at 64 and 240 us at 256; the sample logo 1.2 ms at 256 px, 4 ms at 512 and 16 ms at 1024.

    .img layout (raster, version 1)

    All numbers are little-endian.

    OffsetSizeField
    04MIMG
    41version, 1
    51channels: 3 (RGB) or 4 (RGBA)
    61tile size as a power of two: 6 (64 pixels)
    71flags, 0
    84width (1 to 16384)
    124height (1 to 16384)
    164tile count: ceil(width / 64) x ceil(height / 64)
    204reserved, 0
    244 x (count + 1)where each tile starts, counted from the end of this table; the last entry is where the data ends

    Then the tiles, left to right and top to bottom. A tile with rows rows:

    • ceil(rows / 4) bytes of filters, 2 bits a row, row 0 in the low bits: 0 none, 1 the row above (never on row 0), 2 the previous frame (videos only);
    • the operations for all its pixels, row by row:
    ByteMeaning
    00iiiiiithe value at index i (index = (r x 3 + g x 5 + b x 7 + a x 11) mod 64)
    01rrggbbthe previous value plus (r - 2, g - 2, b - 2), same alpha
    10gggggg, rrrrbbbbgreen changes by g - 32, red by that plus r - 8, blue by that plus b - 8
    11nnnnnn (n < 62)the previous value n + 1 times
    0xFE r g bthat colour, same alpha
    0xFF r g b athat colour and alpha

    The pixel is the decoded value plus the filter's reference pixel. The previous value starts at 0 and the index at all zeros in every tile.

    .vid layout

    OffsetSizeField
    04MVID
    41version: 1 (always the tiles codec) or 2 (the codec is at offset 60)
    51channels, 3 or 4 (motion: 3)
    61tile size as a power of two, 6
    71flags: bit 0 = has a soundtrack
    84width
    124height
    164frame rate numerator
    204frame rate denominator
    244frame count
    284duration in milliseconds
    328where the index starts
    408where the soundtrack starts
    488soundtrack size
    564keyframe interval (information only)
    604version 2: the codec, 0 tiles, 1 motion or 2 h264; version 1: 0

    The tiles codec writes version 1, so players from before the motion codec still read those files; a motion file is version 2, which they reject cleanly.

    Frames follow the header. A tiles frame has:

    • a flags byte (bit 0: keyframe) and 3 zero bytes;
    • a bitmap with one bit per tile: set means the tile is stored, clear means it is unchanged from the previous frame (a keyframe stores every tile);
    • a 4-byte size for each stored tile, then the tiles (coded as in .img; keyframes never use the previous-frame filter).

    A motion frame has a flags byte (bit 0: keyframe), its QP, 2 zero bytes, then the range-coded frame.

    An h264 frame has a flags byte (bit 0: keyframe), 3 zero bytes, then one H.264 access unit in Annex B form.

    The index has 16 bytes per frame: 8-byte offset, 4-byte size and 4-byte flags (bit 0: keyframe). To show frame n, a player decodes from the keyframe at or before it. The next frame decodes over the last one in place, so one frame buffer is enough.

    The soundtrack is an ordinary .adi file stored unchanged. The kernel plays it from inside the video: SYS_AUDIO_OPEN takes the soundtrack's offset in value (mos_audio_open_at(path, offset)). The player uses the sound's position as its clock, so picture and sound stay in step.

    In programs

    #include "mosmedia.h"

// Pictures
mimg_info_t info;
if (mimg_info(data, size, &info)) {
    uint32_t* px = malloc(info.width * info.height * 4);
    mimg_decode(data, size, px, info.width);          // 0xAARRGGBB
}
size_t n = mimg_encode(px, w, h, w, true, out, mimg_encode_bound(w, h));

// Vector pictures (and raster ones, scaled) at any size
mimg_info_t info;
mimg_info(data, size, &info);                      // info.vector, info.current_color, view box
mimg_render_opts_t o;
mimg_render_opts_init(&o);                         // black "current color", cleared, aspect kept
o.current_color = 0xFFEAF2F8;                      // tint for icons that use "current color"
o.clear = false;                                   // or composite over what is in the buffer
o.alloc = malloc; o.free = free;                   // scratch memory (or o.scratch / o.scratch_size)
mimg_render_ex(data, size, window_px, 24, 24, win_stride, &o);
mimg_render(data, size, px, 64, 64, 64);           // the short form (built-in scratch)
size_t scratch = mimg_scratch_size(data, size, 64, 64);   // recommended scratch for a size

// Making a vector picture in code (mimg_vw_*; see the header)
mimg_vwriter_t w;
mimg_vw_begin(&w, buf, cap, mimg_vw_default_shift(24, 24), 0, 0, 24, 24);
int p = mimg_vw_paint_current(&w, 255);
mimg_vstyle_t st = mimg_vstyle_stroke(p, 2);
mimg_vw_shape_begin(&w, &st);
mimg_vw_move(&w, 4, 12); mimg_vw_line(&w, 20, 12);
mimg_vw_shape_end(&w);
size_t n = mimg_vw_finish(&w);

// Videos: give it a read function (offset, buffer, length)
mvid_reader_t r;
mvid_open(&r, my_read, &fd, file_size, malloc);
mvid_decode(&r, mvid_frame_at(&r.info, ms), frame);    // frame: width x height
mos_audio_open_at(path, (uint32_t)r.info.audio_offset);

// Recording: frames in, one at a time (`fast` for live capture)
mvid_writer_t v;
mvid_writer_begin(&v, w, h, 30, 1, false, 60, true, my_write, &fd, malloc, free);
v.codec = MVID_CODEC_MOTION;   // optional, before the first frame (then v.qp)
mvid_writer_frame(&v, pixels, stride);
mvid_writer_finish(&v, adi_bytes, adi_size);

    apps/video.c and apps/photos.c in MOSdesk are complete examples. make test-host runs tests/host/media_tests.c: exact round trips of many picture and video shapes, lossy limits, motion videos that must decode to exactly the encoder's reference frames, seeking, and damaged files, which must fail cleanly.

    Hardware decoding

    What runs where:

    Steptilesmotionh264
    Entropy decoding, prediction, transform, deblockingCPU, changed tiles in parallel on the kernel's SMP workersCPU, one coreGPU (NVDEC) once it has proven itself on the file, else CPU
    Colour conversion (4:2:0 YCbCr to RGB)-GPU when FarcadeGL runs on the card (hw-3d), else CPUthe same, for full-range BT.601 streams (what the converter writes)

    .vid uses its own codecs, so the card's fixed-function video decoder (NVDEC), which only knows H.264, HEVC, VP9 and AV1 bitstreams, cannot read it. What a GPU can take over is what a 3D engine is good at: the same small computation for every pixel.

    Motion codec, on the GPU. The decoder's result is three planes (Y, Cb, Cr). mvid_decode hands them to the kernel (SYS_MEDIA_CONVERT_YCBCR); the NVIDIA backend uploads them as one-byte textures, draws one triangle with a shader that upsamples the colour planes and converts to RGB, and copies the picture back with the copy engine. The shader does mmc_to_argb's arithmetic on whole numbers, so the pixels are exactly the CPU's (tests/host/video_gpu_tests.c runs the same shader bytecode on the CPU rasterizer and compares every pixel). Without hw-3d the call answers "not now" once and the file is converted on the CPU as before. Every player gets this without changes: the Video app, Mxplorer, anything using mvid_decode. gpu nvidia counts the frames converted on the GPU. Like the 3D path it rides on, this has not run on a card yet.

    Why not more of the motion codec. The range coder carries its state from one macroblock to the next, intra prediction reads the pixels of the blocks before it, and the deblocking filter's output is the next frame's reference, bit for bit. Those steps are sequential by design; a rasterizer cannot run them, and hardware decoders do them in dedicated circuits for the standard codecs only. Decoding has no motion search, so this part is cheap.

    H.264 on the card's video decoder (NVDEC). H.264 is one of the formats NVIDIA's NVDEC decodes completely in hardware. On an RTX 20 / GTX 16 card where gpu nvidia boot brought up the video decoder's channel (step 5a) and the 3D engine (step 4), h264 videos are decoded like this:

    1. mosmedia_h264.h still reads every frame's headers: the parameter sets, the picture order count, the reference picture list. It describes the picture to the kernel (SYS_MEDIA_DECODE_H264, syscall_media_h264_t): parameter sets, the picture's numbers, its reference pictures, and the slice data as it is in the file.
    2. The NVIDIA backend fills NVIDIA's picture setup structure (nvdec_h264_pic_s, from nvdec_drv.h in open-gpu-doc) and sends one decode job to NVDEC (nv_nvdec.c). NVDEC writes an NV12 picture into VRAM. The 17 picture buffers stay in VRAM, so reference pictures never travel.
    3. The 3D engine converts NV12 to RGB with a shader doing the CPU decoder's arithmetic (NV_VIDEO_NV12_FS), and the copy engine brings the RGB picture back.

    It has to prove itself first. H.264 output is exact, so the first pictures of every file are decoded on both: from the first keyframe, the CPU decoder and NVDEC each decode every picture and the two are compared pixel for pixel. After 12 equal pictures NVDEC takes over alone at the next keyframe, and the CPU only reads headers (cheap). One different pixel and the file stays on the CPU, and the kernel is told (SYS_MEDIA_H264_MISMATCH): it stops offering NVDEC for every file and gpu nvidia says so. If NVDEC fails later (a job that does not finish), the CPU decoder starts again from the last keyframe and the video goes on. Streams NVDEC is not used for: anything not full-range BT.601 or with cropping at the top or left (the converter never writes those), and anything the CPU decoder refuses.

    Only full pictures from the CPU decoder are ever shown before NVDEC has passed the comparison, so a mistake in this path costs speed, never a wrong picture. It has not run on a card yet. The NVDEC interface is taken from NVIDIA's published nvdec_drv.h / clc5b0.h and from Mesa's NVK, which decodes H.264 on NVDEC the same way; the host tests check the setup structure, the methods, the hand-over and fallback logic (with a stand-in decoder), and that the NV12 shader gives exactly the CPU's pixels.

    Tiles codec. Each changed tile is independent, so the kernel decodes the tiles of a frame in parallel on its CPU cores (SYS_MEDIA_DECODE_TILES). A tile itself is a byte-by-byte code (runs, an index of recent values), which a GPU cannot split up; this stays CPU work.
