    GPU and 3D

    On this pageAdapters and video memoryFGPU command processorFarcadeGLNVIDIA cards and hardware rendering

    Adapters and video memory

    gpu_core_init() (after the display driver is up) gives every display-class PCI device a gpu_adapter_t (src/intf/x86_64/gpucore.h):

    • vram_size – total video memory,
    • aperture_* – the PCI BAR through which the CPU sees VRAM, mapped write-combining,
    • scanout_* – where the framebuffer the screen shows sits in VRAM,
    • heap_start/heap_end – the rest of the window, handed out by gpu_vram_alloc(); it is only enabled after a write/read-back test.

    gpu in the terminal prints all of this.

    NVIDIA (GTX 10 "Pascal", RTX 20 / GTX 16 "Turing")

    gpu_nvidia.c reads the chip from PMC_BOOT_0, the board name from the PCI device id (GT 1030, GTX 1050/1050 Ti/1060/1070/1080, RTX 2060/2070/ 2080 and their variants, GTX 1650/1660), the VRAM size from the memory controller (register 0x100CE0, as nouveau does for Pascal through Turing) and the core temperature. BAR1 is the VRAM window; it is only used for allocations while BAR1 is in physical mode, which is how the firmware leaves it.

    The display mode is the one the firmware set (GOP/VBE). FGPU work is rendered on the CPU into VRAM; see NVIDIA cards and hardware rendering for what running it on the card itself takes.

    QEMU / Bochs

    gpu_bochs.c reads the VRAM size and can page flip (show any line of VRAM). Because VRAM is ordinary host memory there, the kernel's screen back buffer is moved into VRAM as well. Give QEMU more VRAM with -vga none -device VGA,vgamem_mb=64 (make run does).

    FGPU command processor

    SYS_GPU (40) is the GPU interface for programs (fgpu_abi.h, shared word for word with the SDK). A process creates *surfaces* (color XRGB8888, depth float32), *buffers* (vertices, indices) and *shader programs*, records a command buffer (bind target, viewport, clear, state, program or shader, constants, vertex layout, textures, draw) and submits it; then presents a color surface to the screen (copy, or page flip when the surface is in VRAM and the adapter can flip) or into a window. Everything is freed when the process exits.

    ABI version 2 added shader programs (CREATE_PROGRAM, DESTROY_PROGRAM), texture uploads (WRITE_SURFACE) and the commands SET_SHADER, SET_CONSTANTS, SET_VERTEX_LAYOUT and BIND_TEXTURE, plus the FGPU_STATE_BLEND state. The kernel still accepts version-1 requests, so older programs keep working.

    ABI version 3 adds asynchronous submits. SUBMIT with FGPU_SUBMIT_ASYNC copies the command buffer, queues it and returns at once with a fence in handle (increasing, never 0); SYS_GPU_WAIT (handle = fence, 0 for all; bytes = timeout in ns, 0 to poll, ~0 forever) waits for it, returns the triangles drawn by async submits since the last WAIT in handle, and SYS_ERR_INVAL once when one of those buffers was rejected. A program's queued buffers run in order, and every other call of that program (readback, present, uploads, destroys, a plain SUBMIT) first waits for them, so results are always seen. At most 4 are queued per program; a fifth SUBMIT waits for room. FGPU_CAP_ASYNC in SYS_GPU_INFO says the kernel has this. Version-2 requests ignore the flag. A kernel process, fgpu-worker, runs the queued buffers; it is preemptible like any process.

    ABI version 4 (OS-6, first part) adds the scissor test, mipmapped textures with trilinear filtering and 16 texture units, all drawn by the CPU backend whatever the adapter:

    • FGPU_OP_SCISSOR (enable, x, y, w, h): draws and clears only touch the rectangle, clipped to the target. The origin is the top-left pixel (y down), like FGPU_OP_VIEWPORT. The state belongs to the command buffer (every SUBMIT starts with it off). See "Scissor" below.
    • FGPU_SURFACE_MIPMAPS (create flag, color only): the surface is allocated with a whole mip chain after level 0 (level k is max(1, w >> k) by max(1, h >> k), tightly packed, fgpu_mip_layout), in system memory. WRITE_SURFACE takes the level in offset (version 4 requests only); FGPU_OP_GENERATE_MIPMAPS rebuilds levels 1.. with a 2x2 box filter in command order (pending draws land first). BIND_TEXTURE flags FGPU_TEXTURE_MIP_NEAREST / FGPU_TEXTURE_MIP_LINEAR select the filter and three optional words add a level-of-detail bias and min/max clamps. See "Mipmaps and quads" below.
    • FGPU_TEXTURE_UNITS (16) texture units. FGPU_MAX_TEXTURE_UNITS stays at 4: it is the number of units the NVIDIA backend can sample (its constant buffer and texture pools are laid out for four), and draws that use a higher unit or a mip chain are not offered to a hardware backend (fgpu.c, and a second guard in nv_draw, both marked TODO(nv)). The scissor reaches the NVIDIA backend: draws set the hardware's scissor 0, clears get the rectangle in fgpu_hw_target_t and use SET_CLEAR_SURFACE_CONTROL.USE_SCISSOR0 on the 3D engine, or fill just the rectangle on the copy engine. Shaders that sample a unit above 3 do not compile for the NVIDIA backend either, so they run on the CPU.
    • SYS_GPU_INFO accepts the shorter structure of version 3 (SYS_GPU_INFO_SIZE_BASE) and the full one, which ends with a limits block (max_texture_units, max_mip_levels, max_varyings, max_uniform_vec4, max_storage_buffers, max_surface_size, max_buffer_bytes). Capability bits: FGPU_CAP_SCISSOR, FGPU_CAP_MIPMAPS, FGPU_CAP_TEXTURE_UNITS16.

    Objects and contexts. Objects belong to a program, not a thread: all threads of a program share its surfaces, buffers and shaders, and a thread that ends frees nothing. They live in one table per type (grown on demand); a handle encodes slot, type and a generation, so a stale or wrong-type handle is not found. Each program may hold 1024 surfaces, 4096 buffers and 1024 shader programs. Each program has a context: a lock (its calls and queued buffers run one at a time), its counts, its fences. Drawing and presenting share one render lock (the CPU rasterizer keeps one pass and per-worker scratch). With the CPU backend alone, creating, uploading, reading back and freeing need only the program's own lock, so they overlap another program's rendering; with a hardware backend or VRAM they take the render lock too. A thread killed in the middle of a GPU call leaves its locks to the next waiter, and its recorded draws are dropped. When a program ends, its queued buffers are dropped and its objects freed then, or by the worker or the next GPU call if a lock is busy at that moment.

    CPU backend

    fgpu_raster.c runs the pipeline: vertex stage, near-plane clipping, perspective-correct rasterization with the top-left rule, depth test, back/front face culling, wireframe, fragment stage and alpha blending. The built-in programs (vertex color, Gouraud, per-pixel Phong with Blinn-Phong highlights) are hard-wired C code.

    Scissor

    The rectangle (fgpu_pipeline_t.scissor, sc_x .. sc_h) only shrinks the area a draw can touch: the binned path intersects it with the viewport and the target when it records the draw (bstate_t.cx0..cy1), so triangle setup clips its bounding box to it, the tile lists only hold the tiles it reaches and no pixel test is added; the immediate path (fgpuold) intersects its clip rectangle, its bands and the wireframe line plotter the same way. A clear with a scissor cannot be merged into a pass (that merge is for whole-target clears): fgpu_pass_clear_rect renders what is pending and then clears the rectangle in parallel bands. A full-target rectangle takes the normal merged path. host tests: fgpu_bin_tests checks, on exact and general scenes, that pixels outside the rectangle keep their contents, pixels inside equal the unscissored picture, and the immediate and binned paths agree on any worker count.

    Mipmaps and quads

    fgpu_texture_t carries the chain (mip_count, mip_offset[], bias and clamps). fgpu_texture_sample() is unchanged (level 0, the no-mip path costs what it did); fgpu_texture_sample_lod() picks the level (MIP_NEAREST: nearest; MIP_LINEAR: two levels blended; the in-level filter is the LINEAR flag, so LINEAR | MIP_LINEAR is trilinear; lod <= 0 is magnification and uses level 0).

    The level of detail needs screen-space derivatives of whatever coordinate the shader computes, so a fragment stage that samples a texture with a chain and a mip flag runs on 2x2 pixel quads (fgpu_shader_batch_t.quad = 1; lane 4q + 2 * row + column; shader_uses_mips() decides per draw, everything else keeps one pixel per lane). The rasterizer collects the pixels a triangle covers (early depth test and depth writes as before), then shades every touched quad with all four pixels: pixels the triangle does not cover (or that lie outside the clip rectangle, the band or the tile) are *helper* pixels whose varyings come from the triangle's plane equations at their centers; they are shaded but never written. So a pixel's level does not depend on which neighbours are covered, which keeps tile and band splits, worker counts and triangle seams invisible. The binned path does this in quad_flush after each triangle (a bit per pixel in the tile's qmask); the immediate path has the same loop in raster_triangle. TEX takes the differences inside the quad (fine derivatives: u[lane | 1] - u[lane & ~1], u[(lane & 1) + 2] - u[lane & 1]), lod = 0.5 * log2(max(|d/dx|^2, |d/dy|^2)) with the derivative of each coordinate scaled by the level-0 size. The JIT calls the same C code (fgpu_texture_sample_batch) for such samples and learns about quads through bit 0 of its textures argument, so both agree bit for bit; the vertex stage and single-lane runs sample level 0. fgpu_jit_tests runs every third batch as quads on textures with chains, bias and clamps; fgpu_mip_tests checks layout and box filter, level selection and blending against hand computed references, quads drawn at known scales (nearest and trilinear, diagonal seams, 1 and 3 workers, interpreter and JIT), a receding plane (the level grows toward the horizon) and 16 texture units.

    Binned rasterizer (default)

    Draws are not drawn when they are submitted. fgpu_raster.c records them in a pass (fgpu_pass_t: one render target at a time) with a snapshot of everything they depend on, and renders the pass at a flush:

    1. Record. A draw stores its pipeline state, uniforms, shader constants and vertex layout (copied, and deduplicated against the last 8 states), the viewport clipped to the target, and pointers to its vertex and index data. A full clear at the start of a pass is not executed: it is remembered and merged into the tile stage. Lines (FGPU_STATE_WIREFRAME) and draws that sample the surface they draw into are not recorded; they flush the pass and run through the immediate path, so submission order holds.
    2. Geometry (one parallel phase). Workers take *items* (up to 32 triangles of one draw) from an atomic counter. An item shades its vertices with all 8 shader lanes full (built-in programs run a cut-down vertex stage that computes only what the fragment stage reads), clips against the near plane (and, for triangles that reach beyond +-32768 px, against a guard band in screen space), culls, transforms, snaps the vertices to 16.8 fixed point and sets up integer edge functions (top-left rule, exact and independent of the order the pixels are visited in). The triangle record and its bin entries go into the worker's arena and are added to the bin list of every 64x64 tile the triangle may cover (long thin triangles are tested against each tile). Lists are per worker and per tile.
    3. Tiles (one parallel phase). Workers take tiles from an atomic counter. A tile merges the per-worker lists by item number, which restores the submission order exactly (blending and depth-equal results are the same as one core drawing in order), loads color and depth into a local 64x64 copy (or fills it from the pending clear: a tile that only needs the clear is written straight to the target), rasterizes, and stores the copy back. Triangles with a bounding box of at most 400 pixels (this includes the 2x2-pixel case) evaluate their edge functions directly at the sample centers. Bigger ones walk 8x8 blocks: a block is rejected, or accepted without per-pixel coverage tests, from the edge functions at its corners, and with depth testing a block is also rejected when the triangle's nearest depth in the block is behind the farthest depth stored there (hierarchical Z, min/max per block, kept conservative as pixels are written) or its depth test is skipped when it is entirely in front. A tile entirely inside a triangle skips the coverage tests.
    4. Fragments of consecutive triangles with the same state are shaded in batches of 8 lanes (the shader interface is unchanged); shaders that can discard flush per triangle so a later triangle sees the final depth.

    Memory. Records and bins come from the heap (fgpu_raster_set_allocator; the kernel passes alloc_unzeroed/free_mem) in 64 KB chunks that the main thread allocates before each phase (nothing allocates inside a parallel phase). Bin memory is bounded by a budget (8 MB, fgpu_raster_set_bin_budget). The geometry stage runs in *rounds*; when a round does not fit, the items that did are rasterized and the rest goes to the next round. An allocation failure doubles the pool if the budget allows, and as a last resort an item is drawn by the immediate path: a draw never fails because bins are full.

    Flush points. The rasterizer flushes by itself when the target changes (fgpu_pass_clear/draw with another color or depth buffer), when a clear comes after draws, when a draw is a line or reads its own target, when 65536 draws or 2^24 items are pending, and when memory for the record runs out. The kernel (fgpu.c) flushes at the end of every SYS_GPU_SUBMIT (so the triangle count it returns is exact and nothing is pending between system calls), before the hardware backend gets a clear or a draw, at the start of every other SYS_GPU operation (readback, present, buffer upload, surface or buffer or program create and destroy, WRITE_SURFACE), and fgpu_process_exit drops what a dead process left pending. Pipeline state, uniforms and constants are snapshotted, so changing them between draws needs no flush; vertex buffers, index buffers, textures and shader programs are referenced, which is why every operation that writes or frees them flushes first. FGPU_DRAW_COPY copies vertex and index data at record time for callers whose memory does not stay put.

    Results. Coverage, depth tests, interpolated values and blending order are bit-identical to the immediate path whenever the immediate path evaluates its float edge functions exactly, which is the case when vertices sit on a coarse grid (the differential test generates such scenes). Otherwise they differ at the borders of triangles: the immediate path computes edges in float with an accumulating row step, and the binned path snaps vertices to 1/256 pixel and computes edges exactly, so a sample very close to an edge can fall on the other side, and interpolated depth and attributes move by the snapping (a few parts in 1e5; for slivers more). The binned path is the more accurate of the two (the shared-edge meshes of the watertightness test are covered exactly once; the immediate path has no such guarantee). Vertices are clamped as before.

    Mode switch. fgpu_raster_set_mode(FGPU_RASTER_IMMEDIATE) selects the previous rasterizer (one barrier per draw, scalar); the kernel does this with the fgpuold boot flag (GRUB entry "Minimal-OS (RamFS, fgpuold)", two above the last entry). The host benchmark (make bench-fgpu) and the differential tests use the switch.

    Helpers. The parallel phases run on smp_par (smp_par.h): the calling core plus one preemptible kernel process smp-par per other core (not the master core), woken for each job. A busy core's helper starts at its next tick and the scheduler shares the core with programs; parts nobody took are done by the caller. The boot flag smpparipi brings back the older helpers, which run inside an IPI handler with interrupts off until the job ends.

    One pass for everyone. The kernel keeps a single pass, used under the render lock (see "Objects and contexts" above). The pass itself keeps its scratch in the pass, but the batch buffers in fgpu_raster.c are still static per worker, so two passes could not render at once yet.

    Present: scaled, paced, no back buffer (OS-5)

    SYS_GPU_PRESENT to the screen (the screen owner only) used to copy the surface into the kernel back buffer (graphics_backbuffer_blit) and then copy the back buffer into the framebuffer (graphics_backbuffer_present): two full-frame copies, the second one with plain stores into write-combining memory. Now it is one: graphics_present_scaled() (graphics.c) calls gfx_scale_blit() (gfx_blit.c), which expands each source row into a 960-pixel stack chunk (SSE2 shuffles, no <emmintrin.h>: the freestanding build has no hosted headers) and writes the chunk to every destination row it covers with 16-byte non-temporal stores (movntdq) and an sfence at the end. Scale 1, 2 and 3 are nearest neighbour; the image is placed at x, y and clipped on all four sides. The work is done in bands of 16 source rows with the graphics lock (interrupts off) dropped between bands. No damage rectangle: every present copies the whole surface.

    The back buffer is only used by SYS_GRAPHICS_BLIT / SYS_GRAPHICS_PRESENT (the terminal and its cursor draw straight into the framebuffer and stay off while a program owns the screen), so it is kept lazily: a direct present marks it stale, and the next back-buffer blit or rectangle present first reads the framebuffer back into it. A program that mixes both kinds of present pays one slow read of write-combining memory at each switch; a program that only uses SYS_GPU_PRESENT never does. Screens that are not 32-bit XRGB with the usual channel order scale into the back buffer and use the old converting present. Page flipping (FGPU_PRESENT_FLIP) is unchanged and excludes scaling.

    New flags (new bits of FGPU_PRESENT_*, everything else is rejected with SYS_ERR_INVAL): SCALE2, SCALE3 (screen only; exclusive with each other and with FLIP) and PACED. Caps: FGPU_CAP_SCALED_PRESENT (1<<8), FGPU_CAP_PACED_PRESENT (1<<9). The ABI version is not changed by this.

    PACED waits for the next frame boundary of the pace interval (default 1/60 s; SYS_GPU_SET_PACE, op 16, bytes = interval in ns, 0 = default, 1 ms to 1 s) on clock_monotonic_ns() before presenting (screen or window). Boundaries are last + n * interval; a present that is late by less than one interval goes straight through and keeps the phase, later than that restarts the phase. The wait is sleep() in whole milliseconds minus one, then a spin of under 2 ms with interrupts on; the adapters here have no vblank to wait for. If out is non-NULL, the present time (ns, taken just after the wait, before the copy) is written there. Each program has its own pacer (in its GPU context), and the wait happens before the render lock is taken, so other programs' GPU calls do not wait for it.

    Benchmark (make bench-gfx-scale, host memory, not write-combining, so only a CPU-side indication): 960x540 -> 1920x1080 2x about 0.6 ms standard stores, about 0.7 ms with non-temporal stores. On the plan's budget (C4.7, 1.5 ms) the real figure is set by write-combining throughput to the framebuffer, which only a card can show. tests/host/gfx_blit_tests.c checks the scaler against a pixel-by-pixel reference (1x/2x/3x, odd sizes, strides, offsets, clipping on every side, both store kinds); os0test checks the flag combinations, the timestamp pointer and the pace interval; SCALE_CHECK=2 FGLCUBE_ARGS="--scale 2" ONLY=new bash tools/debug/ci_fglcube.sh checks a screenshot is made of 2x2 blocks.

    Shader machine

    Shaders are FGPU bytecode (described at the end of fgpu_abi.h): vec4 registers in a few files (temporaries, inputs, outputs, uniforms, constants, fragment specials), five-word instructions with swizzles, write masks and negate/abs modifiers, and about forty opcodes (arithmetic, dot products, pow/exp2/log2/sin/cos, mix/clamp/ smoothstep, comparisons and select, texture sampling, discard, jumps). The SDK's FGSL compiler (fglsl.h) produces it from GLSL-style source.

    fgpu_shader.c:

    • fgpu_program_check validates a program once, on the kernel's own copy: every opcode, register index, write mask, texture unit and section bound. Jumps may only go forward, so a program runs at most its instruction count (2048 per stage) and cannot hang the kernel. Rejected programs are logged to serial (fgpu: shader program rejected: ...).
    • The interpreter runs 8 invocations at once, like a GPU warp: registers are stored per component as 8-lane rows and the lane loops use SSE (GCC vector extensions). Branches are handled per lane with a "resume at" instruction: lanes that jump wait until execution reaches their target, so divergent if/else runs correctly. Temporaries are zeroed for every draw, so a shader never sees other data.
    • The rasterizer queues covered pixels and shades them 8 at a time, and runs each triangle's three vertices as one batch. A shader that can discard writes depth after the fragment stage instead of before it.

    make test-host runs the compiler, checker, machine and rasterizer end to end (tests/host/fgsl_tests.c), including a check that a shader version of a built-in program gives the same pixels.

    Speed: the fglcube scene at 640 × 480 on one 2.8 GHz core takes about 11 ms per frame with the built-in Phong program and about 42 ms with fglcube --shader (a 60-instruction fragment shader over about 180,000 pixels).

    CPU JIT (OS-4)

    fgpu_jit_x64.c compiles each shader stage to x86-64 machine code, with an SSE4.1 path (4 lanes per XMM register) and an AVX2 path (8 lanes per YMM). The interpreter stays the reference and the fallback: a program whose stage does not compile, a CPU with only SSE2 (QEMU's default qemu64 has no SSE4.1) and the nojit boot flag all keep running on it. Nothing about the call interface changed: fgpu_shader_run_batch, run_vertex and run_fragment use the compiled code when the program has any.

    Pipeline. bytecode -> fgpu_ir_lower_ex(..., FGPU_IR_EXACT) -> linear scan register allocation (fgpu_ir_allocate) -> emitter -> code. The IR is the branch-free SSA form the NVIDIA backend uses (jumps are if-converted to selects, so the code has no branches at all). FGPU_IR_EXACT makes the IR mean what the interpreter computes instead of what GPU hardware would: IEEE division instead of multiply-by-reciprocal, a real subtraction, no algebraic simplifications that change -0/NaN results (x*1, x+0, fma(a,0,c), min(a,a)), no commuting of min/max, step as !(b < a), abs as the interpreter's x < 0 ? -x : x (which keeps -0), and a pending negation is materialized before an abs reads it. The transcendental ops (EX2, LG2, SIN, COS, RSQ) are emitted as the interpreter's own polynomial sequences, one vector instruction per vector operation, with the same constants; fma is multiply, round, add (no FMA instruction, so results are bit-identical; the code uses AVX2 but not FMA).

    Results are bit-identical to the interpreter for every opcode, including -0, denormals, infinities, float-to-int conversions, min/max operand order and comparisons with NaN. The one allowed difference: the sign/payload of a NaN that comes out of arithmetic on two NaNs (operand order, which FGPU does not define) -- a NaN is compared as a NaN. Also, discarded lanes keep unspecified outputs (the interpreter freezes them at the discard, the JIT runs on), and temporaries are not preserved (the interpreter leaves its last values in batch->temp; the JIT uses that area as its spill space). Lanes not asked for (lanes mask) get the default outputs in both.

    Registers. xmm0 is the blend mask (SSE blendvps), xmm1..xmm8 hold IR values (virtual registers 0..7 of the allocator; the allocator hands out the lowest free number, so the hot values land there), the other virtual registers are spill slots, xmm9..xmm15 are scratch. Spill slots, the texture helper's arguments and results, and the registers saved around a helper call all live in the batch's temp rows (128 slots of 32 bytes; a stage that needs more does not compile). General registers: rbx = the batch (+16 bytes for the SSE upper half), rbp = uniforms, r12 = textures, saved and restored; rax, rcx, rdx, rsi, rdi, r8, r9 only for helper calls.

    One emitter, two ISAs. A small layer (v3, v2, cmp, shift, sel) takes AVX-style three-operand requests. For AVX2 it emits 3-byte VEX with L=1; for SSE4.1 it emits the legacy two-operand form, inserting a movaps when the destination is not the first source, and blendvps with the mask in xmm0 for selects. The IR code generation is shared. The SSE path runs the code twice, once per half of the 8-lane batch (base pointer +16 bytes); empty halves are skipped. The AVX2 path ends with vzeroupper (and has one before every helper call) so SSE code afterwards pays no transition penalty.

    Calling convention. uint32_t code(char* batch, const float* uniforms, const fgpu_texture_t* textures) (System V): returns the lanes that were not discarded (4 or 8 bits). The wrapper masks that with the lanes argument, and writes the default outputs for lanes that were not asked for.

    Helper-call ABI. The only call is texture sampling: jit_tex_helper (C, in the same file), at a fixed address, called with rdi = textures, esi = unit, rdx/rcx = rows of u and v, r8 = result rows, r9d = lanes. It calls the interpreter's own fgpu_texture_sample per lane, so the results are identical. Before the call the code stores every live value that is in an XMM register to its save slot and reloads it afterwards (all vector registers are caller-saved in System V); results stay in slots, 4 per sample, until the last use.

    Safety (the JIT output runs in ring 0).

    • It is generated only from IR that was lowered from a program that passed fgpu_program_check; the emitter checks again that every register file, input/output/special/uniform slot and texture unit index is in range and fails the compile otherwise.
    • Memory the code can touch, all at offsets fixed when it is generated: the batch's input, special, output and temp rows (inputs are only read), the uniforms (read only), and its own constant pool (read only, 32-byte aligned). Nothing is computed from shader data: there are no indirect jumps or calls, no jumps at all, no data-dependent addresses. The one call goes to a fixed helper that clamps every texel coordinate.
    • The code buffer is a fixed-size scratch area; the emitter checks every byte and the compile fails (the stage stays on the interpreter) on overflow, too many constants, too many texture samples or spill slots, or more than 4096 IR operations. Compile time and code size are therefore bounded (at most 128 KiB of code per stage; real shaders are 2-10 KiB). The finished code is copied to an exactly sized block.
    • Compilation allocates, so it happens when the program is created (op_create_program, process context), never in a worker. The code is cached in fgpu_program_t.jit and freed with the program (fgpu_program_release, called from program_free).
    • W^X: on the host the code is mapped RW, copied, then mprotected RX. In the kernel the code comes from the heap, which is in the low identity map and is writable and executable today; there is nothing to flip yet. What should change: allocate whole pages from the page pool, map them RW while writing, then RX (and keep the rest of the heap NX).
    • Vector state: AVX code only exists as JIT output (the kernel is compiled without AVX). Every kernel entry stub (simd_save.inc: exceptions, IRQs, int 0x80, and the smp_par IPI wrapper in idt_.asm) saves the full XSAVE area, including the upper YMM halves, before C code runs and restores it on the way out, so JIT code running in a syscall or in a helper core's IPI handler cannot corrupt the interrupted program's state. vzeroupper before returning keeps the kernel's SSE code fast. Exceptions the JIT code could raise are masked in MXCSR like everywhere in the kernel; both machines run under the same MXCSR.
    • CPU gating: SSE4.1 from CPUID; AVX2 only when cpu_simd_features() says the OS enabled the state (XSAVE, noavx flag not given). nojit forces the interpreter. All CPUs are assumed to match the boot CPU (as the entry stubs already do).

    Flags and API. Boot flag nojit (GRUB entry "Minimal-OS (RamFS, nojit)"); fgpu_jit_set_mode(OFF|AUTO|SSE41|AVX2) for tests and benchmarks; gpu jit in the terminal runs the kernel self-check (below).

    Tests. tests/host/fgpu_jit_tests.c (part of make test-host): per-opcode tests over all pairs/triples of ~50 special operands with modifiers, swizzles and write masks; control flow; texture units; real FGSL shaders (including both fglcube --shader shaders); a deterministic differential fuzzer over random valid programs; safety and negative tests. make fuzz-fgpu-jit FUZZ_SECONDS=300 runs the fuzzer longer. Kernel: gpu jit compiles FGSL shaders in the kernel and compares interpreter, SSE4.1 and AVX2 code on random batches, also on the other cores through smp_par (tools/debug/ci_fgpu_jit.sh drives it in QEMU). tools/debug/ci_fgpu_jit_cube.sh takes screendumps of fglcube --shader --still to compare JIT and nojit.

    Speed (make bench-fgpu-jit, one thread of a 2.1 GHz Xeon, through the rasterizer's batch interface; lane-instructions are FGSL bytecode instructions x 8 lanes):

    shader (stage)                instr     interp     SSE4.1       AVX2    SSE x   AVX2 x
                                    G lane-i/s G lane-i/s G lane-i/s
arith vertex (~25 instr)         28      0.399      4.185      7.098    10.5x    17.8x
arith fragment                   15      0.508      2.360      3.842     4.6x     7.6x
fragment + bilinear tex           5      0.116      0.137      0.152     1.2x     1.3x
fglcube vertex                   20      0.454      3.119      5.615     6.9x    12.4x
fglcube fragment                 61      0.377      0.940      1.194     2.5x     3.2x

    The plan's target (16 G lane-instr/s AVX2, 0.6x of it with SSE4.1) is for a 4 GHz core on shaders that are mostly arithmetic: the 28-instruction vertex shader reaches 7.1 G (AVX2) and 4.2 G (SSE4.1) here, about 44% of the target on AVX2 (the SSE path is 59% of the AVX2 one); the fragment shaders with pow/sin/log2/texture are far from it. The interpreter number is this host's (GCC -O3), not the kernel's 0.1-0.2.

    Where the time goes: arithmetic is now limited by the number of vector instructions (the transcendentals are 25-60 each), not by dispatch. Two things cap the next factor, and both are interface/design limits: (1) texture sampling runs through a scalar C helper per lane (about 30 ns per bilinear sample), so a shader with one sample is dominated by it; an inline AVX2 gather sampler for the common ARGB8 path would remove that; (2) marshalling: the rasterizer scatters its per-pixel data into the 8-lane SoA rows and gathers the outputs back, which costs about twice the shader for a short fragment shader (see the benchmark line). A call that takes the interpolants and writes pixels itself (fused kernels, as in the plan) would remove it, as would larger batches (16/32 lanes per call, so the 4-6 ns call and per-batch constant loads amortize).

    FarcadeGL

    The SDK's farcadegl.h wraps all of this in an OpenGL/Vulkan-like API with GLSL-style shaders. Guides: farcadegl.md (API) and fgsl.md (shading language), also in Minimal-OS-SDK/docs/. fglcube (terminal, full screen; fglcube --shader for the shader version) and MOSdesk's *Cube* app (press S) are examples.

    NVIDIA cards and hardware rendering

    Today FGPU renders on the CPU on every adapter. Running it on the graphics card's own engines is the next step, and on NVIDIA cards it is possible with open code. This section explains what stands in the way and how open drivers get around it.

    What has to be signed

    Since the GTX 900 series, an NVIDIA GPU only lets firmware signed by NVIDIA run on its internal microcontrollers ("falcons", and on RTX 20 and later the GSP, a RISC-V core). That firmware sets up the graphics engine's context-switching units (FECS/GPCCS), power management and memory protection; without it the graphics engine does not run.

    What does *not* have to be signed:

    • the command streams (pushbuffers) a driver sends to a channel: "set this register of the 3D class, draw these vertices";
    • the shader programs the shader cores (SMs) execute.

    Both are written by the driver. So an open driver needs NVIDIA's firmware files, but nothing it produces itself has to be signed.

    How open drivers do it

    nouveau (Linux) and NVIDIA's own open kernel modules load NVIDIA's signed firmware files, which NVIDIA publishes for redistribution in the linux-firmware repository (nvidia/gp10x/..., nvidia/tu10x/..., under NVIDIA's firmware licence, LICENCE.nvidia). Minimal-OS can do the same: ship those files unchanged on the system volume and load them at boot. Then:

    GTX 10 (Pascal)RTX 20 / GTX 16 (Turing)
    FirmwareACR + graphics (FECS/GPCCS) + SEC2 images from linux-firmware, booted through the secure-boot falcon as nouveau doesThe GSP firmware (gsp-*.bin) plus its boot loader; GSP then sets up most of the chip itself
    Driver talks toRegisters directlyGSP through a message queue (RPC), as nouveau's GSP mode and NVIDIA's open kernel modules do
    Clock speedsStays at boot clocks: NVIDIA never released the PMU firmware needed to raise them, so 3D runs much slower than the card's real speedFull speed (GSP manages clocks)
    CommandsChannels with a GPFIFO of pushbuffers; 3D class PASCAL_A/PASCAL_BSame, 3D class TURING_A

    The class methods (register meanings) are published by NVIDIA in open-gpu-doc. The shader instruction set (SASS) is not officially documented, but Mesa's open compilers (the nouveau codegen and NAK, used by the NVK Vulkan driver) generate it, and envytools documents much of it.

    The plan for Minimal-OS

    1. Firmware loading: read the linux-firmware files from 0:/firmware/nvidia/, check them, and boot GSP on Turing (simpler and full speed) or ACR on Pascal.
    2. Channels: allocate a channel, a GPFIFO and pushbuffers in VRAM, and submit a "clear the screen" through the 3D class to prove the path.
    3. An FGPU hardware backend: translate FGPU command buffers to pushbuffers (surfaces → render targets, DRAW → vertex buffer setup and draw methods) and FGPU shader bytecode to SASS. The bytecode was designed for this: straight-line code with forward jumps, vec4 registers and a small instruction set map well onto a GPU compiler.
    4. Programs do not change: FarcadeGL and FGSL stay the same, and syscall_gpu_info_t.backend reports the hardware backend.

    This needs testing on real cards (QEMU cannot emulate an NVIDIA GPU); steps 1-2 are the first milestone.

    What is in place (Turing, e.g. RTX 2060)

    Everything below builds into the kernel and changes nothing until the hardware backend's init() succeeds; until then all work runs on the CPU as before.

    FGPU draws - and so FarcadeGL - go to the card's 3D engine once the backend's own test passes (step 4b below): gpu then shows hw-3d and the backend nvidia 3D engine. Until then clears use the copy engine and draws the CPU, as before. Steps 4a and 4b are written from NVIDIA's published class headers and Mesa's NVK/NAK and checked on the build PC, but have not run on a card yet; the test and its log lines exist to find out what the hardware disagrees with.

    PieceWhereState

    Video decoder (NVDEC, NVC4B0_VIDEO_DECODER): channel, H.264 picture setup (nvdec_h264_pic_s) and decode jobs, NV12 to RGB on the 3D enginenv_nvdec.h, nv_nvdec.c, nv_rm_chan.c, fgpu_backend_nv.cwritten, not yet run on a card
    Readback: the copy engine copies VRAM to staging memory in system RAM (16 MiB, mapped once), so presenting a frame never reads through BAR1nv_rm_ce_readwritten, not yet run on a card

    gpu nvidia prints the bring-up state. It only reads registers, so it is safe on any card: which firmware files are present and well-formed, and each microcontroller (GSP, SEC2, PMU, FECS, GPCCS, NVDEC) with its memory sizes and whether it is running.

    Firmware files

    tools/gpu/setup-gpu.sh (or make gpu-setup) sets them up:

    make gpu-setup                      # RTX 2060 (tu106), the default
make gpu-setup GPU="GTX 1660 Ti"    # another card, a chip (GPU=tu104)
                                    # or a PCI id (GPU=10de:1f08)
make gpu-setup GPU=--detect         # the NVIDIA card in the build PC
make mosdesk                        # or make / make run-mosdesk
make gpu-remove                     # build without firmware again

    It copies the files from the build PC's /lib/firmware (unpacking .zst/.xz), or downloads them from linux-firmware on git.kernel.org, checks them, and puts them in firmware/nvidia/<chip>/ (ignored by git; NVIDIA's licence goes along as firmware/nvidia/LICENCE.nvidia). Every build then packs firmware/ into the ISO as boot/mosfirmware.mpkg. GRUB loads it as the mosfirmware module when it is there, and the kernel unpacks it into 0:/firmware whenever it sets up a system volume: RamFS boot (which then gets a 192 MiB RAM disk), format and install. A disk formatted before the firmware was added does not get it; format it again or boot RamFS.

    The files, by hand: copy these from linux-firmware (nvidia/tu106/ for an RTX 2060; follow the symbolic links, MinimaFS has none) to 0:/firmware/nvidia/tu106/:

    gsp/booter_load-535.113.01.bin
gsp/booter_unload-535.113.01.bin
gsp/bootloader-535.113.01.bin
gsp/gsp-535.113.01.bin          (about 30 MB)

    TU102/TU104 use tu102/tu104, the GTX 16 series tu116/tu117.

    The shader IR

    GPU shader cores run 32 threads in step, each on scalar 32-bit registers, so fgpu_ir.c turns each vec4 instruction into scalar operations that correspond one to one to Turing instructions (FFMA, FMNMX, MUFU.RSQ, FSET.BF, FSEL, TEX, IPA, ...):

    • the edge cases FGPU defines (x / 0 = 0, sqrt/rsq of x <= 0, log2(x <= 0) = -126, pow of x <= 0) become explicit selects, so GPU and CPU agree;
    • atan2, smoothstep, mod and sign become short instruction sequences (the same polynomial as the CPU backend);
    • jumps are if-converted: each thread keeps the instruction it resumes at, as the CPU interpreter does per lane, and writes inside a skipped range become selects. The result has no branches at all; turning long skipped ranges back into real branches (BRA with BSSY/BSYNC) is a later optimization.

    make test-host compiles FGSL shaders (lighting, every built-in function, nested if/else with discard, loops with break/continue, textures, gl_FragCoord) and hand-written bytecode with divergent jumps, runs them on random inputs through both the IR (with a reference evaluator) and the CPU shader machine, and checks that they agree. FGPU_IR_LIST=1 ./build/tests/host/fgpu_ir_tests prints a listing:

    // fragment stage: 35 ops, 7 registers
  IPA R0, v3.x
  IPA R1, v3.y
  TEX.2D R0+, R0, R1, tex0
  FSET.BF.LT R3, R3, 0.5
  ...
  KIL if R3 != 0

    At every boot

    Once gpu nvidia boot has brought FarcadeGL onto the card, it sets NvidiaAutoBoot=true in 0:/etc/System.conf and the bring-up runs at every boot from then on, after 0: is mounted and before the services (mosWM) start, so the desktop's FarcadeGL programs find the card. It logs to the serial port only. mossettings set nvidiaboot false turns it off (and gpu nvidia boot succeeding turns it on again). A boot that hangs or crashes in the bring-up leaves NvidiaAutoBootTrying=true behind; the next boot then skips it and switches NvidiaAutoBoot off.

    Checking the card against the CPU

    gpu verify [frames] arms a comparison: the card's draws of the next frame (or frames frames) are also drawn by the CPU, starting from the same pixels and depth, and the results are compared pixel by pixel. Then gpu verify report lists one line per shader (its vertex and fragment instruction counts, uniforms, texture units, storage buffers and state): how many draws differ, the share of bad pixels, the mean card minus CPU difference in r, g and b over those pixels (negative = the card is darker), and the worst pixel with both colours. The program runs slowly while it is armed: every draw waits for the card and copies its target three times.

    Surfaces between the card and the CPU

    A target the card draws with depth lives in a block-linear copy in VRAM. Only the surface the CPU needs is brought back: the frame it presents or reads back, or one it writes (cpu_access). Before, every present and buffer upload copied all of them back (the shadow map, the HDR and post targets) and the next frame loaded each one again. CPU draws still bring everything back first (finish).

    Next steps on a card

    1. Run gpu nvidia with the firmware copied: every file should show ok, GSP/SEC2 should be reachable, and step 2a should list the ROM images and end with ok: FWSEC can be patched with the FRTS command.
    2. gpu nvidia boot: FWSEC-FRTS (works), then booter_load on SEC2 and GSP-RM, following nouveau's r535 code (nvkm/subdev/gsp/r535.c, tu102.c), then a first RPC (step 3a). Everything it prints is also saved to 0:/gsp_boot.log, in case the screen goes dark. What to look for: booter_load halted, mailbox 0x0 0x0 (non-zero mailbox 0 is booter's error code), GSP RISC-V running, then GSP-RM is running and the GPU's name from the first RPC. First run on an RTX 2060 (2026-11-06): booter_load worked, GSP-RM's init task logged two entries (the second right after mapping RMARGS) and stopped with GSP mailbox 0xCA. Cause: the RMARGS region was 0x50 bytes; LibOS's region mapper (init task, ~0x568de1c) asserts that sizes are whole 4 KiB pages, logs the address and size, and panics (its panic routine at 0x402521c writes 0xCA to mailbox 0 and halts). RMARGS is now one page, as in nouveau. Mailbox 0xCA in general means a LibOS crash; the last LOGINIT/LOGRM entries say where. Next run: GSP-RM booted, read both queued RPCs and sent RUN_CPU_SEQUENCER; our CORE_RESUME reset the GSP core before restarting booter, which killed it. Now it only rewrites the GSP mailboxes and restarts SEC2, as nouveau does.
    3. gpu nvidia boot continues on its own once GSP-RM answers: step 3b allocates the RM objects, builds the page tables and opens a channel on an async copy engine (it lists the copy engines it found and which one took the channel), submits a first job and reads it back. Step 3c draws four squares (red, green, blue, white) in the top right corner of the screen with the copy engine and reads them back through BAR1. Then FGPU sends clears of surfaces in VRAM to the copy engine. Failure lines to look for: RM error 0x.. (with the object or control that failed), no semaphore after 2000 ms (with GP_GET/GP_PUT: GP_GET still 0 means the doorbell or the channel setup, GP_GET moved means the copy engine or its page tables), channel error (RC) and GPU page fault from GSP-RM. A failed job switches the GPU path off again, so the desktop keeps working. First run (2026-11-06): everything up to the channel worked (CE2, runlist 8), but the job's USERD read back 0xBAD0ACC5 and the desktop froze: GSP-RM switches BAR1 into virtual mode with its own page tables while it starts (nouveau adopts them, bar/r535.c), so the kernel's 1:1 BAR1 window onto VRAM - the screen, the VRAM heap, our page tables - stopped working. nv_bar1_keep_physical puts BAR1 back into physical mode (0xB80F40 bit 31) after GSP-RM starts and before each job, and says so (BAR1: ... back to physical). Second run: the first job and the four test squares read back right, and FGPU switched its VRAM clears to the copy engine.
    4. gpu nvidia boot goes on by itself. Step 4a (3D channel) prints golden context recorded, the channel, and first 3D clear: reads back 0xffff8000 (ok). Step 4b compiles the built-in shader, then draws in two stages: first the near triangle alone, without depth, into a pitch-linear 64x64 surface; then both triangles with depth test and back-face culling into a block-linear target, which the copy engine copies back to the surface before three pixels are checked:

    text Step 4b: FarcadeGL draws on the 3D engine shaders: vertex and pixel stage compiled (19 + 13 registers) without depth: centre 0xff4080bf, corner 0xff102030 (ok) clockwise front: centre 0xff4080bf, left 0xffff0000, corner 0xff102030 ok: triangles, shaders, depth test and culling work on the 3D engine.

    First run on an RTX 2060 (2026-11-17): the clears of step 4a worked, but the first job of step 4b failed with GSP-RM: channel error (RC) on engine 0x1, channel 8, exception 69 (69 = ROBUST_CHANNEL_GR_CLASS_ERROR, Xid 69: the graphics engine refused a method or its data). That job cleared and drew into a pitch-linear color target with a depth buffer bound, which the hardware does not allow (nouveau's data error name: RT_LINEAR_WITH_ZETA; NVK renders linear images through a tiled shadow for the same reason). Changes: - draws with depth (and clears of color with depth) go to a block-linear copy of the color surface that the backend keeps (tiled in fgpu_backend_nv.c); the copy engine brings it back to the FGPU surface (nv_rm_ce_copy_surface, block-linear to pitch) in finish(), before a read, before a draw samples that surface, and before a draw falls back to the CPU; a depth-only clear binds no color target; - vertex attributes that come from no stream now carry a valid format (R32 float, as nouveau's nvc0 does) instead of 0, which is no value of COMPONENT_BIT_WIDTHS or NUMERICAL_TYPE; - when a 3D job fails, the log shows what PGRAPH trapped: PGRAPH trap: status ..., subchannel S method 0xMMMM data 0x..., error 0xE NAME (from 0x400100/0x400704/0x400708/0x400110, as nouveau's gf100_gr_intr reads them), which names the method.

    Second run (2026-11-18): NVDEC came up (ok: the video decoder's channel runs) and the 3D clear worked, but the draw failed with Graphics Exception: Shader Program Header 11 Error, ESR 0x405840 = 0xa0000800 (NV_PGRAPH_PRI_DS_HWW_ESR: SPH11, pipe stage 0x20 = pixel) and RC exception 13. The pixel shader header lacked IMAP_POSITION_W (bit 191); the card wants it in every pixel header, as Mesa's nvc0 driver notes ("getting a trap if FRAG_COORD_UMASK.w = 0"). nv_sass.c now sets it, nv_sass_tests checks it, and a failed 3D job also prints DS trap: shader header errors 0x... in the ... stage from that register.

    Third run (2026-11-18): no header error any more, but every SM reported Graphics SM Warp Exception: Out Of Range Register (warp ESR 0x...730 = 0x..0d, PC 0x174) and RC exception 13. Since Volta each thread's program counter lives in two registers after the ones the code uses (NAK's hw_reserved_gprs), so SET_PIPELINE_REGISTER_COUNT has to count them; we gave the bare count. nv_sass_encode now adds NV_SASS_HW_RESERVED_REGS (2) to regs, and nv_sass_tests checks that the code stays below regs - 2.

    Fourth run (2026-11-18): the 3D engine draws, but the Farcade editor took 800 ms a frame on Medium and 80 ms on Low. Medium's lit shader reads its lights and shadow data from a storage buffer, and nv_sass.c refused every storage buffer load, so every lit draw ran on the CPU between GPU passes, and each one copied the render target out of its block-linear copy and back. Mipmapped textures did the same. Now: - storage buffer b is bound as constant buffer 1 + b (up to 64 KiB, the constant cache dropped on each draw), and loads with a constant index, which is every load in the engine's shaders, are c[1+b][16 * index + 4 * comp] operands. A computed index still stays on the CPU (it would need LDC with a register offset); - mipmapped textures are drawn on the card from level 0 (pitch-linear textures cannot have mips); - a job no longer polls the GSP-RM queue before it has waited 5 ms; - gpu reports the jobs and their average time, the time spent in block-linear copies, the draws offered to the card and the ones the CPU did with the reason. Run it twice around a few seconds in the editor to see where a slow frame goes.

    Fifth run (2026-11-19): 33 jobs ran, then every SM reported Graphics SM Warp Exception: Misaligned Register (RC exception 13). Turing wants register vectors aligned to their size; the TEX coordinate pair sat at scratch + 3 and the four results at tex_base, both wherever the IR's register count put them. The coordinates now start on an even register and the results on a multiple of 4, and nv_sass_tests refuses unaligned TEX operands.

    The centre is inside both triangles (the near, blue-ish one must win), left only inside the far red one, corner in neither. If the first try shows only the clear color, the test repeats with the other winding as "front" and keeps what works. What other results mean:

    | Result | Look at | | --- | --- | | the draw without depth did not finish or the test draw did not finish, with channel error (RC) or GPU page fault above it | a method or address the engine rejects: nv3d_push_init / nv3d_push_draw in nv_3d.c; the PGRAPH trap line names the method offset and the error | | all three pixels are the clear color with both windings | nothing was rasterized: vertex stream/attribute setup, the vertex stage's code or header (nv_sass.c), or the viewport | | centre and left have a color, but the wrong one | the pixel stage: interpolation (IPA), the output registers, or the constant buffer | | centre is red | the depth buffer: block-linear layout or depth state |

    After ok, FGPU puts new color surfaces, textures and buffers in VRAM and sends clears and draws to the 3D engine. gpu nvidia shows how many ran. A job that does not finish later switches the 3D path off and rendering continues on the CPU.

    1. Step 5a (video decoder): a channel on NVDEC with the decoder class (NVC4B0_VIDEO_DECODER); GSP-RM runs NVDEC's firmware itself, but like every falcon engine NVDEC needs an engine context buffer from the driver, promoted to the channel before the class is allocated (nouveau fifo/r535.c: r535_fifo_ectx_size, r535_flcn_ctor). The size comes from RM's internal GET_CONSTRUCTED_FALCON_INFO for NVDEC's engine descriptor (engine context: N KiB). Without it the first run on an RTX 2060 got video decoder object (class 0xC4B0): RM error 0x1F (NV_ERR_INVALID_ARGUMENT). Then it prints channel N on NVDEC (runlist R) and ok: the video decoder's channel runs. after an empty first job. gpu nvidia then shows step 5 with the number of H.264 pictures NVDEC decoded, or that it was switched off because its pictures differed from the CPU decoder's (see docs/media.md for how files are checked). A failed decode job switches NVDEC off and H.264 goes on on the CPU.

    How a draw runs on the card

    • Shaders. nv_sass.c turns each IR operation into one to three instructions. An immediate goes into the instruction's 32-bit operand slot; operands with modifiers the instruction cannot take go through scratch registers. Texture results get a block of four registers only from the lookup to its last use, so blocks are shared. Two passes then work on the finished code: - Reordering (nv_sass_reorder). The shader is one block (control flow is flattened), so a list scheduler orders the instructions by their longest latency path to the end. Every register and predicate dependency is kept, and stores and KILL keep their order. Texture lookups and interpolation start early, and independent chains fill each other's stalls. - Scheduling (nv_sass_schedule). Fixed-latency results get only the stall the next reader needs: 6 cycles for FP32, 13 for a predicate. Texture lookups, interpolation, attribute and constant loads, MUFU and stores use the six scoreboard barriers, waited for only by the instructions that use those registers.

    nv_sass_tests checks both passes. Every shader runs in the simulator against the CPU, and a hazard checker walks the cycle each instruction issues at, flagging any read or overwrite that comes too early. The dependency decoder both passes rely on is checked against what each instruction really touches in the simulator. Uniforms are constant buffer 0, loaded with every draw; texture handles sit behind them. The vertex stage writes every varying and the pixel stage's header lists every varying as read, so the two always agree. Not encoded yet: front-facing (gl_FrontFacing); such a program stays on the CPU.

    • Built-in programs (color, Gouraud, Phong) are FGSL source in nv_builtin_fgsl.h, compiled in the kernel with the SDK's fglsl.h the first time they are drawn.
    • Memory. Color targets are pitch-linear in VRAM, pitch a multiple of 128 bytes (FGPU pads surfaces to 32 pixels when draws run on the card). Depth is a block-linear ZF32 buffer of the backend's own per depth surface, because the hardware has no pitch-linear depth. The CPU depth buffer only follows the clears, so a frame that mixes GPU draws with a draw that must fall back to the CPU (a refused shader, memory outside VRAM, a full-screen page-flip surface whose pitch does not fit) does not depth-test between the two.
    • One job per clear or draw, submitted and waited for. Batching a frame into one job is the obvious next speed-up.
    • Reading back. fglPresent into a window and fglReadPixels copy the frame out of VRAM with the copy engine (nv_rm_ce_read).

    make test-host runs tests/host/nv_sass_tests.c: it decodes the machine code with a small simulator and compares every output with the CPU shader machine on random inputs (built-in programs, textures with discard, math and branches), and checks the pushbuffers word by word. That proves the encoder against the IR; only a card can prove the encodings themselves.

    Storage And Packages

    On this pageMinimaFS ModelDisks, partitions and drivesEmbedded Install PackagesMPKG FormatFile OperationsSafety Rules

    MinimaFS Model

    MinimaFS stores a directory tree in 4 KiB blocks on an AHCI-backed disk. Mounted drives use paths such as 0:/, 1:/, and 0:/programs. Metadata records file type, format, size, timestamps, runnable state, and block layout. Directory descriptors contain entries and storage descriptors track the volume root, block counts, and free space.

    The filesystem API is declared in src/intf/x86_64/minimafs.h. Commands should use resolved MinimaFS paths and the API rather than constructing raw disk structures.

    Disks, partitions and drives

    disks                                  list disks, partitions, filesystems
part sata1                             show sata1's partition table
part sata1 init gpt --yes              new empty GPT (or mbr)
part sata1 add 500G minimafs data      add a partition (sizes: 512M, 20G, 2T, rest)
part sata1 del 2                       delete partition 2
format sata1p1 1 data                  MinimaFS on sata1p1, mounted as 1:
mount sata1p2 2                        mount an existing volume as 2:
umount 2
drives                                 mounted drives and their usage
format                                 (no arguments) the boot volume as 0:, with system files

    At boot the system volume is mounted as 0: (the one named by root=<partition GUID or device> on the kernel command line, else the first MinimaFS volume found), and every other MinimaFS volume as 1:, 2:, ... in disk order.

    A MinimaFS volume can hold up to 2^32 - 2 blocks of 4 KiB, just under 16 TiB. Free space is tracked as a list of used extents rebuilt at mount time, so memory use does not grow with the volume size. MBR can address disks up to 2 TiB; use GPT beyond that (the default).

    MinimaFS partitions use GPT type 4D696E69-6D61-4653-B0A7-4D4F534D4653 or MBR type 0x7F.

    To make a disk boot by itself, use install (see Installing).

    Embedded Install Packages

    The root Makefile packages these directories as MPKG0001 archives:

    SourceDestination after format
    src/resources/install10:/etc
    src/resources/install20:/programs
    src/resources/install30:/services

    The archives are converted to ELF binary objects with objcopy and linked into the kernel. This is intentional: a newly formatted disk has no files from which the format command could load an installer.

    install1 receives the generated minimaSSL.slib. A service file added to install3 is therefore present at 0:/services before service discovery runs.

    MPKG Format

    The host builder is tools/mkpkg/mkpkg.py. It writes:

    • an 8-byte MPKG0001 magic;
    • a version and entry count;
    • fixed-size entry records with names, flags, compression method, sizes, and payload offsets;
    • stored or LZSS-compressed payload data.

    Directory entries have no payload. File entries use either MPKG_METHOD_STORE or MPKG_METHOD_LZSS. The kernel validates names, table bounds, payload ranges, and decompression output before writing an entry.

    Use the command interface to work with packages already on disk:

    pkg zip 0:/source store
pkg unzip 0:/archive.mpkg 0:/target
pkginfo 0:/archive.mpkg
installpkg 0:/archive.mpkg 0:/target

    User programs use mos_pkg_zip(), mos_pkg_unzip(), and mos_pkg_info() over SYS_PKG.

    File Operations

    Kernel code can create, open, read, write, list, delete, and remove files through MinimaFS. User code uses the corresponding SDK wrappers:

    • mos_open() and mos_close() manage existing files;
    • mos_read() and mos_fwrite() transfer data;
    • mos_seek(), mos_tell(), mos_size(), and mos_feof() inspect position;
    • mos_create() creates an empty file before opening it writable;
    • mos_listdir(), mos_exists(), and mos_is_dir() inspect paths;
    • mos_get_metadata() returns stable user-facing metadata.

    Filesystem paths are strings, not user-space integer descriptors in the public SDK. Open file handles are kernel-owned values returned by SYS_OPEN and must be closed.

    Safety Rules

    Package extraction must reject absolute paths and .. traversal. Validate sizes before allocating or reading payloads. Use heap memory for directory structures and large file buffers instead of kernel stacks. When adding a new format or package feature, keep the host encoder and kernel decoder constants synchronized.

    Installing

    On this pageFrom the terminalFrom MOSdeskBuildingReal hardware notes

    From the terminal

    Boot the ISO (CD/USB stick), then:

    disks                      find the target disk
install sata1              asks for confirmation, then erases sata1
install nvme0 --mbr --yes  MBR instead of GPT, no question
install sata1 --size 64G   leave the rest of the disk unpartitioned
install --system sata1p3 --boot sata1p1     use existing partitions

    The installed disk boots on both BIOS and UEFI PCs:

    GPT (default)MBR (--mbr, disks up to 2 TiB)
    p1 EFI System Partition, FAT32, 256 MiBp1 FAT32 boot partition, 256 MiB
    p2 BIOS boot partition (GRUB core)p2 MinimaFS system
    p3 MinimaFS systemGRUB core in the gap before p1

    The FAT32 partition holds GRUB for UEFI (EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI), the kernel, the install payload and boot/grub/grub.cfg, which passes root=<GUID of the system partition> so the kernel mounts it as 0:. The system partition gets the same files format installs. An installed system can install again.

    From MOSdesk

    Run make run-mosdesk, sign in and open Installer. It lists the disks (the system disk cannot be chosen), lets you pick GPT or MBR, asks for your account password and shows the progress. make run attaches an empty 8 GiB install-target.img as a second disk for this; afterwards make run-installed (BIOS) or make run-installed-uefi (needs the ovmf package) boots it without the CD.

    Building

    The ISO is BIOS + UEFI bootable and the installer can write UEFI boot files when the build machine has grub-pc-bin, grub-efi-amd64-bin, xorriso and mtools installed.

    Real hardware notes

    What has been made to work for real PCs:

    • more than 1 GiB of RAM, memory holes and ACPI tables above 1 GiB,
    • UEFI boot (GOP framebuffer, PS/2 controller initialised by the OS),
    • USB 3 (xHCI) keyboards and mice, PS/2 keyboards,
    • SATA (AHCI, all controllers and ports) and NVMe disks, GPT, large disks,
    • write-combining framebuffer mapping.

    Not yet: USB hubs and USB storage, EHCI, network cards other than the RTL8139 and RTL8111/8168, audio other than AC'97/PC speaker, GPU acceleration.

    Networking

    On this pageStack LayersInitializationDHCPDNSTCPUDPTLS And Wget

    Stack Layers

    The kernel network path is:

    RTL8139 / RTL8168 -> Ethernet -> IPv4/ARP -> UDP/TCP -> syscall handles

    network_manager selects the NIC driver. Ethernet frames are passed to IPv4, which dispatches UDP and TCP payloads. ARP resolves next-hop IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses. The protocol implementations live in src/impl/net.

    The stack uses host-order IPv4 addresses in its internal and user syscall APIs. Only wire headers use network byte order.

    Initialization

    kernel_main() registers the network drivers, RTL8139 (QEMU's default card) and RTL8111/8168 (the gigabit NIC on most desktop boards, rtl8168.c); the network manager uses the first one whose card is present. Then it initializes Ethernet, IP, UDP, TCP, and net_syscall. Both drivers are polled. The RTL8168 driver has not been run on real hardware yet (QEMU has no RTL8168), so RTL8168: lines in the serial log are the first thing to check if networking does not come up on such a board. The NIC must be initialized before protocol traffic can be sent. network_manager_poll() pumps received frames and is called from blocking protocol operations and user polling wrappers.

    The stack has bounded connection, listener, handle, and receive-queue tables. The SYS_ERR_BUSY result means another caller currently owns a non-reentrant network operation; retry it rather than treating it as a permanent failure.

    DHCP

    The terminal dhcp command sends a DISCOVER, waits for an OFFER, sends a REQUEST, and waits for an ACK. It configures:

    • guest IPv4 address;
    • netmask;
    • gateway;
    • DNS server.

    DHCP is intentionally an operator action. A user .run program calling mos_net_dhcp() receives SYS_ERR_PERM because changing the lease changes the machine-wide interface configuration.

    DNS

    dns_resolve() sends a UDP A-record query to the configured DNS server. The resolver registers a temporary UDP handler, pumps the NIC while waiting, and removes the handler when the query completes or times out.

    The terminal wget command resolves a hostname when the URL does not contain a numeric address. DNS failures are reported separately from TCP and TLS failures.

    TCP

    TCP supports active connections, listeners, accept queues, retransmission, ACKs, receive buffers, and bounded send windows. User programs receive integer handles rather than raw tcp_conn_t* pointers. Handles are owned by the creating process and are closed when the owner dies.

    Client pattern:

    long h = mos_tcp_connect(ip, 80, 5000);
if (h > 0) {
    mos_tcp_send(h, request, request_len);
    mos_net_poll();
    mos_tcp_recv(h, buffer, sizeof buffer);
    mos_tcp_close(h);
}

    Server pattern:

    long listener = mos_tcp_listen(8080, 4);
long client = mos_tcp_accept(listener, &peer_ip, &peer_port);

    mos_tcp_accept() is non-blocking. It returns zero when the backlog is empty and SYS_ERR_AGAIN is normalized to zero by the SDK wrapper. A server should sleep briefly between attempts. mos_tcp_handoff() transfers an accepted connection to a child process.

    UDP

    A user program binds a UDP handle, receives queued datagrams, and sends to a host-order destination address. Datagrams larger than the destination buffer are truncated and the remainder is discarded.

    Broadcast uses SYSCALL_NET_IP_BROADCAST. The QEMU user-mode network backend does not forward LAN broadcasts beyond the guest, so broadcast discovery needs a tap or bridged network configuration.

    TLS And Wget

    The kernel wget command performs a TLS 1.3 client handshake over TCP. The current tested cipher path is TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256:

    1. create a ClientHello with X25519 key share;
    2. parse ServerHello and derive handshake traffic secrets;
    3. authenticate encrypted handshake records;
    4. verify the server Finished message;
    5. derive application traffic secrets;
    6. send the HTTP request in an encrypted application record;
    7. decrypt the HTTP response.

    The TLS client defers certificate verification. It is suitable for the current controlled integration test but should not be treated as a complete web PKI client. tools/debug/https_test.sh runs an OpenSSL TLS 1.3 server and verifies this path end to end.

    Discovery And Registration

    Services are filesystem definitions, not C registration calls. After the boot disk is mounted, terminal_program_entry() calls service_manager_init(). The manager scans 0:/services, accepts files whose names end in .service, parses them, and creates a monitor process for each valid entry.

    A service is registered only when it has at least one [STARTUP] action: exec or script. The terminal command services lists entries that parsed and registered successfully.

    Services are optional modules. In particular, the window manager is not required to boot or use the built-in terminal. Installing its executable alone does not start it; automatic startup is enabled by placing its mosWM.service definition in 0:/services. If the definition or executable is missing, service discovery skips the entry and the OS continues without a window manager. Remove the service definition and reboot to disable automatic startup.

    [GENERAL]
name="mosWM"
desc="Optional graphical window manager"
exit=None

[STARTUP]
exec="0:/programs/mosWM/mosWM.run"

    File Format

    [GENERAL]
name="Example Service"
desc="Runs an example"
exit=Restart
exitscript="run 0:/programs/recovery.run"

[STARTUP]
exec="0:/programs/example.run"

    Supported general keys:

    • name: display name; defaults to the filename;
    • desc: text shown by services;
    • exit: None, Restart, or Script;
    • exitscript: command used by Script after a monitored process exits.

    Supported startup keys:

    • exec: direct .run path, run <path>, or an arbitrary terminal command;
    • script: run <path> for a launchable .run, or another command string.

    Values may be quoted. // starts a comment outside quotes.

    Startup Forms

    A directly monitored executable uses a path:

    [STARTUP]
exec="0:/programs/worker.run"

    The equivalent command form is also recognized:

    [STARTUP]
exec="run 0:/programs/worker.run"

    An arbitrary command can be run once:

    [STARTUP]
exec="echo service started"

    Command-style entries call the terminal command dispatcher and do not expose a process ID to the service monitor. exit=Restart and exit=Script therefore cannot supervise their completion. Use a .run path when restart or exit handling is required.

    Supervision

    For a direct .run launch, the manager:

    1. normalizes the path to a 0:/... path;
    2. launches the bundle as a process;
    3. waits for its process ID;
    4. applies the exit policy.

    None stops after exit. Restart waits briefly and starts again. Script executes exitscript once and then stops.

    A failed launch is logged on serial and does not create a usable monitored service. A malformed file, missing startup action, or unsupported startup configuration is skipped.

    Packaging A Service

    Place the definition in src/resources/install3:

    src/resources/install3/example.service

    make build-x86_64 packages install3 and embeds it in the kernel. Running format extracts it to 0:/services before service discovery. A referenced .run program should be placed in src/resources/install2, which becomes 0:/programs.

    The complete install mapping is:

    install1 -> 0:/etc
install2 -> 0:/programs
install3 -> 0:/services

    Troubleshooting

    Use services after mounting to inspect registrations. Use the serial console to distinguish these cases:

    • no services directory: install3 was empty or format did not run;
    • parse failure: the file syntax or section/key names are invalid;
    • no startup action: add exactly one exec or script key;
    • failed to start: the referenced .run path is missing or invalid;
    • repeated starts: the service has exit=Restart and exits normally.
    PreviousNetworkingNextInstall and services

    Edit this page on GitHub

    Install Packages and Services

    Minimal-OS builds three resource packages into the kernel image:

    Source directoryDestination after format
    src/resources/install10:/etc
    src/resources/install20:/programs
    src/resources/install30:/services

    Each directory is packaged as an .mpkg archive during make build-x86_64. The archives are embedded in the kernel because formatting happens before the new MinimaFS disk contains any files. The format command extracts the archives into their destination directories.

    Programs built from the SDK during make and placed in install2:

    FileWhat it is
    dlr.run, dlrconnect.runDeliver, the LAN package manager (dlr in the terminal)
    DeliverManager.runDeliver Manager, a MOSdesk app for getting and sharing Deliver packages (README)
    fglcube.runFarcadeGL demo

    Adding A Service

    Place a .service file in src/resources/install3. No C registration call is needed. The file is packaged automatically, extracted to 0:/services, and discovered after the boot disk is mounted.

    Example: src/resources/install3/example.service

    [GENERAL]
name="Example Service"
desc="Runs the example program"
exit=Restart

[STARTUP]
exec="0:/programs/example.run"

    [STARTUP] must contain exactly one startup action:

    • exec="0:/programs/example.run" starts a .run bundle directly.
    • exec="run 0:/programs/example.run" starts a .run bundle through the

    command system and monitors it like a direct exec path.

    • exec="echo service started" runs any terminal command once.
    • script="run 0:/programs/example.run" starts it through the command system.

    Command-style exec and script entries run once without PID tracking, so exit=Restart and exit=Script cannot monitor or react to their completion.

    The exit setting controls what happens after the startup process exits:

    • None stops monitoring the service.
    • Restart starts it again after a short delay.
    • Script runs the command in exitscript.

    Example with an exit script:

    [GENERAL]
name="Worker"
desc="Background worker"
exit=Script
exitscript="run 0:/programs/worker-failed.run"

[STARTUP]
exec="0:/programs/worker.run"

    After boot, use:

    services

    to list successfully parsed and registered services. Invalid files, files without a .service extension, and services without exec or script are skipped.

    Build And Clean

    Build the kernel and regenerate all install packages:

    make build-x86_64

    minimaSSL.slib is generated into src/resources/install1 and installed as 0:/etc/minimaSSL.slib during format.

    Remove kernel, SDK, generated package, and .run build artifacts with:

    make clean

    The current kernel links the freestanding minimaSSL crypto implementation statically. The installed .slib is the filesystem distribution artifact; the OS does not currently dynamically load .slib code.

    User Programs And SDK

    On this pageProgram Model.run BundlesAddress SpaceWindow FramesArguments And ExitSDK Runtime.slib BundlesWriting A ProgramSecurity And Capability Notes

    Program Model

    The SDK produces self-contained x86_64 PIE programs with no dynamic linker. The kernel loads these programs as user processes and enters them in ring 3. The current process model still shares the kernel PML4, so the syscall ABI is a capability boundary but not yet a fully isolated address-space boundary.

    Build a program with:

    Minimal-OS-SDK/build.sh Minimal-OS-SDK/examples/hello.c

    The output is a .run bundle. Import it into MinimaFS, normally under 0:/programs, and run it with:

    run 0:/programs/hello.run

    .run Bundles

    A .run contains a MINIRUN1 header, an entry table, main.elf, and optional resource files. The kernel extracts main.elf, loads its PT_LOAD segments, and applies supported R_X86_64_RELATIVE relocations.

    The loader validates:

    • ELF64 little-endian format;
    • x86_64 machine type;
    • ET_EXEC or ET_DYN image type;
    • program-header bounds;
    • segment file-size and memory-size relationships;
    • maximum file and image sizes.

    The loader reads main.elf from the file one segment at a time, straight into the program's pages, so a large program needs no large kernel buffer. A file may be up to 256 MiB and an image up to 1 GiB; .bss takes memory only as it is used.

    Address Space

    AddressesContents
    below 4 GiBSYS_HEAP memory (malloc); the rest belongs to the kernel and is not accessible
    0x10000000000 (1 TiB)the image, each segment with its own protection
    from 0x20000000000 (2 TiB)SYS_VM mappings
    up to 0x7FFFF0000000the main stack: 8 MiB unless SYS_SPAWN sets stack_size, with 64 KiB of no-access guard below it
    0x7FFFF8000000argv, envp and their strings

    Stack and SYS_VM pages take physical memory on first use. The stack, SYS_HEAP memory and SYS_VM mappings without SYS_VM_PROT_EXEC cannot be executed. The SDK's link.ld still links everything into one segment, so an SDK program's image is readable, writable and executable as a whole.

    The SDK linker script keeps the image base-relative. External symbols are not available because there is no dynamic linker or libc at runtime.

    Window Frames

    SYS_WINDOW_PRESENT copies pixels into a kernel frame and mosWM copies them out again (SYS_WINDOW_GET_FRAME); that path is unchanged. Three ops, appended to syscall_window_op_t, share the frame instead (syscall_window_shared_t, passed in the shared member of the request, which shares storage with frame):

    • SYS_WINDOW_MAP_FRAME maps the window's two buffers (one object, buffer_count 2, buffer_stride bytes apart, width * 4 bytes per row). The owner gets them writable, the registered manager read-only, nobody else (SYS_ERR_PERM). The first call by the owner turns the window into a shared one (its pixels become buffer 0); the manager asking about a window that is not shared gets SYS_ERR_AGAIN and keeps using GET_FRAME. SYS_ERR_NOMEM: no contiguous memory, or over the 128 MiB limit for shared frames (counted separately from the 64 MiB of the copy path). Every call makes a new mapping; the caller unmaps it (SYS_VM_UNMAP, 2 * buffer_stride).
    • SYS_WINDOW_PRESENT_SHARED: owner only; flags is the buffer number that is ready, x/y/width/height the damage (both 0: everything). That buffer becomes the front one (what the manager shows); the owner draws into the other. Damage is the part that differs from the buffer shown before.
    • SYS_WINDOW_TAKE_DAMAGE: manager only. Returns the geometry, generation, front, frame_version and the union of damage rectangles since the last call (copy-path presents are included; buffer_count is 0 for those windows), and clears it.

    Resizing replaces the object: the window drops its reference, generation increases, front becomes 0 and the old front pixels are copied into the new buffer 0. Existing mappings stay valid, show the old frame and are no longer updated; mapping again gives the new buffers. The old frames are freed when the last process unmaps them or ends, and a closed window's frames likewise. window_manager_present_target() / window_manager_present_done() (the target holds its own reference on the frames) let kernel code (FGPU op_present) render into the back buffer and publish it with a damage rectangle; they fall back to the copy path (return false) when the window cannot be shared.

    Arguments And Exit

    The first argument is the program path. Extra arguments follow it. The SDK runtime calls mos_exit(code) to terminate, passing the low 8 bits of code back to the kernel. Returning from main() passes its return value as the exit code. A user-mode CPU fault terminates the program with code 0xff and prints a crash reason, such as Program crashed! Code 0xff: Memory page fault.

    Use mos_register_cleanup() when a user program needs a chance to save state before Ctrl+C or a requested termination. The kernel gives the cleanup callback a bounded period before force termination.

    Heap allocations made through the SDK are tracked by their owning process. Explicitly free allocations when practical; any remaining allocations are reclaimed when the process exits or is terminated. Invalid or cross-process heap pointers are rejected by the heap syscalls. This is exit-time reclamation, not tracing garbage collection, so it does not collect unreachable objects while a process is still running.

    SDK Runtime

    The SDK provides freestanding headers and small wrappers rather than a normal libc. Common facilities include:

    • stdio.h: terminal output helpers;
    • stdlib.h: heap, random bytes, and integer conversion;
    • string.h: memory and string operations;
    • minimalos.h: core syscalls and package/file wrappers;
    • net.h: TCP, UDP, DNS, and polling;
    • graphics.h: graphics operations;
    • x86_64/user_sysinfo.h: system and memory statistics.

    The runtime is built with freestanding flags, no stack protector, no exceptions, no RTTI, and no dynamic linker. See SDK syscalls for API contracts and examples.

    .slib Bundles

    The SDK can build a shared-library bundle:

    Minimal-OS-SDK/build.sh --slib Minimal-OS-SDK/libraries/minimaSSL

    A .slib contains:

    • library.elf;
    • exports.txt with global symbols;
    • public headers under include/.

    The bundle format is MINISLIB1. It is package metadata for a future/runtime loader; Minimal-OS does not currently dynamically load .slib code. The current kernel TLS path statically links the freestanding minimaSSL implementation and also installs the .slib at 0:/etc/minimaSSL.slib for distribution.

    Writing A Program

    A minimal program should include the SDK headers, perform work, and terminate:

    #include "minimalos.h"
#include "stdio.h"

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    (void)argc;
    (void)argv;
    puts("hello from user space");
    mos_exit(0);
    return 0;
}

    For long-running programs, sleep or poll rather than busy-looping. Network programs must call mos_net_poll() or use the deadline helpers so the kernel network stack can process incoming frames.

    Security And Capability Notes

    User programs can access only syscall operations permitted by the kernel's privilege table. DHCP is privileged. File, network, process, graphics, USB, heap, random, and package operations have individual validation paths.

    Do not pass kernel pointers through the ABI. Use the public request structures, user buffers, and returned handles. Always close file, TCP, UDP, and TLS handles.
