    User SDK Syscalls

    This is the user-space ABI reference for .run programs. The canonical numbers and request structures are in Minimal-OS-SDK/include/syscall.h; the inline wrappers are in minimalos.h, net.h, stdlib.h, x86_64/user_syscalls.h, and related headers.

    On this pageCalling ConventionResult CodesCore Process And Console CallsFilesystem CallsHeap And RandomnessGraphicsDevice Managers And USBPackagesSystem Information And ProcessesNetworkingABI Rules And Lifecycle

    Calling Convention

    The SDK invokes the kernel with int 0x80:

    • rax: syscall number;
    • rdi, rsi, rdx: the first three arguments;
    • rax on return: result value.

    Pointer arguments must point to user-readable or user-writable memory as required by the operation. Request-structure syscalls pass a pointer in rdi. Do not pass kernel-internal structures or pointers through the ABI.

    Most wrappers return long. Success is usually non-negative; failures are negative values represented in the unsigned syscall type. Use the constants rather than comparing against a raw magic number.

    Result Codes

    ConstantMeaning
    SYS_SUCCESSoperation succeeded
    SYS_ERR_GENERICunspecified failure
    SYS_ERR_BADFDinvalid or closed handle
    SYS_ERR_NOTFOUNDpath, peer, or resource not found/closed
    SYS_ERR_INVALinvalid argument or request
    SYS_ERR_PERMoperation is not allowed for this process
    SYS_ERR_BUSYshared non-reentrant subsystem is busy; retry
    SYS_ERR_AGAINnon-blocking operation has no result yet

    Core Process And Console Calls

    WrapperSyscallContract
    mos_write(fd, buf, len)SYS_WRITEwrites to terminal output; SDK programs normally use fd 1 or 2
    mos_puts(text)SYS_WRITEconvenience wrapper for a NUL-terminated string
    mos_getpid()SYS_GETPIDreturns the current process ID
    mos_exit(code)SYS_EXITterminates and reports the low 8 bits of code; does not return
    mos_sleep(ms)SYS_SLEEPyields/sleeps for approximately the requested interval
    mos_uptime()SYS_UPTIMEreturns uptime in milliseconds
    mos_gettime()SYS_GETTIMEreturns the current kernel time representation
    mos_register_cleanup(fn)SYS_REGISTER_CLEANUPregisters a bounded cleanup callback for termination
    mos_exec(path, argv, argc)SYS_EXEClaunches another .run, returning its PID
    mos_pslist(entries, max)SYS_PSLISTlists visible process information

    mos_exec() treats argv as extra arguments. The launched program receives the path as argv[0] and the supplied values starting at argv[1].

    Filesystem Calls

    MinimaFS paths are strings such as 0:/etc/System.conf. SYS_OPEN opens an existing file; use mos_create() before opening a new file for writing.

    WrapperSyscallContract
    mos_open(path, flags)SYS_OPENreturns an open handle; SYS_O_RDONLY is read-only and SYS_O_RDWR is writable
    mos_create(path, type, format)SYS_CREATEcreates an empty file; NULL type/format defaults to binary/bin
    mos_read(fd, buf, len)SYS_READreads from an open handle
    mos_fwrite(fd, buf, len)SYS_FWRITEwrites to an open writable handle
    mos_close(fd)SYS_CLOSEcloses the handle
    mos_seek(fd, offset)SYS_SEEKchanges the current file position
    mos_tell(fd)SYS_TELLreturns the current position
    mos_size(fd)SYS_SIZEreturns file data size
    mos_feof(fd)SYS_EOFreports whether the handle is at EOF
    mos_exists(path)SYS_EXISTStests path existence
    mos_is_dir(path)SYS_IS_DIRtests whether a path is a directory
    mos_mkdir(path)SYS_MKDIRcreates a directory
    mos_listdir(path, entries, max)SYS_LISTDIRwrites directory entries to a caller buffer
    mos_delete(path)SYS_DELETEdeletes a file
    mos_rmdir(path)SYS_RMDIRremoves an empty directory
    mos_get_metadata(path, out)SYS_GET_METADATAfills stable file metadata

    Example:

    int fd = mos_open("0:/etc/config.txt", SYS_O_RDONLY);
if (fd >= 0) {
    char buf[128];
    long got = mos_read(fd, buf, sizeof buf - 1);
    if (got > 0) {
        buf[got] = '\0';
        mos_puts(buf);
    }
    mos_close(fd);
}

    Open handles belong to the process and should always be closed. The public metadata structure is intentionally separate from the kernel's internal minimafs_file_metadata_t so kernel structure growth does not change the ABI.

    Heap And Randomness

    stdlib.h maps the standard allocation names to SYS_HEAP:

    char* data = malloc(4096);
if (!data) mos_exit(1);
/* use data */
free(data);

    Available operations are malloc, calloc, realloc, and free. Allocation failure becomes NULL. realloc() leaves the original allocation valid when it fails. mos_random_bytes() uses the kernel random source and returns a byte count; mos_random_u64() is a convenience wrapper.

    The current implementation backs user heap allocations with the kernel heap. That is an implementation detail and should not be used to infer unrestricted kernel access.

    Graphics

    SYS_GRAPHICS receives a syscall_graphics_request_t. The SDK headers provide wrappers for:

    • width and height queries;
    • bounded opaque or alpha surface blits into a kernel back buffer;
    • dirty-rectangle presentation and packed framebuffer information;
    • clear, pixel, line, rectangle, circle, triangle, and ellipse drawing;
    • text output and text measurement;
    • resolution changes;
    • terminal clear.

    Screen ownership uses mos_graphics_acquire(), mos_graphics_release(), and mos_graphics_owner(). A process must acquire the screen before drawing; only the owner may perform drawing operations. Acquire fails with SYS_ERR_PERM if another process owns the screen. Release redraws the terminal, and ownership is reported as a PID or SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND when no process owns it.

    mos_graphics_blit_surface() accepts an ARGB8888 source surface, byte pitch, source rectangle, destination origin, and either SYS_GRAPHICS_BLIT_OPAQUE or SYS_GRAPHICS_BLIT_ALPHA. The complete source range must belong to one live user-heap allocation. The kernel caps each source at 64 MiB and stages it before compositing. mos_graphics_present(x, y, width, height) copies a clipped dirty rectangle to the framebuffer and is owner-only. mos_graphics_info() fills a versioned syscall_graphics_info_t with dimensions, pitch, framebuffer channel layout, and the back-buffer format SYS_GRAPHICS_PIXEL_FORMAT_ARGB8888.

    Use graphics.h for the shorter API or x86_64/user_graphics.h for raw-style wrappers. Coordinates and sizes are passed in the request's integer argument array; strings and output dimensions use validated pointers.

    Device Managers And USB

    SYS_MANAGER selects a manager and operation. The SDK exposes manager IDs for GPU, audio, storage, and USB, with operations such as init, update, start, has-data, and sample-rate configuration.

    SYS_USB supports:

    • mos_usb_init();
    • mos_usb_poll();
    • keyboard presence checks;
    • scancode/modifier to ASCII translation;
    • pressed-key queries;
    • keyboard device metadata.

    SYS_MOUSE provides mouse initialization, polling, presence, and accumulated relative state (dx, dy, wheel, and button bitmask).

    SYS_INPUT_READ consumes key down/up, mouse motion/button, and wheel events from a 256-entry bounded queue. Only the graphics screen owner may read it. mos_input_read(events, capacity, timeout_ms, dropped_count) caps each read at 256 events and the blocking timeout at 5 seconds; a zero timeout polls once. When no graphics owner is active, the queue ignores hardware input so the terminal remains the input consumer. Overflow drops the newest event and increments the optional dropped-event counter.

    Packages

    SYS_PKG uses a syscall_pkg_request_t structure:

    uint32_t installed = 0, failed = 0;
long rc = mos_pkg_unzip("0:/packages/app.mpkg", "0:/programs",
                        &installed, &failed);

    Wrappers:

    • mos_pkg_unzip(archive, target, installed, failed);
    • mos_pkg_zip(source, algorithm, output, output_size);
    • mos_pkg_info(archive, entry_count).

    Algorithms are "lzss" or "store"; NULL selects the default. Package extraction validates archive names and reports individual entry failures separately from whole-archive failures.

    System Information And Processes

    user_sysinfo.h exposes statistics through SYS_SYSINFO:

    • CPU usage;
    • total, used, and free RAM;
    • uptime;
    • process and online-core counts;
    • heap used/free bytes;
    • physical page used/free counts;
    • per-core usage using SYS_SYSINFO_CORE_USAGE_BASE + core_id.

    mos_pslist() writes process records containing PID, name, state, privilege, CPU assignment, and scheduler level. Its buffer belongs to the caller.

    Networking

    SYS_NET uses a syscall_net_request_t pointer. IPv4 addresses and ports are host-order values. net.h provides wrappers for status, resolve, polling, TCP, UDP, and the experimental TLS handle namespace.

    Status And DNS

    syscall_net_status_t status;
mos_net_status(&status);
uint32_t ip;
mos_net_resolve("example.com", &ip, 5000);

    mos_net_dhcp() is privileged and returns SYS_ERR_PERM from ordinary user programs. Run dhcp in the terminal first.

    TCP Client

    long conn = mos_tcp_connect(ip, 80, 5000);
if (conn > 0) {
    mos_tcp_send(conn, request, request_len);
    while (mos_net_poll() == 0) mos_sleep(10);
    long got = mos_tcp_recv(conn, buffer, sizeof buffer);
    mos_tcp_close(conn);
}

    mos_tcp_recv() returns zero when no data is ready and a negative error when the handle is invalid or the peer is closed. Deadline helpers in net.h pump polling and sleep between attempts.

    TCP Server And Ownership

    mos_tcp_listen() creates a listener handle. mos_tcp_accept() is non-blocking and returns zero when no client is queued. After starting a child, mos_tcp_handoff(connection, child_pid) transfers ownership so the child can use the accepted handle. The handle number is normally passed as an argument.

    UDP

    mos_udp_bind() creates a handle. mos_udp_recv() returns a datagram and fills source address/port outputs. mos_udp_send() sends to a host-order destination; SYSCALL_NET_IP_BROADCAST is the broadcast address.

    TLS Handles

    The ABI defines separate TLS connect, accept, state, send, receive, and close operations. TLS handshakes advance when SYS_NET_TLS_STATE or other TLS calls pump the session. SYS_ERR_AGAIN means the session is still progressing. The terminal wget command currently uses the kernel's dedicated TLS client; user TLS handles and certificate policy should be treated as evolving APIs.

    ABI Rules And Lifecycle

    • Check every return value, especially handle allocation and network operations.
    • Retry SYS_ERR_BUSY and non-blocking SYS_ERR_AGAIN where documented.
    • Close every file, TCP, UDP, and TLS handle before exit.
    • Keep request structures alive until the syscall returns.
    • Keep input/output buffers valid for the entire call.
    • Do not call privileged operations from an ordinary .run process.
    • Use mos_sleep() between polling attempts to yield CPU time.
    • Do not assume kernel structure layouts match SDK structures.

    Minimal-OS SDK function reference

    Every function the SDK headers give a .run program, one entry per function: its signature, what each parameter means, what it returns, the errors to expect, and a short example. The headers are the source of truth; these pages describe them as of SDK v1.1 and the kernel's syscall.c.

    PageHeaderWhat is in it
    Conventions and errorssyscall.hCalling convention, result codes, privilege rules, which header to include
    Process and terminalminimalos.hOutput to the terminal, exit, sleep, time, PIDs, launching programs, cleanup on Ctrl+C
    Filesminimalos.hMinimaFS: open, create, read, write, seek, list, delete, metadata
    Memory and randomnessstdlib.hmalloc, calloc, realloc, free, random bytes, atoi
    Strings and memorystring.hstrlen, strcmp, strstr, memcpy, constant-time compare …
    Formatted outputstdio.h, iostreamprintf and std::cout
    Windowswindow.hmosWM windows: create, draw, present, events
    easyui widgetseasyui.hButtons, sliders, text inputs, radio buttons, lists and more, in the MOSdesk theme
    Text in your own pixelsfont.hdraw_text / text_width: smooth Inter text (bitmap fallback) in any pixel buffer
    Graphicsgraphics.h, x86_64/user_graphics.hFull-screen framebuffer: acquire, blit, present, primitives
    Inputx86_64/user_syscalls.h, user_mouse.h, user_usb.hRaw keyboard and mouse events for full-screen programs
    Networkingnet.hDNS, TCP client and server, UDP, the ktls transport
    System informationuser_sysinfo.hCPU, RAM, heap, cores, uptime, processes
    Packagesminimalos.h.mpkg archives: unzip, zip, inspect
    Device managersx86_64/user_managers.hGPU, audio, storage and USB manager calls
    FarcadeGL 3Dfarcadegl.h, fgpu_abi.hGPU-backed 3D: buffers, vertex layouts, shaders, textures, blending, drawing into a window or the screen
    FGSL shading languagefglsl.hThe GLSL-style language FarcadeGL shaders are written in, and its compiler
    Disks and root commandsstorage.hList disks and partitions, run kernel commands as root (installer)
    Playing audioaudio.hPlay, pause, seek and query .adi audio files

    Reading an entry

    Each function has the same parts:

    • Signature - the declaration exactly as the header has it. Every wrapper is static inline, so including a header never adds a symbol to your program.
    • Parameters - one row per argument.
    • Returns - the success value and the SYS_ERR_* values the kernel can return for that call.
    • Notes - limits, ownership rules and anything surprising.
    • Example - a minimal fragment. Examples assume the headers named at the top of the page are included.

    A complete program

    #include "minimalos.h"
#include "stdio.h"

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    printf("hello from pid %ld, %d argument(s)\n", mos_getpid(), argc);
    for (int i = 0; i < argc; i++) printf("argv[%d] = %s\n", i, argv[i]);
    mos_exit(0);
}

    Build it with ./build.sh hello.c and run it inside Minimal-OS with run 0:/programs/hello.run. Returning from main also ends the program; crt0.c calls mos_exit() with the return value.

    Build Targets

    The default Make target is build-x86_64. The build uses the x86_64-elf cross-compiler at $HOME/cross/bin and host tools including Make, NASM, Python 3, GRUB utilities, and xorriso.

    On this pageCommon targetsBuild productsQEMU disk imagesMOSdesk buildQEMU variantsCleanup

    Common targets

    CommandResult
    make or make build-x86_64Build and link the kernel, package resources, and produce dist/x86_64/kernel.iso
    make minimaSSL-slibBuild the SDK minimaSSL library used by the package build
    make test-hostCompile and run the host-side C tests without booting the OS
    make ci-testBuild the ISO and boot a headless QEMU smoke test
    make ci-interactBuild and run the scripted serial-console test
    make runBuild the ISO, create the install target image if needed, and boot the ISO in QEMU
    make mosdeskBuild the ISO with MOSdesk included
    make run-mosdeskBuild and run the MOSdesk ISO in QEMU
    make mosdesk-doomBuild the MOSdesk ISO with Doom (1993) included
    make run-mosdesk-doomBuild and run the MOSdesk ISO with Doom in QEMU
    make allBuild the MOSdesk ISO with everything: Doom and the Farcade editor (make mosdesk-fe DOOM=1)
    make packagesBuild Deliver install packages in build/dlrpackages: MOSdesk.mpkg, Doom.mpkg, Farcade.mpkg, each with its folder and .pkg manifest. Copy them into 0:/var/dlrd/packages and dlr serve offers them (dlr install Doom). DLR_PACKAGES_DIR= puts them elsewhere
    make netbootServe the built ISO for PXE boot on the LAN; requires elevated network setup
    make run-installedBoot INSTALL_DISK as a BIOS-installed system
    make run-installed-uefiBoot INSTALL_DISK with OVMF UEFI firmware
    make run-hypervRun the Hyper-V-oriented QEMU test environment
    make cleanRemove build outputs and all files ending in .run under the repository

    The full build and debugging overview is in Build and Debugging. The host and QEMU test coverage is detailed in Testing.

    Build products

    The kernel link output is dist/x86_64/kernel.bin. The build copies it into targets/x86_64/iso/boot/kernel.bin, embeds the install and firmware packages, then writes the bootable ISO to dist/x86_64/kernel.iso.

    The resource package inputs are:

    src/resources/install1 -> 0:/etc
src/resources/install2 -> 0:/programs
src/resources/install3 -> 0:/services

    The source resources are not build output. Edit them in place; the Makefile repackages them as part of the kernel build.

    QEMU disk images

    The default make run expects sata256.img to exist for the guest's primary disk. Create a blank image if you do not already have one:

    fallocate -l 256M sata256.img

    The second disk for the installer is install-target.img. It is created sparsely by Make when needed and defaults to 8 GiB. It is separate from the primary disk image.

    Useful overrides include:

    make run INSTALL_DISK=install-target.img INSTALL_DISK_SIZE=16G
make run QEMU_SOUND=hda
make run-two QEMU_TWO_MCAST=230.0.0.1:12345

    run-two needs sata256.img; if sata256-2.img does not exist, the target copies the first image as its starting point. Use disposable test images for filesystem and installer experiments.

    MOSdesk build

    make mosdesk builds the desktop ISO; make run-mosdesk builds and launches it. The targets build MOSdesk programs against this checkout's SDK. The MOSDESK_DIR variable can point to another MOSdesk checkout, and MOSDESK_USE_LOCAL=1 tells the build to use already checked-out submodule contents without fetching pinned revisions.

    make mosdesk-doom builds the same desktop ISO with Doom on it: id Software's GPL Doom engine, ported in Minimal-OS-SDK/programs/doom (its README has the controls and details), drawing through FarcadeGL. The game data is Freedoom: Phase 1, which the build downloads once and checks against its SHA-256; make mosdesk-doom DOOM_WAD=/path/to/DOOM.WAD uses your own copy of Doom instead (id's WADs are not free to redistribute, so none is bundled). Doom and its data go on the ISO as the mosgames boot module, which setup (format, install, RamFS) unpacks into 0:/programs; the launcher then lists Doom. RamFS boots get a larger RAM disk when the module is there. A plain make mosdesk afterwards leaves Doom out again.

    NVIDIA firmware is an optional build input. make gpu-setup downloads firmware for the default supported card; choose another supported model with, for example, make gpu-setup GPU="GTX 1660 Ti". See GPU documentation before distributing an image that contains firmware.

    QEMU variants

    The Makefile has additional targets for hardware and debugging scenarios:

    TargetUse
    run-audioCapture QEMU audio to WAV files
    run-sdlUse QEMU's SDL audio backend
    run-alsaUse QEMU's ALSA audio backend
    run-ps2Boot with PS/2 input instead of the configured USB devices
    run-intLog interrupt activity
    run-deKeep QEMU running after guest errors for debugging
    run-dexStart QEMU paused with the GDB stub enabled
    run-twoStart two guests on a multicast network

    Some audio and network variants assume host audio devices, tap interfaces, or other local setup. Check the target command in the root Makefile before using one on a host with different devices.

    Cleanup

    make clean removes build/, dist/, Minimal-OS-SDK/build, and generated minimaSSL bundles. It also executes find . -type f -name '*.run' -delete, which removes every .run file beneath the repository, including any hand-authored or otherwise valuable bundle. Back up or move .run files you need before running make clean.

    The clean target does not remove disk images such as sata256.img or install-target.img.

    Conventions and errors

    How SDK calls reach the kernel, what they return, and which calls an ordinary .run program is allowed to make.

    On this pageCalling conventionResult codesPrivilegeWhich headerUnitsMemory

    Calling convention

    Every wrapper ends in one int 0x80:

    RegisterInOut
    raxsyscall number (SYS_*)result
    rdifirst argument
    rsisecond argument
    rdxthird argument

    Calls with more data than three registers (graphics, windows, network, packages, input) pass one pointer to a request structure in rdi. Keep the structure and every buffer it points to alive until the call returns. Versioned structures (syscall_graphics_info_t, syscall_blit_request_t, syscall_input_read_request_t, syscall_window_request_t) must have their size and version fields set and their reserved fields zero; the SDK wrappers do this for you.

    Result codes

    Results come back in rax as a 64-bit value. Failures are small negative numbers, which as unsigned values sit at the very top of the range:

    ConstantValueMeaning
    SYS_SUCCESS0The operation succeeded
    SYS_ERR_GENERIC-1Unspecified failure (out of memory, the driver refused, the file system said no)
    SYS_ERR_BADFD-2Invalid or closed handle; mos_write to an fd other than 1 or 2
    SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND-3Path, window, peer or resource not found, or a connection that has closed
    SYS_ERR_INVAL-4Invalid argument: NULL pointer, out-of-range value, bad structure size or version
    SYS_ERR_PERM-5The calling process may not do this (see privilege)
    SYS_ERR_BUSY-6A shared subsystem (the network stack, a full event queue) is in use: retry
    SYS_ERR_AGAIN-7Non-blocking call with nothing to report yet: call again later

    The constants are defined as ((uint64_t)-N). Compare against them directly, or cast to long and test for a negative value:

    long r = mos_mkdir("0:/data");
if (r == (long)SYS_ERR_INVAL) printf("bad path\n");
else if (r < 0)               printf("mkdir failed: %ld\n", r);

    Some wrappers fold errors into a friendlier value (malloc returns NULL, mos_window_create returns 0, mos_tcp_accept returns 0 for "nobody waiting"); each entry says so.

    Privilege

    .run programs start as PROC_PRIVILEGE_USER processes. Before dispatching, the kernel checks the call against a deny list (syscall_user_may_call() in syscall.c); a denied call returns SYS_ERR_PERM and does nothing.

    Denied to .run programsWhy
    SYS_GRAPHICS drawing primitives (clear, pixel, line, rectangle, circle, triangle, ellipse, text, measure text, set resolution, terminal clear)User programs draw into their own surface and use mos_graphics_blit_surface + mos_graphics_present
    SYS_MANAGER init, update, start, set sample rateThey reconfigure hardware every process shares
    SYS_USB_INIT, SYS_MOUSE_INITThey re-enumerate devices the whole system uses
    SYS_NET_DHCPIt rewrites the address of the shared interface
    SYS_USB_KEY_IS_PRESSED, SYS_MOUSE_GET_STATE, SYS_INPUT_READAllowed only to the process that owns the screen

    Everything else - files, heap, network connections, windows, packages, sysinfo, process list - is open to user programs. The table is not a memory-protection boundary; it closes the specific hole of a program reconfiguring shared hardware through the syscall gate.

    Which header

    IncludeYou get
    minimalos.hCore calls: terminal output, exit, time, files, packages, exec, process list, framebuffer ownership and blit
    stdio.hprintf (includes minimalos.h)
    stdlib.hmalloc and friends, random bytes, atoi (includes minimalos.h)
    string.hString and memory helpers (no syscalls)
    window.hmosWM windows and their events
    graphics.hShort graphics_* names for the framebuffer API
    net.hNetworking (includes minimalos.h)
    user_sysinfo.hSystem statistics
    iostreamstd::cout for C++
    x86_64/user_syscalls.hRaw uint64_t wrappers: mos_syscall3, mos_graphics, mos_mouse, mos_usb, mos_manager, mos_sysinfo, mos_input_read
    x86_64/user_mouse.h, x86_64/user_usb.h, x86_64/user_managers.hMouse, USB keyboard and manager wrappers

    Both header families include x86_64/user_common.h, so every wrapper is defined exactly once and any combination of headers can be included together.

    Units

    • Time: milliseconds. mos_uptime() and mos_sleep() both use milliseconds; so do every timeout_ms argument.
    • Colours: window.h and mos_graphics_blit_surface take ARGB8888 pixels, 0xAARRGGBB. Use 0xFF alpha for opaque pixels. The mos_graphics_* primitives take separate r, g, b bytes.
    • IPv4 addresses and ports in net.h are host order: 192.168.1.10 is 0xC0A8010A.
    • Paths are MinimaFS paths such as 0:/programs/app.run. Relative paths are resolved against the terminal's current directory.

    Memory

    There is no libc and no dynamic linker. Everything a program uses is either an inline wrapper from these headers or code compiled into the program. crt0.c supplies _start, runs global constructors (.init_array), calls main(argc, argv) and then mos_exit() with its return value. It also defines out-of-line memcpy, memmove, memset and memcmp, which the compiler may call on its own.

    Development Workflow

    This guide helps you choose where a change belongs, wire it into a build, and select a useful validation command. For subsystem behavior, start with the matching guide in the documentation index.

    On this pageFind the right layerPreserve public contractsAdd or configure a hardware moduleAdd a built-in resourceBuild and validateGenerated files and cleanup

    Find the right layer

    ChangeStart here
    Boot protocol, page tables, interrupts, scheduler, syscallssrc/impl/boot, src/impl/kernel, src/impl/proc; shared contracts in src/intf/x86_64
    Shell command behaviorsrc/impl/commands and its declarations in src/intf/commands
    MinimaFS, block devices, partitioning, installationsrc/impl/filesystem, src/impl/storage, src/impl/install
    Ethernet and network protocolssrc/impl/net and src/modules/Network
    Optional hardware modulessrc/modules; module selection is generated into config.mk
    Built-in program, service, or configuration filesrc/resources/install1, install2, or install3
    User program, SDK header, or user libraryMinimal-OS-SDK
    Host-side packaging, test, or developer utilitytools and, for host tests, tests/host

    The high-level boot and component relationships are in Boot and Kernel. Driver registration and hardware fallbacks are described in Hardware.

    Preserve public contracts

    Before changing a shared interface, check who consumes it. Kernel interfaces and data structures are declared in src/intf; user programs call the syscall ABI through the SDK. The syscall register frame and process fields also have assembly consumers, so a layout change may require synchronized updates to assembly and ABI checks. See SDK conventions and Boot and Kernel.

    Keep kernel-only functionality in the kernel. User syscall access is governed by the privilege table as well as by the syscall-number table; an operation that changes machine-wide state may intentionally remain unavailable to ordinary user programs.

    Add or configure a hardware module

    config.sh discovers C and assembly files under src/modules and edits the generated config.mk interactively:

    ./config.sh

    The interface groups source files by directory. Use arrow keys or j/k to navigate, Space to toggle an item, and Enter to save. q exits without saving. Known dependencies are enabled or disabled together; review the resulting config.mk before building. Add dependency relationships to config.sh when a new module requires other optional modules.

    The module key is derived from the source path, for example src/modules/Audio/audio.c becomes MODULE_Audio_audio_c. Newly discovered modules default to enabled. Use make build-x86_64 to check the selected configuration.

    When adding a driver, keep device detection in the driver and expose subsystem-level operations through the existing manager pattern. Define a degraded behavior for absent or unsupported devices rather than making an optional device a boot requirement. See Hardware.

    Add a built-in resource

    The build embeds three resource trees in the kernel image:

    Source directoryInstalled path after format
    src/resources/install10:/etc
    src/resources/install20:/programs
    src/resources/install30:/services

    Put a service definition in install3 and its .run program in install2. Services are discovered after the system volume has been mounted; no C registration call is needed. See Services and Storage and Packages.

    Build and validate

    For a kernel change, a useful baseline is:

    make build-x86_64
make test-host

    build-x86_64 also produces the BIOS/UEFI ISO. test-host runs focused tests without booting a VM. For boot-time or command behavior, use make ci-test or make ci-interact; use the smallest applicable test first. See Build Targets and Testing.

    For syscall or user-program changes, build the relevant SDK program as well as the kernel. Keep the kernel and user SDK headers in sync: MOSdesk programs are built against this checkout's Minimal-OS-SDK headers.

    Generated files and cleanup

    Build outputs go under build/ and dist/; the ISO input tree is under targets/x86_64/iso. Package inputs in src/resources are source files and should be edited directly.

    Review the clean target before running it: it deletes every *.run file it finds under the repository, not only generated bundles. Preserve any .run files you need. See Build Targets.

    Keep local logs and generated images out of source changes unless they are intentional deliverables. Before handing off a change, inspect git status and git diff --check.

    easyui

    Buttons, sliders, text inputs, radio buttons and more for mosWM apps, in one header. Include easyui.h.

    easyui opens one window, keeps a list of widgets, draws them, and turns mouse and keyboard events into callbacks. Text is smooth, anti-aliased Inter drawn by the same OpenType renderer mosWM uses. Its colours follow the MOSdesk theme picked in Settings > Appearance, and they change while the app is running when the user picks another theme.

    Functionseasyui.initeasyui.runeasyui.updateeasyui.quiteasyui.settitleeasyui.widtheasyui.heighteasyui.windoweasyui.redraweasyui.setdarkmodeeasyui.setaccenteasyui.accenteasyui.themeeasyui.loadfonteasyui.setsmoothtexteasyui.smoothtexteasyui.createbuttoneasyui.createlabeleasyui.createslidereasyui.createcheckboxeasyui.createradioeasyui.createtoggleeasyui.createtextinputeasyui.createprogresseasyui.createdropdowneasyui.createlistboxeasyui.createpaneleasyui.createimageeasyui.createcanvaseasyui.createseparatoreasyui.removeeasyui.recallfunceasyui.currenteasyui.settexteasyui.gettexteasyui.setvalueeasyui.getvalueeasyui.setrangeeasyui.setstepeasyui.additemeasyui.clearitemseasyui.getitemeasyui.itemcounteasyui.setenabledeasyui.setvisibleeasyui.setpositioneasyui.setsizeeasyui.setanchoreasyui.setcoloreasyui.settextsizeeasyui.setaligneasyui.setstyleeasyui.setpasswordeasyui.setmaxlengtheasyui.setimageeasyui.setfocuseasyui.focusedeasyui.typeeasyui.getxeasyui.getyeasyui.getwidtheasyui.getheighteasyui.settimereasyui.stoptimereasyui.messageboxeasyui.pixelseasyui.fillrecteasyui.drawrecteasyui.fillroundrecteasyui.fillcircleeasyui.drawlineeasyui.drawtexteasyui.textwidtheasyui.drawpixelseasyui.addfonteasyui.setfonteasyui.setfontsizeeasyui.settextcoloreasyui.setbackgroundeasyui.setbordereasyui.setradiuseasyui.setpaddingeasyui.copystyleeasyui.drawtextfonteasyui.textwidthfonteasyui.setlookeasyui.lookeasyui.pickfileeasyui.savefileeasyui.pickfoldereasyui.pickedpatheasyui.mouse
    #include "easyui.h"

static int label1;

static void clicked(int value) {
    easyui.settext(label1, "Thanks!");
}

int main(void) {
    easyui.init("Hello", 320, 160);
    int button1 = easyui.createbutton(20, 20, 200, 40, "Click me!");
    label1 = easyui.createlabel(20, 80, 280, 24, "Nobody clicked yet");
    easyui.recallfunc(button1, ONCLICK, clicked);
    return easyui.run();
}

    Build it like any program (./build.sh hello.c), or open the Widgets (easyui) sample in Run Studio. examples/easyui-demo.c uses every widget.

    How it works

    • One object. Every function is called through easyui: easyui.createbutton(...), easyui.setvalue(...). It is a constant structure of function pointers, so it works the same from C and C++.
    • Widgets are ints. Each create... call returns a widget number (1 … 128), or 0 if there was no room. Keep it in an int and pass it to the other calls. Calls with an invalid widget do nothing.
    • Coordinates are pixels inside the window's content area: (0, 0) is the top-left corner below the title bar. Widgets are drawn in the order they were created, so create a panel before the widgets on it.
    • Callbacks take one int, the event's value (see Events). Register them with easyui.recallfunc. Inside a callback, easyui.current says which widget fired, so one function can serve several widgets.
    • The main loop is easyui.run. It handles events, runs timers, redraws only when something changed and sleeps between frames. Callbacks can change any widget; the window is repainted afterwards.
    • Memory. Widgets live in a fixed table (EASYUI_MAX_WIDGETS, 128). Widget text holds up to 127 bytes. List and dropdown items are copied to the heap and freed by clearitems and remove.

    Several source files

    The implementation is inside the header. In a program with more than one .c file, include easyui.h normally in one file, and in every other file write:

    #define EASYUI_NO_IMPLEMENTATION
#include "easyui.h"

    Events

    Pass one of these to recallfunc. The short names (ONCLICK) are macros for EASYUI_ONCLICK and friends; define EASYUI_NO_SHORT_NAMES before the include if they clash with your own names.

    EventWhenValue passed to the callback
    ONPRESSThe left mouse button goes down on the widget, or Space/Enter is pressed while it has focus1
    ONRELEASEThe button comes up again after an ONPRESS, wherever the pointer is0
    ONCLICKPressed and released on the same widget0
    ONCELike ONCLICK, but only the first time; the callback is then removed0
    ONCHANGEThe widget's value changed, by the user or by setvaluethe new value (see below)
    ONSUBMITEnter in a text input; Enter or a double-click in a list boxtext length, or the item index
    ONHOVERThe pointer moved onto the widget0
    ONLEAVEThe pointer moved off it0
    ONFOCUSIt got keyboard focus0
    ONBLURIt lost keyboard focus0
    ONKEYA key went down while it had focus (on EASYUI_WINDOW: any key)key | (modifiers << 8)
    ONDRAWCanvas only: draw your content now0
    ONFRAMEWindow only: once per frame, about 60 times a seconduptime in ms
    ONCLOSEWindow only: the close button was clicked0
    ONRESIZEWindow only: the window changed sizethe new width
    ONWHEELCanvas only: the mouse wheel turned over it1 up, -1 down

    ONCHANGE values by widget:

    WidgetValue
    Slider, progress barThe new value
    Checkbox, toggle1 checked / on, 0 not
    Radio button1 when it becomes selected, 0 when another in its group does
    Text inputThe text's new length (read the text with gettext)
    Dropdown, list boxIndex of the selected item

    Window events use EASYUI_WINDOW (0) as the widget:

    static void closing(int value) {
    easyui.messagebox("Not yet", "Save your work first.");   /* or easyui.quit() */
}
easyui.recallfunc(EASYUI_WINDOW, ONCLOSE, closing);

    Without an ONCLOSE callback, clicking the close button ends run().

    Keyboard

    Click a widget or press Tab (Shift+Tab backwards) to give it focus; a ring in the accent colour shows which one has it.

    WidgetKeys
    Button, checkbox, toggleSpace or Enter clicks it
    Radio buttonSpace selects; arrow keys move to the previous/next button of the same group and select it
    SliderArrows step by setstep (default 1); Home and End jump to the ends
    Text inputTyping, Backspace, Delete, Left, Right, Home, End; Enter submits; Escape leaves the field
    DropdownSpace or Enter opens it; Up and Down change the selection
    List boxUp and Down move the selection; Enter submits

    Key codes are USB HID usage codes. easyui.h defines the common ones: EASYUI_KEY_ENTER (40), _ESCAPE (41), _BACKSPACE (42), _TAB (43), _SPACE (44), _HOME (74), _DELETE (76), _END (77), _RIGHT (79), _LEFT (80), _DOWN (81), _UP (82). Letters are 4 (a) … 29 (z).

    Theme

    MOSdesk stores the chosen theme as an accent colour in 0:/programs/mosdesk/settings.dat. easyui reads it when the window opens and again twice a second, and repaints when it changes. Without MOSdesk (no settings file), the accent is MOSdesk's default blue, 0xFF3DAEE9.

    The other colours match mosWM: the light palette of its dialogs and the Settings app by default, or the dark palette of its menus and Files window after easyui.setdarkmode(1).

    ThemeAccent
    Blue0xFF59A6D8
    Teal0xFF48B8A5
    Copper0xFFD28C54
    Forest0xFF69A86A
    Rose0xFFD66B83
    Gold0xFFE1B64C

    Text

    easyui draws text the way mosWM does:

    • Smooth text (normal). easyui_text.h is a bundled copy of ttrend_outline, the anti-aliased OpenType/TrueType renderer mosWM uses (integer maths only, no libc). When the window opens, easyui loads the Inter fonts mosWM installs, 0:/programs/mosWM/assets/fonts/Inter-Regular.otf and Inter-Medium.otf. Text size 1 is 12 px Inter Regular; size 2 and up is 8 × size px Inter Medium, the same sizes mosWM uses for its own text. Text is proportional: wrapping, alignment and the text-input caret are measured with the real glyph widths.
    • Bitmap fallback. If neither font can be read (mosWM is not installed, or the files are missing), or after easyui.setsmoothtext(0), text uses the 8 × 8 bitmap font mosWM falls back to, scaled by the text size.
    • Your own font. easyui.loadfont loads any .otf or .ttf file instead.

    Run Studio's preview has the same Inter files at the same path, so smooth text looks the same there as on MOSdesk.

    include/easyui_text.h is generated from MOSdesk's mosdesk/libraries/ttrend_outline by tools/bundle-ttrend.py; do not edit it by hand.

    Styling widgets

    Every widget can have its own font, text size, text and background colour, border, corner radius and padding:

    int save = easyui.createbutton(20, 20, 160, 44, "Save");
easyui.setfont(save, EASYUI_FONT_MEDIUM);
easyui.setfontsize(save, 18);                 /* 18 px text */
easyui.setbackground(save, 0xFF2E7D32);       /* green; hover and pressed shades follow */
easyui.setradius(save, 12);
easyui.setborder(save, 0xFF1B5E20, 2);

    Pass EASYUI_WINDOW instead of a widget to set the default for every widget that has no setting of its own (setbackground(EASYUI_WINDOW, ...) colours the window itself):

    int mono = easyui.addfont("0:/programs/notes/Resources/Mono.ttf");
easyui.setfont(EASYUI_WINDOW, mono);          /* the whole app in Mono */
easyui.setfontsize(EASYUI_WINDOW, 14);

    A widget's own setting wins over the window's, which wins over the theme. 0 (colours, setfontsize) or -1 (setborder width, setradius, setpadding) goes back to the default. easyui.copystyle gives one widget another's whole style.

    CallButtonsLabelsText inputs, lists, dropdowns, panelsOthers
    setfont, setfontsizelabeltexttext and rowslabel text; canvases' drawtext
    settextcolorlabeltexttextlabel text
    setbackgroundfillbox behind the textfillbox behind (checkbox, radio, toggle, image, canvas); track (slider, progress)
    setborder, setradiusoutline, cornersoutline, cornersoutline, cornersoutline, corners
    setpaddingtext inset (8)text inset (0)text inset (8, rows 10)space before the box

    Looks: Modern and 2000s Aero

    When the user picks 2000s Aero under Settings > Appearance > Window style, easyui windows follow it: grey glass push buttons that turn light blue on hover, Windows 7 style check boxes, radio buttons, sunken text fields, a green progress bar, blue list selections and a white message box over a grey button strip. Like the accent colour, it changes while the app runs. easyui.setlook fixes one look for an app.

    File and folder pickers

    easyui.pickfile, easyui.savefile and easyui.pickfolder open a dialog over the window, in the current look: Home, its Documents, Pictures and Desktop folders and System on the left; Home, System and Up buttons and the current folder on top; the folder's contents in the middle (folders first); a name field and Cancel / Open (Save, Select) at the bottom. They return at once; the callback runs when the user is done, with 1 for a choice and 0 for Cancel or Escape, and easyui.pickedpath gives the path.

    static void opened(int chosen) {
    if (chosen) load_document(easyui.pickedpath());
}
easyui.pickfile("Open a note", 0, "txt;md", opened);
    Keys
    Up, DownMove the selection
    EnterOpen the selected folder, or choose (same as the main button)
    BackspaceUp one folder (in the save dialog: edit the name)
    EscapeCancel
    Double-clickOpen a folder, or choose a file

    While a picker is up the window's widgets ignore input; timers and ONFRAME keep running. One picker at a time.

    Limits

    LimitValue
    WidgetsEASYUI_MAX_WIDGETS (128)
    Fonts from addfontEASYUI_MAX_FONTS (8)
    Picker pathsEASYUI_PATH_MAX - 1 (255) bytes; 256 entries per folder
    Widget textEASYUI_TEXT_MAX - 1 (127) bytes
    TimersEASYUI_MAX_TIMERS (8)
    WindowsOne per program
    TextInter via the OpenType renderer (8 × 8 bitmap fallback); ASCII from the keyboard. No kerning or right-to-left text

    easyui.init

    int easyui.init(const char* title, int width, int height);

    Opens the app's window and loads the MOSdesk theme. Call it before creating any widget.

    ParameterDescription
    titleTitle bar text (63 bytes at most)
    width, heightContent size in pixels, at least 64 × 48

    Returns 1, or 0 if the window could not be created (no window manager running, or out of memory). Calling it again does nothing and returns 1.

    Example

    if (!easyui.init("Notes", 480, 320)) {
    mos_puts("Start MOSdesk first\n");
    return 1;
}

    easyui.run

    int easyui.run(void);

    Runs the app until the window is closed or easyui.quit is called, then closes the window.

    Returns 0, so return easyui.run(); ends main with exit code 0.

    Notes Each frame handles all pending window events, polls the theme, runs due timers, fires ONFRAME, repaints if anything changed and sleeps 16 ms.

    easyui.update

    int easyui.update(void);

    One frame of easyui.run without the sleep, for programs with their own loop.

    Returns 1 while the app should keep running, 0 once it is closing.

    Example

    while (easyui.update()) {
    simulate_step();
    mos_sleep(10);
}

    easyui.quit

    void easyui.quit(void);

    Makes run() return (and update() return 0) after the current frame.

    easyui.settitle

    void easyui.settitle(const char* title);

    Changes the window's title.

    easyui.width

    int easyui.width(void);

    Returns the current content width. It changes when the user resizes the window.

    easyui.height

    int easyui.height(void);

    Returns the current content height.

    easyui.window

    uint32_t easyui.window(void);

    Returns the mosWM window ID, for calls from window.h such as mos_window_set_flags.

    Example

    mos_window_set_resizable(easyui.window(), false);   /* fixed-size window */

    easyui.redraw

    void easyui.redraw(void);

    Asks for a repaint on the next frame. Only needed after changing something easyui cannot see, such as the pixels behind an image widget or the state a canvas draws.

    easyui.setdarkmode

    void easyui.setdarkmode(int on);

    Switches between the light palette (default) and the dark one. The accent colour is unchanged.

    Example

    easyui.recallfunc(dark_toggle, ONCHANGE, easyui.setdarkmode);

    easyui.setaccent

    void easyui.setaccent(uint32_t argb);

    Uses argb as the accent colour instead of MOSdesk's. Pass 0 to follow MOSdesk again.

    easyui.accent

    uint32_t easyui.accent(void);

    Returns the accent colour in use, as 0xFFRRGGBB. Use it to draw your own content in the theme colour.

    easyui.theme

    const easyui_theme_t* easyui.theme(void);

    Returns every colour easyui is using. The structure is read-only.

    FieldUsed for
    backgroundWindow content
    surfaceText inputs, lists, panels, slider knobs
    borderOutlines and separators
    text, mutedNormal text; placeholders and panel titles
    button, button_hover, button_pressedSecondary buttons and dropdowns
    accent, accent_hover, accent_pressed, accent_textPrimary buttons, selection, focus rings; text on accent
    trackSlider, progress and toggle tracks
    disabled, disabled_textDisabled widgets
    dangerEASYUI_DANGER buttons

    Example

    easyui.fillrect(x, y, w, h, easyui.theme()->surface);

    easyui.loadfont

    int easyui.loadfont(const char* path, int bold);

    Loads an OpenType (.otf, CFF outlines) or TrueType (.ttf) font file and uses it for every widget.

    ParameterDescription
    pathFont file, for example a resource of your app: "0:/programs/myapp/Resources/Font.ttf"
    bold0 for size-1 text, 1 for size 2 and larger. Load the same file into both to use one face everywhere

    Returns 1, or 0 if the file could not be read or is not a font the renderer understands (CID-keyed CFF, variable or colour fonts). The font already loaded stays in use when it fails.

    Notes Call it after init, which has already loaded Inter. The file is read into the heap and kept for the life of the program.

    Example

    if (!easyui.loadfont("0:/programs/notes/Resources/Mono.ttf", 0))
    mos_puts("using Inter\n");

    easyui.setsmoothtext

    void easyui.setsmoothtext(int on);

    0 draws every text with the 8 × 8 bitmap font even when a font is loaded (for a retro look, or pixel-exact layouts); 1 (the default) goes back to smooth text.

    easyui.smoothtext

    int easyui.smoothtext(void);

    Returns 1 if text is being drawn with an outline font, 0 if it is using the bitmap fallback.

    Example

    if (!easyui.smoothtext()) easyui.settext(status, "Install mosWM for nicer text");

    easyui.createbutton

    int easyui.createbutton(int x, int y, int w, int h, const char* text);

    A push button. By default it is filled with the accent colour; see easyui.setstyle for the other styles.

    ParameterDescription
    x, y, w, hBounds
    textLabel, centred; wraps onto several lines if it is too wide

    Returns the widget, or 0.

    Events ONPRESS, ONRELEASE, ONCLICK, ONCE, ONHOVER, ONLEAVE, ONFOCUS, ONBLUR, ONKEY.

    Example

    int save = easyui.createbutton(20, 20, 120, 36, "Save");
easyui.recallfunc(save, ONCLICK, save_file);

    easyui.createlabel

    int easyui.createlabel(int x, int y, int w, int h, const char* text);

    Text. It wraps at word boundaries to fit w, and \n starts a new line; the block is centred vertically in h. Change it with settext, its colour with setcolor, its size with settextsize and its alignment with setalign.

    Returns the widget, or 0.

    Notes Labels get ONCLICK too, which makes them usable as links.

    easyui.createslider

    int easyui.createslider(int x, int y, int w, int h, int min, int max, int value);

    A slider. It is horizontal, or vertical when h is greater than w (the top is max).

    ParameterDescription
    min, maxRange
    valueStarting value, clamped to the range

    Returns the widget, or 0.

    Events ONCHANGE with the new value whenever it moves (dragging, clicking the track, the mouse wheel, arrow keys or setvalue), plus ONPRESS / ONRELEASE around a drag.

    Example

    static void volume_changed(int value) { set_volume(value); }

int vol = easyui.createslider(20, 60, 200, 24, 0, 100, 50);
easyui.recallfunc(vol, ONCHANGE, volume_changed);
easyui.setstep(vol, 5);   /* arrow keys and wheel move by 5 */

    easyui.createcheckbox

    int easyui.createcheckbox(int x, int y, int w, int h, const char* text, int checked);

    A checkbox with a label to its right. Clicking anywhere on the widget toggles it.

    Returns the widget, or 0. Read the state with getvalue (1 or 0).

    Events ONCHANGE (1 / 0), ONCLICK.

    easyui.createradio

    int easyui.createradio(int x, int y, int w, int h, const char* text, int group);

    A radio button. Radio buttons with the same group number exclude each other: selecting one clears the others. The first one created in a group starts selected.

    ParameterDescription
    groupAny number you choose; one per set of choices

    Returns the widget, or 0.

    Events ONCHANGE with 1 on the button that became selected and 0 on the one that was cleared.

    Example

    static int small, medium, large;

static void size_picked(int selected) {
    if (!selected) return;                  /* ignore the one being cleared */
    int w = easyui.current();
    set_size(w == small ? 1 : w == medium ? 2 : 3);
}

small  = easyui.createradio(20, 20, 120, 24, "Small", 1);
medium = easyui.createradio(20, 48, 120, 24, "Medium", 1);
large  = easyui.createradio(20, 76, 120, 24, "Large", 1);
easyui.recallfunc(small, ONCHANGE, size_picked);
easyui.recallfunc(medium, ONCHANGE, size_picked);
easyui.recallfunc(large, ONCHANGE, size_picked);

    easyui.createtoggle

    int easyui.createtoggle(int x, int y, int w, int h, const char* text, int on);

    An on/off switch with a label. Behaves like a checkbox.

    Returns the widget, or 0.

    Events ONCHANGE (1 / 0), ONCLICK.

    easyui.createtextinput

    int easyui.createtextinput(int x, int y, int w, int h, const char* placeholder);

    A one-line text field. placeholder is shown in grey while the field is empty and not focused.

    Returns the widget, or 0.

    Events ONCHANGE after every edit (value: the new length), ONSUBMIT when Enter is pressed (value: the length), ONFOCUS, ONBLUR, ONKEY.

    Notes

    • Typing uses a US keyboard layout. Text is limited to 127 bytes, or less with easyui.setmaxlength.
    • easyui.setpassword shows * instead of the characters.
    • Read the text with gettext, change it with settext.

    Example

    static int search;

static void run_search(int length) {
    if (length) find(easyui.gettext(search));
}

search = easyui.createtextinput(20, 20, 260, 32, "Search");
easyui.recallfunc(search, ONSUBMIT, run_search);

    easyui.createprogress

    int easyui.createprogress(int x, int y, int w, int h, int max);

    A progress bar from 0 to max. Set it with setvalue; change the range with setrange.

    Returns the widget, or 0.

    Example

    int bar = easyui.createprogress(20, 20, 300, 10, total_files);
...
easyui.setvalue(bar, files_done);

    easyui.createdropdown

    int easyui.createdropdown(int x, int y, int w, int h);

    A drop-down list. Add choices with additem. Until one is selected it shows its text ("Choose..."; change it with settext). Clicking opens a list of up to 8 rows below it (above, if there is no room), which scrolls with the wheel.

    Returns the widget, or 0. getvalue is the selected index (-1 for none) and gettext the selected item's text.

    Events ONCHANGE with the selected index.

    Example

    int lang = easyui.createdropdown(20, 20, 200, 30);
easyui.additem(lang, "English");
easyui.additem(lang, "Svenska");
easyui.setvalue(lang, 0);
easyui.recallfunc(lang, ONCHANGE, language_changed);

    easyui.createlistbox

    int easyui.createlistbox(int x, int y, int w, int h);

    A scrolling list. Add rows with additem. Clicking a row selects it; the wheel scrolls.

    Returns the widget, or 0. getvalue is the selected index (-1 for none).

    Events ONCHANGE with the selected index, ONSUBMIT with the index on a double-click or Enter.

    Example

    static int files;

static void open_file(int index) { open(easyui.getitem(files, index)); }

files = easyui.createlistbox(20, 20, 240, 200);
for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) easyui.additem(files, entries[i].name);
easyui.recallfunc(files, ONSUBMIT, open_file);

    easyui.createpanel

    int easyui.createpanel(int x, int y, int w, int h, const char* title);

    A rounded box with an optional title in its top-left corner, for grouping widgets. Create it before the widgets that sit on it. setcolor changes its fill.

    Returns the widget, or 0.

    easyui.createimage

    int easyui.createimage(int x, int y, int w, int h, const uint32_t* pixels,
                       int image_w, int image_h);

    Shows an ARGB8888 image, scaled to w × h. Pixels with alpha below 255 are blended.

    ParameterDescription
    pixelsimage_w × image_h pixels, row by row. Not copied: keep the buffer alive while the widget exists
    image_w, image_hImage size

    Returns the widget, or 0.

    Notes After changing the pixels, call easyui.redraw(). Images get ONCLICK, ONPRESS and the hover events.

    easyui.createcanvas

    int easyui.createcanvas(int x, int y, int w, int h);

    An area you draw yourself. Its ONDRAW callback runs whenever the window is repainted, with drawing clipped to the canvas. Use the drawing calls below, in window coordinates.

    Returns the widget, or 0.

    Example

    static int chart;

static void draw_chart(int value) {
    int x = easyui.getx(chart), y = easyui.gety(chart), h = easyui.getheight(chart);
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++)
        easyui.fillrect(x + i * 20, y + h - data[i], 16, data[i], easyui.accent());
}

chart = easyui.createcanvas(20, 20, 200, 120);
easyui.recallfunc(chart, ONDRAW, draw_chart);

    easyui.createseparator

    int easyui.createseparator(int x, int y, int w);

    A one-pixel horizontal line in the border colour.

    Returns the widget, or 0.

    easyui.remove

    void easyui.remove(int widget);

    Deletes a widget and frees its items. Its number may be reused by the next create... call.

    easyui.recallfunc

    int easyui.recallfunc(int widget, int event, easyui_callback fn);

    Sets the function called when event happens on widget. Each widget has one callback per event; registering again replaces it.

    ParameterDescription
    widgetA widget, or EASYUI_WINDOW (0) for window events
    eventOne of the events
    fnvoid fn(int value), or NULL to remove the callback

    Returns 1, or 0 for an unknown widget or event.

    Example

    static void pressed(int v)  { easyui.settext(status, "Holding..."); }
static void released(int v) { easyui.settext(status, "Let go"); }

int button1 = easyui.createbutton(0, 0, 200, 100, "Click me!");
easyui.recallfunc(button1, ONPRESS, pressed);
easyui.recallfunc(button1, ONRELEASE, released);

    easyui.current

    int easyui.current(void);

    Returns the widget whose callback is running (0 for window events and timers).

    Example

    static void digit(int v) { append(easyui.gettext(easyui.current())); }

for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    char t[2] = { (char)('0' + i), 0 };
    easyui.recallfunc(easyui.createbutton(20 + i * 44, 20, 40, 40, t), ONCLICK, digit);
}

    easyui.settext

    void easyui.settext(int widget, const char* text);

    Changes the text of a button, label, checkbox, radio button, toggle, text input (the cursor moves to the end), panel title or the dropdown's "nothing selected" text. Longer text is cut at 127 bytes. Does not fire ONCHANGE.

    easyui.gettext

    const char* easyui.gettext(int widget);

    Returns the widget's text; for a dropdown or list box, the selected item's text. The pointer stays valid until the text changes. An invalid widget returns "".

    easyui.setvalue

    void easyui.setvalue(int widget, int value);

    Sets the value: a slider or progress bar position (clamped to the range), a checkbox or toggle (0 / 1), a radio button (1 selects it), or the selected index of a dropdown or list box (-1 for none). Fires ONCHANGE if the value changed.

    easyui.getvalue

    int easyui.getvalue(int widget);

    Returns the value described under setvalue.

    easyui.setrange

    void easyui.setrange(int widget, int min, int max);

    Changes a slider's or progress bar's range and clamps its value into it.

    easyui.setstep

    void easyui.setstep(int widget, int step);

    How far a slider moves per arrow key or wheel notch, and what dragging snaps to. Default 1.

    easyui.additem

    int easyui.additem(int widget, const char* text);

    Adds a row to a dropdown or list box. The text is copied.

    Returns the new item's index, or -1 if memory ran out.

    easyui.clearitems

    void easyui.clearitems(int widget);

    Removes every item and clears the selection (to -1).

    easyui.getitem

    const char* easyui.getitem(int widget, int index);

    Returns an item's text, or "" for an index out of range.

    easyui.itemcount

    int easyui.itemcount(int widget);

    Returns the number of items.

    easyui.setenabled

    void easyui.setenabled(int widget, int enabled);

    Disables (0) or enables (1) a widget. A disabled widget is drawn grey, cannot get focus and ignores clicks and keys.

    easyui.setvisible

    void easyui.setvisible(int widget, int visible);

    Hides (0) or shows (1) a widget. Hidden widgets get no events.

    Example

    /* simple tabs: show one page's widgets at a time */
for (int i = 0; i < page1_count; i++) easyui.setvisible(page1[i], tab == 0);

    easyui.setposition

    void easyui.setposition(int widget, int x, int y);

    Moves a widget.

    easyui.setsize

    void easyui.setsize(int widget, int width, int height);

    Resizes a widget.

    easyui.setanchor

    void easyui.setanchor(int widget, uint32_t anchors);

    Says which window edges the widget keeps its distance to when the window is resized. The default is EASYUI_ANCHOR_LEFT | EASYUI_ANCHOR_TOP: it stays put.

    AnchorsEffect when the window grows
    RIGHTMoves right with the right edge
    LEFT | RIGHTStretches horizontally
    BOTTOMMoves down with the bottom edge
    TOP | BOTTOMStretches vertically

    (Each name is prefixed with EASYUI_ANCHOR_.) The distances are measured when setanchor is called.

    Example

    int ok = easyui.createbutton(easyui.width() - 110, easyui.height() - 46, 90, 32, "OK");
easyui.setanchor(ok, EASYUI_ANCHOR_RIGHT | EASYUI_ANCHOR_BOTTOM);   /* stays in the corner */

    easyui.setcolor

    void easyui.setcolor(int widget, uint32_t argb);

    Gives one widget its own colour: the accent of a button, slider, checkbox, radio, toggle, progress bar, list or dropdown; the text colour of a label; the fill of a panel. Pass 0 to go back to the theme.

    easyui.settextsize

    void easyui.settextsize(int widget, int size);

    Text size, 1 … 8. With smooth text, size 1 is 12 px Inter Regular and size n (2 and up) is 8 × n px Inter Medium, as in mosWM. With the bitmap font, each size is 8 × n pixels tall. Checkbox, radio and toggle boxes and list rows grow with it.

    Example

    int title = easyui.createlabel(20, 10, 300, 30, "Settings");
easyui.settextsize(title, 2);

    easyui.setalign

    void easyui.setalign(int widget, int align);

    EASYUI_ALIGN_LEFT, EASYUI_ALIGN_CENTER or EASYUI_ALIGN_RIGHT, for labels and buttons. Buttons are centred by default, labels left-aligned.

    easyui.setstyle

    void easyui.setstyle(int widget, int style);

    A button's look:

    StyleLook
    EASYUI_PRIMARYFilled with the accent colour (default)
    EASYUI_SECONDARYGrey, like mosWM's Cancel buttons
    EASYUI_DANGERRed, for destructive actions
    EASYUI_FLATNo background until hovered; accent-coloured text

    Example

    easyui.setstyle(cancel, EASYUI_SECONDARY);
easyui.setstyle(delete_button, EASYUI_DANGER);

    easyui.setpassword

    void easyui.setpassword(int widget, int hidden);

    Shows a text input's characters as * when hidden is 1.

    easyui.setmaxlength

    void easyui.setmaxlength(int widget, int length);

    The most characters a text input accepts, at most 127.

    easyui.setimage

    void easyui.setimage(int widget, const uint32_t* pixels, int image_w, int image_h);

    Changes an image widget's pixels.

    easyui.setfocus

    void easyui.setfocus(int widget);

    Gives a widget keyboard focus (0 removes focus). Useful to put the cursor in a text input when the window opens.

    easyui.focused

    int easyui.focused(void);

    Returns the widget with keyboard focus, or 0.

    easyui.type

    int easyui.type(int widget);

    Returns the kind of widget: EASYUI_BUTTON, EASYUI_LABEL, EASYUI_SLIDER, EASYUI_CHECKBOX, EASYUI_RADIO, EASYUI_TOGGLE, EASYUI_TEXTINPUT, EASYUI_PROGRESS, EASYUI_DROPDOWN, EASYUI_LISTBOX, EASYUI_PANEL, EASYUI_IMAGE, EASYUI_CANVAS, EASYUI_SEPARATOR, or EASYUI_NONE for an invalid one.

    easyui.getx

    int easyui.getx(int widget);

    Returns the widget's left edge. gety, getwidth and getheight return the rest of its bounds, which change when anchors move it.

    easyui.gety

    int easyui.gety(int widget);

    Returns the widget's top edge.

    easyui.getwidth

    int easyui.getwidth(int widget);

    Returns the widget's width.

    easyui.getheight

    int easyui.getheight(int widget);

    Returns the widget's height.

    easyui.settimer

    int easyui.settimer(int interval_ms, easyui_callback fn);

    Calls fn every interval_ms milliseconds while run() (or update()) is running. The value passed is the timer number.

    Returns a timer number (1 … 8), or 0 if all timers are in use.

    Notes Timers run between frames, so their resolution is about 16 ms. To run something once, stop the timer in its own callback.

    Example

    static int clock_label;

static void tick(int timer) {
    char t[16];
    format_time(t, mos_uptime() / 1000);
    easyui.settext(clock_label, t);
}

easyui.settimer(1000, tick);

    easyui.stoptimer

    void easyui.stoptimer(int timer);

    Stops a timer from settimer.

    Example

    static void once_later(int timer) {
    easyui.stoptimer(timer);
    easyui.settext(status, "Ready");
}
easyui.settimer(2000, once_later);

    easyui.messagebox

    void easyui.messagebox(const char* title, const char* text);

    Shows a message over the window with an OK button. It returns at once; while the message is up, the window's widgets ignore input. OK, Enter, Space or Escape closes it.

    ParameterDescription
    titleHeading, up to 63 bytes
    textMessage, up to 255 bytes, word-wrapped

    easyui.pixels

    uint32_t* easyui.pixels(void);

    Returns the window's ARGB8888 pixel buffer, easyui.width() pixels per row. easyui repaints it completely each time something changes, so draw from a canvas's ONDRAW rather than writing here directly.

    easyui.fillrect

    void easyui.fillrect(int x, int y, int w, int h, uint32_t argb);

    Fills a rectangle. Colours with alpha below 255 are blended. Like all the drawing calls, it is clipped to the window (and to the canvas inside ONDRAW).

    easyui.drawrect

    void easyui.drawrect(int x, int y, int w, int h, uint32_t argb);

    Draws a one-pixel rectangle outline.

    easyui.fillroundrect

    void easyui.fillroundrect(int x, int y, int w, int h, int radius, uint32_t argb);

    Fills a rectangle with rounded corners.

    easyui.fillcircle

    void easyui.fillcircle(int cx, int cy, int radius, uint32_t argb);

    Fills a circle centred on (cx, cy).

    easyui.drawline

    void easyui.drawline(int x1, int y1, int x2, int y2, uint32_t argb);

    Draws a one-pixel line.

    easyui.drawtext

    void easyui.drawtext(int x, int y, const char* text, uint32_t argb, int size);

    Draws text with its top-left corner at (x, y), in the same font as the widgets (blended onto what is underneath). \n starts a new line one line height lower.

    easyui.textwidth

    int easyui.textwidth(const char* text, int size);

    Returns the width in pixels of the longest line of text at size.

    Example

    int w = easyui.textwidth(msg, 1);
easyui.drawtext(x + (cw - w) / 2, y + 10, msg, easyui.theme()->text, 1);

    easyui.drawpixels

    void easyui.drawpixels(int x, int y, const uint32_t* pixels, int w, int h);

    Copies a w × h ARGB8888 image with its top-left at (x, y), blending pixels that are not opaque.

    easyui.addfont

    int easyui.addfont(const char* path);

    Loads another OpenType (.otf) or TrueType (.ttf) font for easyui.setfont, next to the Inter fonts.

    Returns the font's number (EASYUI_FONT_CUSTOM and up), or 0 if the file could not be read or used, or 8 fonts are already loaded.

    easyui.setfont

    void easyui.setfont(int widget, int font);

    The font a widget's text is drawn in:

    Font
    EASYUI_FONT_DEFAULTBy text size: Inter Regular at size 1, Inter Medium above (the default)
    EASYUI_FONT_REGULARInter Regular
    EASYUI_FONT_MEDIUMInter Medium, for bolder text
    EASYUI_FONT_BITMAPThe 8 × 8 bitmap font
    a number from addfontThat font

    EASYUI_WINDOW sets the font of every widget that has none of its own.

    easyui.setfontsize

    void easyui.setfontsize(int widget, int pixels);

    Text height in pixels, 6 … 128, for any size between the steps of settextsize. Whichever of the two was called last applies; 0 goes back to the text size. With the bitmap font the size is rounded down to a multiple of 8 (at least 8). Check, radio and toggle boxes and list rows grow with it.

    easyui.settextcolor

    void easyui.settextcolor(int widget, uint32_t argb);

    The colour of a widget's text (a button's label, a label's text, a text input's characters ...). 0 goes back to the theme. Disabled widgets keep the theme's disabled colour.

    easyui.setbackground

    void easyui.setbackground(int widget, uint32_t argb);

    A widget's fill (see the table in Styling widgets). Buttons derive their hover and pressed shades from it and pick black or white text to suit. On EASYUI_WINDOW it is the window's background. 0 goes back to the theme.

    easyui.setborder

    void easyui.setborder(int widget, uint32_t argb, int width);

    Draws an outline width pixels thick (at most 16) along the widget's edge, following its corner radius. Width 0 means no outline; -1 goes back to the widget's own look. A colour of 0 uses the theme's border colour.

    easyui.setradius

    void easyui.setradius(int widget, int radius);

    Corner radius in pixels of the widget's box (buttons, text inputs, lists, panels, progress bars, dropdowns, and the background or border of the others). -1 goes back to the default.

    easyui.setpadding

    void easyui.setpadding(int widget, int pixels);

    Space between a widget's edge and its text. -1 goes back to the default.

    easyui.copystyle

    void easyui.copystyle(int to, int from);

    Gives widget to the font, sizes, colours, border, radius, padding, alignment and button style of from.

    Example

    int ok = easyui.createbutton(20, 20, 100, 36, "OK");
easyui.setfontsize(ok, 16);
easyui.setradius(ok, 18);
int cancel = easyui.createbutton(130, 20, 100, 36, "Cancel");
easyui.copystyle(cancel, ok);
easyui.setstyle(cancel, EASYUI_SECONDARY);

    easyui.drawtextfont

    void easyui.drawtextfont(int x, int y, const char* text, uint32_t argb, int font, int pixels);

    Like easyui.drawtext, in a given font (EASYUI_FONT_... or a number from addfont) and pixel size. For canvases.

    easyui.textwidthfont

    int easyui.textwidthfont(const char* text, int font, int pixels);

    Returns the width of text in that font and size.

    easyui.setlook

    void easyui.setlook(int look);

    EASYUI_LOOK_AUTO (the default) follows MOSdesk's window style; EASYUI_LOOK_MODERN or EASYUI_LOOK_AERO keeps one look whatever the user picks.

    easyui.look

    int easyui.look(void);

    Returns the look in use: EASYUI_LOOK_MODERN or EASYUI_LOOK_AERO.

    easyui.pickfile

    int easyui.pickfile(const char* title, const char* folder, const char* extensions,
                    easyui_callback done);

    Asks the user for a file to open.

    ParameterDescription
    titleDialog title, or NULL for "Open a file"
    folderFolder to start in, or NULL for the user's home
    extensionsFiles to offer, separated by ; ("txt;md"), or NULL for all
    donevoid done(int chosen): 1 with a file, 0 if cancelled

    Returns 1, or 0 if a picker is already open or there is no window.

    easyui.savefile

    int easyui.savefile(const char* title, const char* folder, const char* name,
                    easyui_callback done);

    Asks where to save, with name (or NULL) already typed in. Clicking a file takes its name. The chosen path may be an existing file; ask before replacing it if that matters.

    easyui.pickfolder

    int easyui.pickfolder(const char* title, const char* folder, easyui_callback done);

    Asks for a folder. Select chooses the folder selected in the list, or the one shown when none is.

    easyui.pickedpath

    const char* easyui.pickedpath(void);

    Returns the full path from the last picker ("0:/users/ann/notes.txt"), or "" after Cancel.

    easyui.mouse

    void easyui.mouse(int* x, int* y, int* buttons);

    The pointer in window coordinates (-1, -1 when it is outside the window) and its buttons (bit 0 = left). Any argument may be NULL. Useful in a canvas's ONPRESS or ONFRAME to see where a click landed or to follow a drag.

    Edit this page on GitHub

    Farcade Engine (working name): a high-performance game engine for Minimal-OS

    > How to read this plan. *Overview* says what is being built and the four decisions. *Where things stand* is the current state. *Architecture* is the layer diagram. *Roadmap* has the milestones, a short list of small fixes to do first, and every milestone cut into small steps. Parts A, B and C give the detail for the OS track, the SDK/toolchain track and the engine. *Risks*, *Verification* and *After approval* close the plan. Step IDs (H1, OS-6.1, S1.2, E0.3 ...) are used in the roadmap. A step is meant to be about one pull request.

    On this pageOverview: goals and decisionsWhere things standArchitectureRoadmap: milestones and small stepsPart A: OS track (Minimal-OS)Part B: SDK track and the native toolchain (the "Minimal-OS port of Minimal-OS-SDK")Part C: The engine (new repository)Main risks and mitigationsVerificationAfter approval

    Overview: goals and decisions

    Goals

    Farcade Engine:

    • It compiles and exports games to Minimal-OS and includes a Minimal-OS port of the SDK.
    • Its editor is easy to use but capable.
    • Gameplay code can be Lua and C++, mixed in one project.
    • It has modern graphics: CLOD virtual geometry with voxels as the far representation (no impostors), a screen-space + voxel hybrid GI (no ray tracing), and far-away proxies that carry no instance data.
    • It is fast.

    Decisions

    1. The editor and toolchain run on Minimal-OS only. Game makers never need a PC. The engine developer (you) still builds the engine and editor on the PC (WSL/Docker) and tests them in QEMU.
    2. All rendering goes through FarcadeGL. It already falls back between the kernel's CPU backend and the NVIDIA Turing backend, so speed work goes into FGPU itself.
    3. Scripting is Lua 5.4.
    4. Kernel and SDK changes run as a parallel OS track.

    ---

    Where things stand

    Minimal-OS today (the facts that shape this plan)

    Updated after OS-0 to OS-5 (see the status list under Part A). Everything in the "Today" column has only run in QEMU, not on real hardware.

    AreaTodayWhat it means for the engine
    3DFGPU (SYS_GPU 40) runs in the kernel, with one context per program and one render lock. The CPU backend has a tile-binning rasterizer, an x86 shader JIT (SSE4.1 and AVX2) and asynchronous submits with fences. Read-only shader storage buffers (4 slots, vec4 loads) were added on 2026-11-16. Scissor, 2D mips with trilinear filtering and 16 texture units were added on 2026-11-17 (ABI 4; the NVIDIA backend does the scissor, mips and units above 4 still run on the CPU backend). It still has no MRT, compute, writable SSBOs, instancing or integer formats (OS-6 and OS-7).The CPU backend *is* the renderer on QEMU, Intel and AMD. The engine can use scissor and mips now; MRT waits for OS-6.
    NVIDIATuring GSP-RM, the copy engine and 3D clears work on an RTX 2060. The first draw failed with Xid 69 (a pitch-linear color target next to a depth buffer) and NVDEC with RM error 0x1F (no engine context); both are fixed in code (block-linear color copies; falcon context promote, 2026-11-17) but not yet rerun on the card.A bonus path, not a dependency.
    CPUAVX and AVX2 work (XSAVE state saving, OS-2; AVX-512 untested). A program's threads run on all cores (OS-3), with affinity and priority calls. One intermittent kernel crash in the thread tests is still open.The job system can use every core. AVX2 code paths are picked by hand at startup (no ifunc).
    MemoryPrograms live above 4 GiB with SYS_VM (map, unmap, protect, decommit; demand-zero pages, NX, guard pages). ELF files up to 256 MiB are streamed in, the main stack is 8 MiB (configurable), and the page pool is sized from RAM, including RAM above 4 GiB. The SDK's own malloc is still one syscall per call.The engine's allocator sits on SYS_VM. GCC on the OS has the address space it needs.
    RuntimeTLS, futex, clocks, spawn/wait and the environment exist (OS-0). The SDK's C library is still tiny: no libm, STL or operator new. Static PIE with RELATIVE relocations only (so no ifunc).Until mlibc is ported, the engine carries a small C/C++ runtime of its own (runtime/minimalos in the engine repo).
    On-OS toolsNothing compiles or interprets on the OS except the FGSL compiler and Mxplorer's JS.The native toolchain is on the critical path.
    Display/input/audioFull-screen present is one copy straight to the framebuffer, scaled 1x to 3x and paced by a timer (no vsync). Programs and the window manager can share window frames (OS-5), but mosWM's use of them is untested. Only the USB HID boot keyboard and mouse work: no hubs or gamepads. 8 PCM16 kernel-mixed streams.The editor runs full screen and as a window under MOSdesk (copy path for now). Gamepads are on the OS track (OS-8).
    FilesMinimaFS: 32-bit offsets, no modification times. stat, rename, chdir and / paths exist (OS-0). File reads are synchronous.Content-hash builds; pak parts of at most 2 GiB; streaming reads on their own thread.
    LicenceOS, SDK, MOSdesk and the engine repository are GPLv3. farcadegl.h, fglsl.h and crt0.c get compiled into every game.Decide before release: relicense the runtime files (MIT, or GPL plus a linking exception).

    Architecture

     Game project (Lua 5.4 scripts + optional C++ module + assets)
 ┌────────────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────────┐
 │ Editor (runs on MOSdesk)       │   │ Player runtime (.run)        │
 │ Dear ImGui on FarcadeGL        │   │ static: libfe.a + game code  │
 └───────────────┬────────────────┘   └───────────────┬──────────────┘
 Engine runtime libfe.a: core · jobs · flecs ECS · assets/paks · gfx (feature levels)
                 · vgeo/voxel/proxy · GI · Jolt · ozz · audio mixer · Lua · RmlUi
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Minimal-OS SDK: mlibc + libstdc++ · FarcadeGL v3 + FGSL v2 · msdk (native)
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Kernel: FGPU (CPU backend v2: binning + x86 JIT | NVIDIA Turing backend)
         threads/futex/TLS · mmap/NX · XSAVE/AVX · spawn/wait · shared surfaces

    The work runs in three tracks:

    • OS track: the Minimal-OS repo.
    • SDK track: the Minimal-OS-SDK repo, plus the native toolchain.
    • Engine track: the new repo.

    Part A: OS track (Minimal-OS)

    Status (merged into main through PR #13; it was branch claude/os0-process-basics-bq26wb):

    • OS-0 done. TLS, futex, clocks, stat/rename/chdir, spawn/wait, environment.
    • OS-1 done. Program memory above 4 GiB with demand-zero pages (SYS_VM), NX, guard pages, a streaming ELF loader, 8 MiB stacks, a page pool sized from RAM, and RAM above 4 GiB used for program pages.
    • OS-2 done, AVX-512 untested. XSAVE-based state saving, AVX/AVX2 usable, noavx flag, CPU features in SYSINFO. QEMU's emulation has no AVX-512, so that path has never run.
    • OS-3 done, QEMU only. Threads of one program run on different CPUs by default (threads1cpu pins them as before; smpthreads forces it on). It includes: - TLB shootdown IPIs, with a per-space mask of the CPUs that have the space loaded; - a reschedule IPI so idle cores start work at once; - thread placement and migration like processes; - affinity and priority in SYS_THREAD (thread.h: mos_thread_set_affinity/priority, mos_cpu_count); - a group exit/crash that stops threads running on other CPUs; - an audit of the shared state (docs/boot-and-kernel.md, Processes And Threads).

    Thread entry points outside the image were already allowed in OS-1. Tested at -smp 1/2/4/8 in TCG only; real SMP hardware (including TSC and APIC timing) has not been tried. - Known bug (open, not diagnosed): an intermittent kernel crash (a jump to address 3 with an empty kernel stack, then the CPU idles) right after os0test's smp_priority checks, around joining a low-priority thread. Seen twice in about ten runs (once on 1 CPU, once on 2, the second before the OS-4/OS-5 changes); reruns of the same build pass.

    • OS-4 done, QEMU only. - Rasterizer: tile binning, hierarchical Z and a small-triangle path (default; fgpuold selects the previous one). - Shader JIT (fgpu_jit_x64.c): SSE4.1 and AVX2 code, checked against the interpreter by a fuzzer (nojit turns it off). - Per-program GPU contexts: objects shared by a program's threads, grown tables with O(1) handles and quotas of 1024/4096/1024, and a per-program lock plus one render lock instead of g_busy. - Asynchronous submit with fences (ABI 3: FGPU_SUBMIT_ASYNC, SYS_GPU_WAIT), run by the fgpu-worker kernel process. - Preemptible smp-par helper processes instead of IPI handlers (smpparipi brings the IPI helpers back). - Measured on one 2.1 GHz core: about 8 M small triangles/s (C4.7 target 30 M/s) and 7 G lane-instructions/s at best (target 16 G). The engine targets a real GPU, so these targets are no longer pursued. Fused rasterizer/shader kernels and SIMD texture sampling were dropped from OS-4 and remain possible later work.
    • OS-5 mostly done, QEMU only. - Scaled present (1x/2x/3x, nearest) straight into the framebuffer with non-temporal stores: one copy instead of two (FGPU_PRESENT_SCALE2/3). - Frame pacing per program on the monotonic clock (FGPU_PRESENT_PACED, SYS_GPU_SET_PACE; the adapters here have no vblank). - Window frames shared between a program and the window manager (reference-counted shared memory in user VM, SYS_WINDOW_MAP_FRAME, PRESENT_SHARED with damage rectangles, TAKE_DAMAGE). FGPU presents into a window's shared back buffer. - Left: mosWM compositing from the mapped frames is on MOSdesk main (commit 7b3bf89, marked untested) but has not been run on a desktop, so the Minimal-OS submodule still pins the older copy-path mosWM (19ee8b0). The 1.5 ms present budget is unmeasured on real hardware.
    • System-call pointer checks done (not in the original plan): every user pointer is checked before use; what is left is listed in docs/syscall-pointers.md.
    • Everything was tested in QEMU without KVM (make ci-os0); nothing has run on real hardware yet.
    • The SDK half is merged into Minimal-OS-SDK main (4eb00ba). The Minimal-OS submodule now pins 584f118, which is ahead of main (see Repository status).
