    Part B: SDK track and the native toolchain (the "Minimal-OS port of Minimal-OS-SDK")

    1. S1 mlibc port (MIT; built for hobby OSes). Its sysdeps sit on OS-0/OS-1: tcb_set, futex_wait/wake, anon_allocate/free, vm_map, clock_get, open/read/write/seek/close/stat, spawn/wait and exit, with / ↔ 0:/ translation. It produces libc.a, libm.a and pthreads. mlibc beats newlib or the 846-line Doom shim because GCC on the OS needs POSIX spawn, stat and threads.
    2. S2 GCC target x86_64-minimalos (GCC 15.1 + binutils 2.45, the versions build_gccbinutils.sh already uses): - an entry in config.gcc; - gcc/config/minimalos.h: LINK_SPEC -static-pie -z max-page-size=0x1000, a built-in __minimalos__ define, and gthr-posix through mlibc; - libgcc t-files, plus a binutils alias to elf_x86_64; - libstdc++ with --disable-shared; - a CMake toolchain file for the engine developer's PC build.

    GCC is the only compiler, on both the PC and the OS.

    1. S3 msdk rewritten in C (keeping today's name and CLI from MOSdesk/msdk and build.sh). It builds C/C++, incrementally by content hash (xxh3 over the -MD dependency list plus flags, since MinimaFS has no mtime), and makes MINIRUN1 .run, .slib, .mpkg and Deliver packages (replacing mkrun.sh/runbundle.py). It runs on the PC and on the OS. Old freestanding programs keep building with msdk --freestanding; hosted mode uses mlibc.
    2. S4 Canadian cross: binutils, GCC, cc1plus and libstdc++ *hosted on* Minimal-OS: - Configure flags: --disable-lto --disable-plugin --without-isl --disable-nls --disable-multilib --enable-languages=c,c++ --enable-threads=posix, with GMP, MPFR and MPC static. libiberty's pex goes through posix_spawn, with no -pipe. - It ships as an msdk-native package installed to 0:/sdk/, built in CI. - Needs OS-0 and OS-1 (big ELFs, stacks, spawn/wait), and a VM with 4–8 GiB of RAM.
    3. S5 FarcadeGL v3 + FGSL v2 in the SDK, with docs (follows OS-6/OS-7).

    Part C: The engine (new repository)

    C1. Repository layout

    Current state: the repo builds with a Makefile and one mk/*.mk fragment per part (no CMake yet). It has engine/{core,ecs,gfx,script,physics,scene,audio,mof}, editor/, runtime/minimalos/, tools/, tests/ and external/ (imgui, imguizmo, stb, cgltf, fast_obj, flecs, lua, dr_libs, the FGPU copy and the SDK submodule). engine/mof is a .mof model format with glTF and OBJ importers, which the layout below does not list. engine/core has only the math code so far.

    Target layout:

    farcade-engine/
  cmake/toolchains/minimalos-x86_64.cmake   # developer's PC build; headless-host.cmake for CI
  external/      lua-5.4, flecs, meshoptimizer, MaskedOcclusionCulling, JoltPhysics, ozz-animation,
                 recastnavigation, imgui(docking), ImGuizmo, imnodes, implot, textedit(fork), RmlUi,
                 cgltf, fast_obj, ufbx, stb, dr_libs, zstd, lz4, xxhash, msdfgen, doctest
  engine/core/       memory, jobs, simd math, containers, strings, log, profiler, reflection, serialize, vfs/pak
  engine/platform/   minimalos/ (window, input, audio, time, threads, fs, net), headless/ (CI)
  engine/ecs/        flecs integration, scene, prefabs, transform hierarchy, world cells
  engine/gfx/        FarcadeGL layer, feature levels, pass list, resource pools, upload rings
  engine/render/     vgeo/ voxel/ proxy/ gi/ shadows/ post/ materials/ debug/
  engine/assets/     importers, cooker, derived-data cache (DDC), paks
  engine/script/     Lua runtime, bindings, scheduler, debugger
  engine/{physics,anim,audio,ui,nav,module}/
  editor/            app, panels, gizmos, material graph, code editor, build/export, Lua debugger
  player/            feplayer runtime (also runs Lua-only games without a compiler)
  shaders/           FGSL sources per feature level
  templates/         empty, first-person, third-person, top-down
  tests/             unit, golden image diffs, perf scenes

    C2. Language and core

    • C++20 (GCC 15) subset: -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti, no template-heavy libraries in public headers. Game code includes only a light fe.h/fe.hpp (target under 3k lines; no STL-heavy, flecs, Jolt or RmlUi headers), so C++ compiles quickly *on* the OS. The engine ships prebuilt as libfe.a.
    • SIMD: in-house wrapper types. The baseline is SSE4.1 (x86-64-v2); AVX2 paths are dispatched by hand at startup (no ifunc, since the loader only handles RELATIVE relocations).
    • Memory: - Today: carve 64 MiB SYS_HEAP chunks into size-class pools, per-frame linear allocators and per-thread caches. - After OS-1: back it with mmap reserve/commit. - Every library gets allocator hooks: Lua's lua_Alloc, Jolt and flecs.
    • Jobs: a work-stealing job graph with one worker per core (falls back to a single thread until OS-3). Frames are pipelined: simulation of frame N+1 overlaps rendering of frame N.
    • Reflection: X-macro descriptors FE_REFLECT(T, (field, type)...), so no libclang is needed and it works with GCC on the OS. It drives the inspector, serialization, the Lua bindings, editor autocomplete and hot-reload snapshots.
    • Profiler: its own rdtsc ring buffer per thread with an editor timeline (Tracy is dropped: it needs threads and networking first).
    • Large worlds: 64-bit world positions (cell + float offset), rendered relative to the camera.

    C3. ECS, scene, world

    • flecs v4 (MIT, C99), used through its C API inside the engine. Its meta addon is filled from engine reflection, and its os_api hooks run on engine jobs. Components from Lua and C++ live in one world.
    • Started (farcade-engine engine/ecs): - flecs v4.1.6 behind fe::World, with its own single-threaded os_api; it runs in QEMU. - Components: modules (Rigidbody 3D, Collider 3D, listener, audio stream and sampler, light) and scene-object settings (camera, sky, sky light, post processing), with flecs meta filled from the same field tables as the editor. - The transform hierarchy runs as a system, and the "one current camera/sky/listener" rule is enforced in the world. - The editor's Play runs the scene as a world.
    • Scenes are text for editing (diff-friendly) and cooked to binary. Prefabs use flecs prefabs.
    • A world-partition grid of 32 m streaming cells feeds the proxy hierarchy (C4.6).

    C4. Rendering (FarcadeGL only)

    C4.1 The gfx layer and feature levels

    Started (farcade-engine engine/gfx):

    • An FL0-style forward renderer on farcadegl.h: up to 8 lights, hemisphere ambient, a gradient sky with a sun, and post processing folded into the shaders. It renders offscreen and reads the frames back for the editor viewport.
    • On the PC it runs on a host copy of the FGPU CPU backend (external/fgpu). In QEMU its smoke test gives the same checksum as the host.
    • A GPU tier (Settings > Graphics) adds a sun shadow map with PCF, point and spot light shadows from a shadow atlas, GGX PBR, SSAO, bloom, FXAA and fog. It is on by default only when FGPU runs on a graphics card (FGPU_CAP_HW_3D) and can be forced on the CPU backend. Its QEMU smoke test also matches the host checksum.
    • On the CPU backend the editor redraws only what changed. While the view moves it renders the viewport at a lower resolution with draft shaders, then refines in bands. In QEMU TCG a FarcadeGL orbit went from 3.4 s to about 0.2 s per frame.
    • Mesh objects have a material in the editor's Inspector: roughness, metal, unlit and shadows. Roughness, metal and shadows show in the GPU tier only.
    • Not started: CLOD, voxels, GI and the rest of C4.
    • The host FGPU copy is pinned to Minimal-OS a00577e, so it lacks later kernel changes (read-only SSBOs). Update it when the kernel changes.

    gfx is a thin layer over FarcadeGL:

    • Resources are pooled and sub-allocated from FGPU buffers of at most 16 MiB until OS-6 lifts the limit, within handle budgets.
    • Uploads go through rings of 2–3 buffers, and passes are an ordered list.
    • FGSL is compiled at cook time and cached in paks.
    • The feature level is picked from fglGetDeviceInfo caps, and the same game runs on all three:
    LevelNeedsPipeline
    FL0Today's FGPU v2 + scissor + more texture units + additive blendForward shading. DAG cut and Masked Occlusion Culling (Intel, SSE4.1/AVX2) run on the CPU and build a compacted index buffer each frame. Packed 20-byte vertices. 2 cached shadow cascades. Voxel far LOD as greedy-meshed quads. CPU GI into a probe atlas.
    FL1OS-6 (FGPU v3 graphics + FGSL v2)Visibility buffer (R32UI + depth), Nanite-style material resolve (material-ID depth, one full-screen quad per material with depth EQUAL), TAA at internal resolution with scaled present, full hybrid GI, SSR, GTAO, ray-marched voxel bricks.
    FL2OS-7 (compute, SSBOs, 64-bit atomics)GPU-driven culling and LOD, compute micro-triangle raster and voxel splatting into a 64-bit visibility buffer, compute GI, cached virtual shadow maps. Stretch goal.

    Rule for the CPU path: every pass runs at *internal* resolution (for example 960×540 for 1080p output) and is upscaled at present.

    C4.2 Virtual geometry (CLOD)

    • Offline DAG build with meshoptimizer ≥0.23 (MIT): meshopt_buildMeshlets, meshopt_partitionClusters, and meshopt_simplifyWithAttributes with vertex_lock on group borders and absolute errors. Its cluster-LOD demo is the starting reference.
    • Clusters and groups: clusters hold up to 128 triangles and 64 vertices (7-bit local indices). Groups target 8 clusters (allowed 4–16) and are simplified to 50%, then split again. Errors are monotonic: a parent's error is ≥ its children's, and its LOD sphere encloses theirs.
    • Runtime cut: err_px = err · k / max(d_nearest, near) with k = 0.5·h / tan(fov/2). A cluster is drawn when its parent's projected error is above τ and its own is not. Each cluster decides independently, so the cut runs as parallel jobs. τ = 2 px (FL0), 1–1.25 px (FL1 with TAA), 1 px (FL2).
    • Culling: an 8-wide BVH over groups (culled by maximum parent error), then frustum and normal-cone tests, then two-pass occlusion. Masked Occlusion Culling runs at 640×360, using last frame's cut at 4τ plus proxies as occluders.
    • Streaming: - Page format: 64 KiB pages (about 30–40 clusters). Positions are quantized on a mesh-wide power-of-two grid so border vertices match and cracks can't appear. - Normals are octahedral and UVs quantized per cluster. - On disk: a delta/byte-plane transform plus zstd. - The top 2–3 levels and the voxel roots always stay resident. - Pools are 256 MB on the desktop and 64 MB in the VM, prioritized by projected error, with I/O on a worker thread. - At FL0/FL1, pages decode to float vertex pools; FL2 decodes in the shader from SSBOs.

    C4.3 Voxels as the far representation (no impostors)

    • Switch rule, at build time: DAG level L and everything coarser become voxels when any of these holds: - triangle reduction stalls below 1.4×; - voxels reach error ≤ e_tri(L) in fewer bytes than triangles; - the geometry is thin or aggregate (foliage, fences): a high area/volume ratio or many connected components.

    The first voxel edge is set to ≥ e_tri(L), so the error stays monotonic.

    • Bricks: 8³ with a 512-bit occupancy mask, plus 8 bytes per occupied voxel: albedo RGB8 + coverage, octahedral normal 8:8, roughness and metal 4:4, and opacity per axis. Parents are built by 2×2×2 coverage-weighted downsampling, with normal variance folded into roughness (Toksvig).
    • Rendering per level: - FL0: greedy-meshed quads, switched at a projected voxel edge of ≤2.5 px with 10% hysteresis. - FL1: a ray march through each brick's bounding box (3D texture plus gl_FragDepth) at ≤1.25 px, with a 15% dithered cross-fade that TAA resolves. - FL2: compute splatting with stochastic coverage at ≤1 px.
    • The same per-mesh bricks feed the GI voxel scene (C4.5), so they are built once.

    C4.4 Far proxies without instance data

    For distant rings, each world cell has a baked proxy: one merged voxel/cluster CLOD of all its static instances. No per-instance transforms, bounds or culling data are loaded or processed. Ring k starts at d_k = 2·cell_k, with finest error e_k = d_k·τ/k:

    RingCellStarts atFinest error (τ = 1.5 px, h = 540)
    L032 m streaming cells with real instances0per asset
    L1128 m proxy256 m≈1.0 m
    L2512 m1 km≈3.9 m
    L32 km4 km≈16 m
    L48 km16 km≈62 m
    • Bake pipeline (incremental by a hash of each cell's contents, run as editor background jobs): 1. Assign static instances to cells; instances larger than half a cell move up a level. 2. Flatten each instance's cut at e/2 into world space. 3. Voxelize conservatively with 4³ supersampled coverage. 4. Keep triangles only where they win (large flat surfaces). 5. Build L(k+1) by merging 4×4 cells of Lk and downsampling 2×2×2.
    • Drawing: one draw per cell, which suits FL0. The working set scales with pixels, not with world area (about 1.5 M voxels, around 12 MB; pool 48–64 MB).
    • Dynamic objects never go into proxies.

    C4.5 Hybrid GI: screen space + voxels (no ray tracing)

    • The voxel scene is a camera-centred clipmap built by instancing cooked per-mesh bricks. - Size: 4 levels of 64³ on the desktop, 3 in the VM; base voxel 0.5 m; coverage 32/64/128/256 m. - Scrolling is toroidal in 8-voxel slabs, and dynamic objects are re-splatted at 10 Hz. - Storage: a sparse table of surface voxels at 10 B each (albedo, normal, flags, R11G11B10 radiance) plus 64-bit occupancy masks per 4³ brick.
    • Light injection (amortized over 1/4 of surface voxels per frame; 1/8 in the VM): - sun: CSM in range, beyond it a hierarchical voxel shadow ray of at most 64 steps; - up to 8 local lights and emissives; - albedo × last frame's irradiance, which gives multi-bounce lighting one frame late.
    • FL0 (CPU jobs, about 8 core-ms): - Probes: 3 levels of 24×12×24 L1-SH probes at 1/4/16 m spacing, 32 rays per update, 1/16 of probes updated per frame, hysteresis 0.93. - Probes are moved out of geometry and invalidated on back-face hits, which limits leaks. - The probe atlas is uploaded as ARGB8 textures and sampled with a manual slice lerp (4 taps). - Specular comes from probe SH plus an octahedral sky atlas with 5 roughness bands.
    • FL1 (about 8 core-ms in the kernel + 4 in userland): - The clipmap goes to the GPU as 4×64³ RGBA16F 3D textures (8 MiB), with at most 2 MB of dirty-brick uploads per frame. - Screen probes every 32 px on the CPU backend (16 px on NVIDIA), 32 rays each in 8×4 octahedral texels. Each ray marches in screen space over depth mips first (at most 16 steps), then continues in the voxel clipmap (at most 32 steps, level chosen by cone width), then falls back to sky or probes. - Denoising: temporal α = 0.1 with reprojection and depth/normal rejection, a 3×3 probe filter weighted by hit distance, then integration into L1 SH. Interpolation runs at half resolution with a joint-bilateral upsample. - Specular: SSR (half resolution, roughness < 0.45), then a voxel cone, then probes and sky. - GTAO at half resolution (2 slices × 6 steps) for short-range occlusion only.
    • Shadows: 3 cached CSM cascades (1024²) plus voxel sun shadow beyond 128 m. Virtual shadow maps come at FL2.
    • Post: TAA + temporal upscaling, dynamic resolution to hold the frame target, bloom, auto exposure, AgX tonemapping, and FXAA at FL0 (which has no TAA).

    C4.6 Materials

    • A node graph in the editor (imnodes) plus hand-written FGSL. Both generate per-level FGSL: a forward variant (FL0), a material-resolve variant (FL1) and a compute variant (FL2).
    • The model is PBR metallic-roughness with layered inputs.
    • The kernel compiles FGSL bytecode to x86 (OS-4 JIT) or to SASS, so there is one material path for CPU and GPU.

    C4.7 Performance contract

    > Status (open decision): OS-4 measured about 8 M small triangles/s and 7 G lane-instructions/s on one 2.1 GHz core, and the CPU-backend targets are no longer pursued (the engine targets a real GPU). The tables below stay as the reference for what the CPU path would need. The FL1/FL2 frame budgets and the E5/E7 exit criteria assume that speed, so either re-baseline them against measured numbers or treat them as real-GPU goals (NVIDIA path, OS-7).

    What the kernel CPU backend must reach (OS-4), per core, AVX2 at about 4 GHz (the SSE4.1 JIT reaches about 0.6× of this):

    StageTarget
    Per-draw overhead≤1.5 µs (one parallel phase per pass)
    Vertex shading (25 instructions)≥40 M vertices/s
    Clip, cull, set up and bin≥25 M triangles/s
    Depth-tested pixels (large triangles, hierarchical Z)≥1.5 G px/s
    Small triangles (≤2×2 px)≥30 M triangles/s
    Fragment shader arithmetic≥16 G lane-instructions/s (today about 0.1–0.2; fglcube --shader takes 42 ms)
    ARGB8 bilinear sampling≥300 M samples/s (stochastic sampling ≥1 G/s)
    Present at 1080p including 2× upscale≤1.5 ms

    Frame budgets (the core-ms are a starting point, to be checked with the benchmarks):

    • 8-core AVX2 desktop, FL1, 960×540 → 1080p at 60 fps (133 core-ms available): - kernel about 63: geometry 15, visibility buffer 6, resolve + light 18, GI 8, SSR/GTAO 4, TAA/post 9, UI/present 2.5; - userland about 39: simulation, physics, animation and Lua 20; cut + occlusion 5; GI upkeep 8; commands, streaming and audio 6; - ≈77% use.
    • 2-core QEMU+KVM, FL0/FL1-low, 640×360 → 720p at 30 fps: ≈53 of 66 core-ms.
    • FL0 on today's kernel, before OS-4: demo quality only (about 10–20 fps at 640×480 for small scenes).

    C4.8 Streaming: maps, objects and textures

    One streaming system serves all three. It reads only cooked paks (never .mof or source files), on its own I/O thread with decode jobs, and nothing in it blocks a frame. Each pool has a fixed memory budget; what is loaded is decided by priority, and the lowest priority is evicted first.

    • Maps (the world): - The world is cut into 32 m cells (C3). A cell holds its entity list (instances, lights, script references), collision and a navigation tile. - Cells load in a ring around the camera, widened in the direction of travel, with hysteresis so a player on a border does not make cells flap. States: unloaded, loading, active, asleep. - Things that must always exist (the player, game rules, the sky) live in an always-loaded layer. - Beyond the loaded ring the cell proxies of C4.4 are drawn, so an unloaded cell never disappears from view.
    • Objects: - Every asset has a small record that is always in memory (bounds, material ids, its coarsest LOD or voxel root) and a payload that streams: CLOD pages (C4.2), voxel bricks (C4.3), collision meshes, animation clips, audio. - Pages are requested by projected error, so detail arrives where it is visible. The top levels stay resident, so there is always something to draw.
    • Textures: - The cooker writes each texture as a mip chain: a small resident tail (64x64 and below, stored with the material) plus one chunk per larger mip. - What to load comes from the texel density on screen: computed on the CPU per cluster or instance at FL0, read from a feedback pass at FL1 and up. - FL0 (today's GPU interface: no mips): a texture streams in whole steps. Its surface is rebuilt at the next size (64, 256, 1024) and swapped when the upload is done. - FL1 (OS-6: mips and trilinear): mips stream one at a time, with the lowest loaded mip clamped and faded in. - FL2 (stretch): virtual textures with sparse pages.
    • Budgets (starting values): geometry 256 MB on a desktop and 64 MB in a VM (C4.2); textures 512 MB and 96 MB; cell data 64 MB and 16 MB.
    • Pak layout for streaming: chunks aligned to 64 KiB, each compressed on its own (zstd, LZ4 for the hot path), with neighbours in the world stored next to each other so one read brings several.
    • In the editor: a streaming overlay (what is loaded, queued and evicted, per pool), and a "keep loaded" flag per asset.
    • What it needs from the OS: threads on all cores (done), file reads that do not hold up other threads (a dedicated I/O thread is enough today), mips (OS-6), and later faster storage paths (OS-8).
    • When: the pak reader and the asynchronous loader come with E1. Map and object streaming come with E5, FL0 texture steps with E5, and per-mip streaming with E7.

    C5. Scripting: Lua 5.4 and C++ in one project

    • How mixing works: both languages register into the same flecs world, through the same reflection. - C++ components: struct Health { float hp, max; }; FE_REFLECT(Health, (hp,f32), (max,f32));. They appear automatically in Lua (e:get(Health).hp) and in the inspector. - Lua components: fe.component("Velocity", { x="f32", y="f32", z="f32" }). C++ reads them by name through a dynamic view, or through a generated typed header. - Systems in either language: Lua fe.system("Move", {Position, Velocity}, fn), C++ FE_SYSTEM(Move, Position&, const Velocity&), ordered in one pipeline. - Calls across: Lua calls C++ functions exported with FE_FUNCTION, C++ calls Lua with fe::lua::call("player.on_hit", ...), and both share one event bus. - Easy mode: a Script component with on_start/on_update/on_event callbacks (Unity/Godot style). Capable mode: plain ECS systems. - Scripts on objects (editor side done in farcade-engine, see its docs/scripting.md): - An object holds several scripts, run in Inspector order. - Each script declares inputs in -- @prop comments, which the editor reads without Lua. Types: number (optionally with a range), text, toggle, list, object link. - Scripts on different objects reach each other through object links: self.door:script("door"), obj:send(event, ...), fe.broadcast. - Started (farcade-engine engine/script): - Lua 5.4.7 runs scripts in Play: one sandboxed instance per script, inputs in self, object handles, module fields through the ECS (including camera.current), events and physics callbacks. - Errors are logged with file:line and a traceback. - Generational GC. - It runs in QEMU, with its own setjmp/longjmp for the OS runtime. - Not yet: the C++ game module, hot reload, the debugger, and time limits for runaway scripts.
    • Fast Lua 5.4: - Generational GC stepped within about 0.5 ms per frame, and an engine allocator through lua_Alloc. - Entities as light userdata (the 64-bit flecs id, generation checked on use, no allocation). Multi-return accessors (x,y,z = fe.pos(e)). - Batch column APIs (struct-of-arrays tables, refilled and reused). - Stripped precompiled bytecode in paks, tagged with the engine build hash. API functions cached in locals. - Pooled coroutines for sequences and AI (wait(t), wait_event). - One VM on the game thread, a sandboxed _ENV per script, pcall with tracebacks into the editor console.
    • Bindings: the stack API, generated from the reflection data (no sol2). Component get/set is data-driven, and function trampolines use shallow templates.
    • Lua hot reload: swap the function tables and keep the state tables. The debugger uses lua_sethook (only while breakpoints are set): breakpoints, stepping, locals and upvalues, and a REPL. A count-hook sampling profiler covers scripts.
    • C++ game module: - Built as ET_DYN with -fPIC -shared -nostdlib, with one entry point fe_game_entry(const fe_api_v1*) and every engine call going through that function table. - The engine's own ELF loader (about 1k lines) handles RELATIVE/64/GLOB_DAT/JUMP_SLOT relocations. Modules use no TLS, and new/malloc are routed through the API. - Hot reload keeps state with a reflection-driven ECS snapshot and restore. - Exported games link statically into one .run.
    • C++ debugging on the OS: crash handler with stack traces (frame pointers + ELF symbols), asserts sent to the editor, serial log. The engine developer gets QEMU's gdbstub. A gdbserver-lite over TCP is a later stretch goal.

    C6. Other systems and libraries

    Started: a built-in physics step (engine/physics) stands in for Jolt until the engine can meet Jolt's C++ standard library needs. It covers gravity, box, sphere, capsule, cylinder and convex-hull mesh colliders (GJK/EPA, contact manifolds of up to 4 points, sequential impulses with warm starting), rotation from contacts, friction, bounciness, layers, triggers and an upright-capsule character controller. Concave triangle meshes are not done.

    Vendored so far (external/VERSIONS.md): Dear ImGui (docking), ImGuizmo, stb, cgltf, fast_obj, flecs 4.1.6, Lua 5.4.7, dr_libs and the FGPU copy. The other libraries in the table are not added yet.

    Every library here must build with GCC against mlibc, and the heavy ones live only inside libfe.a.

    C7. Editor (runs on Minimal-OS)

    Started (farcade-engine editor/):

    • The shell, panels, gizmos and Play exist and are drawn by a software rasterizer (SwRenderer, the fallback described below), not yet through FarcadeGL with scissor. On Minimal-OS the editor runs full screen, and as a resizable "Farcade Editor" window under MOSdesk (changed regions go through mos_window_present; F11 toggles borderless fullscreen).
    • Scenes save and open as text .fscene files. Module fields are written by name from the reflection tables, so older files load. The commands are File > Save scene (Ctrl+S), Save scene as, and double-click in Files.
    • In QEMU, farcade-editor --scene-test saves, overwrites and reopens the demo scene. This needed a fix to the editor's MinimaFS file writer: create a .part file, write it with SYS_FWRITE, then rename it over the target.
    • Undo and redo (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y) keep whole-scene snapshots, taken when an edit settles; a drag counts as one step.
    • New scene, Open and Quit ask before unsaved changes are lost.
    • Scripts read and write the material through obj.material.
    • Prefabs, the material graph and autosave are not started.
    • Shell: - Dear ImGui docking in a mosWM window (or full screen). It is drawn through FarcadeGL with scissor and a 6-float vertex layout in ring buffers. - Fallback until scissor lands: a userland 2D rasterizer (fast quads and glyphs) blitted with SYS_WINDOW. - It redraws only on input or animation, which is critical on a CPU-rendered OS. - The viewport is an FGPU surface shown as an ImGui texture. - The theme matches MOSdesk (Modern/Aero) with Inter text.
    • Panels: - Scene hierarchy; inspector generated from reflection; viewports with gizmos, snapping and a grid. - Asset browser with thumbnails rendered by the engine; material graph. - Code editor (Lua/C++ with error markers from parsed GCC file:line:col output and luaL_loadbuffer checks while typing). - Build and console panels; profiler timeline; Lua debugger; SDK docs viewer (the existing markdown docs); project settings; export dialog.
    • Ease of use: project templates, one-click Play (instant for Lua; C++ does an incremental build + hot reload), undo/redo, prefabs, drag and drop, a Ctrl+P command palette, autocomplete from the reflection database, and automatic LOD/voxel/proxy builds with no manual bake steps.
    • Getting assets onto the OS: - "Import from URL" over HTTP/HTTPS (SYS_NET + minimaSSL), or Deliver (dlr) packages. - .mpkg boot modules. - tools/minimafs-explorer/mfs-explorer.py (writes files into a disk image from the PC). - A FAT32 disk, and later USB mass storage (OS-8).
    • Background work: cooking into a derived-data cache 0:/projects/<name>/.cache/, keyed by content hash. Autosave.

    C8. Project format, build and export

    MyGame/
  project.fe      name, version, minimum feature level, entry scene, modules
  assets/         meshes, textures, audio, *.fmat materials, *.fscene scenes, prefabs
  scripts/*.lua
  src/*.cpp *.h   (optional C++ module)
  .cache/  build/

    Export (in the editor, or msdk export):

    1. Cook assets: CLOD pages, voxel bricks, cell proxies, FGSL bytecode, Lua bytecode, textures, audio.
    2. Write .fepak files (zstd, parts of at most 2 GiB, 64-bit index).
    3. Choose the binary: - Lua-only: use the prebuilt feplayer runtime. No compiler needed. - C++: the native msdk compiles the module and statically links libfe.a + liblua.a into main.elf, then wraps it in a MINIRUN1 .run.
    4. Package the .run + paks as an .mpkg / Deliver package. It installs to 0:/programs/<Game>.run + 0:/games/<Game>/, with a MOSdesk icon (from Resources/icon.bmp).
    5. "Run standalone" spawns the exported game as its own process.

    The runtime. There is one engine runtime, libfe (renderer, ECS, physics, audio, Lua, streaming). It is not installed separately on the player's machine: every exported game carries it inside its own .run. A Lua-only game is the prebuilt player (feplayer, which is libfe plus a main) next to the game's paks; a game with C++ code is linked with libfe.a into its own binary. The editor links the same library, which is what "Play" runs.

    ---

    Main risks and mitigations

    1. The kernel CPU backend is the renderer's single point of failure. Mitigation: the contract in C4.7, performance tests built on tests/host/fgpu_raster_tests.c, and keeping the backend free of kernel dependencies so it could also run in-process.
    2. The JIT runs in ring 0. Mitigation: generate code only from checked IR, allow memory access only through helpers that clamp bounds, differential fuzzing against the interpreter, and a boot flag that falls back to the interpreter.
    3. The native toolchain is on the critical path (cc1plus size, stack, RAM, spawn). Mitigation: ship Lua-only games first, keep OS-0/OS-1 small, pin GCC/binutils versions, build the Canadian cross in CI.
    4. Multicore races and XSAVE corruption in the kernel. Mitigation: multicore threads opt-in at first, stress tests at -smp 8, YMM torture tests, a noavx flag.
    5. System-wide FGPU handle limits and the 16 MiB buffer cap. Mitigation: pooled sub-allocation now, per-process quotas in v3.
    6. Editor latency (4 copies per frame through mosWM). Mitigation: redraw only on change, damage rectangles, OS-5 shared surfaces.
    7. GPLv3 SDK headers compiled into every game. Mitigation: relicense the SDK runtime files before release.
    8. Scope. Mitigation: strict tiers, FL0-first, stretch goals labelled.
    9. The open intermittent kernel crash in the thread tests (OS-3). E5 and E6 depend on multicore threads. Mitigation: diagnose it before building on OS-3, and keep threads1cpu as the fallback.
    10. Version drift between repos. The SDK branch pinned by Minimal-OS and Farcade-Engine is ahead of SDK main, and the engine's FGPU copy is behind the kernel. Mitigation: merge the SSBO branch, and refresh external/fgpu whenever the kernel's FGPU changes.

    Verification

    • Headless host CI (Linux): - doctest unit tests for core, math, ECS and the Lua bindings. - DAG invariants: monotonic errors, crack-free borders. - Voxelizer and proxy baker checked against reference output and for determinism. - FGPU JIT checked against the interpreter by differential fuzzing; the existing make test-host pattern extends to new IR/raster tests.
    • Golden images: fixed camera paths per feature level, rendered in QEMU and read back with fglReadPixels, then compared with tolerances. CPU and NVIDIA backends must match the same goldens.
    • Performance CI: the Sponza, Bistro-style and foliage-field scenes on fixed paths, with frame times logged per pass against the C4.7 budgets (desktop under KVM with -cpu host -smp 8, plus a 2-core profile).
    • Self-hosting test on the OS: the editor creates a template project, builds the C++ module with native GCC, hot-reloads it, exports a .run, and runs it as a separate process.
    • Real hardware: an 8-core AVX2 desktop for the CPU path; an RTX 2060 for the NVIDIA path (gpu nvidia self-tests).

    After approval

    The plan is saved as docs/farcade-engine-plan.md in Minimal-OS. The engine repository (fsminecrafter/Farcade-Engine) now exists and points to it; the plan can move there when you choose. OS-0 to OS-5 are done and E1 and E3 have started. Still open: the rest of E0 (allocator, jobs, profiler, reflection, VFS/pak), the toolchain (E2), the OS-3 crash and the SDK branch merge.

    PreviouseasyuiNextFarcadeGL (farcadegl.h)

    Edit this page on GitHub

    FarcadeGL (farcadegl.h)

    FarcadeGL is the 3D library of Minimal-OS. It sits on the kernel's FGPU interface (SYS_GPU, described in fgpu_abi.h) and borrows from both OpenGL and Vulkan:

    On this pageHow it runsA first programContextsBuffers and vertex layoutsState and drawingBuilt-in programsShadersTexturesBlendingMathErrors and limitsPerformanceFunction referenceThe FGPU interface underneath
    • Like Vulkan, drawing is recorded into a command buffer and sent to the GPU in one call (fglSubmit / fglPresent). GPU memory is explicit: you create and destroy buffers, textures and shaders.
    • Like OpenGL, state is a handful of simple calls (fglEnable, fglUseShader, fglSetModel ...), matrices are column-major, and shaders are written in a GLSL-style language, FGSL (fgsl.md).

    It is header only: include farcadegl.h and build with ./build.sh.

    Contents:

    1. How it runs
    2. A first program
    3. Contexts
    4. Buffers and vertex layouts
    5. State and drawing
    6. Built-in programs
    7. Shaders
    8. Textures
    9. Blending
    10. Math
    11. Errors and limits
    12. Performance
    13. Function reference
    14. The FGPU interface underneath

    Examples: programs/fglcube (shipped as 0:/programs/fglcube.run; run fglcube --shader for the shader version) and MOSdesk's *Cube* app (press S for the shader).

    How it runs

    The kernel executes command buffers through its FGPU command processor, on one of two backends:

    • The graphics card (NVIDIA RTX 20 / GTX 16, after gpu nvidia boot passed its draw test): shaders are translated to the card's machine code when you create them, and clears and draws run on its 3D engine. Surfaces, textures and buffers live in video memory. This path is new and has not been confirmed on a card yet; see docs/gpu.md in Minimal-OS.
    • The CPU (everything else, and the fallback): vertex stage, clipping, perspective-correct rasterization, depth test, fragment stage and blending in software, on every core.

    Programs do not choose: the same calls and the same shader bytecode run on both. A shader the card's compiler does not take yet (one that reads gl_FrontFacing) is drawn by the CPU.

    The kernel reports the active adapter and available caps through fglGetDeviceInfo(). If you want to auto-detect the 3D path in user code, check info.caps & FGPU_CAP_HW_3D, or use the convenience helpers fglHasHardware3D() and fglHasShaders() from farcadegl.h.

    A first program

    #include "farcadegl.h"
#include "window.h"

static const char* vs =
    "uniform mat4 fgl_ModelViewProjection;\n"
    "attribute vec3 position;\n"
    "attribute vec4 color;\n"
    "varying vec4 v_color;\n"
    "void main() {\n"
    "    v_color = color;\n"
    "    gl_Position = fgl_ModelViewProjection * vec4(position, 1.0);\n"
    "}\n";

static const char* fs =
    "uniform float time;\n"
    "varying vec4 v_color;\n"
    "void main() {\n"
    "    float pulse = 0.75 + 0.25 * sin(time * 4.0);\n"
    "    gl_FragColor = vec4(v_color.rgb * pulse, 1.0);\n"
    "}\n";

int main(void) {
    uint32_t win = mos_window_create(0, 100, 100, 640, 480, "Hello 3D");
    FGLContext* gl = fglCreateContext(&(FGLContextDesc){
        .width = 640, .height = 480, .window_id = win, .depth = 1 });

    FGLVertex cube[36];
    fglMakeCube(cube, 1.0f, NULL);
    FGLBuffer vb = fglCreateBuffer(gl, sizeof cube);
    fglBufferData(gl, vb, 0, cube, sizeof cube);

    FGLShader* sh = fglCreateShader(gl, vs, fs);
    if (!sh) { /* fglShaderLog(gl) says why */ return 1; }
    int u_time = fglUniformLocation(sh, "time");

    for (int frame = 0; frame < 600; frame++) {
        fglClearColor(gl, 0.05f, 0.07f, 0.12f);
        fglClear(gl, FGL_COLOR_BUFFER_BIT | FGL_DEPTH_BUFFER_BIT);
        fglEnable(gl, FGL_DEPTH_TEST | FGL_CULL_FACE);
        fglUseShader(gl, sh);
        fglUniform1f(sh, u_time, frame / 60.0f);
        fglSetProjection(gl, fglPerspective(0.9f, 640.0f / 480.0f, 0.1f, 50));
        fglSetView(gl, fglLookAt(fglVec3(0, 1, 4), fglVec3(0, 0, 0), fglVec3(0, 1, 0)));
        fglSetModel(gl, fglRotate(frame * 0.02f, fglVec3(0, 1, 0)));
        fglDraw(gl, vb, 0, 36);
        fglPresent(gl);
    }
    fglDestroyShader(gl, sh);
    fglDestroyContext(gl);
    mos_window_close(win);
    return 0;
}

    Without the shader lines, fglUseProgram(gl, FGL_PROGRAM_PHONG) draws the same cube with the built-in per-pixel lighting.

    Contexts

    typedef struct {
    uint32_t width, height;     // render size
    uint32_t window_id;         // present into this window; 0 = the screen
    int32_t x, y;               // screen position when window_id == 0
    int depth;                  // create a depth buffer
    int page_flip;              // screen only: flip between two VRAM buffers
} FGLContextDesc;

FGLContext* fglCreateContext(const FGLContextDesc* desc);
void fglDestroyContext(FGLContext* gl);

    A context owns the color surface(s) you draw into, an optional depth buffer, and the command buffer being recorded.

    • In a window (MOSdesk): create the window with mos_window_create and pass its id. fglPresent copies each frame into the window.
    • Full screen (terminal): take the screen with mos_graphics_acquire() first. With page_flip set and a GPU that can flip (the QEMU/Bochs adapter can), frames are shown by switching the display to the buffer just drawn instead of copying it.

    Returns NULL when the surfaces cannot be created. fglGetDeviceInfo fills a syscall_gpu_info_t (GPU name, driver, VRAM, backend, caps; caps & FGPU_CAP_SHADERS says shaders are available).

    Buffers and vertex layouts

    FGLBuffer fglCreateBuffer(FGLContext* gl, uint32_t bytes);
int fglBufferData(FGLContext* gl, FGLBuffer b, uint32_t offset, const void* data, uint32_t bytes);
void fglDestroyBuffer(FGLContext* gl, FGLBuffer b);

    A buffer is up to 16 MiB of GPU memory. Index buffers hold uint32_t indices. Everything a process creates is freed when it exits.

    Vertex buffers hold FGLVertex by default:

    StructFloatsAttributes (location)
    FGLVertex10position xyz (0), normal xyz (1), color rgba (2)
    FGLVertexUV12the same, plus texture coordinates uv (3)

    Call fglVertexLayoutUV(gl) before drawing FGLVertexUV data, and fglVertexLayoutDefault(gl) to go back. For your own vertex struct, describe where each attribute location sits:

    typedef struct { float x, y; float u, v; float shade; } MyVertex;

static const FGLAttribute attrs[] = {
    { offsetof(MyVertex, x), 2 },       // location 0: vec2 (z = 0, w = 1)
    { offsetof(MyVertex, u), 2 },       // location 1
    { offsetof(MyVertex, shade), 1 },   // location 2
};
fglVertexLayout(gl, sizeof(MyVertex), 3, attrs);

    Offsets and the stride are in bytes and must be multiples of 4; a vertex is at most 64 floats; there are 8 locations. Missing components read as (0, 0, 0, 1), so a 2-float position is a point at z = 0. The layout is context state: it applies to every following draw, with shaders and with the built-in programs (which read locations 0, 1 and 2).

    In a shader, attributes get their location from layout(location = N), or from their name: position, normal, color, uv / texcoord (also with a_, in_, a or in prefixes) are 0, 1, 2 and 3. See fgsl.md.

    State and drawing

    CallEffect
    fglClearColor(gl, r, g, b) / fglClear(gl, bits)Clear color and/or depth (FGL_COLOR_BUFFER_BIT, FGL_DEPTH_BUFFER_BIT).
    fglEnable / fglDisableFGL_DEPTH_TEST, FGL_CULL_FACE (back faces; counter-clockwise is front), FGL_WIREFRAME, FGL_BLEND.
    fglUseProgram(gl, p)Use a built-in program (and stop using a shader).
    fglUseShader(gl, sh)Use a shader.
    fglSetModel, fglSetView, fglSetProjectionThe usual three matrices.
    fglSetLight(gl, direction, color, ambient)One directional light; direction is where the light travels.
    fglSetMaterial(gl, specular, shininess)Highlight strength (0-1) and sharpness (1-128).
    fglViewport(gl, x, y, w, h)Area of the surface to draw into (defaults to all of it).
    fglDraw(gl, vertices, first, count)Triangles from consecutive vertices.
    fglDrawIndexed(gl, vertices, indices, first_index, count)Triangles from an index buffer.
    fglSubmit(gl)Run the recorded commands.
    fglPresent(gl)Submit and show the frame. Returns 0, or -1 with gl->error set.
    fglReadPixels(gl, out, pitch)Copy the frame into your memory.

    Calls only *record*; nothing is drawn until fglSubmit/fglPresent. State changes between draws apply to the draws after them, in order, so you can change a uniform, draw, change it again and draw again in one frame.

    Built-in programs

    ProgramWhat it does
    FGL_PROGRAM_COLORVertex colors, no lighting.
    FGL_PROGRAM_GOURAUDLighting per vertex (diffuse + Blinn-Phong highlight), interpolated.
    FGL_PROGRAM_PHONGThe same lighting per pixel.

    They use fglSetLight and fglSetMaterial. They are faster than an equivalent shader, so they remain a good choice for simple scenes.

    Shaders

    FGLShader* fglCreateShader(FGLContext* gl, const char* vertex_src, const char* fragment_src);
const char* fglShaderLog(FGLContext* gl);
void fglUseShader(FGLContext* gl, FGLShader* sh);
void fglDestroyShader(FGLContext* gl, FGLShader* sh);

    fglCreateShader compiles both stages with the FGSL compiler (fglsl.h), links them (varyings and uniforms are matched by name), and loads the program onto the GPU. On failure it returns NULL and fglShaderLog(gl) holds a message such as

    fragment shader line 12: unknown identifier 'normall'

    The language is GLSL ES 1.0 / GLSL 1.30 with a few limits (no structs, no while, loops must have constant bounds); fgsl.md has the full reference. The compiler runs inside your program and takes well under a millisecond for typical shaders; create shaders once at startup, not every frame.

    Uniforms

    int fglUniformLocation(FGLShader* sh, const char* name);    // -1 if not declared
void fglUniform1f(FGLShader* sh, int loc, float x);
void fglUniform2f(FGLShader* sh, int loc, float x, float y);
void fglUniform3f(FGLShader* sh, int loc, float x, float y, float z);
void fglUniform4f(FGLShader* sh, int loc, float x, float y, float z, float w);
void fglUniformVec3(FGLShader* sh, int loc, FGLVec3 v);
void fglUniformMatrix4(FGLShader* sh, int loc, FGLMat4 m);
void fglUniformArray(FGLShader* sh, int loc, uint32_t first, const float* values, uint32_t count);
void fglUniformTexture(FGLContext* gl, FGLShader* sh, int loc, FGLTexture t, uint32_t flags);

    Uniform values belong to the shader and keep their value until you set them again (also across frames and while another shader is in use). Setting a location of -1 does nothing, so you can skip checks. fglUniformArray takes count elements packed tightly in the uniform's type (vec3 = 3 floats, mat4 = 16).

    Automatic uniforms

    Declare any of these and FarcadeGL keeps them up to date from the context's state, so shaders work with fglSetModel, fglSetLight and friends:

    UniformTypeValue
    fgl_ModelViewProjectionmat4projection × view × model
    fgl_Model, fgl_View, fgl_Projectionmat4the matrices as set
    fgl_ModelViewmat4view × model
    fgl_NormalMatrixmat4inverse transpose of the model matrix (use with vec4(normal, 0.0))
    fgl_LightDirectionvec3fglSetLight direction (normalized; the way light travels)
    fgl_LightColor, fgl_Ambientvec3fglSetLight colors
    fgl_CameraPositionvec3the eye position, from the view matrix
    fgl_Materialvec2fglSetMaterial specular strength, shininess

    Textures

    FGLTexture fglCreateTexture(FGLContext* gl, uint32_t width, uint32_t height, const uint32_t* pixels);
int fglTextureData(FGLContext* gl, FGLTexture t, const uint32_t* pixels, uint32_t pitch);
void fglDestroyTexture(FGLContext* gl, FGLTexture t);
void fglBindTexture(FGLContext* gl, uint32_t unit, FGLTexture t, uint32_t flags);

    Textures are ARGB8888 (0xAARRGGBB), rows top to bottom, up to 4096 × 4096. In a shader, texture(sampler, uv) returns vec4(r, g, b, a) in 0..1. uv = (0, 0) is the top-left corner of the image and (1, 1) the bottom-right; fglMakeCubeUV maps each face upright.

    Each sampler2D uniform gets a texture unit (0-3, in declaration order). fglUniformTexture(gl, sh, loc, tex, flags) binds a texture to that sampler's unit; fglBindTexture binds to a unit directly. Flags:

    FlagEffect
    FGL_TEXTURE_LINEARBilinear filtering (default: nearest texel).
    FGL_TEXTURE_CLAMPCoordinates outside 0..1 use the edge texels (default: the texture repeats).

    Bindings are context state, like the vertex layout.

    Blending

    fglEnable(gl, FGL_BLEND) mixes each new pixel with what is already there using the fragment's alpha: color = src.rgb * src.a + dst.rgb * (1 - src.a). Draw opaque geometry first, then transparent geometry back to front. With the built-in programs, alpha comes from the vertex color.

    Math

    FGLVec3, FGLMat4 and: fglVec3, fglAdd, fglSub, fglScale3, fglDot, fglCross, fglNormalize, fglIdentity, fglMul, fglTranslate, fglScale, fglRotate(angle, axis), fglPerspective(fovy, aspect, near, far), fglLookAt(eye, center, up), fglNormalMatrix, and fglSin, fglCos, fglTan, fglSqrt (the SDK has no libm).

    fglMakeCube(out, half_size, face_colors) writes the 36 vertices of a cube with one color per face (NULL for the default colors); fglMakeCubeUV does the same with texture coordinates.

    Errors and limits

    • fglPresent/fglSubmit return -1 and set gl->error to the first failed SYS_GPU result (SYS_ERR_INVAL for a bad command, SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND for a destroyed buffer or texture).
    • fglCreateShader returns NULL; see fglShaderLog. If the kernel rejects a program the compiler produced, the reason is written to the serial log (fgpu: shader program rejected: ...).
    LimitValue
    Surface / texture size4096 × 4096
    Buffer size16 MiB
    Command buffer1 MiB per submit (FarcadeGL grows its buffer as needed)
    Shader program2048 instructions per stage, 32 temporary vec4s, 8 varyings, 64 uniform vec4s (a mat4 uses 4), 256 constant vec4s, 4 texture units
    Objects per process1024 surfaces (contexts and textures), 4096 buffers, 1024 shaders; shared by the threads of a program

    Performance

    The CPU backend runs on one core. Measured for the fglcube scene in a 640 × 480 window on a 2.8 GHz Xeon core: about 11 ms per frame with the built-in Phong program and about 42 ms (24 fps) with fglcube --shader (a 60-instruction fragment shader over about 180,000 pixels), so a full shader costs roughly 4 times a built-in program. Fragment shaders run 8 pixels at a time with SSE. Under QEMU without KVM everything is many times slower. Tips:

    • Do per-vertex work in the vertex shader and pass it as a varying; the fragment shader runs for every pixel.
    • Fewer varyings and fewer instructions are faster. discard makes the depth buffer update after the fragment shader instead of before it.
    • Use the built-in programs for objects that need nothing special.

    Function reference

    FunctionSection
    fglGetDeviceInfoContexts
    fglCreateContext, fglDestroyContextContexts
    fglCreateBuffer, fglBufferData, fglDestroyBufferBuffers
    fglVertexLayout, fglVertexLayoutUV, fglVertexLayoutDefaultBuffers
    fglEnable, fglDisable, fglViewport, fglClearColor, fglClearState and drawing
    fglUseProgramBuilt-in programs
    fglSetModel, fglSetView, fglSetProjection, fglSetLight, fglSetMaterialState and drawing
    fglDraw, fglDrawIndexed, fglSubmit, fglPresent, fglReadPixelsState and drawing
    fglCreateShader, fglShaderLog, fglUseShader, fglDestroyShaderShaders
    fglUniformLocation, fglUniform1f … fglUniform4f, fglUniformVec3, fglUniformMatrix4, fglUniformArray, fglUniformTextureUniforms
    fglCreateTexture, fglTextureData, fglDestroyTexture, fglBindTextureTextures
    fglMakeCube, fglMakeCubeUV and the math functionsMath

    The FGPU interface underneath

    SYS_GPU (40) takes a syscall_gpu_request_t. Operations: INFO, CREATE_SURFACE, DESTROY_SURFACE, CREATE_BUFFER, UPLOAD_BUFFER, DESTROY_BUFFER, SUBMIT, READBACK, PRESENT, RELEASE_DISPLAY, and (ABI version 2) CREATE_PROGRAM, DESTROY_PROGRAM, WRITE_SURFACE.

    A command buffer is a list of 32-bit words; each command starts with FGPU_CMD(opcode, length_in_words): BIND_TARGET, VIEWPORT, CLEAR, SET_STATE, SET_PROGRAM, SET_UNIFORMS, DRAW, and (version 2) SET_SHADER, SET_CONSTANTS, SET_VERTEX_LAYOUT, BIND_TEXTURE. Every submit starts from default state.

    A shader program is a blob of FGPU bytecode: a header, the vertex and fragment instructions (five words each: opcode, destination, three sources, with swizzles and negate/abs modifiers on vec4 registers) and a constant pool. The instruction set and register files are described at the end of fgpu_abi.h. Jumps only go forward, so every program finishes; the kernel checks every instruction when the program is created. You can produce blobs yourself, but fglsl_compile (fglsl.h) is the supported way.

    PreviousFarcade Engine (working name): a high-performance game engine for Minimal-OSNextFGSL shading language (fglsl.h)

    Edit this page on GitHub

    FGSL shading language (fglsl.h)

    FGSL (Farcade GL Shading Language) is the language FarcadeGL shaders are written in. It is a subset of GLSL: if you know GLSL ES 1.0 (WebGL 1) or desktop GLSL 1.30, you already know it. Shaders are compiled inside your program by fglsl.h (FarcadeGL's fglCreateShader does this), into FGPU bytecode that the kernel checks and runs.

    On this pageProgram structureTypesVariablesStatementsExpressionsFunctionsLimitsErrorsUsing the compiler directly
    // vertex shader
uniform mat4 fgl_ModelViewProjection;
attribute vec3 position;
attribute vec2 uv;
varying vec2 v_uv;

void main() {
    v_uv = uv;
    gl_Position = fgl_ModelViewProjection * vec4(position, 1.0);
}
    // fragment shader
uniform sampler2D tex;
uniform float time;
varying vec2 v_uv;

void main() {
    vec4 c = texture(tex, v_uv);
    if (c.a < 0.1) discard;
    gl_FragColor = vec4(c.rgb * (0.8 + 0.2 * sin(time)), 1.0);
}

    Program structure

    A shader is a list of global declarations and functions, with one void main(). Both GLSL styles work:

    GLSL ES 1.0 styleGLSL 1.30 style
    Vertex inputattribute vec3 position;in vec3 position;
    Vertex → fragmentvarying vec3 v_normal;out vec3 v_normal; / in vec3 v_normal;
    Fragment outputgl_FragColor = ...;out vec4 color; then color = ...;

    #version, #extension and other # lines are ignored, as are precision ...; statements and the qualifiers highp, mediump, lowp, flat, smooth, centroid, invariant. Comments are // and /* */.

    Types

    TypeNotes
    float32-bit float.
    vec2, vec3, vec4Float vectors.
    mat44 × 4 float matrix, column-major, as in GLSL. m[i] is column i.
    sampler2DA texture; uniforms and function parameters only.
    int, bool, uint, ivecN, bvecNAccepted, stored as floats. true is 1.0, false 0.0. Integer division is not truncated: use floor() or int().

    mat2, mat3, structs and samplers other than sampler2D are not supported. Arrays are supported for uniforms and local variables, with a size up to 64 (uniforms) or 16 (locals), indexed by a constant or a loop counter.

    Constructors

    vec4(1.0), vec4(v3, 1.0), vec3(v4) (takes .xyz), vec2(x, y), float(x), int(x) (truncates toward zero), bool(x), mat4(c0, c1, c2, c3) (four vec4 columns) and mat4(1.0) (diagonal). Constructors whose arguments are all constants are folded at compile time.

    Swizzles

    .xyzw, .rgba and .stpq, in any order and with repeats when reading (v.zyx, c.rrr); without repeats when writing (v.xz = ...).

    Variables

    DeclarationMeaning
    uniform T name;Set by the program with fglUniform*. The same name in both shaders is one uniform.
    attribute T name; / in T name; (vertex)Per-vertex input, float to vec4.
    varying T name; / out T name; (vertex)Output to the fragment shader, float to vec4, interpolated perspective-correctly.
    varying T name; / in T name; (fragment)Input from the vertex shader, matched by name and type.
    out vec4 name; (fragment)The fragment color (same as gl_FragColor).
    const T name = expr;A constant; folded when the value is known at compile time.
    T name; (global or local)A variable; starts at zero.

    Attributes

    Each attribute reads one location of the vertex layout (see farcadegl.md). The location is layout(location = N) if given, otherwise taken from the name:

    Name (also with an a_, in_, a or in prefix, any case)LocationIn FGLVertex / FGLVertexUV
    position, pos, vertex0px, py, pz
    normal1nx, ny, nz
    color, colour2r, g, b, a
    uv, texcoord, texcoord03u, v

    Other names get the first free location from 4. Components the layout does not provide read as 0, 0, 0, 1.

    Built-in variables

    VariableStageTypeMeaning
    gl_Positionvertexvec4Clip-space position (write).
    gl_FragColorfragmentvec4Color, rgba in 0..1 (write).
    gl_FragCoordfragmentvec4Pixel center (x + 0.5, y + 0.5, depth 0..1, 1/w). y grows downwards.
    gl_FrontFacingfragmentboolTrue for counter-clockwise (front) triangles.

    FarcadeGL also fills the fgl_* uniforms when you declare them (fgl_ModelViewProjection, fgl_NormalMatrix, fgl_LightDirection, ...): see farcadegl.md.

    Statements

    • Assignment =, +=, -=, *=, /=, and ++ / -- (as statements).
    • if (...) ... else ...
    • for (int i = A; i < B; i++) ... — the start, end and step must be constants (<, <=, >, >=, !=; i++, i--, ++i, i += n, i -= n). Loops are unrolled, at most 256 times. break and continue work. Inside the loop, i is a constant, so it can index arrays.
    • discard; (fragment shader) drops the pixel.
    • return; / return expr;
    • while and do loops are not supported (every program must finish in a known number of steps).

    Expressions

    Operators, from lowest to highest precedence: ?:, ||, &&, == !=, < > <= >=, + -, * /, unary - + !, then calls, [] and swizzles. Arithmetic works component by component; a float mixes with any vector (v * 2.0). mat4 * vec4, vec4 * mat4 and mat4 * mat4 are matrix products. Comparisons and &&, ||, ! work on scalars and give 0.0 or 1.0.

    Functions

    User functions are supported and inlined at each call: parameters are copies (in); out / inout parameters and recursion are not supported. A function must be declared before main is compiled, in any order.

    float rim(vec3 n, vec3 v, float power) {
    return pow(1.0 - max(dot(n, v), 0.0), power);
}

    Built-in functions

    T is float or a vector; arguments marked float may also be a single float with vector arguments (as in GLSL).

    FunctionNotes
    radians, degrees
    sin, cos, tan, atan(y, x), atan(y_over_x)Error about 1e-5.
    pow, exp, exp2, log, log2, sqrt, inversesqrtpow(x, y) is 0 for x <= 0 (GLSL leaves it undefined).
    abs, sign, floor, ceil, fract, mod(x, y)
    min, max, clamp(x, lo, hi), mix(a, b, t), step(edge, x), smoothstep(e0, e1, x)
    length, distance, dot, cross, normalize, reflect(I, N)
    texture(sampler, uv), texture2D(sampler, uv)Returns vec4, see textures.

    Not available: asin, acos, refract, faceforward, derivatives (dFdx...), texture with a bias or LOD, matrix functions.

    Limits

    Limit
    Instructions per stage (after inlining and unrolling)2048
    Temporary registers (vec4)32
    Varyings8
    Uniform registers64 vec4 (mat4 = 4, arrays count every element)
    Constants256 vec4
    Samplers4
    Attributes8

    The compiler reports when a shader goes over a limit ("shader too complex", "too many varyings ...").

    Errors

    Errors name the stage and line:

    vertex shader line 7: unknown identifier 'positon'
fragment shader line 3: the vertex shader does not write varying 'v_uv'
fragment shader line 9: type mismatch in assignment

    Using the compiler directly

    #include "fglsl.h"

static fglsl_program_t prog;    // about 160 KiB: keep it static or malloc it
if (fglsl_compile(&prog, vertex_src, fragment_src) != 0)
    printf("%s\n", prog.error);
// prog.words / prog.size: the blob for SYS_GPU_CREATE_PROGRAM
// prog.uniforms[0 .. uniform_count-1]: name, type, first register (or unit)
// prog.attribs[0 .. attrib_count-1]: name, type, location

    fglsl.h needs no libc, so it also builds on a Linux or macOS host, for example to check shaders at build time. The bytecode format is described in fgpu_abi.h ("Shader programs").

    Files

    MinimaFS file and directory calls. Include minimalos.h.

    Paths look like 0:/etc/System.conf: a drive number, a colon, then an absolute path. A path without a drive prefix is resolved against the terminal's current directory (see mos_getcwd).

    A file handle is a long. Keep it in a long: it is a 64-bit value, and truncating it to int can corrupt it. Valid handles are positive; errors are negative.

    Functionsmos_openmos_createmos_readmos_fwritemos_closemos_seekmos_tellmos_sizemos_feofmos_existsmos_is_dirmos_mkdirmos_listdirmos_deletemos_rmdirmos_get_metadata

    mos_open

    long mos_open(const char* path, long flags);

    Opens an existing file.

    ParameterDescription
    pathFile to open
    flagsSYS_O_RDONLY (0) for read-only; SYS_O_RDWR (or any non-zero value) for read and write

    Returns a handle (positive), SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND if the file does not exist or cannot be opened, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL or invalid path.

    Notes

    • mos_open never creates a file. Call mos_create first.
    • The position starts at 0. Writing at position 0 overwrites the start of the file; to append, mos_seek to mos_size first.
    • Writes are kept in memory and saved to disk by mos_close. Always close a handle you wrote to.

    Example

    long fd = mos_open("0:/etc/motd.txt", SYS_O_RDONLY);
if (fd < 0) { printf("no motd (%ld)\n", fd); mos_exit(1); }
char buf[256];
long n = mos_read(fd, buf, sizeof buf - 1);
if (n > 0) { buf[n] = '\0'; mos_puts(buf); }
mos_close(fd);

    mos_create

    long mos_create(const char* path, const char* filetype, const char* fileformat);

    Creates a new, empty file. Open it afterwards with SYS_O_RDWR to write to it.

    ParameterDescription
    pathFile to create. The parent directory must exist
    filetypeMinimaFS file type such as "text" or "binary". NULL means "binary"
    fileformatFormat tag such as "txt" or "bin". NULL means "bin"

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL or invalid path, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if the file system refused (missing parent, no space).

    Example

    const char* path = "0:/data/notes.txt";
if (!mos_exists(path)) mos_create(path, "text", "txt");
long fd = mos_open(path, SYS_O_RDWR);
mos_seek(fd, mos_size(fd));          /* append */
mos_fwrite(fd, "new line\n", 9);
mos_close(fd);

    mos_read

    long mos_read(long fd, void* buf, size_t len);

    Reads up to len bytes from the current position and advances it.

    ParameterDescription
    fdHandle from mos_open
    bufDestination buffer
    lenMaximum number of bytes

    Returns the number of bytes read; 0 at end of file. SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL handle or buffer.

    Notes The result is not NUL-terminated. Leave a byte free when reading text.

    Example

    /* read a whole file into the heap */
long fd = mos_open(path, SYS_O_RDONLY);
long size = mos_size(fd);
char* data = malloc((size_t)size + 1);
long got = 0, n;
while ((n = mos_read(fd, data + got, (size_t)(size - got))) > 0) got += n;
data[got] = '\0';
mos_close(fd);

    mos_fwrite

    long mos_fwrite(long fd, const void* buf, size_t len);

    Writes len bytes at the current position and advances it, growing the file if needed.

    ParameterDescription
    fdHandle opened with SYS_O_RDWR
    bufBytes to write
    lenNumber of bytes

    Returns the number of bytes written, 0 if the handle is read-only or memory ran out, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL handle or buffer.

    Notes

    • Writing never shortens a file. To replace a file's contents, delete it, create it again and write.
    • The data reaches disk when the handle is closed.

    mos_close

    long mos_close(long fd);

    Closes a handle and saves anything written to it.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL handle.

    Notes Do not use the handle afterwards. Closing twice is undefined.

    mos_seek

    long mos_seek(long fd, long offset);

    Moves the position to offset bytes from the start of the file.

    ParameterDescription
    fdOpen handle
    offsetNew position. Values past the end are clamped to the file size

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL handle.

    mos_tell

    long mos_tell(long fd);

    Returns the current position in bytes, or SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL handle.

    mos_size

    Returns 1 if the position is at the end of the file, 0 if not, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL handle.

    Example

    char c;
while (!mos_feof(fd) && mos_read(fd, &c, 1) == 1) count++;

    Returns 1 if path is a directory, 0 if it is a file or does not exist, SYS_ERR_INVAL for an invalid path.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if it could not be created (it already exists, or the parent is missing), SYS_ERR_INVAL for an invalid path.

    Example

    if (!mos_is_dir("0:/data")) mos_mkdir("0:/data");

    syscall_dirent_t items[64];
long n = mos_listdir("0:/programs", items, 64);
for (long i = 0; i < n; i++)
    printf("%s%s\n", items[i].name, items[i].type == SYSCALL_DIRENT_TYPE_DIR ? "/" : "");

    ParameterDescription

    syscall_file_metadata_t fields:

    FieldMeaning
    filetype[64]File type, such as text or binary
    fileformat[16]Format tag, such as txt or run
    data_lengthSize of the data in bytes

    hidden1 for hidden files

    created_date[32]Creation date as text
    last_changed[32]Last-modified date as text

    Example

    syscall_file_metadata_t m;
if (mos_get_metadata("0:/programs/hello.run", &m) == 0)
    printf("%s/%s, %u bytes, changed %s\n", m.filetype, m.fileformat, m.data_length, m.last_changed);

    Text in your own pixels (font.h)

    font.h draws text into any ARGB8888 pixel buffer, for programs that render their own window contents (games, canvases, clocks) instead of using easyui widgets. It uses the same OpenType renderer and Inter fonts as mosWM and easyui, so text looks like the rest of MOSdesk: smooth and anti-aliased. When the fonts cannot be read (mosWM is not installed), it falls back to the 8 × 8 bitmap font, scaled by the text size.

    Header only; it can be included together with easyui.h.

    Functionsdraw_texttext_widthtext_heightfont_load
    #include "window.h"
#include "font.h"

static uint32_t pixels[320 * 120];

draw_text(pixels, 320, 120, 10, 10, "Score 120", 0xFFEAF2F8, 1);
int w = text_width("Game over", 2);
draw_text(pixels, 320, 120, (320 - w) / 2, 50, "Game over", 0xFFFFD166, 2);

    Sizes

    SizeSmooth textBitmap fallback
    112 px Inter Regular8 × 8
    2 and up8 × size px Inter Medium(8 × size) square glyphs

    These match easyui's text sizes and mosWM's own text.

    Functions

    draw_text

    void draw_text(uint32_t* pixels, uint32_t width, uint32_t height,
               int x, int y, const char* text, uint32_t color, int size);

    Draws text with its top-left corner at (x, y) into a width × height buffer whose rows are width pixels long. Clipped to the buffer. '\n' starts a new line. The color is 0xAARRGGBB; text is blended with the pixels underneath, so a lower alpha draws translucent text. Text is UTF-8; the bundled Inter files are a subset that may lack some characters, and the bitmap fallback has ASCII only.

    text_width

    int text_width(const char* text, int size);

    Width in pixels of the widest line, for centring and right alignment.

    text_height

    int text_height(int size);

    Height of one line (ascent + descent).

    font_load

    int font_load(const char* path, int bold);

    Uses another .otf / .ttf file instead of Inter: bold = 0 for size-1 text, 1 for size 2 and up. Returns 1 on success. Call it before the first draw_text.

    font_set_smooth, font_is_smooth

    void font_set_smooth(int on);
int font_is_smooth(void);

    font_set_smooth(0) always uses the bitmap font. font_is_smooth() says whether the OpenType fonts were found.

    Notes

    • The fonts are read from 0:/programs/mosWM/assets/fonts/ the first time text is drawn or measured (about 50 KiB of memory for both faces).
    • Glyphs are cached, so redrawing the same text every frame is cheap.
    • MOSdesk's Snake, Clock and Paint use it.

    Graphics

    Full-screen framebuffer access over SYS_GRAPHICS, for programs that take over the whole display instead of opening a mosWM window. The ownership, info, blit and present calls are in minimalos.h (from x86_64/user_common.h); the size queries and drawing primitives are in x86_64/user_graphics.h. Include graphics.h to get all of them plus the short graphics_* names.

    Most apps should use windows instead. Under MOSdesk, mosWM already owns the screen and a second program cannot acquire it.

    Functionsmos_graphics_acquiremos_graphics_releasemos_graphics_ownermos_graphics_infomos_graphics_blit_surfacemos_graphics_presentmos_graphics_get_widthmos_graphics_get_heightmos_graphics_clearmos_graphics_pixelmos_graphics_linemos_graphics_rectanglemos_graphics_fill_rectanglemos_graphics_trianglemos_graphics_fill_trianglemos_graphics_circlemos_graphics_fill_circlemos_graphics_ellipsemos_graphics_textmos_graphics_measure_textmos_graphics_set_resolutionmos_graphics_callmos_graphics

    How drawing works

    The kernel keeps a back buffer the size of the screen. A program:

    1. takes ownership of the screen with mos_graphics_acquire;
    2. draws into its own ARGB8888 surface (a malloced uint32_t array);
    3. copies the surface into the back buffer with mos_graphics_blit_surface;
    4. shows the changed rectangle with mos_graphics_present;
    5. gives the screen back with mos_graphics_release, which redraws the terminal.
    #include "graphics.h"
#include "stdlib.h"

int main(void) {
    if (mos_graphics_acquire() != SYS_SUCCESS) { mos_puts("screen busy\n"); return 1; }
    uint32_t w = mos_graphics_get_width(), h = mos_graphics_get_height();
    uint32_t* surf = malloc((size_t)w * h * 4);
    for (uint32_t f = 0; f < 300; f++) {
        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < w * h; i++) surf[i] = 0xFF000000 | ((i + f * 4) & 0xFF);
        mos_graphics_blit_surface(surf, w, h, w * 4, 0, 0, (int32_t)w, (int32_t)h, 0, 0,
                                  SYS_GRAPHICS_BLIT_OPAQUE);
        mos_graphics_present(0, 0, (int32_t)w, (int32_t)h);
        mos_sleep(16);
    }
    mos_graphics_release();
    return 0;
}

    Privilege

    On Minimal-OS a .run program is a user process, and the kernel only lets user processes call these graphics operations: get width, get height, owner, acquire, release, info, blit and present. The drawing primitives - clear, pixel, line, rectangle, circle, triangle, ellipse, text, measure text and set resolution - return SYS_ERR_PERM to a user process; they exist for kernel-privileged callers. Draw shapes and text into your own surface and blit it.

    The Run Studio preview runs the primitives for any program, so code that uses them works there but not on the real system.

    mos_graphics_acquire

    long mos_graphics_acquire(void);

    Makes the calling process the owner of the screen. Only the owner may blit, present, draw or read raw input.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_PERM if another process owns the screen.

    Notes While a program owns the screen, keyboard and mouse input goes to the raw input queue (mos_input_read) instead of the terminal.

    mos_graphics_release

    long mos_graphics_release(void);

    Gives up ownership and redraws the terminal.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_PERM if the caller does not own the screen.

    mos_graphics_owner

    uint64_t mos_graphics_owner(void);

    Returns the PID that owns the screen, or SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND if nobody does.

    Example

    if (mos_graphics_owner() != SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND) mos_puts("a desktop is running; open a window instead\n");

    mos_graphics_info

    long mos_graphics_info(syscall_graphics_info_t* info);

    Describes the display. The wrapper sets info->size, info->version and info->reserved before the call.

    syscall_graphics_info_t fieldMeaning
    width, heightScreen size in pixels
    pitchFramebuffer bytes per row
    pixel_formatBack-buffer format; always SYS_GRAPHICS_PIXEL_FORMAT_ARGB8888
    bytes_per_pixelFramebuffer bytes per pixel
    red_position, red_mask_size, and green/blueFramebuffer channel layout

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL or malformed structure, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if there is no framebuffer.

    Notes Surfaces you blit are always ARGB8888; the channel layout is only informative.

    mos_graphics_blit_surface

    long mos_graphics_blit_surface(const uint32_t* src, uint32_t width, uint32_t height,
                               uint32_t pitch, int32_t sx, int32_t sy, int32_t sw, int32_t sh,
                               int32_t dx, int32_t dy, uint32_t flags);

    Copies a rectangle of an ARGB8888 surface into the kernel back buffer. Nothing appears until mos_graphics_present.

    ParameterDescription
    srcSurface pixels, 4-byte aligned. The whole surface must be one live heap allocation of this process
    width, heightSurface size, 1 … 16384 each
    pitchSurface bytes per row: a multiple of 4, at least width × 4. pitch × height at most 64 MiB
    sx, sy, sw, shSource rectangle; must lie inside the surface and have positive size
    dx, dyWhere its top-left lands on screen; parts off screen are clipped
    flagsSYS_GRAPHICS_BLIT_OPAQUE copies pixels as they are; SYS_GRAPHICS_BLIT_ALPHA blends them using their alpha byte

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_PERM if the caller does not own the screen, SYS_ERR_INVAL for any argument outside the rules above, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if the blit failed.

    Example

    /* draw a 32x32 sprite with transparency at (x, y) */
mos_graphics_blit_surface(sprite, 32, 32, 32 * 4, 0, 0, 32, 32, x, y, SYS_GRAPHICS_BLIT_ALPHA);
mos_graphics_present(x, y, 32, 32);

    mos_graphics_present

    long mos_graphics_present(int32_t x, int32_t y, int32_t width, int32_t height);

    Copies a rectangle of the back buffer to the visible framebuffer. The rectangle is clipped to the screen.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_PERM if the caller does not own the screen, SYS_ERR_INVAL for an empty rectangle or no framebuffer.

    Notes Present only what changed: a small dirty rectangle is much cheaper than the whole screen.

    Returns the screen width in pixels. Allowed for any process.

Every wrapper on this page builds one and calls this (or mos_graphics, its uint64_t twin in x86_64/user_syscalls.h).

    Input

    Raw keyboard and mouse input for programs that own the screen. Window apps do not need any of this: mosWM delivers key and mouse events to their window (see mos_window_next_event).

    mos_input_read is in x86_64/user_syscalls.h; the mouse calls are in x86_64/user_mouse.h and the USB keyboard calls in x86_64/user_usb.h.

    Functionsmos_input_readmos_mouse_get_statemos_mouse_pollmos_mouse_has_mousemos_mouse_initmos_mousemos_mouse_callmos_usb_has_keyboardmos_usb_key_to_asciimos_usb_key_is_pressedmos_usb_keyboard_infomos_usb_pollmos_usb_initmos_usb

    mos_input_read

    uint64_t mos_input_read(syscall_input_event_t* events, uint32_t capacity,
                        uint32_t timeout_ms, uint64_t* dropped_count);

    Takes queued keyboard and mouse events off the kernel's input queue. Only the screen owner may call it; while nobody owns the screen, hardware input goes to the terminal instead.

    ParameterDescription
    eventsArray to fill
    capacitySize of events, 1 … SYSCALL_INPUT_MAX_READ (256)
    timeout_msHow long to wait when the queue is empty, at most 5000. 0 returns at once
    dropped_countIf not NULL, receives the total number of events dropped because the queue was full

    Returns the number of events written (0 on timeout), SYS_ERR_PERM if the caller does not own the screen, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a bad argument.

    syscall_input_event_t fields:

    FieldMeaning
    typeSYSCALL_INPUT_KEY_DOWN, _KEY_UP, _MOUSE_MOVE, _MOUSE_BUTTON or _MOUSE_WHEEL
    keyUSB HID usage code (key events)
    modsSYSCALL_INPUT_MOD_SHIFT, _CTRL, _ALT bits
    buttonsSYSCALL_INPUT_BTN_LEFT, _RIGHT, _MIDDLE bits: the current button state
    dx, dyRelative motion (MOUSE_MOVE)
    wheelRelative scroll (MOUSE_WHEEL)
    time_msUptime when the event was queued

    Notes The queue holds SYSCALL_INPUT_QUEUE_CAPACITY (256) events. When it is full the newest event is dropped and the drop counter increases.

    Example

    syscall_input_event_t ev[32];
uint64_t n = mos_input_read(ev, 32, 16, NULL);   /* wait up to one frame */
if (n > 32) n = 0;                               /* an SYS_ERR_* value */
for (uint64_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (ev[i].type == SYSCALL_INPUT_KEY_DOWN && ev[i].key == 41) quit = 1;   /* Esc */
    if (ev[i].type == SYSCALL_INPUT_MOUSE_MOVE) { mx += ev[i].dx; my += ev[i].dy; }
}

    mos_mouse_get_state

    uint64_t mos_mouse_get_state(syscall_mouse_state_t* out_state);

    Reads the USB mouse's accumulated motion since the last call, and resets it. Screen owner only.

    syscall_mouse_state_t fieldMeaning
    dx, dyMotion since the last call
    wheelScroll since the last call
    buttonsCurrent SYSCALL_MOUSE_BTN_LEFT, _RIGHT, _MIDDLE bits

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_PERM if the caller does not own the screen, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL pointer.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS.

    Device managers

    Calls into the kernel's GPU, audio, storage and USB managers over SYS_MANAGER. Include x86_64/user_managers.h.

    These exist for kernel-privileged code such as the boot sequence and the terminal. A .run program may only call mos_audio_has_data; every other operation returns SYS_ERR_PERM to a user process, because it reconfigures hardware the whole system shares.

    Memory and randomness

    Heap allocation over SYS_HEAP, random bytes over SYS_RANDOM, and atoi. Include stdlib.h.

    Heap blocks come from the kernel allocator and are tracked per process: free and realloc only accept blocks this process allocated, and any block still allocated when the process ends is reclaimed.

    Functionsmalloccallocreallocfreemos_heap_failedmos_random_bytesmos_random_u64mos_randomatoi

    malloc

    void* malloc(size_t size);

    Allocates size bytes. The memory is not cleared.

    ParameterDescription
    sizeNumber of bytes. Must be greater than 0

    Returns a pointer to the block, or NULL if size is 0 or there is not enough memory.

    Example

    uint32_t* pixels = malloc(width * height * sizeof(uint32_t));
if (!pixels) { mos_puts("out of memory\n"); mos_exit(1); }

    calloc

    void* calloc(size_t count, size_t size);

    Allocates an array of count elements of size bytes, cleared to zero.

    Returns a pointer, or NULL if count * size overflows, is 0, or memory runs out.

    Example

    int* grid = calloc(rows * cols, sizeof(int));

    realloc

    void* realloc(void* ptr, size_t size);

    Resizes a block, moving it if needed. The contents are kept up to the smaller of the two sizes.

    ParameterDescription
    ptrBlock from malloc, calloc or realloc, or NULL to allocate a new one
    sizeNew size. 0 frees the block

    Returns the (possibly moved) block, or NULL on failure. On failure the original block is unchanged and still yours, so keep the old pointer until the call succeeds. realloc(ptr, 0) frees ptr and returns NULL.

    Example

    char* bigger = realloc(buf, cap * 2);
if (!bigger) { free(buf); mos_exit(1); }
buf = bigger; cap *= 2;

    free

    void free(void* ptr);

    Releases a block. free(NULL) does nothing.

    Notes Passing a pointer this process did not allocate is rejected by the kernel (SYS_ERR_INVAL, ignored by free) rather than corrupting the heap. Using a block after freeing it is still a bug.

    mos_heap_failed

    int mos_heap_failed(long value);

    Tells whether a raw SYS_HEAP result is an error code rather than an address. malloc, calloc and realloc use it to return NULL; you only need it when calling SYS_HEAP through mos_syscall.

    Returns non-zero if value is one of the SYS_ERR_* codes.

    mos_random_bytes

    long mos_random_bytes(void* buf, size_t len);

    Fills buf with random bytes from the kernel's entropy source.

    ParameterDescription
    bufDestination
    lenNumber of bytes. Must be greater than 0

    Returns len, or SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL buffer or zero length.

    Notes The kernel uses RDRAND when the CPU has it, which is suitable for keys and nonces. Without it, the bytes are derived from the TSC and RTC and must not be used for cryptography.

    Example

    uint8_t key[32];
mos_random_bytes(key, sizeof key);

    mos_random_u64

    uint64_t mos_random_u64(void);

    Returns 64 random bits from mos_random_bytes.

    Example

    int die = (int)(mos_random_u64() % 6) + 1;

    mos_random

    long mos_random(void* buf, uint32_t len);

    The same call as mos_random_bytes, declared in net.h with a 32-bit length.

    atoi

    int atoi(const char* s);

    Converts a decimal string to an int. Skips leading spaces and tabs, accepts one + or -, then reads digits until the first non-digit.

    Returns the value, or 0 if there are no digits. Overflow is not detected.

    Example

    int port = argc > 1 ? atoi(argv[1]) : 8080;
