    Network boot (PXE)

    Boot Minimal-OS on another PC on the same LAN, straight from dist/x86_64/kernel.iso on this machine. No USB stick needed.

    On this pageRun itHow it worksNetwork logTarget PC BIOS setup (ASRock)Troubleshooting

    Run it

    make                # or make mosdesk: build the ISO as usual
make netboot        # = sudo tools/netboot/netboot.sh serve

    Leave it running, then boot the other PC from the network. Press Ctrl+C to stop. Rebuilt the ISO? Stop it and run make netboot again.

    How it works

    1. tools/netboot/netboot.sh unpacks /boot from the ISO into build/netboot/tftp/ and builds GRUB network images for BIOS (core.0) and UEFI (core.efi), with this machine's IP built in.
    2. dnsmasq runs in proxy DHCP mode. The router still hands out IP addresses; dnsmasq only tells PXE clients which file to load.
    3. The PC loads GRUB over TFTP. GRUB reads the ISO's own grub.cfg and loads kernel.bin, mosinst.mpkg and mosfirmware.mpkg over TFTP, so the boot menu is the same as when booting the ISO.

    While it runs, the script opens UDP ports 67, 69 and 4011 in ufw on the LAN interface and removes them again when it stops.

    Settings: NETBOOT_IFACE (default: the default-route interface, wired first) and NETBOOT_ISO.

    Network log

    While make netboot runs, the booted PC sends its whole log back: boot messages, everything the kernel writes to serial, program output, and Mxplorer's console (site errors, failed loads, navigations). It appears in the make netboot terminal as [<pc ip>] ... and is saved to build/netboot/logs/ (latest.log is the newest run).

    How: the script adds netlog=<this pc>:5140 to the kernel arguments in the served grub.cfg. The kernel keeps every log line in a 512 KiB buffer from the start of boot and sends it over UDP once the network has an address (it runs DHCP itself if nothing else did after 20 s). Programs write to the log, without showing it on screen, with mos_log() from minimalos.h (file descriptor 3).

    NETBOOT_LOG_PORT=0 make netboot turns it off; another number changes the port. UDP 5140 is opened in ufw along with the PXE ports.

    Target PC BIOS setup (ASRock)

    In the UEFI setup (press F2 or Del at power on):

    • Advanced > Network Stack Configuration: Network Stack = Enabled, IPv4 PXE Support = Enabled.
    • Security > Secure Boot: Disabled (the GRUB image is not signed).
    • Save, reboot, press F11 for the boot menu and pick UEFI: PXE IPv4 Realtek ....

    The PC must be cabled into the same network as this machine; PXE does not work over Wi-Fi.

    Troubleshooting

    • dnsmasq prints a PXE(enp2s0) ... proxy line when the PC asks. If nothing shows up, the PC is not on the same network or PXE is off in its BIOS.
    • If the server's IP changes, restart make netboot (the IP is built into GRUB).
    • Loading the ~68 MB of boot files over TFTP takes a little while.

    Networking

    IPv4 networking over SYS_NET: interface status, DNS, TCP clients and servers, UDP and the experimental ktls transport. Include net.h.

    Before a program can use the network the interface needs an address. Run dhcp in the terminal first; a .run program cannot do it itself (see mos_net_dhcp).

    Things to know about every call here:

    Functionsmos_net_statusmos_net_is_upmos_net_pollmos_net_resolvemos_net_lookupmos_net_dhcpmos_tcp_connectmos_tcp_sendmos_tcp_send_allmos_tcp_recvmos_tcp_recv_exactmos_tcp_statemos_tcp_closemos_tcp_listenmos_tcp_acceptmos_tcp_unlistenmos_tcp_handoffmos_udp_bindmos_udp_unbindmos_udp_recvmos_udp_recv_timeoutmos_udp_sendmos_tls_connectmos_tls_wait_establishedmos_tls_acceptmos_tls_statemos_tls_sendmos_tls_recvmos_tls_closemos_ip_parsemos_ip_to_stringmos_htonsmos_htonlmos_net_call
    • Host order. IPv4 addresses are uint32_t in host order (192.168.1.10 is 0xC0A8010A), and ports are plain numbers. You only swap bytes for values you put inside your own packets (mos_htons).
    • Polled. The kernel stack only makes progress when a process calls into it. A program that stops calling recv stops receiving. Loop with a short mos_sleep, or use the blocking helpers at the end of this page.
    • One at a time. The stack is not reentrant. A call that finds it in use by another process returns SYS_ERR_BUSY; retry it.
    • Handles. Connections, listeners, UDP bindings and TLS sessions are small positive integers in separate namespaces. They belong to the process that made them; a dead process's handles are closed the next time any process connects, listens or accepts.
    • No driver. With no network card every call except mos_net_status and mos_tcp_state returns SYS_ERR_GENERIC.

    A small HTTP client

    #include "net.h"
#include "stdio.h"

int main(void) {
    if (!mos_net_is_up()) { mos_puts("run dhcp first\n"); return 1; }
    uint32_t ip = mos_net_lookup("example.com", 5000);
    if (!ip) { mos_puts("lookup failed\n"); return 1; }

    long c = mos_tcp_connect(ip, 80, 5000);
    if (c <= 0) { printf("connect failed (%ld)\n", c); return 1; }

    const char* req = "HEAD / HTTP/1.0\r\nHost: example.com\r\n\r\n";
    uint32_t len = 0; while (req[len]) len++;
    mos_tcp_send_all(c, req, len);

    char buf[512];
    long idle = mos_uptime();
    for (;;) {
        long n = mos_tcp_recv(c, buf, sizeof buf - 1);
        if (n < 0) break;                                  /* closed */
        if (n == 0) {
            if (mos_uptime() - idle > 5000) break;
            mos_sleep(5);
            continue;
        }
        buf[n] = '\0'; mos_puts(buf); idle = mos_uptime();
    }
    mos_tcp_close(c);
    return 0;
}

    mos_net_status

    long mos_net_status(syscall_net_status_t* out);

    Reports the interface configuration. Never touches the stack, so it never returns SYS_ERR_BUSY.

    syscall_net_status_t fieldMeaning
    has_driver1 if a network card driver is loaded
    configured1 if the interface has an IPv4 address
    mac[6]MAC address
    local_ip, netmask, gateway, dnsHost-order IPv4 addresses

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL pointer.

    Example

    syscall_net_status_t st;
char ip[16];
mos_net_status(&st);
mos_ip_to_string(st.local_ip, ip);
printf("address %s\n", ip);

    mos_net_is_up

    bool mos_net_is_up(void);

    Returns true if there is a driver and the interface has an address.

    mos_net_poll

    long mos_net_poll(void);

    Processes whatever the network card has received, once. Cheap; safe in a loop. recv, accept and udp_recv already poll, so most programs never call this directly.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_BUSY, or SYS_ERR_GENERIC with no driver.

    mos_net_resolve

    long mos_net_resolve(const char* hostname, uint32_t* out_ip, uint32_t timeout_ms);

    Looks up a host name with DNS.

    ParameterDescription
    hostnameName to resolve
    out_ipReceives the host-order address
    timeout_msHow long to wait; 0 means 5000

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND if the name did not resolve, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if the interface has no address, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL argument, SYS_ERR_BUSY.

    mos_net_lookup

    uint32_t mos_net_lookup(const char* host, uint32_t timeout_ms);

    Accepts either a dotted-quad address or a host name.

    Returns the host-order address, or 0 on failure.

    Example

    uint32_t ip = mos_net_lookup(argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "10.0.2.2", 3000);

    mos_net_dhcp

    long mos_net_dhcp(uint32_t timeout_ms);

    Acquires an address with DHCP. Kernel-privileged: a .run program always gets SYS_ERR_PERM, because a lease changes the address for every process on the machine. Use the terminal's dhcp command.

    mos_tcp_connect

    long mos_tcp_connect(uint32_t ip, uint16_t port, uint32_t timeout_ms);

    Opens a TCP connection and waits for it to be established.

    ParameterDescription
    ipHost-order address, not 0
    portRemote port, not 0
    timeout_msConnect timeout; 0 means 5000

    Returns a connection handle (> 0), SYS_ERR_GENERIC if the connection failed or timed out, there is no address or no free handle, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a zero address or port, SYS_ERR_BUSY.

    mos_tcp_send

    long mos_tcp_send(long handle, const void* buf, uint32_t len);

    Sends up to 4096 bytes of buf.

    Returns the number of bytes sent, which can be fewer than len - a short count is not an error. SYS_ERR_BADFD for a bad handle, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL buffer or zero length, SYS_ERR_GENERIC on failure, SYS_ERR_BUSY.

    Notes Use mos_tcp_send_all to send a whole buffer.

    mos_tcp_send_all

    bool mos_tcp_send_all(long handle, const void* buf, uint32_t len);

    Calls mos_tcp_send until all of buf is sent.

    Returns true when everything was sent, false as soon as a send fails.

    mos_tcp_recv

    long mos_tcp_recv(long handle, void* buf, uint32_t len);

    Reads whatever has arrived, without waiting.

    Returns the number of bytes read; 0 if nothing has arrived yet; SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND once the peer has closed and everything has been read; SYS_ERR_BADFD, SYS_ERR_INVAL or SYS_ERR_BUSY.

    Notes 0 means "try again later", not end of stream. Sleep a few milliseconds between empty reads.

    mos_tcp_recv_exact

    bool mos_tcp_recv_exact(long handle, void* buf, uint32_t len, uint32_t timeout_ms);

    Reads exactly len bytes, sleeping between empty reads.

    ParameterDescription
    timeout_msGives up after this long with no new data. The timer restarts whenever data arrives

    Returns true when len bytes were read, false if the peer closed or the timeout passed.

    Example

    uint8_t header[4];
if (!mos_tcp_recv_exact(c, header, 4, 2000)) goto fail;

    mos_tcp_state

    long mos_tcp_state(long handle);

    Returns one of SYSCALL_NET_TCP_CLOSED, _CONNECTING, _ESTABLISHED, _CLOSING or _PEER_CLOSED, or SYS_ERR_BADFD. Never returns SYS_ERR_BUSY.

    mos_tcp_close

    long mos_tcp_close(long handle);

    Closes the connection and frees the handle.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_BADFD or SYS_ERR_BUSY.

    mos_tcp_listen

    long mos_tcp_listen(uint16_t port, uint32_t backlog);

    Starts accepting connections on port.

    ParameterDescription
    portLocal port, not 0. Only one listener per port machine-wide
    backlogConnections to queue before accepting; 0 for a small default. Clamped by the kernel

    Returns a listener handle (> 0), valid only for mos_tcp_accept and mos_tcp_unlisten. SYS_ERR_INVAL if the port is 0 or already has a listener, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if there is no address or no free listener slot, SYS_ERR_BUSY.

    mos_tcp_accept

    long mos_tcp_accept(long listener, uint32_t* out_ip, uint16_t* out_port);

    Takes the oldest waiting client. Never blocks.

    ParameterDescription
    listenerHandle from mos_tcp_listen
    out_ip, out_portIf not NULL, receive the client's address and port

    Returns a connection handle (> 0); 0 if nobody is waiting (or every connection handle is in use); SYS_ERR_BADFD, SYS_ERR_BUSY.

    Example

    long ls = mos_tcp_listen(8080, 0);
for (;;) {
    uint32_t ip; uint16_t port;
    long c = mos_tcp_accept(ls, &ip, &port);
    if (c > 0) { serve(c); mos_tcp_close(c); }
    else mos_sleep(10);
}

    mos_tcp_unlisten

    long mos_tcp_unlisten(long listener);

    Stops listening and frees the listener handle. Connections already accepted stay open.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_BADFD or SYS_ERR_BUSY.

    mos_tcp_handoff

    long mos_tcp_handoff(long handle, uint32_t pid);

    Gives a connection you own to another process, typically a child started with mos_exec to serve it. The connection then closes when that process dies instead of when you do.

    ParameterDescription
    handleConnection handle you own
    pidNew owner, not 0

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_PERM if you do not own the handle, SYS_ERR_BADFD, SYS_ERR_INVAL for pid 0.

    Notes The child needs nothing special: pass it the handle number on its command line and it can use it once the handoff is done. Until then the parent still owns it.

    Example

    char num[24]; /* format c into num */
const char* args[] = { num };
long pid = mos_exec("0:/programs/worker.run", args, 1);
if (pid > 0) mos_tcp_handoff(c, (uint32_t)pid);

    mos_udp_bind

    long mos_udp_bind(uint16_t local_port);

    Opens a UDP port for receiving (and as a default source port).

    Returns a UDP handle (> 0), SYS_ERR_INVAL for port 0, an error if the port is taken or all 4 bindings are in use, SYS_ERR_BUSY.

    mos_udp_unbind

    long mos_udp_unbind(long handle);

    Closes a UDP binding.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS or an error for a bad handle.

    mos_udp_recv

    long mos_udp_recv(long handle, void* buf, uint32_t len,
                  uint32_t* out_from_ip, uint16_t* out_from_port);

    Takes the next queued datagram. Polls the card first; never blocks.

    Returns the datagram's length (bytes copied), 0 if none is waiting, SYS_ERR_BADFD, SYS_ERR_INVAL, SYS_ERR_BUSY.

    Notes A datagram larger than len is truncated and the rest is lost.

    mos_udp_recv_timeout

    long mos_udp_recv_timeout(long handle, void* buf, uint32_t len,
                          uint32_t* out_from_ip, uint16_t* out_from_port,
                          uint32_t timeout_ms);

    Waits up to timeout_ms for a datagram.

    Returns its length, 0 on timeout, or a negative error.

    mos_udp_send

    long mos_udp_send(long handle, uint32_t dst_ip, uint16_t dst_port,
                  uint16_t src_port, const void* buf, uint32_t len);

    Sends one datagram.

    ParameterDescription
    handleA UDP handle; used for its port when src_port is 0
    dst_ipDestination, or SYSCALL_NET_IP_BROADCAST for 255.255.255.255
    dst_portDestination port
    src_portSource port, or 0 to use the handle's
    buf, lenPayload, 1 … 1024 bytes

    Returns len, SYS_ERR_INVAL for an empty or oversize payload or no source port, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if sending failed or there is no address, SYS_ERR_BUSY.

    Example

    long u = mos_udp_bind(40000);
mos_udp_send(u, SYSCALL_NET_IP_BROADCAST, 40000, 0, "hello?", 6);
char reply[256]; uint32_t from; uint16_t fport;
long n = mos_udp_recv_timeout(u, reply, sizeof reply, &from, &fport, 2000);

    Notes Under QEMU's -netdev user the guest is behind NAT and LAN broadcasts never reach it; use a tap or bridge network to test discovery.

    TLS 1.3 client sessions

    mos_tls13_connect(ip, port, host, timeout_ms) opens a TCP connection and completes the kernel's TLS 1.3 client handshake using host for SNI. It returns a positive owned handle or a negative SYS_ERR_* value. The TLS 1.3 client is a separate API from the KTLS transport below, which does not speak HTTPS.

    Use mos_tls13_send(handle, buf, len) to send encrypted data (up to 4096 bytes per call), mos_tls13_recv(handle, buf, len, timeout_ms) to receive data, and mos_tls13_close(handle) to close the session. Handles are owned by the creating process and reclaimed if that process exits.

    The current TLS 1.3 client does not authenticate server certificates. It encrypts traffic but cannot establish the server's identity, so applications must not use it for credentials or other sensitive data.

    mos_tls_connect

    long mos_tls_connect(uint32_t ip, uint16_t port, uint32_t timeout_ms);

    Opens a ktls session: a TCP connection plus a hello. The handshake finishes in the background.

    Returns a TLS handle (> 0) or a negative error.

    Notes ktls is a transport shape, not real TLS: there are no certificates and the session key crosses the wire in the clear. It does not talk to ordinary HTTPS servers and gives no security. (The terminal's wget uses the kernel's separate TLS 1.3 client.)

    mos_tls_wait_established

    bool mos_tls_wait_established(long handle, uint32_t timeout_ms);

    Polls mos_tls_state until the handshake completes.

    Returns true when established, false if it failed or timeout_ms passed.

    mos_tls_accept

    long mos_tls_accept(long tcp_handle);

    Turns a TCP connection you own into a server-side ktls session.

    Returns a TLS handle (> 0) or a negative error. On success the TCP handle must no longer be used (closing the TLS handle closes it); on failure it is still yours.

    mos_tls_state

    long mos_tls_state(long handle);

    Advances the handshake and reports the session state.

    Returns SYSCALL_NET_TLS_CLOSED (failed or closed), SYSCALL_NET_TLS_HANDSHAKING or SYSCALL_NET_TLS_ESTABLISHED, or a negative error (SYS_ERR_BUSY: retry).

    mos_tls_send

    long mos_tls_send(long handle, const void* buf, uint32_t len);

    Returns bytes sent (at most 4096 per call; short counts are normal), SYS_ERR_AGAIN while the handshake is still running, SYS_ERR_BUSY.

    mos_tls_recv

    long mos_tls_recv(long handle, void* buf, uint32_t len);

    Returns bytes read, 0 if nothing has arrived, SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND once the session is closed and drained.

    mos_tls_close

    long mos_tls_close(long handle);

    Closes the session and its TCP connection.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS or a negative error.

    mos_ip_parse

    uint32_t mos_ip_parse(const char* dotted);

    Parses "a.b.c.d".

    Returns the host-order address, or 0 if the string is not exactly four decimal octets of 0-255.

    Example

    uint32_t gw = mos_ip_parse("10.0.2.2");   /* 0x0A000202 */

    mos_ip_to_string

    void mos_ip_to_string(uint32_t ip, char* out);

    Formats a host-order address as dotted decimal. out must hold at least 16 bytes.

    mos_htons

    uint16_t mos_htons(uint16_t v);

    Swaps the bytes of a 16-bit value (host to network order). mos_ntohs is the same function. Only needed for fields inside your own packet formats.

    mos_htonl

    uint32_t mos_htonl(uint32_t v);

    Swaps the bytes of a 32-bit value. mos_ntohl is the same function.

    mos_net_call

    long mos_net_call(syscall_net_request_t* request);

    Issues SYS_NET with a filled syscall_net_request_t. Every function on this page builds a zeroed request, sets op and the fields that operation uses, and calls this.

    Formatted output

    printf from stdio.h and std::cout from iostream. Both are header-only and write to stdout through mos_write.

    Functionsprintfmos_vprintfstd::cout

    printf

    long printf(const char* format, ...);

    Formats its arguments and writes the result to stdout.

    ParameterDescription
    formatFormat string
    ...One argument per conversion

    Supported conversions:

    ConversionArgumentOutput
    %d, %iintSigned decimal
    %uunsigned intUnsigned decimal
    %x, %Xunsigned intHexadecimal, lower or upper case
    %ldlongSigned decimal
    %luunsigned longUnsigned decimal
    %cintOne character
    %sconst char*String; NULL prints (null)
    %%noneA %

    Returns the number of bytes written.

    Notes

    • There are no flags, widths or precisions (%5d, %-10s, %02x), no floating point and no %p or %lx. An unsupported conversion is printed as is.
    • To print a 64-bit value in hex, split it: printf("%x%x", (unsigned)(v >> 32), (unsigned)v) (pad the low half yourself), or format it into a buffer by hand.
    • There is no sprintf. Build strings by hand or with string.h.
    • Output is buffered in 128-byte chunks inside one call, so a single printf is one or a few mos_write calls.

    Example

    printf("%s: %d of %u done (%ld ms)\n", name, done, total, mos_uptime() - start);

    mos_vprintf

    long mos_vprintf(const char* format, va_list args);

    The va_list form of printf, for writing your own logging functions.

    Example

    static void logf(const char* fmt, ...) {
    va_list ap;
    va_start(ap, fmt);
    mos_puts("[app] ");
    mos_vprintf(fmt, ap);
    va_end(ap);
}

    std::cout

    namespace std { class ostream; static ostream cout; }
ostream& operator<<(const char*);
ostream& operator<<(char);
ostream& operator<<(int);
ostream& operator<<(unsigned int);
ostream& operator<<(long);
ostream& operator<<(unsigned long);
ostream& operator<<(bool);

    A minimal std::cout for C++ programs. Include <iostream>.

    Notes

    • bool prints true or false; a NULL const char* prints (null).
    • There is no std::endl, manipulators, std::string or std::cin. Write "\n" for a newline.

    Example

    #include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::cout << "2 + 2 = " << 2 + 2 << "\n";
    return 0;
}

    Packages

    .mpkg archives over SYS_PKG. Include minimalos.h.

    An .mpkg holds files and directories, stored or LZSS-compressed. The terminal's pkg command and the dlr package client use the same calls.

    Functionsmos_pkg_unzipmos_pkg_zipmos_pkg_info

    mos_pkg_unzip

    long mos_pkg_unzip(const char* archive_path, const char* target_dir,
                   uint32_t* out_installed, uint32_t* out_failed);

    Extracts an archive into a directory.

    ParameterDescription
    archive_pathThe .mpkg file
    target_dirDirectory to extract into, for example "0:/"
    out_installedIf not NULL, receives the number of entries extracted
    out_failedIf not NULL, receives the number of entries that failed

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS if the archive was processed, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if it could not be read, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL path or target.

    Notes Success means the archive was read; individual entries can still fail (invalid names are rejected, for one). Check out_failed.

    Example

    uint32_t ok = 0, bad = 0;
if (mos_pkg_unzip("0:/downloads/app.mpkg", "0:/", &ok, &bad) == 0)
    printf("installed %u entries, %u failed\n", ok, bad);

    mos_pkg_zip

    long mos_pkg_zip(const char* source_path, const char* algorithm,
                 char* out_path, uint32_t out_path_size);

    Archives a file or directory as <source_path>.mpkg.

    ParameterDescription
    source_pathFile or directory to pack
    algorithm"lzss", "store", or NULL for the default (LZSS)
    out_pathIf not NULL, receives the path of the archive written
    out_path_sizeSize of out_path

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_GENERIC on failure, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL source.

    Example

    char made[128];
if (mos_pkg_zip("0:/projects/game", NULL, made, sizeof made) == 0)
    printf("wrote %s\n", made);

    mos_pkg_info

    long mos_pkg_info(const char* archive_path, uint32_t* out_entry_count);

    Reads an archive's entry count without extracting it.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if the archive is invalid, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL path.

    Process and terminal

    Terminal output, ending the program, time, sleeping, process IDs, launching other programs and the Ctrl+C cleanup hook. Include minimalos.h.

    Functionsmos_writemos_write_fdmos_write_textmos_putsmos_exitmos_exit_withmos_exit_codemos_getpidmos_uptimemos_sleepmos_gettimemos_register_cleanupmos_execmos_pslistmos_getcwdmos_syscallmos_syscall3mos_syscall1

    mos_write

    long mos_write(int fd, const void* buf, size_t len);   /* form 1 */
long mos_write(const char* text, uint64_t len);        /* form 2 */

    Writes bytes to the terminal. mos_write is a macro that picks a form by argument count: three arguments call mos_write_fd, two call mos_write_text (always stdout).

    ParameterDescription
    fd1 (stdout) or 2 (stderr). Both go to the terminal and the serial log
    buf / textBytes to write. Not required to be NUL-terminated
    lenNumber of bytes

    Returns len on success, SYS_ERR_BADFD for any other fd, SYS_ERR_INVAL if buf is NULL.

    Notes

    • To write to a file use mos_fwrite; mos_write only reaches the terminal.
    • Inside mosWM the terminal is the Terminal window that launched the program.

    Example

    mos_write(1, "ready\n", 6);
mos_write("also stdout\n", 12);

    mos_write_fd

    long mos_write_fd(int fd, const void* buf, size_t len);

    The three-argument form of mos_write, as a function. Useful where a macro cannot go, such as taking its address.

    Returns the same values as mos_write.

    mos_write_text

    long mos_write_text(const char* text, uint64_t length);

    Writes length bytes of text to stdout. The two-argument form of mos_write.

    mos_puts

    long mos_puts(const char* str);

    Writes a NUL-terminated string to stdout. No newline is added, unlike the C library's puts.

    ParameterDescription
    strNUL-terminated string. Must not be NULL

    Returns the number of bytes written.

    Example

    mos_puts("Hello, Minimal-OS!\n");

    mos_exit

    void mos_exit(int code);   /* noreturn */
void mos_exit(void);       /* exit code 0 */

    Ends the calling process. Never returns. A macro over mos_exit_with: mos_exit() with no argument exits with code 0.

    ParameterDescription
    codeExit status. Only the low 8 bits are reported; the terminal prints [exited with code N] for a non-zero code

    Notes

    • Global destructors (.fini_array) do not run. Release resources yourself, or from a cleanup callback.
    • The kernel closes the process's windows, network handles and heap blocks when it reaps it, but files should be closed explicitly so their data is flushed.
    • Returning from main calls mos_exit with the return value.

    Example

    if (!buffer) {
    mos_puts("out of memory\n");
    mos_exit(1);
}

    mos_exit_with

    __attribute__((noreturn)) void mos_exit_with(int code);

    The function behind mos_exit. Issues SYS_EXIT and never returns.

    mos_exit_code

    void mos_exit_code(uint8_t code);

    Older spelling from x86_64/user_syscalls.h. Same effect as mos_exit(code).

    mos_getpid

    long mos_getpid(void);

    Returns the PID of the calling process.

    Notes A server passes this, or a child's PID from mos_exec, to mos_tcp_handoff.

    mos_uptime

    long mos_uptime(void);

    Returns the time since boot in milliseconds.

    Notes Use it to measure intervals and frame times. For wall-clock time see mos_gettime.

    Example

    long start = mos_uptime();
do_work();
printf("took %ld ms\n", mos_uptime() - start);

    mos_sleep

    long mos_sleep(long ms);

    Puts the process to sleep for at least ms milliseconds and lets other processes run.

    ParameterDescription
    msMilliseconds to sleep. 0 returns at once

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS.

    Notes

    • Call it in every polling loop (window events, network receive, accept) so the program does not spin a core at 100%.
    • A frame loop typically sleeps 10-16 ms per frame.

    Example

    for (;;) {
    handle_events();
    draw_frame();
    mos_sleep(16);   /* about 60 frames per second */
}

    mos_gettime

    long mos_gettime(void);

    Wrapper for SYS_GETTIME, the real-time clock.

    Returns SYS_ERR_INVAL with the current kernel: SYS_GETTIME expects a pointer to a datetime_t in rdi, and this wrapper passes none.

    Notes Until the wrapper takes a buffer, call the syscall directly with a structure laid out like the kernel's datetime_t:

    typedef struct {
    uint16_t year;
    uint8_t month, day;           /* 1-12, 1-31 */
    uint8_t hour, minute, second; /* 0-23, 0-59, 0-59 */
} mos_datetime_t;

mos_datetime_t now;
if (mos_syscall(SYS_GETTIME, (long)(uintptr_t)&now, 0, 0) == 0)
    printf("%d-%d-%d %d:%d\n", now.year, now.month, now.day, now.hour, now.minute);

    mos_register_cleanup

    long mos_register_cleanup(void (*cleanup)(void));

    Registers a function the kernel calls when the user presses Ctrl+C in the terminal running this program.

    ParameterDescription
    cleanupFunction to call. Must not be NULL

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL callback.

    Notes

    • The callback runs on the program's next syscall after Ctrl+C. It should save what it needs and call mos_exit().
    • If the program has not exited one second after Ctrl+C, the kernel terminates it. A second Ctrl+C within 800 ms terminates it at once.
    • Without a callback, Ctrl+C terminates the program immediately.
    • Registering again replaces the previous callback.

    Example

    static long log_fd;

static void on_ctrl_c(void) {
    mos_fwrite(log_fd, "interrupted\n", 12);
    mos_close(log_fd);
    mos_exit(130);
}

int main(void) {
    log_fd = mos_open("0:/tmp/log.txt", SYS_O_RDWR);
    mos_register_cleanup(on_ctrl_c);
    for (;;) mos_sleep(100);
}

    mos_exec

    long mos_exec(const char* path, const char** argv, long argc);

    Starts another .run bundle as a new process, the way the terminal's run command does. Does not wait for it.

    ParameterDescription
    pathPath of the .run file
    argvExtra arguments. The child sees path as argv[0] and these from argv[1] on. May be NULL when argc is 0
    argcNumber of entries in argv, at most 16

    Returns the new process's PID, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL or invalid path or more than 16 arguments, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if the program could not be loaded.

    Example

    const char* args[] = { "--port", "8080" };
long pid = mos_exec("0:/programs/server.run", args, 2);
if (pid < 0) printf("could not start server (%ld)\n", pid);

    mos_pslist

    long mos_pslist(syscall_process_info_t* entries, size_t max_entries);

    Copies a snapshot of the process list into a caller buffer.

    ParameterDescription
    entriesArray to fill
    max_entriesCapacity of entries

    Returns the number of entries written (0 if entries is NULL or max_entries is 0).

    Each syscall_process_info_t holds:

    FieldMeaning
    pidProcess ID
    name[128]Process name, NUL-terminated
    stateSYSCALL_PROC_STATE_READY, _RUNNING, _WAITING, _PAUSED, _ZOMBIE or _TERMINATED
    privilegeSYSCALL_PROC_PRIV_KERNEL or SYSCALL_PROC_PRIV_USER
    sched_cpuCore the scheduler assigned
    sched_levelScheduler queue level

    Example

    syscall_process_info_t procs[32];
long n = mos_pslist(procs, 32);
for (long i = 0; i < n; i++)
    printf("%lu %s\n", (unsigned long)procs[i].pid, procs[i].name);

    mos_getcwd

    long mos_getcwd(char* path, size_t path_size);

    Copies the terminal's current directory, which relative paths are resolved against.

    ParameterDescription
    pathOutput buffer
    path_sizeSize of path in bytes, including room for the NUL

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_INVAL if the buffer is NULL or too small.

    Example

    char cwd[256];
if (mos_getcwd(cwd, sizeof cwd) == 0) printf("in %s\n", cwd);

    mos_syscall

    long mos_syscall(long num, long a1, long a2, long a3);

    Issues syscall num with up to three arguments. Every other wrapper is built on this (or on mos_syscall3). Use it for calls that have no wrapper yet.

    ParameterDescription
    numA SYS_* number from syscall.h
    a1, a2, a3Arguments for rdi, rsi, rdx; pass 0 for unused ones

    Returns the raw rax value.

    uint64_t mos_syscall3(uint64_t number, uint64_t arg1, uint64_t arg2, uint64_t arg3);

    Same as mos_syscall with unsigned types, from x86_64/user_syscalls.h.

    mos_storage_list

    long mos_storage_list(syscall_storage_device_t* devices, uint32_t capacity);

    Fills devices with every disk, each followed by its partitions, and returns how many there are (which can be more than capacity). Read-only; any program may call it.

    name, parentsata0, nvme0p2; partitions name their disk

    Running kernel commands as root

    long mos_root_auth(const char* username, const char* password);
long mos_root_run(const char* command);
long mos_root_read(char* out, size_t out_size);

    mos_root_auth checks the password of the MOSdesk account and gives the process a ticket for a few minutes (SYS_ERR_PERM when wrong). mos_root_run starts a kernel terminal command such as install sata1 --yes; one command runs at a time. mos_root_read appends the command's output to out and returns 1 while it still runs, 0 once it has finished. The MOSdesk Installer is built this way.

    Strings and memory

    Freestanding string and memory helpers. Include string.h. None of these make a syscall.

    memcpy, memmove, memset and memcmp are real functions defined in crt0.c, because the compiler emits calls to them on its own (struct assignment, = {0} initialisers); the rest are static inline.

    Functionsstrlenstrcmpstrncmpstrcpystrlcpy_safestrchrstrrchrstrstrmemcpymemmovememsetmemcmpmos_memcmpmos_memeq_ct

    strlen

    size_t strlen(const char* s);

    Returns the number of bytes before the terminating NUL.

    strcmp

    int strcmp(const char* a, const char* b);

    Compares two strings byte by byte as unsigned char.

    Returns 0 if they are equal, a negative value if a sorts first, a positive value if b does.

    Example

    if (argc > 1 && strcmp(argv[1], "--help") == 0) usage();

    strncmp

    int strncmp(const char* a, const char* b, size_t n);

    Like strcmp but compares at most n bytes.

    Example

    if (strncmp(line, "GET ", 4) == 0) handle_get(line + 4);

    strcpy

    char* strcpy(char* dst, const char* src);

    Copies src, including its NUL, into dst.

    Returns dst.

    Notes Does not check the size of dst. Prefer strlcpy_safe.

    strlcpy_safe

    char* strlcpy_safe(char* dst, const char* src, size_t size);

    Copies at most size - 1 bytes of src and always NUL-terminates, truncating if src does not fit. Unlike the C library's strncpy, it never leaves dst unterminated and never pads with zeros.

    ParameterDescription
    dstDestination buffer
    srcNUL-terminated source
    sizeSize of dst in bytes. 0 copies nothing

    Returns dst.

    Example

    char name[16];
strlcpy_safe(name, argv[1], sizeof name);

    strchr

    char* strchr(const char* s, int c);

    Returns a pointer to the first c in s, or NULL. Searching for '\0' returns a pointer to the terminator.

    strrchr

    char* strrchr(const char* s, int c);

    Returns a pointer to the last c in s, or NULL.

    Example

    const char* slash = strrchr(path, '/');
const char* file = slash ? slash + 1 : path;

    strstr

    char* strstr(const char* haystack, const char* needle);

    Returns a pointer to the first occurrence of needle in haystack, haystack itself if needle is empty, or NULL.

    memcpy

    void* memcpy(void* dst, const void* src, size_t n);

    Copies n bytes. The ranges must not overlap; use memmove if they might.

    Returns dst.

    memmove

    void* memmove(void* dst, const void* src, size_t n);

    Copies n bytes; the ranges may overlap.

    Returns dst.

    Example

    /* shift an array one slot right */
memmove(&items[1], &items[0], (count - 1) * sizeof items[0]);

    memset

    void* memset(void* dst, int value, size_t n);

    Sets n bytes to (unsigned char)value.

    Returns dst.

    memcmp

    int memcmp(const void* a, const void* b, size_t n);

    Compares n bytes.

    Returns 0 if equal, otherwise the difference of the first differing bytes.

    Notes Stops at the first difference, so its timing reveals where the inputs differ. For secrets use mos_memeq_ct.

    mos_memcmp

    int mos_memcmp(const void* a, const void* b, size_t n);

    An inline copy of memcmp with the same result.

    mos_memeq_ct

    int mos_memeq_ct(const void* a, const void* b, size_t n);

    Compares n bytes in constant time: it always reads every byte, whatever the contents.

    Returns 1 if the ranges are equal, 0 if not. Note the sense is the opposite of memcmp.

    Notes Use it for authentication tags, MACs and password hashes. An early-exit comparison leaks how many leading bytes matched, which is enough to forge a tag one byte at a time.

    Example

    if (!mos_memeq_ct(tag, expected_tag, 16)) reject();

    System-call pointer arguments

    Every pointer a program passes to the kernel, and how the kernel checks it. Programs run in ring 3; the kernel dereferences their pointers directly while running on the program's page tables. A pointer that is not the program's own memory must come back as an error (SYS_ERR_INVAL unless noted) before the call has any effect, and never as a kernel-mode page fault.

    On this pageThe checksTableNot fixed, and whyFGPU and SYS_MEDIA: do they keep program pointers?Cost of the checks

    The checks

    HelperWhereUse
    syscall_user_range_ok(ptr, len, write)syscall.c, declared in x86_64/user_ptr.h[ptr, ptr+len) is the program's (SYS_HEAP block, image, stack, SYS_VM mapping with the right protection); gives uvm pages their frame. NULL and len == 0 are false.
    syscall_user_str_ok(s, max)sameNUL-terminated string of at most max bytes (NUL included), page by page.
    syscall_user_copy_in/out(...)samerange check plus memcpy; used to take one kernel copy of a request struct.
    proc_user_strlen(s, max, &len)spawn.cwhat syscall_user_str_ok uses.
    syscall_resolve_path(...)syscall.cevery path syscall goes through it; it checks the string (MINIMAFS_MAX_PATH).

    All of them accept anything for kernel-privilege callers (isCurrentProcessUser() false): kernel code calls many syscalls with kernel pointers.

    Rules used throughout: output (kernel writes) means write = true; where programs have always been free to pass a capacity larger than their buffer, only the bytes the kernel really writes are checked (SYS_READ: what is left in the file; SYS_LISTDIR/SYS_PSLIST: the entries found; SYS_GETCWD: the string; SYS_NET UDP/TCP send: the slice sent); a request struct holding pointers is copied into a kernel local first and the nested pointers are checked and used from the copy (no double fetch). Results are written back to the program only after the checks.

    Table

    "Before" says what was checked before this audit; "now" is the state after it.

    SYS_OPEN, EXISTS, IS_DIR, MKDIR, DELETE, RMDIR, GET_METADATA path, LISTDIR path, STAT path, RENAME from/to, CHDIR, GETCWDpath stringreadNUL, MINIMAFS_MAX_PATHSTAT, RENAME, EXEC, CHDIR onlyall, in syscall_resolve_path
    SYS_CREATEpath; type, format strings (optional)readNULnonepath, type, format
    SYS_READbufwritemin(len, bytes left in file)nonechecked (position unchanged on error)
    SYS_FWRITEbufread(uint32_t)lennonechecked
    SYS_LISTDIRoutwriteentries found (<= max_entries, <= MINIMAFS_MAX_ROOT_ENTRIES)nonechecked after listing, before writing
    SYS_STAToutwritesizeof(syscall_stat_t)yesyes
    SYS_GET_METADATAoutwritesizeof(syscall_file_metadata_t)nonechecked
    SYS_GETCWDoutwritestrlen(cwd)+1 (capacity may be larger)yesyes
    SYS_GETTIMEoutwritesizeof(datetime_t)nonechecked
    SYS_RANDOMbufwritelennonechecked
    SYS_PSLISToutwriteentries written (<= max_entries)nonechecked
    SYS_PKGrequest; path, extra strings; out_path (size out_path_size); out_count, out_failedread; writeNUL / givennonerequest copied, all checked before the op
    SYS_EXECpath; argv[argc] (argc <= 16); each argv stringreadNUL / argcyesyes; argv pointer array copied once
    SYS_SPAWNrequest; path, argv[] + strings, envp[] + strings, cwd, stdout_path, stderr_pathreadNUL / argcyes (copied into the kernel)unchanged
    SYS_WAIToutwritesizeof(syscall_wait_t)yesyes
    SYS_VM maprequestreadsizeofyesyes (copy)
    SYS_VM unmap/protect/decommitaddress range-lenby uvm itself (not dereferenced)unchanged
    SYS_THREAD create / create_exrequest (entry, stack, exit futex are checked in proc_create_thread_ex)readsizeofyesyes (copy)
    SYS_FUTEXuint32_t*read (wait) / key only (wake)4, alignedyesunchanged

    SYS_GRAPHICSrequest; INFO info (write); BLIT blit (read) and blit->src (read); TEXT / MEASURE_TEXT text (<= 64 KiB), out_width, out_height (write)sizeof, src_pitch * src_h, NULrequest, INFO, BLIT srcrequest and BLIT copied; TEXT, MEASURE_TEXT added
    SYS_USB KEYBOARD_INFOarg1writesizeof(syscall_usb_keyboard_info_t)nonechecked
    SYS_MOUSE GET_STATEarg1writesizeof(syscall_mouse_state_t)nonechecked

    SYS_WINDOWrequest; PRESENT pixels (read); GET_INFO info, LIST windows, NEXT_EVENT event (write); GET_FRAME frame struct (read) and frame->pixels (write); POST_EVENT event (read)formulas in sys_window_implyesyes; request, frame struct and posted event copied
    SYS_GPUrequest; INFO out; UPLOAD_BUFFER, CREATE_PROGRAM, SUBMIT, WRITE_SURFACE data (read); READBACK out (write)bytes, pitch*(h-1)+rowyesyes; request copied once, only handle is written back
    SYS_MEDIArequest; DECODE_TILES frame (read), pixels (write); CONVERT_YCBCR planes struct and planes; DECODE_H264 frame struct, data, pixelsframe_bytes, w*h*4, plane sizesyesyes; request copied; tile frame copied into the kernel (see FGPU/media below)
    SYS_STORAGErequest; LIST deviceswritecapacity * sizeofyesyes; fields read once
    SYS_AUDIOrequest (path inline, status out)in/outsizeofyes (gate)yes; kernel copy, copied back
    SYS_AUDIO_MIXERrequestin/outsizeofyes (gate)yes; kernel copy, copied back
    SYS_AUDIO_STREAMrequest; WRITE samplesreadframes * channels * 2yesyes; request copied (frames validated = frames used)
    SYS_NETrequest; per op: out_status, out_handle, out_ip, out_from_ip, out_from_port (write), buf send (read) / recv (write), host (string <= 256)slice sizes, NET_UDP_DGRAM_MAX, sizeof(syscall_net_adapters_t)none (the gate even read req->op unchecked)request copied, every op's pointers checked before it runs
    SYS_ROOTrequest (inline strings, output buffer)in/outsizeofyesyes; kernel copy (heap), copied back
    SYS_TIMESYNCrequest (inline url, error)in/outsizeofyesyes; kernel copy (heap), copied back
    SYS_MANAGER, SYS_SYSINFO, SYS_CLOCK, SYS_SLEEP, SYS_UPTIME, SYS_GETPID, SYS_EXIT, SYS_POWER, SYS_SEEK/SIZE/TELL/EOF/CLOSEno pointers (file handles: see below)

    Not fixed, and why

    • File handles are kernel pointers. SYS_OPEN returns a minimafs_file_handle_t* and SYS_READ, SYS_FWRITE, SYS_CLOSE, SYS_SEEK, SYS_SIZE, SYS_TELL, SYS_EOF take it back unchecked. A program can forge one and make the kernel read or write there. Closing it needs a handle table (small integers owned by the process, like the SYS_NET handles); that changes the ABI value programs see, so it is a redesign, not part of this audit.
    • SYS_REGISTER_CLEANUP runs program code in ring 0. syscall_dispatch_inner calls cleanup_entry() on the kernel stack. The entry is now required to be executable program memory (so it cannot be an unmapped address that would fault), but the call itself still gives the program ring-0 execution. The fix is to deliver the cleanup as an upcall into ring 3.
    • Races with a sibling thread. Checks happen once, then the kernel uses the memory. A second thread of the same program can SYS_VM_UNMAP or SYS_VM_PROTECT a checked range between the check and the access. Requests and nested pointer values are copied, so *values* cannot change, but memory can disappear. Closing this needs fault-tolerant copies (an exception table for kernel-mode faults inside a syscall) or the uvm lock held across the call. Windows where the kernel holds a spinlock while touching program memory (window manager) are the worst case.
    • Strings are checked in place, not copied (paths, TEXT, host names, argv strings): the length is validated but the bytes are read again later. An unterminated rewrite by a sibling thread could make a kernel read run on; all consumers are bounded by their own buffers except graphics_write_text and graphics_measure_text.
    • SYS_EXEC: argv strings are checked, but proc_exec_inherit reads them from the program's memory again.
    • SYS_NET TCP/UDP handles are small integers with owner checks only for TLS; tcp_slot_get does not compare owners for send/recv/close. Not a pointer issue.

    FGPU and SYS_MEDIA: do they keep program pointers?

    • FGPU (fgpu.c) copies at call time: command streams (SUBMIT) and shader blobs (CREATE_PROGRAM) go into kernel buffers, uploads are memcpyed into surface/buffer memory, readback is written before the call returns. Surfaces, buffers and programs live in kernel memory (or VRAM). The workers started by smp_par_run only touch those kernel copies. No program pointer is kept beyond the call. What was wrong: the request struct was read from program memory throughout a call that runs with interrupts enabled, so bytes could change between its check and the memcpy. The request is now copied once.
    • SYS_MEDIA DECODE_TILES did hand program memory to the parallel workers: each tile job pointed into the program's frame, and the workers run on the kernel's page tables, where memory above 4 GiB does not exist. The frame is now copied into a kernel buffer first (pixels already went through one). The CONVERT_YCBCR and DECODE_H264 paths (NVIDIA hardware only, not run in QEMU) read the planes / slice data on the calling core, with the program's page tables, and are unchanged apart from the request copy.

    Cost of the checks

    syscall_user_range_ok on heap memory walks the process's allocation list; on uvm memory it walks the area list and the page tables per page. Per call:

    • SYS_GPU, SYS_WINDOW, SYS_INPUT_READ, SYS_MEDIA, SYS_STORAGE, SYS_AUDIO*: one request check (gates that used to check the same struct a second time were removed) plus one per nested buffer. Image/blit buffers are large (a frame): that is O(pages) once per call, as before.
    • SYS_GRAPHICS: the gate still checks the request (it needs op) and sys_graphics_impl copies it again: two small checks.
    • SYS_READ / SYS_FWRITE / SYS_WRITE: one check of the buffer; SYS_READ also asks the handle for size and position (two field reads).
    • SYS_NET: one for the request, one or two for buffers.
    • Strings walk byte by byte for NUL but check the range once per page.
    • Largest added cost: SYS_NET (new), SYS_LISTDIR (after the listing, under the listing lock), SYS_ROOT / SYS_TIMESYNC / SYS_AUDIO* (a heap copy, not hot).

    System information

    Machine-wide statistics over SYS_SYSINFO. Include user_sysinfo.h. Every call is allowed for user programs, returns a uint64_t, and returns SYS_ERR_INVAL for an unknown query.

    Example - a one-line status bar:

    Functionsmos_sysinfo_cpu_usagemos_sysinfo_core_usagemos_sysinfo_core_countmos_sysinfo_ram_totalmos_sysinfo_ram_usedmos_sysinfo_ram_freemos_sysinfo_heap_usedmos_sysinfo_heap_freemos_sysinfo_pmm_used_pagesmos_sysinfo_pmm_free_pagesmos_sysinfo_uptime_msmos_sysinfo_process_countmos_sysinfo
    #include "user_sysinfo.h"
#include "stdio.h"

int main(void) {
    printf("cpu %lu%%  ram %lu/%lu MiB  %lu cores  %lu procs  up %lu s\n",
           (unsigned long)mos_sysinfo_cpu_usage(),
           (unsigned long)(mos_sysinfo_ram_used() >> 20),
           (unsigned long)(mos_sysinfo_ram_total() >> 20),
           (unsigned long)mos_sysinfo_core_count(),
           (unsigned long)mos_sysinfo_process_count(),
           (unsigned long)(mos_sysinfo_uptime_ms() / 1000));
    return 0;
}

    mos_sysinfo_cpu_usage

    uint64_t mos_sysinfo_cpu_usage(void);

    Returns average CPU usage across all online cores, in percent (0-100).

    mos_sysinfo_core_usage

    uint64_t mos_sysinfo_core_usage(uint32_t core_id);

    Returns the usage of one core in percent, or SYS_ERR_INVAL if core_id is out of range or that core is not online.

    Example

    uint64_t cores = mos_sysinfo_core_count();
for (uint32_t i = 0; i < cores; i++)
    printf("core %u: %lu%%\n", i, (unsigned long)mos_sysinfo_core_usage(i));

    mos_sysinfo_core_count

    uint64_t mos_sysinfo_core_count(void);

    Returns the number of online cores.

    mos_sysinfo_ram_total

    uint64_t mos_sysinfo_ram_total(void);

    Returns total RAM in bytes.

    mos_sysinfo_ram_used

    uint64_t mos_sysinfo_ram_used(void);

    Returns RAM in use in bytes: kernel heap in use plus physical pages in use. An approximation.

    mos_sysinfo_ram_free

    uint64_t mos_sysinfo_ram_free(void);

    Returns ram_total - ram_used, or 0 if the estimate of used memory exceeds the total.

    mos_sysinfo_heap_used

    uint64_t mos_sysinfo_heap_used(void);

    Returns bytes allocated from the kernel heap, which also backs every program's malloc.

    mos_sysinfo_heap_free

    uint64_t mos_sysinfo_heap_free(void);

    Returns free bytes in the kernel heap.

    mos_sysinfo_pmm_used_pages

    uint64_t mos_sysinfo_pmm_used_pages(void);

    Returns physical 4 KiB pages in use.

    mos_sysinfo_pmm_free_pages

    uint64_t mos_sysinfo_pmm_free_pages(void);

    Returns free physical 4 KiB pages.

    mos_sysinfo_uptime_ms

    uint64_t mos_sysinfo_uptime_ms(void);

    Returns milliseconds since boot, the same value as mos_uptime.

    mos_sysinfo_process_count

    uint64_t mos_sysinfo_process_count(void);

    Returns the number of processes. To list them use mos_pslist.

    mos_sysinfo

    uint64_t mos_sysinfo(uint64_t op);

    Issues SYS_SYSINFO with a SYS_SYSINFO_* query, or SYS_SYSINFO_CORE_USAGE_BASE + core_id for one core. The functions above wrap it.

    Testing

    Minimal-OS has host-side unit tests, QEMU boot checks, interactive serial tests, and focused integration scripts. Pick the narrowest test that exercises the changed behavior, then add a boot test when the change crosses into kernel startup or device integration.

    On this pageHost-side testsQEMU boot smoke testOS0 self-test in QEMUFarcadeGL screenshot test (ci_fglcube.sh)Interactive serial testFocused integration checksChoose a test by changeWhen a test fails

    Host-side tests

    Run the C tests that do not require a guest OS:

    make test-host

    The target builds and runs:

    Test binaryMain coverage
    gfx_blit_testsFramebuffer blit and graphics helper behavior
    fgpu_raster_testsFGPU rasterizer and shader execution
    fgpu_bin_testsBinned rasterizer against the immediate one (see below)
    fgsl_testsFGSL shader compilation and execution path
    fgpu_ir_testsFGPU intermediate representation
    fgpu_jit_testsShader JIT (SSE4.1 and AVX2 machine code) against the interpreter, bit for bit: per-opcode edge cases, real FGSL shaders, a differential fuzzer, safety and negative tests. A path the host CPU lacks is skipped with a message
    nv_hw_testsNVIDIA firmware, VBIOS, and resource-manager data parsing
    hid_mouse_testsHID mouse report decoding
    media_testsHost-testable media interfaces
    os0_testsOS0 host helpers: time conversion, path resolution and the program argument block

    These are ordinary host binaries under build/tests/host. The Makefile uses HOSTCC (default gcc) and HOST_CFLAGS for their compilation.

    Shader JIT checks

    make test-host                       # includes fgpu_jit_tests (a few seconds)
make fuzz-fgpu-jit FUZZ_SECONDS=300  # longer differential fuzzing (FUZZ_SEED=n to change the seed)
make bench-fgpu-jit                  # interpreter vs SSE4.1 vs AVX2, lane-instructions/s (not part of test-host)
FGPU_JIT_DUMP=1 build/tests/host/fgpu_jit_tests --soak 20   # on a failure: shrunk program + listing

    In QEMU (TCG), the JIT needs a CPU with SSE4.1 and AVX2: -cpu max; the default qemu64 CPU has neither, so the shader JIT stays off there.

    QEMU_EXTRA="-cpu max -smp 4" bash tools/debug/ci_fgpu_jit.sh   # `gpu jit`: interpreter vs JIT in the kernel, also on helper cores
bash tools/debug/ci_fgpu_jit.sh                                 # default CPU: reports SKIP
GRUB_UP=3 QEMU_EXTRA="-cpu max" bash tools/debug/ci_fgpu_jit.sh # the nojit entry: reports SKIP
SHOT=/tmp/a.ppm QEMU_EXTRA="-cpu max -smp 4" bash tools/debug/ci_fgpu_jit_cube.sh   # fglcube --shader --still screendump
SHOT=/tmp/b.ppm GRUB_UP=3 QEMU_EXTRA="-cpu max -smp 4" bash tools/debug/ci_fgpu_jit_cube.sh && cmp /tmp/a.ppm /tmp/b.ppm

    QEMU boot smoke test

    make ci-test

    This builds the ISO, launches a headless QEMU guest with 512 MiB of memory, and waits up to 60 seconds for known boot markers on the serial console. It writes ci_serial.log in the repository root and exits nonzero if no marker appears. It verifies that the image reaches a basic boot milestone; it does not validate every device or command.

    Required host tools include the normal kernel build dependencies and qemu-system-x86_64.

    OS0 self-test in QEMU

    make ci-os0

    This builds the ISO, boots it headless in QEMU (2 CPUs, 1024 MiB, KVM only if /dev/kvm is writable, otherwise TCG) and selects the "Minimal-OS (RamFS)" GRUB entry through the QEMU monitor, so no disk image is needed: 0: is a RAM disk filled from the embedded package, including 0:/programs/os0test.run. Once === TERMINAL READY === appears (up to 120 seconds) the script types run 0:/programs/os0test.run over the serial port, which the terminal reads like keyboard input, and waits up to 600 seconds for a line ending in OS0TEST PASS or OS0TEST FAIL in the serial log. The log is ci_os0_serial.log in the repository root. The script exits 0 on PASS and nonzero on FAIL or timeout, printing the tail of the log. Set QEMU_BIN to use another QEMU binary.

    Two more variables select what is tested. QEMU_EXTRA is appended to the QEMU command line (word split): QEMU's default CPU, qemu64, has no AVX, so QEMU_EXTRA="-cpu max" is how the XSAVE/AVX path and the YMM torture test run (-cpu max -smp 4 adds cores; a later -smp wins over the script's -smp 2). GRUB_UP=1 presses up once after the last entry is selected, which picks "Minimal-OS (RamFS, noavx)" (the entry above the RamFS one, so the RamFS entry stays last). The configurations OS-2 was checked in:

    bash tools/debug/ci_os0.sh                                   # qemu64: fxsave path
QEMU_EXTRA="-cpu max" bash tools/debug/ci_os0.sh             # xsave + AVX2
QEMU_EXTRA="-cpu max -smp 4" bash tools/debug/ci_os0.sh      # same on 4 cores
QEMU_EXTRA="-cpu max" GRUB_UP=1 bash tools/debug/ci_os0.sh   # noavx flag

    Binned rasterizer tests and benchmark

    fgpu_bin_tests (tests/host/fgpu_bin_tests.c) renders random scenes through the binned path (default) and through the immediate path (fgpu_raster_set_mode), with random depth/blend/cull/viewport state, several draws, clears in between, indexed and plain draws, the built-in programs and four FGSL shaders (one discards, one reads the fragment coordinate and facing, one samples a texture):

    • *exact scenes* (two thirds): screen vertices on a quarter-pixel grid, orthographic, so both paths evaluate edges exactly; color, depth and the triangle count must match bit for bit. They include degenerate and sliver triangles, tiny (2x2) ones, sample centers exactly on edges, quads with shared diagonals, huge triangles, off-screen parts, clipped viewports, bad indices.
    • *general scenes*: perspective, near-plane clipping, huge triangles. Pixels may differ only at triangle borders (1/256 snapping); the share of differing pixels per scene is bounded (0.4%, and 2% for "hostile" scenes with slivers and triangles crossing the camera; the observed worst case over 7500 scenes is 0.16% and 0.29%).
    • every scene is also rendered on several host threads and through a pass with random flush points and with the pipeline state, constants, layout and vertex data destroyed right after recording (snapshot semantics); the result must be identical to the single thread result.
    • watertightness: shared-edge meshes with interior vertices on a 1/256 grid or on pixel centers (the top-left rule decides), blended with alpha 1/2: every pixel inside the outline is touched exactly once, none outside.
    • a 1 MB bin budget with 30000 triangles (several rounds) and allocation failures every 2nd/7th allocation must give the same picture.

    FGPU_FUZZ_ITERS=n and FGPU_FUZZ_SEED=s change the run (default 600 scenes, seed 1); FGPU_FUZZ_DEBUG=1 prints the first differing pixels and the draws of a failing scene. For memory errors build it with -fsanitize=address,undefined.

    make bench-fgpu (not part of test-host) times the immediate and the binned path on a 640x480 target for 2000 draws of 12 triangles, 8 huge triangles, 200k triangles of about 1.2 px, and 32 layers of overdraw (front to back with hierarchical Z, and back to front), with a built-in program and with a one-instruction FGSL shader, on 1 thread and on FGPU_BENCH_THREADS (default 4) host threads standing in for the kernel's workers (fgpu_raster_set_parallel). It reports triangles/s, pixels/s, the per-draw overhead and the share of time spent inside fgpu_shader_run_batch (measured with a linker wrap). FGPU_BENCH_PHASES=1 adds the cycles spent in the geometry and the tile phase.

    FarcadeGL screenshot test (ci_fglcube.sh)

    bash tools/debug/ci_fglcube.sh                      # builds, then boots twice
FGLCUBE_ARGS=--shader NO_BUILD=1 bash tools/debug/ci_fglcube.sh

    Boots the ISO headless in RamFS mode with the binned rasterizer, runs fglcube 600 --still from the terminal (typed over serial like ci_os0.sh; --still fixes the animation at one instant and prints FGLCUBE READY after the third frame), takes a screenshot with the QEMU monitor (screendump), then does the same with the fgpuold GRUB entry (the previous rasterizer; GRUB_UP=2, the noavx entry stays at GRUB_UP=1). It converts both to PNG in dist/ci_fglcube/ (new.png, old.png, serial logs next to them), checks that the pictures show a cube (at least 2% of the screen differs from the background) and compares them: the default allowance is 2000 ppm of pixels (MAX_DIFF_PPM) because the two rasterizers differ at triangle borders by the 1/256 pixel snapping. ONLY=new or ONLY=old takes one screenshot.

    Interactive serial test

    make ci-interact

    The script builds the ISO, starts headless QEMU with a TCP serial console, and sends a small sequence of terminal commands. By default it uses port 5555, drive number 0, and a 90-second timeout. The command-line options are:

    --drive N       drive number passed to storage commands
--delay S       pause between commands
--port P        serial TCP port
--timeout S     wait limit
--junit FILE    output JUnit XML at this path
--auto-mount    answer yes if the mount prompt appears

    The default JUnit output is tools/debug/ci_interact.xml; serial output is captured in ci_serial_interact.log. QEMU is stopped when the script exits. Use a free local TCP port if the default is already in use.

    Focused integration checks

    Useful focused checks include:

    bash tools/debug/https_test.sh
make dlr-cli-test

    The HTTPS script exercises the TLS client against a local OpenSSL server via QEMU; it is an integration check, not a certificate-trust test. The Deliver CLI test uses the helper in tools/debug/test_dlr_present.sh.

    For a small cryptographic known-answer test, the source and build command are documented in Build and Debugging.

    Choose a test by change

    ChangeSuggested first check
    Pure host helper or parserAdd or update a host test, then make test-host
    Kernel compile/link, resource packagingmake build-x86_64
    Boot sequence, terminal, or kernel service startupmake ci-test
    Terminal commands or storage interactionsmake ci-interact
    TLS/network client behaviorbash tools/debug/https_test.sh
    SDK or Deliver CLI behaviorSDK build and make dlr-cli-test as applicable
    FGPU rasterizer or fgpu.c flush pointsmake test-host, make bench-fgpu, bash tools/debug/ci_fglcube.sh, bash tools/debug/ci_os0.sh
    Audio, USB, GPU, or real-device integrationHost tests first, then an appropriate QEMU or hardware test

    Tests that rely on QEMU hardware emulation do not establish that a driver works on physical hardware. The hardware guide records known device support and limitations.

    When a test fails

    1. Re-run the smallest failing test and preserve its exit status.
    2. Read the serial or QEMU output named by the test before changing code.
    3. Distinguish a build failure from a boot-marker timeout or a guest command failure.
    4. Remove or archive generated logs only after collecting the failure evidence; do not treat logs as source files.
    5. Run git status --short before and after the test to identify generated files and keep them out of the change unless intentionally needed.

    Windows

    mosWM windows over SYS_WINDOW. Include window.h.

    A window is a kernel-owned ARGB8888 frame buffer plus a title, bounds, flags, a style and an event queue. Your program draws into its own pixel buffer and copies it into the window with mos_window_present; mosWM, the window manager, composites every window onto the screen and turns mouse and keyboard input into window events.

    Windows belong to the process that created them (and its descendants). They are closed automatically when that process exits.

    Functionsmos_window_createmos_window_closemos_window_presentmos_window_next_eventmos_window_dispatch_eventsmos_window_set_boundsmos_window_set_titlemos_window_set_flagsmos_window_set_fullscreenmos_window_minimizemos_window_maximizemos_window_restoremos_window_set_resizablemos_window_set_pointer_lockmos_window_set_visiblemos_window_set_stylemos_window_get_infomos_window_listmos_window_get_framemos_window_post_eventmos_window_register_managermos_window_callmos_window_request

    A minimal window app

    #include "window.h"
#include "stdlib.h"

static int running = 1;
static void on_close(uint32_t id) { (void)id; running = 0; }

int main(void) {
    const uint32_t W = 320, H = 200;
    uint32_t id = mos_window_create(0, 120, 80, W, H, "Hello");
    if (!id) mos_exit(1);
    uint32_t* px = malloc(W * H * 4);

    mos_window_callbacks_t cb = { .onwindowclose = on_close };
    while (running) {
        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < W * H; i++) px[i] = 0xFF2845F5;   /* opaque blue */
        mos_window_present(id, px, W * 4, 0, 0, W, H);
        mos_window_dispatch_events(id, &cb);
        mos_sleep(16);
    }
    mos_window_close(id);
    mos_exit(0);
}

    Limits

    LimitValue
    Windows in the systemSYSCALL_WINDOW_MAX_WINDOWS (64)
    Minimum size64 × 48
    Maximum size16384 × 16384, and at most 64 MiB of pixels
    All windows' pixels together64 MiB
    TitleSYSCALL_WINDOW_MAX_TITLE (64) bytes including the NUL
    Queued events per windowSYSCALL_WINDOW_MAX_EVENTS (16)
    Position0 … 32768 on each axis

    Flags

    FlagMeaning
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_VISIBLEDrawn by mosWM
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_RESIZABLEThe user can resize it, and the program may call mos_window_set_bounds
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_FULLSCREENCovers the screen; cannot be combined with MAXIMIZED
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_MAXIMIZEDFills the desktop area
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_MINIMIZEDHidden in the taskbar
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_FOCUSEDHas keyboard focus. Read-only for applications: only mosWM sets it
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_POINTER_LOCKWants the mouse to itself (games): see mos_window_set_pointer_lock

    mos_window_create

    uint32_t mos_window_create(uint32_t parent_id, uint32_t x, uint32_t y,
                           uint32_t width, uint32_t height, const char* title);

    Creates a visible, resizable window. Its frame starts out as whatever the allocator returned, so present a first frame straight away.

    ParameterDescription
    parent_id0 for a top-level window, or the ID of a window this process controls to create a child (a dialog)
    x, yPosition on the desktop
    width, heightContent size in pixels, at least 64 × 48
    titleTitle bar text; truncated to 63 bytes. NULL for none

    Returns the new window ID (1 … 64), or 0 on failure. The raw call fails with SYS_ERR_INVAL (size out of range, bad flags), SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND / SYS_ERR_PERM (bad parent) or SYS_ERR_GENERIC (no free slot, out of frame memory); the wrapper turns all of these into 0.

    Notes To create a window with other flags (not resizable, hidden, full screen), create it and then call mos_window_set_flags.

    mos_window_close

    uint64_t mos_window_close(uint32_t id);

    Destroys a window and frees its frame.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND for an unknown ID, SYS_ERR_PERM for a window this process does not control.

    Notes Clicking the close button does not close the window; it queues a SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_CLOSE_REQUEST. The program decides whether to call mos_window_close.

    mos_window_present

    uint64_t mos_window_present(uint32_t id, const uint32_t* pixels, uint32_t pitch,
                            uint32_t x, uint32_t y, uint32_t width, uint32_t height);

    Copies a rectangle of your pixel buffer into the window's frame. mosWM shows the new frame on its next composite.

    ParameterDescription
    idWindow
    pixelsYour buffer, the same size as the window, ARGB8888 (0xAARRGGBB). Use 0xFF alpha
    pitchBytes per row of pixels, at least window width × 4
    x, y, width, heightThe rectangle to copy, in window coordinates. It must lie inside the window

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a rectangle outside the window, a short pitch or a NULL buffer, SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND / SYS_ERR_PERM for a bad window.

    Notes

    • pixels points at the top-left of your whole buffer, not of the rectangle; the kernel offsets into it. Presenting only the part that changed is cheaper than the whole window.
    • After a SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_RESIZED, reallocate the buffer at the new size before presenting again.
    • Each present increments the window's frame_version.

    Example

    /* redraw only a 32 x 32 cursor area */
mos_window_present(id, px, W * 4, cx, cy, 32, 32);

    mos_window_next_event

    uint64_t mos_window_next_event(uint32_t id, syscall_window_event_t* event);

    Takes the oldest event off the window's queue. Never blocks.

    ParameterDescription
    idWindow
    eventFilled with the event

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS with *event filled, SYS_ERR_AGAIN if the queue is empty, SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND / SYS_ERR_PERM for a bad window.

    syscall_window_event_t fields:

    FieldMeaning
    idWindow the event is for
    typeOne of the event types below
    x, yPointer position in window coordinates (mouse events); how far the mouse moved (MOUSE_RELATIVE)
    width, heightNew content size (RESIZED)
    keyUSB HID usage code (KEY)
    buttonsKEY: 1 = pressed, 0 = released. MOUSE: button mask, bit 0 left, bit 1 right, bit 2 middle
    wheelScroll amount (MOUSE_WHEEL)
    modsSYSCALL_INPUT_MOD_SHIFT, _CTRL, _ALT bits
    time_msUptime when the event was queued

    Event types:

    TypeSent when
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_RESIZEDThe window's size changed
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_CLOSE_REQUESTThe user clicked the close button
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_MINIMIZEDIt was minimised
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_MAXIMIZEDIt was maximised
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_RESTOREDIt returned from minimised or maximised
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_FOCUS_GAINEDIt got keyboard focus
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_FOCUS_LOSTIt lost keyboard focus
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_KEYA key was pressed or released while it had focus
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_MOUSEThe pointer moved over it, or a button changed
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_MOUSE_WHEELThe wheel turned over it
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_MOUSE_RELATIVEThe mouse moved while the window holds pointer lock: x, y are the motion, buttons the button mask

    Notes

    • The queue holds 16 events. Window-state events of the same type are merged (only the newest resize is kept), and consecutive mouse moves with the same buttons are merged, so a slow program loses detail but not clicks. Drain the queue every frame.
    • Common HID codes: a-z 4-29, 1-9 30-38, 0 39, Enter 40, Escape 41, Backspace 42, Tab 43, Space 44, Right 79, Left 80, Down 81, Up 82.

    Example

    syscall_window_event_t ev;
while (mos_window_next_event(id, &ev) == SYS_SUCCESS) {
    if (ev.type == SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_CLOSE_REQUEST) running = 0;
    else if (ev.type == SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_KEY && ev.buttons && ev.key == 41) running = 0;  /* Esc */
    else if (ev.type == SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_MOUSE && (ev.buttons & 1)) paint(ev.x, ev.y);
    else if (ev.type == SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_RESIZED) resize_buffer(ev.width, ev.height);
}

    mos_window_dispatch_events

    uint64_t mos_window_dispatch_events(uint32_t id, const mos_window_callbacks_t* callbacks);

    Drains the window's queue and calls a callback for each window-state event.

    ParameterDescription
    idWindow
    callbacksStructure of function pointers; any may be NULL

    mos_window_callbacks_t members:

    MemberCalled for
    onwindowclose(id)CLOSE_REQUEST
    onwindowminimize(id)MINIMIZED
    onwindowmaximise(id)MAXIMIZED
    windowsizechange_recall(id, width, height)RESIZED
    onwindowfocus(id, focused)FOCUS_GAINED (1) and FOCUS_LOST (0)

    Returns the number of events taken off the queue, SYS_ERR_INVAL if callbacks is NULL, or an error from mos_window_next_event.

    Notes Key, mouse, wheel and RESTORED events are consumed and dropped. A program that needs input should loop over mos_window_next_event itself.

    mos_window_set_bounds

    uint64_t mos_window_set_bounds(uint32_t id, uint32_t x, uint32_t y,
                               uint32_t width, uint32_t height);

    Moves and/or resizes a window. Resizing keeps the overlapping part of the old frame and queues a RESIZED event.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_PERM if the window is not resizable, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a size or position out of range, SYS_ERR_BUSY if its event queue is full, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if frame memory runs out.

    mos_window_set_title

    uint64_t mos_window_set_title(uint32_t id, const char* title);

    Changes the title bar text (truncated to 63 bytes).

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND / SYS_ERR_PERM.

    Example

    mos_window_set_title(id, dirty ? "notes.txt *" : "notes.txt");

    mos_window_set_flags

    uint64_t mos_window_set_flags(uint32_t id, uint32_t flags);

    Replaces the window's flags with flags (see Flags). The FOCUSED bit is kept as it is.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_INVAL if flags has unknown bits, includes FOCUSED, or combines FULLSCREEN with MAXIMIZED.

    Notes The helpers below read the current flags with mos_window_get_info and change one bit, which is usually what you want.

    Example

    /* a fixed-size window */
mos_window_set_flags(id, SYSCALL_WINDOW_VISIBLE);

    mos_window_set_fullscreen

    uint64_t mos_window_set_fullscreen(uint32_t id, bool enabled);

    Turns full screen on or off. Clears MAXIMIZED and MINIMIZED.

    Returns the result of mos_window_set_flags.

    mos_window_minimize

    uint64_t mos_window_minimize(uint32_t id);

    Minimises the window. Clears FULLSCREEN and MAXIMIZED.

    mos_window_maximize

    uint64_t mos_window_maximize(uint32_t id);

    Maximises the window. Clears FULLSCREEN and MINIMIZED.

    mos_window_restore

    uint64_t mos_window_restore(uint32_t id);

    Clears FULLSCREEN, MAXIMIZED and MINIMIZED, returning the window to its normal bounds.

    mos_window_set_resizable

    uint64_t mos_window_set_resizable(uint32_t id, bool resizable);

    Sets or clears SYSCALL_WINDOW_RESIZABLE.

    mos_window_set_pointer_lock

    uint64_t mos_window_set_pointer_lock(uint32_t id, bool locked);

    Sets or clears SYSCALL_WINDOW_POINTER_LOCK, for games that steer with the mouse. While the window has the flag, is focused, visible and not minimised (and no menu, dialog or the lock screen is open), mosWM hides the cursor, stops it at the window, and sends every move as SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_MOUSE_RELATIVE with the distance moved instead of a position. Buttons and the wheel still come as MOUSE and MOUSE_WHEEL. Moves made while the queue is full are added up and sent with the next event, so no motion is lost.

    The lock ends by itself when the window loses focus and comes back when it is focused again. Clear the flag when the mouse is needed as a pointer again (a menu, a paused game). Doom (programs/doom) locks while a level is played.

    Returns the result of mos_window_set_flags.

    mos_window_set_visible

    uint64_t mos_window_set_visible(uint32_t id, bool visible);

    Shows or hides the window by setting or clearing SYSCALL_WINDOW_VISIBLE. A hidden window keeps its frame and events.

    mos_window_set_style

    uint64_t mos_window_set_style(uint32_t id, syscall_window_style_t style);

    Changes the colours mosWM uses for this window's decoration. All colours are ARGB8888.

    syscall_window_style_t memberDefault
    title_bar0xFF24343C
    title_text0xFFFFFFFF
    close_button, close_icon0xFFE35D6A, 0xFFFFFFFF
    minimize_button, minimize_icon0xFFE8B34C, 0xFF17262C
    maximize_button, maximize_icon0xFF4ABF8A, 0xFF17262C
    border0xFF49616B
    content_background0xFF17232A

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND / SYS_ERR_PERM.

    Example

    syscall_window_info_t info;
mos_window_get_info(id, &info);
syscall_window_style_t s = info.style;
s.title_bar = 0xFF2845F5;
mos_window_set_style(id, s);

    mos_window_get_info

    uint64_t mos_window_get_info(uint32_t id, syscall_window_info_t* info);

    Copies a window's current state.

    syscall_window_info_t fieldMeaning
    id, parent_idThe window and its parent (0 for top level)
    x, y, width, heightContent bounds
    flagsCurrent flags
    frame_versionIncremented by every present
    owner_pidProcess that created it
    title[64]Title
    styleDecoration colours

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL info, or SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND / SYS_ERR_PERM.

    Example

    syscall_window_info_t info;
if (mos_window_get_info(id, &info) == 0 && (info.flags & SYSCALL_WINDOW_FOCUSED))
    draw_caret();

    mos_window_list

    uint64_t mos_window_list(syscall_window_info_t* windows, uint32_t capacity);

    Lists the windows this process controls (all windows, for the window manager).

    ParameterDescription
    windowsArray to fill; may be NULL when capacity is 0
    capacitySize of the array, at most 64

    Returns the total number of matching windows, which can be larger than capacity (only capacity are copied), or SYS_ERR_INVAL.

    Example

    uint64_t count = mos_window_list(NULL, 0);   /* just count */

    mos_window_get_frame

    uint64_t mos_window_get_frame(uint32_t id, syscall_window_frame_t* frame);

    Window-manager only. Copies a window's frame into frame->pixels, which must match the window's size. mosWM uses it to composite.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_PERM for any process other than the registered window manager, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a mismatched buffer.

    mos_window_post_event

    uint64_t mos_window_post_event(uint32_t id, syscall_window_event_t* event);

    Window-manager only. Queues an event on a window; this is how mosWM delivers input and close requests.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_PERM for other processes, SYS_ERR_INVAL for an unknown event type, SYS_ERR_BUSY if the queue is full.

    mos_window_register_manager

    uint64_t mos_window_register_manager(void);

    Makes the calling process the window manager. Only a process started as a window manager that also owns the screen (mos_graphics_acquire) may do this.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_PERM if the caller is not allowed, SYS_ERR_BUSY if another manager is registered.

    mos_window_call

    uint64_t mos_window_call(syscall_window_request_t* request);

    Issues SYS_WINDOW with a filled request. Every wrapper above builds a request with mos_window_request and calls this.

    mos_window_request

    syscall_window_request_t mos_window_request(uint32_t op, uint32_t id);

    Returns a zeroed request with size, version, op and id filled in, ready for mos_window_call.

    Minimal-OS SDK function reference

    Every function the SDK headers give a .run program, one entry per function: its signature, what each parameter means, what it returns, the errors to expect, and a short example. The headers are the source of truth; these pages describe them as of SDK v1.1 and the kernel's syscall.c.

    PageHeaderWhat is in it
    Conventions and errorssyscall.hCalling convention, result codes, privilege rules, which header to include
    Process and terminalminimalos.hOutput to the terminal, exit, sleep, time, clocks, PIDs, launching programs, working directory, stat, rename, cleanup on Ctrl+C
    Filesminimalos.hMinimaFS: open, create, read, write, seek, list, delete, metadata
    Spawning and waitingprocess.hStart programs with arguments, environment, working directory and redirected output; wait for them; getenv; clock helpers
    Threadsthread.hThreads in one program, mos_mutex_t locks, futexes, thread-local storage base
    Memory and randomnessstdlib.hmalloc, calloc, realloc, free, random bytes, atoi

    Strings and memorystring.hstrlen, strcmp, strstr, memcpy, constant-time compare …
    Formatted outputstdio.h, iostreamprintf and std::cout
    Windowswindow.hmosWM windows: create, draw, present, events
    easyui widgetseasyui.hButtons, sliders, text inputs, radio buttons, lists and more, in the MOSdesk theme
    Graphicsgraphics.h, x86_64/user_graphics.hFull-screen framebuffer: acquire, blit, present, primitives
    Inputx86_64/user_syscalls.h, user_mouse.h, user_usb.hRaw keyboard and mouse events for full-screen programs
    Networkingnet.hDNS, TCP client and server, UDP, the ktls transport

    Text in your own pixelsfont.hdraw_text / text_width: smooth Inter text (bitmap fallback) in any pixel buffer
    FarcadeGL 3Dfarcadegl.h, fgpu_abi.hGPU-backed 3D: buffers, vertex layouts, shaders, textures, blending, drawing into a window or the screen
    FGSL shading languagefglsl.hThe GLSL-style language FarcadeGL shaders are written in, and its compiler
    Disks and root commandsstorage.hList disks and partitions, run kernel commands as root (installer)
    Playing audioaudio.hPlay, pause, seek and query .adi audio files
    Pictures and iconsmosmedia.hRead .img pictures; draw raster and vector (SVG-like) pictures at any size, tinted with the theme's color

    Reading an entry

    Each function has the same parts:

    • Signature - the declaration exactly as the header has it. Every wrapper is static inline, so including a header never adds a symbol to your program.
    • Parameters - one row per argument.
    • Returns - the success value and the SYS_ERR_* values the kernel can return for that call.
    • Notes - limits, ownership rules and anything surprising.
    • Example - a minimal fragment. Examples assume the headers named at the top of the page are included.

    A complete program

    #include "minimalos.h"
#include "stdio.h"

int main(int argc, char** argv) {   /* or main(argc, argv, envp) */
    printf("hello from pid %ld, %d argument(s)\n", mos_getpid(), argc);
    for (int i = 0; i < argc; i++) printf("argv[%d] = %s\n", i, argv[i]);
    mos_exit(0);
}

    Build it with ./build.sh hello.c and run it inside Minimal-OS with run 0:/programs/hello.run. Returning from main also ends the program; crt0.c calls mos_exit() with the return value.
