    Conventions and errors

    How SDK calls reach the kernel, what they return, and which calls an ordinary .run program is allowed to make.

    On this pageCalling conventionResult codesPrivilegeWhich headerUnitsMemory

    Calling convention

    Every wrapper ends in one int 0x80:

    RegisterInOut
    raxsyscall number (SYS_*)result
    rdifirst argument
    rsisecond argument
    rdxthird argument
    r10fourth argument (only SYS_FUTEX_WAIT's timeout; see mos_syscall4)

    Calls with more data than three registers (graphics, windows, network, packages, input) pass one pointer to a request structure in rdi. Keep the structure and every buffer it points to alive until the call returns. Versioned structures (syscall_graphics_info_t, syscall_blit_request_t, syscall_input_read_request_t, syscall_window_request_t) must have their size and version fields set and their reserved fields zero; the SDK wrappers do this for you.

    Result codes

    Results come back in rax as a 64-bit value. Failures are small negative numbers, which as unsigned values sit at the very top of the range:

    ConstantValueMeaning
    SYS_SUCCESS0The operation succeeded
    SYS_ERR_GENERIC-1Unspecified failure (out of memory, the driver refused, the file system said no)
    SYS_ERR_BADFD-2Invalid or closed handle; mos_write to an fd other than 1 or 2
    SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND-3Path, window, peer or resource not found, or a connection that has closed
    SYS_ERR_INVAL-4Invalid argument: NULL pointer, out-of-range value, bad structure size or version
    SYS_ERR_PERM-5The calling process may not do this (see privilege)
    SYS_ERR_BUSY-6A shared subsystem (the network stack, a full event queue) is in use: retry
    SYS_ERR_AGAIN-7Non-blocking call with nothing to report yet: call again later. SYS_FUTEX_WAIT returns it when the word no longer has the expected value
    SYS_ERR_NOMEM-8Out of kernel memory (heap or video memory)
    SYS_ERR_TIMEDOUT-9A timed wait ran out (SYS_FUTEX_WAIT with a timeout)

    The constants are defined as ((uint64_t)-N). Compare against them directly, or cast to long and test for a negative value:

    long r = mos_mkdir("0:/data");
if (r == (long)SYS_ERR_INVAL) printf("bad path\n");
else if (r < 0)               printf("mkdir failed: %ld\n", r);

    Some wrappers fold errors into a friendlier value (malloc returns NULL, mos_window_create returns 0, mos_tcp_accept returns 0 for "nobody waiting"); each entry says so.

    Privilege

    .run programs start as PROC_PRIVILEGE_USER processes. Before dispatching, the kernel checks the call against a deny list (syscall_user_may_call() in syscall.c); a denied call returns SYS_ERR_PERM and does nothing.

    Denied to .run programsWhy
    SYS_GRAPHICS drawing primitives (clear, pixel, line, rectangle, circle, triangle, ellipse, text, measure text, set resolution, terminal clear)User programs draw into their own surface and use mos_graphics_blit_surface + mos_graphics_present
    SYS_MANAGER init, update, start, set sample rateThey reconfigure hardware every process shares
    SYS_USB_INIT, SYS_MOUSE_INITThey re-enumerate devices the whole system uses
    SYS_NET_DHCPIt rewrites the address of the shared interface
    SYS_USB_KEY_IS_PRESSED, SYS_MOUSE_GET_STATE, SYS_INPUT_READAllowed only to the process that owns the screen

    Everything else - files, heap, network connections, windows, packages, sysinfo, process list - is open to user programs. The table is not a memory-protection boundary; it closes the specific hole of a program reconfiguring shared hardware through the syscall gate.

    Which header

    IncludeYou get
    minimalos.hCore calls: terminal output, exit, time, files, packages, exec, process list, framebuffer ownership and blit
    process.hmos_spawn, mos_waitpid, mos_getenv, environ, clock helpers (includes minimalos.h; see Spawning)
    vm.hmos_vm_map, mos_vm_unmap, mos_vm_protect, mos_vm_decommit, mos_vm_reserve (includes minimalos.h; see Virtual memory)
    thread.hThreads, mutexes, futexes, thread-local storage base (see Threads)
    stdio.hprintf (includes minimalos.h)
    stdlib.hmalloc and friends, random bytes, atoi (includes minimalos.h)
    string.hString and memory helpers (no syscalls)
    window.hmosWM windows and their events
    easyui.hReady-made widgets for window apps (see easyui)
    graphics.hShort graphics_* names for the framebuffer API
    net.hNetworking (includes minimalos.h)
    user_sysinfo.hSystem statistics
    iostreamstd::cout for C++
    x86_64/user_syscalls.hRaw uint64_t wrappers: mos_syscall3, mos_graphics, mos_mouse, mos_usb, mos_manager, mos_sysinfo, mos_input_read
    x86_64/user_mouse.h, x86_64/user_usb.h, x86_64/user_managers.hMouse, USB keyboard and manager wrappers

    Both header families include x86_64/user_common.h, so every wrapper is defined exactly once and any combination of headers can be included together.

    Units

    • Time: milliseconds. mos_uptime() and mos_sleep() both use milliseconds; so do every timeout_ms argument. The exceptions are the mos_clock_* functions (nanoseconds) and the futex timeout (nanoseconds, rounded up to whole milliseconds).
    • Colours: window.h and mos_graphics_blit_surface take ARGB8888 pixels, 0xAARRGGBB. Use 0xFF alpha for opaque pixels. The mos_graphics_* primitives take separate r, g, b bytes.
    • IPv4 addresses and ports in net.h are host order: 192.168.1.10 is 0xC0A8010A.
    • Paths are MinimaFS paths such as 0:/programs/app.run. /dir/file is the root of the working directory's drive; any other path is relative to the program's working directory (the terminal's until the program calls mos_chdir).

    Memory

    There is no libc and no dynamic linker. Everything a program uses is either an inline wrapper from these headers or code compiled into the program. crt0.c supplies _start, runs global constructors (.init_array), calls main(argc, argv, envp) (programs declared main(int, char**) just ignore the third argument), keeps envp in environ and then mos_exit() with its return value. It also defines out-of-line memcpy, memmove, memset and memcmp, which the compiler may call on its own.

    PreviousOverviewNextProcess and terminal

    Edit this page on GitHub

    Process and terminal

    Terminal output, ending the program, time, sleeping, process IDs, launching other programs, clocks, the working directory, stat and rename, and the Ctrl+C cleanup hook. Include minimalos.h. Starting a program and waiting for it with arguments, environment and redirected output is in Spawning and waiting (process.h).

    Functionsmos_writemos_write_fdmos_write_textmos_putsmos_exitmos_exit_withmos_exit_codemos_getpidmos_uptimemos_sleepmos_gettimemos_register_cleanupmos_execmos_pslistmos_getcwdmos_chdirmos_statmos_renamemos_syscallmos_syscall4mos_syscall3mos_syscall1

    mos_write

    long mos_write(int fd, const void* buf, size_t len);   /* form 1 */
long mos_write(const char* text, uint64_t len);        /* form 2 */

    Writes bytes to the terminal. mos_write is a macro that picks a form by argument count: three arguments call mos_write_fd, two call mos_write_text (always stdout).

    ParameterDescription
    fd1 (stdout) or 2 (stderr). Both go to the terminal and the serial log
    buf / textBytes to write. Not required to be NUL-terminated
    lenNumber of bytes

    Returns len on success, SYS_ERR_BADFD for any other fd, SYS_ERR_INVAL if buf is NULL.

    Notes

    • To write to a file use mos_fwrite; mos_write only reaches the terminal.
    • Inside mosWM the terminal is the Terminal window that launched the program.

    Example

    mos_write(1, "ready\n", 6);
mos_write("also stdout\n", 12);

    mos_write_fd

    long mos_write_fd(int fd, const void* buf, size_t len);

    The three-argument form of mos_write, as a function. Useful where a macro cannot go, such as taking its address.

    Returns the same values as mos_write.

    mos_write_text

    long mos_write_text(const char* text, uint64_t length);

    Writes length bytes of text to stdout. The two-argument form of mos_write.

    mos_puts

    long mos_puts(const char* str);

    Writes a NUL-terminated string to stdout. No newline is added, unlike the C library's puts.

    ParameterDescription
    strNUL-terminated string. Must not be NULL

    Returns the number of bytes written.

    Example

    mos_puts("Hello, Minimal-OS!\n");

    mos_exit

    void mos_exit(int code);   /* noreturn */
void mos_exit(void);       /* exit code 0 */

    Ends the calling process. Never returns. A macro over mos_exit_with: mos_exit() with no argument exits with code 0.

    ParameterDescription
    codeExit status. Only the low 8 bits are reported; the terminal prints [exited with code N] for a non-zero code

    Notes

    • Global destructors (.fini_array) do not run. Release resources yourself, or from a cleanup callback.
    • The kernel closes the process's windows, network handles and heap blocks when it reaps it, but files should be closed explicitly so their data is flushed.
    • Returning from main calls mos_exit with the return value.

    Example

    if (!buffer) {
    mos_puts("out of memory\n");
    mos_exit(1);
}

    mos_exit_with

    __attribute__((noreturn)) void mos_exit_with(int code);

    The function behind mos_exit. Issues SYS_EXIT and never returns.

    mos_exit_code

    void mos_exit_code(uint8_t code);

    Older spelling from x86_64/user_syscalls.h. Same effect as mos_exit(code).

    mos_getpid

    long mos_getpid(void);

    Returns the PID of the calling process.

    Notes A server passes this, or a child's PID from mos_exec, to mos_tcp_handoff.

    mos_uptime

    long mos_uptime(void);

    Returns the time since boot in milliseconds.

    Notes Use it to measure intervals and frame times. For wall-clock time see mos_gettime.

    Example

    long start = mos_uptime();
do_work();
printf("took %ld ms\n", mos_uptime() - start);

    mos_sleep

    long mos_sleep(long ms);

    Puts the process to sleep for at least ms milliseconds and lets other processes run.

    ParameterDescription
    msMilliseconds to sleep. 0 returns at once

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS.

    Notes

    • Call it in every polling loop (window events, network receive, accept) so the program does not spin a core at 100%.
    • A frame loop typically sleeps 10-16 ms per frame.

    Example

    for (;;) {
    handle_events();
    draw_frame();
    mos_sleep(16);   /* about 60 frames per second */
}

    mos_gettime

    long mos_gettime(void);

    Wrapper for SYS_GETTIME, the real-time clock.

    Returns SYS_ERR_INVAL with the current kernel: SYS_GETTIME expects a pointer to a datetime_t in rdi, and this wrapper passes none.

    Notes Until the wrapper takes a buffer, call the syscall directly with a structure laid out like the kernel's datetime_t:

    typedef struct {
    uint16_t year;
    uint8_t month, day;           /* 1-12, 1-31 */
    uint8_t hour, minute, second; /* 0-23, 0-59, 0-59 */
} mos_datetime_t;

mos_datetime_t now;
if (mos_syscall(SYS_GETTIME, (long)(uintptr_t)&now, 0, 0) == 0)
    printf("%d-%d-%d %d:%d\n", now.year, now.month, now.day, now.hour, now.minute);

    mos_register_cleanup

    long mos_register_cleanup(void (*cleanup)(void));

    Registers a function the kernel calls when the user presses Ctrl+C in the terminal running this program.

    ParameterDescription
    cleanupFunction to call. Must not be NULL

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL callback.

    Notes

    • The callback runs on the program's next syscall after Ctrl+C. It should save what it needs and call mos_exit().
    • If the program has not exited one second after Ctrl+C, the kernel terminates it. A second Ctrl+C within 800 ms terminates it at once.
    • Without a callback, Ctrl+C terminates the program immediately.
    • Registering again replaces the previous callback.

    Example

    static long log_fd;

static void on_ctrl_c(void) {
    mos_fwrite(log_fd, "interrupted\n", 12);
    mos_close(log_fd);
    mos_exit(130);
}

int main(void) {
    log_fd = mos_open("0:/tmp/log.txt", SYS_O_RDWR);
    mos_register_cleanup(on_ctrl_c);
    for (;;) mos_sleep(100);
}

    mos_exec

    long mos_exec(const char* path, const char** argv, long argc);

    Starts another .run bundle as a new process, the way the terminal's run command does. Does not wait for it.

    ParameterDescription
    pathPath of the .run file
    argvExtra arguments. The child sees path as argv[0] and these from argv[1] on. May be NULL when argc is 0
    argcNumber of entries in argv, at most 16

    Returns the new process's PID, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL or invalid path or more than 16 arguments, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if the program could not be loaded.

    Example

    const char* args[] = { "--port", "8080" };
long pid = mos_exec("0:/programs/server.run", args, 2);
if (pid < 0) printf("could not start server (%ld)\n", pid);

    mos_pslist

    long mos_pslist(syscall_process_info_t* entries, size_t max_entries);

    Copies a snapshot of the process list into a caller buffer.

    ParameterDescription
    entriesArray to fill
    max_entriesCapacity of entries

    Returns the number of entries written (0 if entries is NULL or max_entries is 0).

    Each syscall_process_info_t holds:

    FieldMeaning
    pidProcess ID
    name[128]Process name, NUL-terminated
    stateSYSCALL_PROC_STATE_READY, _RUNNING, _WAITING, _PAUSED, _ZOMBIE or _TERMINATED
    privilegeSYSCALL_PROC_PRIV_KERNEL or SYSCALL_PROC_PRIV_USER
    sched_cpuCore the scheduler assigned
    sched_levelScheduler queue level

    Example

    syscall_process_info_t procs[32];
long n = mos_pslist(procs, 32);
for (long i = 0; i < n; i++)
    printf("%lu %s\n", (unsigned long)procs[i].pid, procs[i].name);

    mos_getcwd

    long mos_getcwd(char* path, size_t path_size);

    Copies the program's working directory, which relative paths are resolved against. It is the terminal's current directory until the program calls mos_chdir; programs started by this one inherit it.

    ParameterDescription
    pathOutput buffer
    path_sizeSize of path in bytes, including room for the NUL

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_INVAL if the buffer is NULL or too small.

    Example

    char cwd[256];
if (mos_getcwd(cwd, sizeof cwd) == 0) printf("in %s\n", cwd);

    mos_chdir

    long mos_chdir(const char* path);

    Sets the program's working directory, which relative paths are resolved against. The setting belongs to the program and is shared by all its threads; it does not change the terminal's directory. Programs started with mos_spawn or mos_exec inherit it.

    ParameterDescription
    pathA directory: 0:/dir, /dir (the working directory's drive), or relative. . and .. are allowed; .. at the root stays at the root

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND if path is not an existing directory, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL, invalid or over-long path.

    Notes

    • mos_getcwd then returns the normalized form: 0:/dir/sub, no trailing slash except for a drive root (0:/).

    Example

    mos_chdir("0:/data");
mos_create("notes.txt", "text", "txt");     /* 0:/data/notes.txt */

    mos_stat

    long mos_stat(const char* path, syscall_stat_t* out);

    Size, type and times of a file or directory, without opening it.

    ParameterDescription
    pathFile or directory
    outFilled in on success

    syscall_stat_t:

    FieldMeaning
    sizeData bytes; 0 for a directory
    typeSYS_STAT_FILE or SYS_STAT_DIR
    flagsSYS_STAT_HIDDEN, SYS_STAT_RUNNABLE (bit mask)
    created, modifiedSeconds since 1970-01-01. MinimaFS keeps only the day. 0 when unknown, and always 0 for a directory

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND when nothing is at path, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL argument or an invalid path.

    Example

    syscall_stat_t st;
if (mos_stat("0:/etc/motd.txt", &st) == 0 && st.type == SYS_STAT_FILE)
    printf("%lu bytes\n", (unsigned long)st.size);

    mos_rename

    long mos_rename(const char* from, const char* to);

    Renames or moves a file or directory on one drive, also into another directory.

    ParameterDescription
    fromExisting file or directory
    toNew path. Its directory must exist

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS; SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND when from does not exist; SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL or invalid path; SYS_ERR_GENERIC for any other refusal.

    Notes

    • A file already at to is replaced. A directory at to is an error (SYS_ERR_GENERIC), whatever from is; so is moving a directory into itself or its own subtree, a missing target directory, a different drive, and the drive root.
    • Renaming a path to itself succeeds and changes nothing.
    • Close files before renaming them: a handle opened earlier still writes back to the old name.

    Example

    mos_rename("0:/data/new.tmp", "0:/data/state.bin");   /* replaces state.bin */

    Clocks

    uint64_t mos_clock_monotonic_ns(void);
uint64_t mos_clock_realtime_ns(void);
uint64_t mos_clock_tsc_hz(void);
    FunctionReturns
    mos_clock_monotonic_nsNanoseconds since boot. Never goes backwards. Read from the CPU's time-stamp counter when it has a usable one, else it has millisecond steps
    mos_clock_realtime_nsNanoseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC by the system clock (UTC when internet time sync is on). Millisecond steps; jumps when the clock is set, so use the monotonic clock for durations
    mos_clock_tsc_hzTime-stamp counter ticks per second when RDTSC is a usable clock in a program (invariant TSC), else 0

    process.h adds mos_monotonic_ms() and mos_time_unix().

    Example

    uint64_t t0 = mos_clock_monotonic_ns();
do_work();
printf("took %lu us\n", (unsigned long)((mos_clock_monotonic_ns() - t0) / 1000));

    mos_syscall

    long mos_syscall(long num, long a1, long a2, long a3);

    Issues syscall num with up to three arguments. Every other wrapper is built on this (or on mos_syscall3). Use it for calls that have no wrapper yet.

    ParameterDescription
    numA SYS_* number from syscall.h
    a1, a2, a3Arguments for rdi, rsi, rdx; pass 0 for unused ones

    Returns the raw rax value.

    mos_syscall4

    long mos_syscall4(long num, long a1, long a2, long a3, long a4);

    mos_syscall with a fourth argument in r10. Only SYS_FUTEX_WAIT uses it (its timeout); mos_futex_wait wraps that.

    mos_syscall3

    uint64_t mos_syscall3(uint64_t number, uint64_t arg1, uint64_t arg2, uint64_t arg3);

    Same as mos_syscall with unsigned types, from x86_64/user_syscalls.h.

    mos_syscall1

    uint64_t mos_syscall1(uint64_t number, uint64_t arg1);

    mos_syscall3(number, arg1, 0, 0).

    Edit this page on GitHub

    Files

    MinimaFS file and directory calls. Include minimalos.h.

    Paths look like 0:/etc/System.conf: a drive number, a colon, then an absolute path. A path without a drive prefix is resolved against the program's working directory (see mos_getcwd and mos_chdir); /dir/file is the root of that directory's drive. mos_stat and mos_rename are documented with the process calls.

    A file handle is a long. Keep it in a long: it is a 64-bit value, and truncating it to int can corrupt it. Valid handles are positive; errors are negative.

    Functionsmos_openmos_createmos_readmos_fwritemos_closemos_seekmos_tellmos_sizemos_feofmos_existsmos_is_dirmos_mkdirmos_listdirmos_deletemos_rmdirmos_get_metadata

    mos_open

    long mos_open(const char* path, long flags);

    Opens an existing file.

    ParameterDescription
    pathFile to open
    flagsSYS_O_RDONLY (0) for read-only; SYS_O_RDWR (or any non-zero value) for read and write

    Returns a handle (positive), SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND if the file does not exist or cannot be opened, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL or invalid path.

    Notes

    • mos_open never creates a file. Call mos_create first.
    • The position starts at 0. Writing at position 0 overwrites the start of the file; to append, mos_seek to mos_size first.
    • Writes are kept in memory and saved to disk by mos_close. Always close a handle you wrote to.

    Example

    long fd = mos_open("0:/etc/motd.txt", SYS_O_RDONLY);
if (fd < 0) { printf("no motd (%ld)\n", fd); mos_exit(1); }
char buf[256];
long n = mos_read(fd, buf, sizeof buf - 1);
if (n > 0) { buf[n] = '\0'; mos_puts(buf); }
mos_close(fd);

    mos_create

    long mos_create(const char* path, const char* filetype, const char* fileformat);

    Creates a new, empty file. Open it afterwards with SYS_O_RDWR to write to it.

    ParameterDescription
    pathFile to create. The parent directory must exist
    filetypeMinimaFS file type such as "text" or "binary". NULL means "binary"
    fileformatFormat tag such as "txt" or "bin". NULL means "bin"

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL or invalid path, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if the file system refused (missing parent, no space).

    Example

    const char* path = "0:/data/notes.txt";
if (!mos_exists(path)) mos_create(path, "text", "txt");
long fd = mos_open(path, SYS_O_RDWR);
mos_seek(fd, mos_size(fd));          /* append */
mos_fwrite(fd, "new line\n", 9);
mos_close(fd);

    mos_read

    long mos_read(long fd, void* buf, size_t len);

    Reads up to len bytes from the current position and advances it.

    ParameterDescription
    fdHandle from mos_open
    bufDestination buffer
    lenMaximum number of bytes

    Returns the number of bytes read; 0 at end of file. SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL handle or buffer.

    Notes The result is not NUL-terminated. Leave a byte free when reading text.

    Example

    /* read a whole file into the heap */
long fd = mos_open(path, SYS_O_RDONLY);
long size = mos_size(fd);
char* data = malloc((size_t)size + 1);
long got = 0, n;
while ((n = mos_read(fd, data + got, (size_t)(size - got))) > 0) got += n;
data[got] = '\0';
mos_close(fd);

    mos_fwrite

    long mos_fwrite(long fd, const void* buf, size_t len);

    Writes len bytes at the current position and advances it, growing the file if needed.

    ParameterDescription
    fdHandle opened with SYS_O_RDWR
    bufBytes to write
    lenNumber of bytes

    Returns the number of bytes written, 0 if the handle is read-only or memory ran out, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL handle or buffer.

    Notes

    • Writing never shortens a file. To replace a file's contents, delete it, create it again and write.
    • The data reaches disk when the handle is closed.

    mos_close

    long mos_close(long fd);

    Closes a handle and saves anything written to it.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL handle.

    Notes Do not use the handle afterwards. Closing twice is undefined.

    mos_seek

    long mos_seek(long fd, long offset);

    Moves the position to offset bytes from the start of the file.

    ParameterDescription
    fdOpen handle
    offsetNew position. Values past the end are clamped to the file size

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL handle.

    mos_tell

    long mos_tell(long fd);

    Returns the current position in bytes, or SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL handle.

    mos_size

    long mos_size(long fd);

    Returns the size of the open file's data in bytes, including anything written but not yet closed. SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL handle.

    mos_feof

    long mos_feof(long fd);

    Returns 1 if the position is at the end of the file, 0 if not, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL handle.

    Example

    char c;
while (!mos_feof(fd) && mos_read(fd, &c, 1) == 1) count++;

    mos_exists

    long mos_exists(const char* path);

    Returns 1 if a file or directory exists at path, 0 if not, SYS_ERR_INVAL for an invalid path.

    mos_is_dir

    long mos_is_dir(const char* path);

    Returns 1 if path is a directory, 0 if it is a file or does not exist, SYS_ERR_INVAL for an invalid path.

    mos_mkdir

    long mos_mkdir(const char* path);

    Creates one directory. The parent must already exist.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if it could not be created (it already exists, or the parent is missing), SYS_ERR_INVAL for an invalid path.

    Example

    if (!mos_is_dir("0:/data")) mos_mkdir("0:/data");

    mos_listdir

    long mos_listdir(const char* path, syscall_dirent_t* entries, size_t max_entries);

    Lists a directory into a caller buffer.

    ParameterDescription
    pathDirectory to list
    entriesArray to fill
    max_entriesCapacity of entries. The kernel also caps it at the most entries one directory can hold

    Returns the number of entries written, or SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL path or buffer, an invalid path, or max_entries of 0.

    Each syscall_dirent_t holds:

    FieldMeaning
    name[64]Entry name, NUL-terminated
    typeSYSCALL_DIRENT_TYPE_FILE, _DIR, _EXECUTABLE or _SYMLINK
    hidden1 for hidden entries

    Example

    syscall_dirent_t items[64];
long n = mos_listdir("0:/programs", items, 64);
for (long i = 0; i < n; i++)
    printf("%s%s\n", items[i].name, items[i].type == SYSCALL_DIRENT_TYPE_DIR ? "/" : "");

    mos_delete

    long mos_delete(const char* path);

    Deletes a file.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if it does not exist or could not be deleted, SYS_ERR_INVAL for an invalid path.

    Notes Use mos_rmdir for directories.

    mos_rmdir

    long mos_rmdir(const char* path);

    Removes an empty directory.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if it is not empty, does not exist or is the drive root, SYS_ERR_INVAL for an invalid path.

    mos_get_metadata

    long mos_get_metadata(const char* path, syscall_file_metadata_t* out);

    Reads a file's MinimaFS metadata without opening it.

    ParameterDescription
    pathFile to inspect
    outStructure to fill

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND if there is no such file, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL argument.

    syscall_file_metadata_t fields:

    FieldMeaning
    filetype[64]File type, such as text or binary
    fileformat[16]Format tag, such as txt or run
    data_lengthSize of the data in bytes
    runnable1 for executables
    hidden1 for hidden files
    entrypointEntry point recorded for executables
    created_date[32]Creation date as text
    last_changed[32]Last-modified date as text

    Example

    syscall_file_metadata_t m;
if (mos_get_metadata("0:/programs/hello.run", &m) == 0)
    printf("%s/%s, %u bytes, changed %s\n", m.filetype, m.fileformat, m.data_length, m.last_changed);

    Edit this page on GitHub

    Memory and randomness

    Heap allocation over SYS_HEAP, random bytes over SYS_RANDOM, and atoi. Include stdlib.h.

    For big blocks, memory that must be given back, reserved address space or code you generate, see Virtual memory (vm.h).

    Heap blocks come from the kernel allocator and are tracked per process: free and realloc only accept blocks this process allocated, and any block still allocated when the process ends is reclaimed.

    Functionsmalloccallocreallocfreemos_heap_failedmos_random_bytesmos_random_u64mos_randomatoi

    malloc or SYS_VM?

    malloc (SYS_HEAP)mos_vm_map (SYS_VM)
    GranularityAny sizeWhole 4 KiB pages
    AddressBelow 4 GiB2 TiB and up
    ContentsNot clearedReads as zero
    Physical memoryTaken when allocatedTaken on first use, can be given back (mos_vm_decommit)
    Guard pagesNoneAn unmapped page on each side
    ExecutableNeverOnly with MOS_VM_PROT_EXEC
    Cost of a callCheap, fine for small objectsA system call and a kernel area per mapping

    Use malloc for ordinary objects, strings and buffers up to some megabytes. Use mos_vm_map for large blocks (images, arenas, caches), for a buffer that should grow in place (reserve, then commit), for memory you want to return to the system while keeping the address range, for stacks and anything that benefits from a guard page, and for code you write at run time. Do not use it for many small allocations: each mapping takes at least one page and two guard pages of address space.

    malloc

    void* malloc(size_t size);

    Allocates size bytes. The memory is not cleared.

    ParameterDescription
    sizeNumber of bytes. Must be greater than 0

    Returns a pointer to the block, or NULL if size is 0 or there is not enough memory.

    Example

    uint32_t* pixels = malloc(width * height * sizeof(uint32_t));
if (!pixels) { mos_puts("out of memory\n"); mos_exit(1); }

    calloc

    void* calloc(size_t count, size_t size);

    Allocates an array of count elements of size bytes, cleared to zero.

    Returns a pointer, or NULL if count * size overflows, is 0, or memory runs out.

    Example

    int* grid = calloc(rows * cols, sizeof(int));

    realloc

    void* realloc(void* ptr, size_t size);

    Resizes a block, moving it if needed. The contents are kept up to the smaller of the two sizes.

    ParameterDescription
    ptrBlock from malloc, calloc or realloc, or NULL to allocate a new one
    sizeNew size. 0 frees the block

    Returns the (possibly moved) block, or NULL on failure. On failure the original block is unchanged and still yours, so keep the old pointer until the call succeeds. realloc(ptr, 0) frees ptr and returns NULL.

    Example

    char* bigger = realloc(buf, cap * 2);
if (!bigger) { free(buf); mos_exit(1); }
buf = bigger; cap *= 2;

    free

    void free(void* ptr);

    Releases a block. free(NULL) does nothing.

    Notes Passing a pointer this process did not allocate is rejected by the kernel (SYS_ERR_INVAL, ignored by free) rather than corrupting the heap. Using a block after freeing it is still a bug.

    mos_heap_failed

    int mos_heap_failed(long value);

    Tells whether a raw SYS_HEAP result is an error code rather than an address. malloc, calloc and realloc use it to return NULL; you only need it when calling SYS_HEAP through mos_syscall.

    Returns non-zero if value is one of the SYS_ERR_* codes.

    mos_random_bytes

    long mos_random_bytes(void* buf, size_t len);

    Fills buf with random bytes from the kernel's entropy source.

    ParameterDescription
    bufDestination
    lenNumber of bytes. Must be greater than 0

    Returns len, or SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL buffer or zero length.

    Notes The kernel uses RDRAND when the CPU has it, which is suitable for keys and nonces. Without it, the bytes are derived from the TSC and RTC and must not be used for cryptography.

    Example

    uint8_t key[32];
mos_random_bytes(key, sizeof key);

    mos_random_u64

    uint64_t mos_random_u64(void);

    Returns 64 random bits from mos_random_bytes.

    Example

    int die = (int)(mos_random_u64() % 6) + 1;

    mos_random

    long mos_random(void* buf, uint32_t len);

    The same call as mos_random_bytes, declared in net.h with a 32-bit length.

    atoi

    int atoi(const char* s);

    Converts a decimal string to an int. Skips leading spaces and tabs, accepts one + or -, then reads digits until the first non-digit.

    Returns the value, or 0 if there are no digits. Overflow is not detected.

    Example

    int port = argc > 1 ? atoi(argv[1]) : 8080;

    Edit this page on GitHub

    Strings and memory

    Freestanding string and memory helpers. Include string.h. None of these make a syscall.

    memcpy, memmove, memset and memcmp are real functions defined in crt0.c, because the compiler emits calls to them on its own (struct assignment, = {0} initialisers); the rest are static inline.

    Functionsstrlenstrcmpstrncmpstrcpystrlcpy_safestrchrstrrchrstrstrmemcpymemmovememsetmemcmpmos_memcmpmos_memeq_ct

    strlen

    size_t strlen(const char* s);

    Returns the number of bytes before the terminating NUL.

    strcmp

    int strcmp(const char* a, const char* b);

    Compares two strings byte by byte as unsigned char.

    Returns 0 if they are equal, a negative value if a sorts first, a positive value if b does.

    Example

    if (argc > 1 && strcmp(argv[1], "--help") == 0) usage();

    strncmp

    int strncmp(const char* a, const char* b, size_t n);

    Like strcmp but compares at most n bytes.

    Example

    if (strncmp(line, "GET ", 4) == 0) handle_get(line + 4);

    strcpy

    char* strcpy(char* dst, const char* src);

    Copies src, including its NUL, into dst.

    Returns dst.

    Notes Does not check the size of dst. Prefer strlcpy_safe.

    strlcpy_safe

    char* strlcpy_safe(char* dst, const char* src, size_t size);

    Copies at most size - 1 bytes of src and always NUL-terminates, truncating if src does not fit. Unlike the C library's strncpy, it never leaves dst unterminated and never pads with zeros.

    ParameterDescription
    dstDestination buffer
    srcNUL-terminated source
    sizeSize of dst in bytes. 0 copies nothing

    Returns dst.

    Example

    char name[16];
strlcpy_safe(name, argv[1], sizeof name);

    strchr

    char* strchr(const char* s, int c);

    Returns a pointer to the first c in s, or NULL. Searching for '\0' returns a pointer to the terminator.

    strrchr

    char* strrchr(const char* s, int c);

    Returns a pointer to the last c in s, or NULL.

    Example

    const char* slash = strrchr(path, '/');
const char* file = slash ? slash + 1 : path;

    strstr

    char* strstr(const char* haystack, const char* needle);

    Returns a pointer to the first occurrence of needle in haystack, haystack itself if needle is empty, or NULL.

    memcpy

    void* memcpy(void* dst, const void* src, size_t n);

    Copies n bytes. The ranges must not overlap; use memmove if they might.

    Returns dst.

    memmove

    void* memmove(void* dst, const void* src, size_t n);

    Copies n bytes; the ranges may overlap.

    Returns dst.

    Example

    /* shift an array one slot right */
memmove(&items[1], &items[0], (count - 1) * sizeof items[0]);

    memset

    void* memset(void* dst, int value, size_t n);

    Sets n bytes to (unsigned char)value.

    Returns dst.

    memcmp

    int memcmp(const void* a, const void* b, size_t n);

    Compares n bytes.

    Returns 0 if equal, otherwise the difference of the first differing bytes.

    Notes Stops at the first difference, so its timing reveals where the inputs differ. For secrets use mos_memeq_ct.

    mos_memcmp

    int mos_memcmp(const void* a, const void* b, size_t n);

    An inline copy of memcmp with the same result.

    mos_memeq_ct

    int mos_memeq_ct(const void* a, const void* b, size_t n);

    Compares n bytes in constant time: it always reads every byte, whatever the contents.

    Returns 1 if the ranges are equal, 0 if not. Note the sense is the opposite of memcmp.

    Notes Use it for authentication tags, MACs and password hashes. An early-exit comparison leaks how many leading bytes matched, which is enough to forge a tag one byte at a time.

    Example

    if (!mos_memeq_ct(tag, expected_tag, 16)) reject();
    PreviousMemory and randomnessNextFormatted output

    Edit this page on GitHub

    Formatted output

    printf from stdio.h and std::cout from iostream. Both are header-only and write to stdout through mos_write.

    Functionsprintfmos_vprintfstd::cout

    printf

    long printf(const char* format, ...);

    Formats its arguments and writes the result to stdout.

    ParameterDescription
    formatFormat string
    ...One argument per conversion

    Supported conversions:

    ConversionArgumentOutput
    %d, %iintSigned decimal
    %uunsigned intUnsigned decimal
    %x, %Xunsigned intHexadecimal, lower or upper case
    %ldlongSigned decimal
    %luunsigned longUnsigned decimal
    %cintOne character
    %sconst char*String; NULL prints (null)
    %%noneA %

    Returns the number of bytes written.

    Notes

    • There are no flags, widths or precisions (%5d, %-10s, %02x), no floating point and no %p or %lx. An unsupported conversion is printed as is.
    • To print a 64-bit value in hex, split it: printf("%x%x", (unsigned)(v >> 32), (unsigned)v) (pad the low half yourself), or format it into a buffer by hand.
    • There is no sprintf. Build strings by hand or with string.h.
    • Output is buffered in 128-byte chunks inside one call, so a single printf is one or a few mos_write calls.

    Example

    printf("%s: %d of %u done (%ld ms)\n", name, done, total, mos_uptime() - start);

    mos_vprintf

    long mos_vprintf(const char* format, va_list args);

    The va_list form of printf, for writing your own logging functions.

    Example

    static void logf(const char* fmt, ...) {
    va_list ap;
    va_start(ap, fmt);
    mos_puts("[app] ");
    mos_vprintf(fmt, ap);
    va_end(ap);
}

    std::cout

    namespace std { class ostream; static ostream cout; }
ostream& operator<<(const char*);
ostream& operator<<(char);
ostream& operator<<(int);
ostream& operator<<(unsigned int);
ostream& operator<<(long);
ostream& operator<<(unsigned long);
ostream& operator<<(bool);

    A minimal std::cout for C++ programs. Include <iostream>.

    Notes

    • bool prints true or false; a NULL const char* prints (null).
    • There is no std::endl, manipulators, std::string or std::cin. Write "\n" for a newline.

    Example

    #include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::cout << "2 + 2 = " << 2 + 2 << "\n";
    return 0;
}

    Windows

    mosWM windows over SYS_WINDOW. Include window.h.

    A window is a kernel-owned ARGB8888 frame buffer plus a title, bounds, flags, a style and an event queue. Your program draws into its own pixel buffer and copies it into the window with mos_window_present; mosWM, the window manager, composites every window onto the screen and turns mouse and keyboard input into window events.

    Windows belong to the process that created them (and its descendants). They are closed automatically when that process exits.

    Functionsmos_window_createmos_window_closemos_window_presentmos_window_next_eventmos_window_dispatch_eventsmos_window_set_boundsmos_window_set_titlemos_window_set_flagsmos_window_set_fullscreenmos_window_minimizemos_window_maximizemos_window_restoremos_window_set_resizablemos_window_set_pointer_lockmos_window_set_visiblemos_window_set_stylemos_window_get_infomos_window_listmos_window_get_framemos_window_post_eventmos_window_register_managermos_window_callmos_window_request

    A minimal window app

    #include "window.h"
#include "stdlib.h"

static int running = 1;
static void on_close(uint32_t id) { (void)id; running = 0; }

int main(void) {
    const uint32_t W = 320, H = 200;
    uint32_t id = mos_window_create(0, 120, 80, W, H, "Hello");
    if (!id) mos_exit(1);
    uint32_t* px = malloc(W * H * 4);

    mos_window_callbacks_t cb = { .onwindowclose = on_close };
    while (running) {
        for (uint32_t i = 0; i < W * H; i++) px[i] = 0xFF2845F5;   /* opaque blue */
        mos_window_present(id, px, W * 4, 0, 0, W, H);
        mos_window_dispatch_events(id, &cb);
        mos_sleep(16);
    }
    mos_window_close(id);
    mos_exit(0);
}

    Limits

    LimitValue
    Windows in the systemSYSCALL_WINDOW_MAX_WINDOWS (64)
    Minimum size64 × 48
    Maximum size16384 × 16384, and at most 64 MiB of pixels
    All windows' pixels together64 MiB
    TitleSYSCALL_WINDOW_MAX_TITLE (64) bytes including the NUL
    Queued events per windowSYSCALL_WINDOW_MAX_EVENTS (16)
    Position0 … 32768 on each axis

    Flags

    FlagMeaning
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_VISIBLEDrawn by mosWM
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_RESIZABLEThe user can resize it, and the program may call mos_window_set_bounds
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_FULLSCREENCovers the screen; cannot be combined with MAXIMIZED
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_MAXIMIZEDFills the desktop area
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_MINIMIZEDHidden in the taskbar
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_FOCUSEDHas keyboard focus. Read-only for applications: only mosWM sets it
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_POINTER_LOCKWants the mouse to itself (games): see mos_window_set_pointer_lock

    mos_window_create

    uint32_t mos_window_create(uint32_t parent_id, uint32_t x, uint32_t y,
                           uint32_t width, uint32_t height, const char* title);

    Creates a visible, resizable window. Its frame starts out as whatever the allocator returned, so present a first frame straight away.

    ParameterDescription
    parent_id0 for a top-level window, or the ID of a window this process controls to create a child (a dialog)
    x, yPosition on the desktop
    width, heightContent size in pixels, at least 64 × 48
    titleTitle bar text; truncated to 63 bytes. NULL for none

    Returns the new window ID (1 … 64), or 0 on failure. The raw call fails with SYS_ERR_INVAL (size out of range, bad flags), SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND / SYS_ERR_PERM (bad parent) or SYS_ERR_GENERIC (no free slot, out of frame memory); the wrapper turns all of these into 0.

    Notes To create a window with other flags (not resizable, hidden, full screen), create it and then call mos_window_set_flags.

    mos_window_close

    uint64_t mos_window_close(uint32_t id);

    Destroys a window and frees its frame.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND for an unknown ID, SYS_ERR_PERM for a window this process does not control.

    Notes Clicking the close button does not close the window; it queues a SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_CLOSE_REQUEST. The program decides whether to call mos_window_close.

    mos_window_present

    uint64_t mos_window_present(uint32_t id, const uint32_t* pixels, uint32_t pitch,
                            uint32_t x, uint32_t y, uint32_t width, uint32_t height);

    Copies a rectangle of your pixel buffer into the window's frame. mosWM shows the new frame on its next composite.

    ParameterDescription
    idWindow
    pixelsYour buffer, the same size as the window, ARGB8888 (0xAARRGGBB). Use 0xFF alpha
    pitchBytes per row of pixels, at least window width × 4
    x, y, width, heightThe rectangle to copy, in window coordinates. It must lie inside the window

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a rectangle outside the window, a short pitch or a NULL buffer, SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND / SYS_ERR_PERM for a bad window.

    Notes

    • pixels points at the top-left of your whole buffer, not of the rectangle; the kernel offsets into it. Presenting only the part that changed is cheaper than the whole window.
    • After a SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_RESIZED, reallocate the buffer at the new size before presenting again.
    • Each present increments the window's frame_version.

    Example

    /* redraw only a 32 x 32 cursor area */
mos_window_present(id, px, W * 4, cx, cy, 32, 32);

    Shared frames (mos_window_surface_*)

    mos_window_present copies your pixels into the window. To avoid the copy, map the window's frame buffers and draw into them directly:

    mos_window_surface_t sf;
if (mos_window_surface_map(id, &sf) == SYS_SUCCESS) {
    uint32_t* px = mos_window_surface_back(&sf);      /* rows: sf.info.pitch bytes */
    /* ... draw ... */
    mos_window_surface_present(id, &sf, x, y, w, h);  /* damage rect; swaps buffers */
}

    A window has two buffers (double buffering). The manager shows the front one, you draw into the other, and mos_window_surface_present publishes it (the kernel only records which buffer and which rectangle changed; mosWM recomposites just that rectangle). The damage is what differs from the buffer shown before: after drawing only a rectangle, copy the old front buffer into the back buffer first, or present everything (width == height == 0).

    CallPurpose
    mos_window_map_frame(id, &shared)Raw SYS_WINDOW_MAP_FRAME: fills syscall_window_shared_t (address, buffer_stride, width, height, pitch, generation, front)
    mos_window_present_shared(id, buffer, x, y, w, h)Raw SYS_WINDOW_PRESENT_SHARED
    mos_window_take_damage(id, &shared)Window manager only: damage since the last call
    mos_window_surface_map / _back / _present / _unmapThe convenient form above

    Resizing. A resize replaces both buffers. After SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_RESIZED call mos_window_surface_map again (new address and size, generation + 1, front 0, the old picture copied into buffer 0) and mos_window_surface_unmap the old surface first. A stale mapping stays readable and writable until you unmap it, but nothing you write there is shown. Closing the window does not unmap anything; the frames are freed when the last mapping (yours, the window manager's) is gone or its process ends.

    mos_window_present still works on a mapped window (it writes into the front buffer). Errors: SYS_ERR_NOMEM (no contiguous memory, or over the 128 MiB limit of shared frames), SYS_ERR_INVAL (bad buffer number or rectangle, or not mapped yet), SYS_ERR_PERM. mos_vm_decommit of the mapping is refused (SYS_ERR_INVAL), and mos_vm_unmap / mos_vm_protect must cover the whole mapping; protect may only lower access.

    mos_window_next_event

    uint64_t mos_window_next_event(uint32_t id, syscall_window_event_t* event);

    Takes the oldest event off the window's queue. Never blocks.

    ParameterDescription
    idWindow
    eventFilled with the event

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS with *event filled, SYS_ERR_AGAIN if the queue is empty, SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND / SYS_ERR_PERM for a bad window.

    syscall_window_event_t fields:

    FieldMeaning
    idWindow the event is for
    typeOne of the event types below
    x, yPointer position in window coordinates (mouse events); how far the mouse moved (MOUSE_RELATIVE)
    width, heightNew content size (RESIZED)
    keyUSB HID usage code (KEY)
    buttonsKEY: 1 = pressed, 0 = released. MOUSE: button mask, bit 0 left, bit 1 right, bit 2 middle
    wheelScroll amount (MOUSE_WHEEL)
    modsSYSCALL_INPUT_MOD_SHIFT, _CTRL, _ALT bits
    time_msUptime when the event was queued

    Event types:

    TypeSent when
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_RESIZEDThe window's size changed
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_CLOSE_REQUESTThe user clicked the close button
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_MINIMIZEDIt was minimised
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_MAXIMIZEDIt was maximised
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_RESTOREDIt returned from minimised or maximised
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_FOCUS_GAINEDIt got keyboard focus
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_FOCUS_LOSTIt lost keyboard focus
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_KEYA key was pressed or released while it had focus
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_MOUSEThe pointer moved over it, or a button changed
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_MOUSE_WHEELThe wheel turned over it
    SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_MOUSE_RELATIVEThe mouse moved while the window holds pointer lock: x, y are the motion, buttons the button mask

    Notes

    • The queue holds 16 events. Window-state events of the same type are merged (only the newest resize is kept), and consecutive mouse moves with the same buttons are merged, so a slow program loses detail but not clicks. Drain the queue every frame.
    • Key repeat: while a key is held, the window manager (mosWM) sends it again as a key-down (buttons 1) after about 420 ms, then about 30 times a second, until it is released. These repeats have reserved[0] == 1; SYSCALL_WINDOW_KEY_IS_REPEAT(&ev) tests it. Text input should take them; toggles and game actions that should happen once per press skip them. Modifier keys never repeat. easyui apps get the repeats as ordinary ONKEY calls.
    • Common HID codes: a-z 4-29, 1-9 30-38, 0 39, Enter 40, Escape 41, Backspace 42, Tab 43, Space 44, Right 79, Left 80, Down 81, Up 82.

    Example

    syscall_window_event_t ev;
while (mos_window_next_event(id, &ev) == SYS_SUCCESS) {
    if (ev.type == SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_CLOSE_REQUEST) running = 0;
    else if (ev.type == SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_KEY && ev.buttons && ev.key == 41) running = 0;  /* Esc */
    else if (ev.type == SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_MOUSE && (ev.buttons & 1)) paint(ev.x, ev.y);
    else if (ev.type == SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_RESIZED) resize_buffer(ev.width, ev.height);
}

    mos_window_dispatch_events

    uint64_t mos_window_dispatch_events(uint32_t id, const mos_window_callbacks_t* callbacks);

    Drains the window's queue and calls a callback for each window-state event.

    ParameterDescription
    idWindow
    callbacksStructure of function pointers; any may be NULL

    mos_window_callbacks_t members:

    MemberCalled for
    onwindowclose(id)CLOSE_REQUEST
    onwindowminimize(id)MINIMIZED
    onwindowmaximise(id)MAXIMIZED
    windowsizechange_recall(id, width, height)RESIZED
    onwindowfocus(id, focused)FOCUS_GAINED (1) and FOCUS_LOST (0)

    Returns the number of events taken off the queue, SYS_ERR_INVAL if callbacks is NULL, or an error from mos_window_next_event.

    Notes Key, mouse, wheel and RESTORED events are consumed and dropped. A program that needs input should loop over mos_window_next_event itself.

    mos_window_set_bounds

    uint64_t mos_window_set_bounds(uint32_t id, uint32_t x, uint32_t y,
                               uint32_t width, uint32_t height);

    Moves and/or resizes a window. Resizing keeps the overlapping part of the old frame and queues a RESIZED event.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_PERM if the window is not resizable, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a size or position out of range, SYS_ERR_BUSY if its event queue is full, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if frame memory runs out.

    mos_window_set_title

    uint64_t mos_window_set_title(uint32_t id, const char* title);

    Changes the title bar text (truncated to 63 bytes).

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND / SYS_ERR_PERM.

    Example

    mos_window_set_title(id, dirty ? "notes.txt *" : "notes.txt");

    mos_window_set_flags

    uint64_t mos_window_set_flags(uint32_t id, uint32_t flags);

    Replaces the window's flags with flags (see Flags). The FOCUSED bit is kept as it is.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_INVAL if flags has unknown bits, includes FOCUSED, or combines FULLSCREEN with MAXIMIZED.

    Notes The helpers below read the current flags with mos_window_get_info and change one bit, which is usually what you want.

    Example

    /* a fixed-size window */
mos_window_set_flags(id, SYSCALL_WINDOW_VISIBLE);

    mos_window_set_fullscreen

    uint64_t mos_window_set_fullscreen(uint32_t id, bool enabled);

    Turns full screen on or off. Clears MAXIMIZED and MINIMIZED.

    Returns the result of mos_window_set_flags.

    mos_window_minimize

    uint64_t mos_window_minimize(uint32_t id);

    Minimises the window. Clears FULLSCREEN and MAXIMIZED.

    mos_window_maximize

    uint64_t mos_window_maximize(uint32_t id);

    Maximises the window. Clears FULLSCREEN and MINIMIZED.

    mos_window_restore

    uint64_t mos_window_restore(uint32_t id);

    Clears FULLSCREEN, MAXIMIZED and MINIMIZED, returning the window to its normal bounds.

    mos_window_set_resizable

    uint64_t mos_window_set_resizable(uint32_t id, bool resizable);

    Sets or clears SYSCALL_WINDOW_RESIZABLE.

    mos_window_set_pointer_lock

    uint64_t mos_window_set_pointer_lock(uint32_t id, bool locked);

    Sets or clears SYSCALL_WINDOW_POINTER_LOCK, for games that steer with the mouse. While the window has the flag, is focused, visible and not minimised (and no menu, dialog or the lock screen is open), mosWM hides the cursor, stops it at the window, and sends every move as SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_MOUSE_RELATIVE with the distance moved instead of a position. Buttons and the wheel still come as MOUSE and MOUSE_WHEEL. Moves made while the queue is full are added up and sent with the next event, so no motion is lost.

    The lock ends by itself when the window loses focus and comes back when it is focused again. Clear the flag when the mouse is needed as a pointer again (a menu, a paused game). Doom (programs/doom) locks while a level is played.

    Returns the result of mos_window_set_flags.

    mos_window_set_visible

    uint64_t mos_window_set_visible(uint32_t id, bool visible);

    Shows or hides the window by setting or clearing SYSCALL_WINDOW_VISIBLE. A hidden window keeps its frame and events.

    mos_window_set_style

    uint64_t mos_window_set_style(uint32_t id, syscall_window_style_t style);

    Changes the colours mosWM uses for this window's decoration. All colours are ARGB8888.

    syscall_window_style_t memberDefault
    title_bar0xFF24343C
    title_text0xFFFFFFFF
    close_button, close_icon0xFFE35D6A, 0xFFFFFFFF
    minimize_button, minimize_icon0xFFE8B34C, 0xFF17262C
    maximize_button, maximize_icon0xFF4ABF8A, 0xFF17262C
    border0xFF49616B
    content_background0xFF17232A

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND / SYS_ERR_PERM.

    Example

    syscall_window_info_t info;
mos_window_get_info(id, &info);
syscall_window_style_t s = info.style;
s.title_bar = 0xFF2845F5;
mos_window_set_style(id, s);

    mos_window_get_info

    uint64_t mos_window_get_info(uint32_t id, syscall_window_info_t* info);

    Copies a window's current state.

    syscall_window_info_t fieldMeaning
    id, parent_idThe window and its parent (0 for top level)
    x, y, width, heightContent bounds
    flagsCurrent flags
    frame_versionIncremented by every present
    owner_pidProcess that created it
    title[64]Title
    styleDecoration colours

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a NULL info, or SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND / SYS_ERR_PERM.

    Example

    syscall_window_info_t info;
if (mos_window_get_info(id, &info) == 0 && (info.flags & SYSCALL_WINDOW_FOCUSED))
    draw_caret();

    mos_window_list

    uint64_t mos_window_list(syscall_window_info_t* windows, uint32_t capacity);

    Lists the windows this process controls (all windows, for the window manager).

    ParameterDescription
    windowsArray to fill; may be NULL when capacity is 0
    capacitySize of the array, at most 64

    Returns the total number of matching windows, which can be larger than capacity (only capacity are copied), or SYS_ERR_INVAL.

    Example

    uint64_t count = mos_window_list(NULL, 0);   /* just count */

    mos_window_get_frame

    uint64_t mos_window_get_frame(uint32_t id, syscall_window_frame_t* frame);

    Window-manager only. Copies a window's frame into frame->pixels, which must match the window's size. mosWM uses it to composite.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_PERM for any process other than the registered window manager, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a mismatched buffer.

    mos_window_post_event

    uint64_t mos_window_post_event(uint32_t id, syscall_window_event_t* event);

    Window-manager only. Queues an event on a window; this is how mosWM delivers input and close requests.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_PERM for other processes, SYS_ERR_INVAL for an unknown event type, SYS_ERR_BUSY if the queue is full.

    mos_window_register_manager

    uint64_t mos_window_register_manager(void);

    Makes the calling process the window manager. Only a process started as a window manager that also owns the screen (mos_graphics_acquire) may do this.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, SYS_ERR_PERM if the caller is not allowed, SYS_ERR_BUSY if another manager is registered.

    mos_window_call

    uint64_t mos_window_call(syscall_window_request_t* request);

    Issues SYS_WINDOW with a filled request. Every wrapper above builds a request with mos_window_request and calls this.

    mos_window_request

    syscall_window_request_t mos_window_request(uint32_t op, uint32_t id);

    Returns a zeroed request with size, version, op and id filled in, ready for mos_window_call.
