    Examples: programs/fglcube (shipped as 0:/programs/fglcube.run; run fglcube --shader for the shader version) and MOSdesk's *Cube* app (press S for the shader).

    How it runs

    The kernel executes command buffers through its FGPU command processor, on one of two backends:

    • The graphics card (NVIDIA RTX 20 / GTX 16, after gpu nvidia boot passed its draw test): shaders are translated to the card's machine code when you create them, and clears and draws run on its 3D engine. Surfaces, textures and buffers live in video memory. This path is new and has not been confirmed on a card yet; see docs/gpu.md in Minimal-OS.
    • The CPU (everything else, and the fallback): vertex stage, clipping, perspective-correct rasterization, depth test, fragment stage and blending in software, on every core.

    Programs do not choose: the same calls and the same shader bytecode run on both. A shader the card's compiler does not take yet (one that reads gl_FrontFacing) is drawn by the CPU.

    A first program

    #include "farcadegl.h"
#include "window.h"

static const char* vs =
    "uniform mat4 fgl_ModelViewProjection;\n"
    "attribute vec3 position;\n"
    "attribute vec4 color;\n"
    "varying vec4 v_color;\n"
    "void main() {\n"
    "    v_color = color;\n"
    "    gl_Position = fgl_ModelViewProjection * vec4(position, 1.0);\n"
    "}\n";

static const char* fs =
    "uniform float time;\n"
    "varying vec4 v_color;\n"
    "void main() {\n"
    "    float pulse = 0.75 + 0.25 * sin(time * 4.0);\n"
    "    gl_FragColor = vec4(v_color.rgb * pulse, 1.0);\n"
    "}\n";

int main(void) {
    uint32_t win = mos_window_create(0, 100, 100, 640, 480, "Hello 3D");
    FGLContext* gl = fglCreateContext(&(FGLContextDesc){
        .width = 640, .height = 480, .window_id = win, .depth = 1 });

    FGLVertex cube[36];
    fglMakeCube(cube, 1.0f, NULL);
    FGLBuffer vb = fglCreateBuffer(gl, sizeof cube);
    fglBufferData(gl, vb, 0, cube, sizeof cube);

    FGLShader* sh = fglCreateShader(gl, vs, fs);
    if (!sh) { /* fglShaderLog(gl) says why */ return 1; }
    int u_time = fglUniformLocation(sh, "time");

    for (int frame = 0; frame < 600; frame++) {
        fglClearColor(gl, 0.05f, 0.07f, 0.12f);
        fglClear(gl, FGL_COLOR_BUFFER_BIT | FGL_DEPTH_BUFFER_BIT);
        fglEnable(gl, FGL_DEPTH_TEST | FGL_CULL_FACE);
        fglUseShader(gl, sh);
        fglUniform1f(sh, u_time, frame / 60.0f);
        fglSetProjection(gl, fglPerspective(0.9f, 640.0f / 480.0f, 0.1f, 50));
        fglSetView(gl, fglLookAt(fglVec3(0, 1, 4), fglVec3(0, 0, 0), fglVec3(0, 1, 0)));
        fglSetModel(gl, fglRotate(frame * 0.02f, fglVec3(0, 1, 0)));
        fglDraw(gl, vb, 0, 36);
        fglPresent(gl);
    }
    fglDestroyShader(gl, sh);
    fglDestroyContext(gl);
    mos_window_close(win);
    return 0;
}

    Without the shader lines, fglUseProgram(gl, FGL_PROGRAM_PHONG) draws the same cube with the built-in per-pixel lighting.

    Contexts

    typedef struct {
    uint32_t width, height;     // render size
    uint32_t window_id;         // present into this window; 0 = the screen
    int32_t x, y;               // screen position when window_id == 0
    int depth;                  // create a depth buffer
    int page_flip;              // screen only: flip between two VRAM buffers
} FGLContextDesc;

FGLContext* fglCreateContext(const FGLContextDesc* desc);
void fglDestroyContext(FGLContext* gl);

    A context owns the color surface(s) you draw into, an optional depth buffer, and the command buffer being recorded.

    • In a window (MOSdesk): create the window with mos_window_create and pass its id. fglPresent copies each frame into the window.
    • Full screen (terminal): take the screen with mos_graphics_acquire() first. With page_flip set and a GPU that can flip (the QEMU/Bochs adapter can), frames are shown by switching the display to the buffer just drawn instead of copying it.

    Returns NULL when the surfaces cannot be created. fglGetDeviceInfo fills a syscall_gpu_info_t (GPU name, driver, VRAM, backend, caps; caps & FGPU_CAP_SHADERS says shaders are available).

    Buffers and vertex layouts

    FGLBuffer fglCreateBuffer(FGLContext* gl, uint32_t bytes);
int fglBufferData(FGLContext* gl, FGLBuffer b, uint32_t offset, const void* data, uint32_t bytes);
void fglDestroyBuffer(FGLContext* gl, FGLBuffer b);

    A buffer is up to 16 MiB of GPU memory. Index buffers hold uint32_t indices. Everything a process creates is freed when it exits.

    Vertex buffers hold FGLVertex by default:

    StructFloatsAttributes (location)
    FGLVertex10position xyz (0), normal xyz (1), color rgba (2)
    FGLVertexUV12the same, plus texture coordinates uv (3)

    Call fglVertexLayoutUV(gl) before drawing FGLVertexUV data, and fglVertexLayoutDefault(gl) to go back. For your own vertex struct, describe where each attribute location sits:

    typedef struct { float x, y; float u, v; float shade; } MyVertex;

static const FGLAttribute attrs[] = {
    { offsetof(MyVertex, x), 2 },       // location 0: vec2 (z = 0, w = 1)
    { offsetof(MyVertex, u), 2 },       // location 1
    { offsetof(MyVertex, shade), 1 },   // location 2
};
fglVertexLayout(gl, sizeof(MyVertex), 3, attrs);

    Offsets and the stride are in bytes and must be multiples of 4; a vertex is at most 64 floats; there are 8 locations. Missing components read as (0, 0, 0, 1), so a 2-float position is a point at z = 0. The layout is context state: it applies to every following draw, with shaders and with the built-in programs (which read locations 0, 1 and 2).

    In a shader, attributes get their location from layout(location = N), or from their name: position, normal, color, uv / texcoord (also with a_, in_, a or in prefixes) are 0, 1, 2 and 3. See fgsl.md.

    Read-only shader buffers

    void fglBindStorageBuffer(FGLContext* gl, uint32_t binding, FGLBuffer buffer);

    Bind a buffer to a shader declaration such as layout(binding = 0) buffer vec4 lights[];. Buffer contents are read-only from FGSL; each element is one 16-byte vec4, and the bound buffer size must be a multiple of 16 bytes. There are FGL_MAX_STORAGE_BUFFERS bindings. Negative and out-of-range shader indices return a zero vector. On the NVIDIA Turing backend, a storage buffer is bound as a constant buffer (the first 64 KiB of it): constant and computed indices both run on the card, and reads past the end return zero there too.

    State and drawing

    CallEffect
    fglClearColor(gl, r, g, b) / fglClear(gl, bits)Clear color and/or depth (FGL_COLOR_BUFFER_BIT, FGL_DEPTH_BUFFER_BIT).
    fglEnable / fglDisableFGL_DEPTH_TEST, FGL_CULL_FACE (back faces; counter-clockwise is front), FGL_WIREFRAME, FGL_BLEND, FGL_SCISSOR_TEST.
    fglUseProgram(gl, p)Use a built-in program (and stop using a shader).
    fglUseShader(gl, sh)Use a shader.
    fglSetModel, fglSetView, fglSetProjectionThe usual three matrices.
    fglSetLight(gl, direction, color, ambient)One directional light; direction is where the light travels.
    fglSetMaterial(gl, specular, shininess)Highlight strength (0-1) and sharpness (1-128).
    fglViewport(gl, x, y, w, h)Area of the surface to draw into (defaults to all of it).
    fglScissor(gl, x, y, w, h)The rectangle FGL_SCISSOR_TEST limits draws and clears to. See Scissor.
    fglDraw(gl, vertices, first, count)Triangles from consecutive vertices.
    fglDrawIndexed(gl, vertices, indices, first_index, count)Triangles from an index buffer.
    fglSubmit(gl)Run the recorded commands.
    fglPresent(gl)Submit and show the frame. Returns 0, or -1 with gl->error set.
    fglPresentScaled(gl, scale)Upscale every later fglPresent by 1, 2 or 3 (nearest neighbour; screen only). See Scaled and paced present.
    fglSwapInterval(gl, n)0 = present at once, n = wait for the next boundary of n/60 s before each present (1 = 60 fps).
    fglSwapIntervalNs(gl, ns)The same with the interval in nanoseconds (1 ms to 1 s).
    fglLastPresentNs(gl)Monotonic time (ns) the last paced present was released.
    fglSetPresentFlags(gl, flags)Raw FGPU_PRESENT_* flags for fglPresent.
    fglReadPixels(gl, out, pitch)Copy the frame into your memory.

    Scissor

    fglEnable(gl, FGL_SCISSOR_TEST);
fglScissor(gl, x, y, w, h);          // pixels of the render target

    While FGL_SCISSOR_TEST is enabled, draws and clears (fglClear, color and depth) only touch pixels inside the rectangle. The origin is the top-left pixel and y grows downward, exactly like fglViewport, so a viewport and a scissor with the same numbers cover the same pixels (this differs from OpenGL, where the origin is bottom-left). The rectangle is clipped to the render target (negative x/y and parts beyond the target are fine); a zero width or height draws nothing; a negative size makes the next fglSubmit fail with SYS_ERR_INVAL. Until you call fglScissor the rectangle is the whole target.

    It costs nothing per pixel: the rectangle only shrinks the area the rasterizer visits (tiles and edge setup are clipped), so a UI that sets a scissor for every widget pays nothing extra for it. A clear with a scissor rectangle first renders the draws recorded before it, then clears the rectangle, so alternate long runs of draws with scissored clears rather than clearing in the middle of every draw sequence. fglHasScissor() tells whether the kernel supports it (FGPU_CAP_SCISSOR in fglGetDeviceInfo); the NVIDIA backend draws scissored work on the CPU backend for now.

    Scaled and paced present

    A full-screen game can render at a lower internal size and let the kernel upscale: create the context at 960x540 (desc.width/height), call fglPresentScaled(gl, 2) and every fglPresent fills a 1920x1080 screen (3 gives 2880x1620, clipped to the screen; desc.x/y place the scaled image, negative values clip). The surface goes straight into the framebuffer with non-temporal SSE2 stores, one copy and no kernel back buffer; page flipping is not used for scaled frames. fglSwapInterval(gl, 1) makes each present wait for the next 1/60 s boundary (the process sleeps; it does not spin), so a loop that renders in less than 16.7 ms runs at a steady 60 fps. A frame that is late by under one interval presents at once and keeps the phase; later than that restarts the phase. fglLastPresentNs reports when the frame was released. Both options need FGPU_CAP_SCALED_PRESENT and FGPU_CAP_PACED_PRESENT in syscall_gpu_info_t.caps; older kernels reject the flags and fglPresent returns -1.

    Calls only *record*; nothing is drawn until fglSubmit/fglPresent. State changes between draws apply to the draws after them, in order, so you can change a uniform, draw, change it again and draw again in one frame.

    Built-in programs

    ProgramWhat it does
    FGL_PROGRAM_COLORVertex colors, no lighting.
    FGL_PROGRAM_GOURAUDLighting per vertex (diffuse + Blinn-Phong highlight), interpolated.
    FGL_PROGRAM_PHONGThe same lighting per pixel.

    They use fglSetLight and fglSetMaterial. They are faster than an equivalent shader, so they remain a good choice for simple scenes.

    Shaders

    FGLShader* fglCreateShader(FGLContext* gl, const char* vertex_src, const char* fragment_src);
const char* fglShaderLog(FGLContext* gl);
void fglUseShader(FGLContext* gl, FGLShader* sh);
void fglDestroyShader(FGLContext* gl, FGLShader* sh);

    fglCreateShader compiles both stages with the FGSL compiler (fglsl.h), links them (varyings and uniforms are matched by name), and loads the program onto the GPU. On failure it returns NULL and fglShaderLog(gl) holds a message such as

    fragment shader line 12: unknown identifier 'normall'

    The language is GLSL ES 1.0 / GLSL 1.30 with a few limits (no structs, no while, loops must have constant bounds); fgsl.md has the full reference. The compiler runs inside your program and takes well under a millisecond for typical shaders; create shaders once at startup, not every frame.

    Uniforms

    int fglUniformLocation(FGLShader* sh, const char* name);    // -1 if not declared
void fglUniform1f(FGLShader* sh, int loc, float x);
void fglUniform2f(FGLShader* sh, int loc, float x, float y);
void fglUniform3f(FGLShader* sh, int loc, float x, float y, float z);
void fglUniform4f(FGLShader* sh, int loc, float x, float y, float z, float w);
void fglUniformVec3(FGLShader* sh, int loc, FGLVec3 v);
void fglUniformMatrix4(FGLShader* sh, int loc, FGLMat4 m);
void fglUniformArray(FGLShader* sh, int loc, uint32_t first, const float* values, uint32_t count);
void fglUniformTexture(FGLContext* gl, FGLShader* sh, int loc, FGLTexture t, uint32_t flags);

    Uniform values belong to the shader and keep their value until you set them again (also across frames and while another shader is in use). Setting a location of -1 does nothing, so you can skip checks. fglUniformArray takes count elements packed tightly in the uniform's type (vec3 = 3 floats, mat4 = 16).

    Automatic uniforms

    Declare any of these and FarcadeGL keeps them up to date from the context's state, so shaders work with fglSetModel, fglSetLight and friends:

    UniformTypeValue
    fgl_ModelViewProjectionmat4projection × view × model
    fgl_Model, fgl_View, fgl_Projectionmat4the matrices as set
    fgl_ModelViewmat4view × model
    fgl_NormalMatrixmat4inverse transpose of the model matrix (use with vec4(normal, 0.0))
    fgl_LightDirectionvec3fglSetLight direction (normalized; the way light travels)
    fgl_LightColor, fgl_Ambientvec3fglSetLight colors
    fgl_CameraPositionvec3the eye position, from the view matrix
    fgl_Materialvec2fglSetMaterial specular strength, shininess

    Textures

    FGLTexture fglCreateTexture(FGLContext* gl, uint32_t width, uint32_t height, const uint32_t* pixels);
int fglTextureData(FGLContext* gl, FGLTexture t, const uint32_t* pixels, uint32_t pitch);
void fglDestroyTexture(FGLContext* gl, FGLTexture t);
void fglBindTexture(FGLContext* gl, uint32_t unit, FGLTexture t, uint32_t flags);
// mipmaps
FGLTexture fglCreateTextureMips(FGLContext* gl, uint32_t width, uint32_t height, const uint32_t* pixels);
int fglTextureLevelData(FGLContext* gl, FGLTexture t, uint32_t level, const uint32_t* pixels, uint32_t pitch);
void fglGenerateMipmap(FGLContext* gl, FGLTexture t);
void fglBindTextureLod(FGLContext* gl, uint32_t unit, FGLTexture t, uint32_t flags, float bias, float min_lod, float max_lod);
uint32_t fglMipLevels(uint32_t width, uint32_t height);

    Textures are ARGB8888 (0xAARRGGBB), rows top to bottom, up to 4096 × 4096. In a shader, texture(sampler, uv) returns vec4(r, g, b, a) in 0..1. uv = (0, 0) is the top-left corner of the image and (1, 1) the bottom-right; fglMakeCubeUV maps each face upright.

    Each sampler2D uniform gets a texture unit (0-15, FGL_MAX_TEXTURE_UNITS, in declaration order; kernels from before ABI 4 had 4). fglUniformTexture(gl, sh, loc, tex, flags) binds a texture to that sampler's unit; fglBindTexture binds to a unit directly. Flags:

    FlagEffect
    FGL_TEXTURE_LINEARBilinear filtering (default: nearest texel).
    FGL_TEXTURE_CLAMPCoordinates outside 0..1 use the edge texels (default: the texture repeats).
    FGL_TEXTURE_MIP_NEARESTMipmapped textures: sample the nearest mip level.
    FGL_TEXTURE_MIP_LINEARMipmapped textures: blend the two nearest levels. With FGL_TEXTURE_LINEAR this is trilinear (FGL_TEXTURE_TRILINEAR).

    Bindings are context state, like the vertex layout.

    Mipmaps

    fglCreateTextureMips makes a texture with room for the whole chain: level k is max(1, w >> k) x max(1, h >> k) texels, down to 1 x 1 (at most 13 levels, fglMipLevels(w, h) counts them); pixels is level 0. Fill the other levels yourself with fglTextureLevelData(gl, t, level, pixels, pitch) (the pixels of that level; level 0 is the texture itself) or let fglGenerateMipmap(gl, t) build levels 1.. from level 0 with a 2x2 box filter. fglGenerateMipmap is a command: it runs after the draws recorded before it, so you can render into a texture and generate its mips in the same frame (render targets and fglReadPixels only see level 0).

    The sampler picks a level from the screen-space derivatives of the texture coordinate: lod = log2(longest side of the pixel's footprint, in texels of level 0). A shader that samples a mipmapped texture with a mip flag runs on 2x2 pixel quads (the differences between the neighbours in the quad give the derivatives, also for coordinates the shader computes); pixels at the edge of a triangle behave the same as the interior. Filtering:

    FlagsResult
    none, or FGL_TEXTURE_LINEARLevel 0 only, as before.
    FGL_TEXTURE_MIP_NEARESTThe level nearest to lod; nearest texel inside it (with FGL_TEXTURE_LINEAR: bilinear).
    FGL_TEXTURE_MIP_LINEARThe two levels around lod, blended by its fraction (with FGL_TEXTURE_LINEAR: trilinear).

    When lod <= 0 (the texture is magnified) level 0 is used with the LINEAR filter. A texture without a chain ignores the mip flags. Textures sampled in the vertex stage use level 0. fglBindTextureLod adds a level-of-detail bias (positive = blurrier), a min_lod (never finer than this level; use it while streaming mips in, 0 = off) and a max_lod (never coarser, 0 = off). Mipmapped textures are kept in system memory and drawn by the CPU backend (the NVIDIA backend does not sample them yet). fglHasMipmaps() reports support (FGPU_CAP_MIPMAPS).

    Blending

    fglEnable(gl, FGL_BLEND) mixes each new pixel with what is already there using the fragment's alpha: color = src.rgb * src.a + dst.rgb * (1 - src.a). Draw opaque geometry first, then transparent geometry back to front. With the built-in programs, alpha comes from the vertex color.

    Math

    FGLVec3, FGLMat4 and: fglVec3, fglAdd, fglSub, fglScale3, fglDot, fglCross, fglNormalize, fglIdentity, fglMul, fglTranslate, fglScale, fglRotate(angle, axis), fglPerspective(fovy, aspect, near, far), fglLookAt(eye, center, up), fglNormalMatrix, and fglSin, fglCos, fglTan, fglSqrt (the SDK has no libm).

    fglMakeCube(out, half_size, face_colors) writes the 36 vertices of a cube with one color per face (NULL for the default colors); fglMakeCubeUV does the same with texture coordinates.

    Errors and limits

    • fglPresent/fglSubmit return -1 and set gl->error to the first failed SYS_GPU result (SYS_ERR_INVAL for a bad command, SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND for a destroyed buffer or texture).
    • fglCreateShader returns NULL; see fglShaderLog. If the kernel rejects a program the compiler produced, the reason is written to the serial log (fgpu: shader program rejected: ...).
    LimitValue
    Surface / texture size4096 × 4096
    Buffer size16 MiB
    Command buffer1 MiB per submit (FarcadeGL grows its buffer as needed)
    Shader program2048 instructions per stage, 32 temporary vec4s, 8 varyings, 64 uniform vec4s (a mat4 uses 4), 256 constant vec4s, 16 texture units (4 before ABI 4), 4 storage-buffer bindings
    Mip levels13 (4096 × 4096 down to 1 × 1)
    Objects per process1024 surfaces (contexts and textures), 4096 buffers, 1024 shaders; shared by the threads of a program

    Performance

    The CPU backend runs on one core. Measured for the fglcube scene in a 640 × 480 window on a 2.8 GHz Xeon core: about 11 ms per frame with the built-in Phong program and about 42 ms (24 fps) with fglcube --shader (a 60-instruction fragment shader over about 180,000 pixels), so a full shader costs roughly 4 times a built-in program. Fragment shaders run 8 pixels at a time with SSE. Under QEMU without KVM everything is many times slower. Tips:

    • Do per-vertex work in the vertex shader and pass it as a varying; the fragment shader runs for every pixel.
    • Fewer varyings and fewer instructions are faster. discard makes the depth buffer update after the fragment shader instead of before it.
    • Use the built-in programs for objects that need nothing special.

    The FGPU interface underneath

    SYS_GPU (40) takes a syscall_gpu_request_t. Operations: INFO, CREATE_SURFACE, DESTROY_SURFACE, CREATE_BUFFER, UPLOAD_BUFFER, DESTROY_BUFFER, SUBMIT, READBACK, PRESENT, RELEASE_DISPLAY, and (ABI version 2) CREATE_PROGRAM, DESTROY_PROGRAM, WRITE_SURFACE (ABI 4: the request's offset is the mip level). INFO reports FGPU_CAP_SCISSOR, FGPU_CAP_MIPMAPS and FGPU_CAP_TEXTURE_UNITS16 in caps and, with the ABI 4 structure size, a limits block (max_texture_units, max_mip_levels, ...); fglGetDeviceInfo fills it in for older kernels too.

    A command buffer is a list of 32-bit words; each command starts with FGPU_CMD(opcode, length_in_words): BIND_TARGET, VIEWPORT, CLEAR, SET_STATE, SET_PROGRAM, SET_UNIFORMS, DRAW, and (version 2) SET_SHADER, SET_CONSTANTS, SET_VERTEX_LAYOUT, BIND_TEXTURE, and (version 4) SCISSOR, GENERATE_MIPMAPS. Every submit starts from default state (scissor off).

    A shader program is a blob of FGPU bytecode: a header, the vertex and fragment instructions (five words each: opcode, destination, three sources, with swizzles and negate/abs modifiers on vec4 registers) and a constant pool. The instruction set and register files are described at the end of fgpu_abi.h. Jumps only go forward, so every program finishes; the kernel checks every instruction when the program is created. You can produce blobs yourself, but fglsl_compile (fglsl.h) is the supported way.

    PreviousDevice managersNextFGSL shading language

    Edit this page on GitHub

    FGSL shading language (fglsl.h)

    FGSL (Farcade GL Shading Language) is the language FarcadeGL shaders are written in. It is a subset of GLSL: if you know GLSL ES 1.0 (WebGL 1) or desktop GLSL 1.30, you already know it. Shaders are compiled inside your program by fglsl.h (FarcadeGL's fglCreateShader does this), into FGPU bytecode that the kernel checks and runs.

    On this pageProgram structureTypesVariablesStatementsExpressionsFunctionsLimitsErrorsUsing the compiler directly
    // vertex shader
uniform mat4 fgl_ModelViewProjection;
attribute vec3 position;
attribute vec2 uv;
varying vec2 v_uv;

void main() {
    v_uv = uv;
    gl_Position = fgl_ModelViewProjection * vec4(position, 1.0);
}
    // fragment shader
uniform sampler2D tex;
uniform float time;
varying vec2 v_uv;

void main() {
    vec4 c = texture(tex, v_uv);
    if (c.a < 0.1) discard;
    gl_FragColor = vec4(c.rgb * (0.8 + 0.2 * sin(time)), 1.0);
}

    Program structure

    A shader is a list of global declarations and functions, with one void main(). Both GLSL styles work:

    GLSL ES 1.0 styleGLSL 1.30 style
    Vertex inputattribute vec3 position;in vec3 position;
    Vertex → fragmentvarying vec3 v_normal;out vec3 v_normal; / in vec3 v_normal;
    Fragment outputgl_FragColor = ...;out vec4 color; then color = ...;

    #version, #extension and other # lines are ignored, as are precision ...; statements and the qualifiers highp, mediump, lowp, flat, smooth, centroid, invariant. Comments are // and /* */.

    Types

    TypeNotes
    float32-bit float.
    vec2, vec3, vec4Float vectors.
    mat44 × 4 float matrix, column-major, as in GLSL. m[i] is column i.
    sampler2DA texture; uniforms and function parameters only.
    int, bool, uint, ivecN, bvecNAccepted, stored as floats. true is 1.0, false 0.0. Integer division is not truncated: use floor() or int().

    mat2, mat3, structs and samplers other than sampler2D are not supported. Arrays are supported for uniforms and local variables, with a size up to 64 (uniforms) or 16 (locals), indexed by a constant or a loop counter.

    Constructors

    vec4(1.0), vec4(v3, 1.0), vec3(v4) (takes .xyz), vec2(x, y), float(x), int(x) (truncates toward zero), bool(x), mat4(c0, c1, c2, c3) (four vec4 columns) and mat4(1.0) (diagonal). Constructors whose arguments are all constants are folded at compile time.

    Swizzles

    .xyzw, .rgba and .stpq, in any order and with repeats when reading (v.zyx, c.rrr); without repeats when writing (v.xz = ...).

    Variables

    DeclarationMeaning
    uniform T name;Set by the program with fglUniform*. The same name in both shaders is one uniform.
    layout(binding = N) buffer vec4 name[];Read-only storage buffer at binding 0-3; bind with fglBindStorageBuffer.
    attribute T name; / in T name; (vertex)Per-vertex input, float to vec4.
    varying T name; / out T name; (vertex)Output to the fragment shader, float to vec4, interpolated perspective-correctly.
    varying T name; / in T name; (fragment)Input from the vertex shader, matched by name and type.
    out vec4 name; (fragment)The fragment color (same as gl_FragColor).
    const T name = expr;A constant; folded when the value is known at compile time.
    T name; (global or local)A variable; starts at zero.

    Storage buffers are unsized vec4 arrays and read-only. An index is truncated toward zero; a negative or out-of-range index returns (0, 0, 0, 0). The bound buffer's size must be a multiple of 16 bytes.

    Attributes

    Each attribute reads one location of the vertex layout (see farcadegl.md). The location is layout(location = N) if given, otherwise taken from the name:

    Name (also with an a_, in_, a or in prefix, any case)LocationIn FGLVertex / FGLVertexUV
    position, pos, vertex0px, py, pz
    normal1nx, ny, nz
    color, colour2r, g, b, a
    uv, texcoord, texcoord03u, v

    Other names get the first free location from 4. Components the layout does not provide read as 0, 0, 0, 1.

    Built-in variables

    VariableStageTypeMeaning
    gl_Positionvertexvec4Clip-space position (write).
    gl_FragColorfragmentvec4Color, rgba in 0..1 (write).
    gl_FragCoordfragmentvec4Pixel center (x + 0.5, y + 0.5, depth 0..1, 1/w). y grows downwards.
    gl_FrontFacingfragmentboolTrue for counter-clockwise (front) triangles.

    FarcadeGL also fills the fgl_* uniforms when you declare them (fgl_ModelViewProjection, fgl_NormalMatrix, fgl_LightDirection, ...): see farcadegl.md.

    Statements

    • Assignment =, +=, -=, *=, /=, and ++ / -- (as statements).
    • if (...) ... else ...
    • for (int i = A; i < B; i++) ... — the start, end and step must be constants (<, <=, >, >=, !=; i++, i--, ++i, i += n, i -= n). Loops are unrolled, at most 256 times. break and continue work. Inside the loop, i is a constant, so it can index arrays.
    • discard; (fragment shader) drops the pixel.
    • return; / return expr;
    • while and do loops are not supported (every program must finish in a known number of steps).

    Expressions

    Operators, from lowest to highest precedence: ?:, ||, &&, == !=, < > <= >=, + -, * /, unary - + !, then calls, [] and swizzles. Arithmetic works component by component; a float mixes with any vector (v * 2.0). mat4 * vec4, vec4 * mat4 and mat4 * mat4 are matrix products. Comparisons and &&, ||, ! work on scalars and give 0.0 or 1.0.

    Functions

    User functions are supported and inlined at each call: parameters are copies (in); out / inout parameters and recursion are not supported. A function must be declared before main is compiled, in any order.

    float rim(vec3 n, vec3 v, float power) {
    return pow(1.0 - max(dot(n, v), 0.0), power);
}

    Built-in functions

    T is float or a vector; arguments marked float may also be a single float with vector arguments (as in GLSL).

    FunctionNotes
    radians, degrees
    sin, cos, tan, atan(y, x), atan(y_over_x)Error about 1e-5.
    pow, exp, exp2, log, log2, sqrt, inversesqrtpow(x, y) is 0 for x <= 0 (GLSL leaves it undefined).
    abs, sign, floor, ceil, fract, mod(x, y)
    min, max, clamp(x, lo, hi), mix(a, b, t), step(edge, x), smoothstep(e0, e1, x)
    length, distance, dot, cross, normalize, reflect(I, N)
    texture(sampler, uv), texture2D(sampler, uv)Returns vec4, see textures.

    texture on a mipmapped texture (see mipmaps) picks its level from the derivatives of the coordinate across the 2x2 pixel quad.

    Not available: asin, acos, refract, faceforward, derivatives (dFdx...), texture with a bias or explicit LOD (textureLod), matrix functions.

    Limits

    Limit
    Instructions per stage (after inlining and unrolling)2048
    Temporary registers (vec4)32
    Varyings8
    Uniform registers64 vec4 (mat4 = 4, arrays count every element)
    Constants256 vec4
    Samplers16
    Storage-buffer bindings4
    Attributes8

    The compiler reports when a shader goes over a limit ("shader too complex", "too many varyings ...").

    Errors

    Errors name the stage and line:

    vertex shader line 7: unknown identifier 'positon'
fragment shader line 3: the vertex shader does not write varying 'v_uv'
fragment shader line 9: type mismatch in assignment

    Using the compiler directly

    #include "fglsl.h"

static fglsl_program_t prog;    // about 160 KiB: keep it static or malloc it
if (fglsl_compile(&prog, vertex_src, fragment_src) != 0)
    printf("%s\n", prog.error);
// prog.words / prog.size: the blob for SYS_GPU_CREATE_PROGRAM
// prog.uniforms[0 .. uniform_count-1]: name, type, first register (or unit)
// prog.attribs[0 .. attrib_count-1]: name, type, location

    fglsl.h needs no libc, so it also builds on a Linux or macOS host, for example to check shaders at build time. The bytecode format is described in fgpu_abi.h ("Shader programs").

    Disks and root commands (storage.h)

    Functionsmos_storage_listmos_storage_status

    mos_storage_list

    long mos_storage_list(syscall_storage_device_t* devices, uint32_t capacity);

    Fills devices with every disk, each followed by its partitions, and returns how many there are (which can be more than capacity). Read-only; any program may call it.

    FieldMeaning
    name, parentsata0, nvme0p2; partitions name their disk
    model, labelDrive model; GPT partition name
    kindSYSCALL_STORAGE_KIND_DISK or _PARTITION
    tableDisks: SYSCALL_STORAGE_TABLE_NONE, _MBR, _GPT
    fs0 unknown, 1 empty, 2 MinimaFS, 3 FAT, 4 partitioned
    part_kind0 MinimaFS, 1 EFI System, 2 BIOS boot, 3 FAT, 4 other

    mos_storage_status

    install_payload is 1 when the kernel can run install (GRUB loaded the install payload, as the ISO and installed systems do). boot_device is the device mounted as 0:.

    Running kernel commands as root

    long mos_root_auth(const char* username, const char* password);
long mos_root_run(const char* command);
long mos_root_read(char* out, size_t out_size);

    mos_root_auth checks the password of the MOSdesk account and gives the process a ticket for a few minutes (SYS_ERR_PERM when wrong). mos_root_run starts a kernel terminal command such as install sata1 --yes; one command runs at a time. mos_root_read appends the command's output to out and returns 1 while it still runs, 0 once it has finished. The MOSdesk Installer is built this way.

    Playing audio (audio.h)

    Plays .adi files through the sound card the kernel found: Intel HD Audio or AC97, and lets programs play sound they make themselves through audio streams (below), mixed together with the file. There is one file player for the whole system. Opening a file replaces whatever was playing, including a file started with the terminal's play command. MOSdesk's Player app (0:/programs/mos_player.run) uses this API.

    Every call returns SYS_SUCCESS (0) or a negative SYS_ERR_* value.

    Functionssyscall_audio_status_t
    CallDoes
    mos_audio_open(path)Loads a file and starts playing it. SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND if it does not exist, SYS_ERR_INVAL if it is not a playable .adi, SYS_ERR_GENERIC if there is no sound card
    mos_audio_pause()Pauses
    mos_audio_resume()Continues; after the end it plays the file again from the start
    mos_audio_stop()Stops and unloads the file
    mos_audio_seek(ms)Jumps to a position in milliseconds
    mos_audio_volume(v)Sets the volume, 0-100. Opening a file resets it to the file's Globalvol
    mos_audio_status(&st)Fills a syscall_audio_status_t; works with nothing loaded

    syscall_audio_status_t

    FieldMeaning
    stateSYSCALL_AUDIO_IDLE (nothing loaded), _PLAYING, _PAUSED, _ENDED
    position_ms, duration_msWhere playback is and how long the file is
    sample_rate, channelsFrom the file's header
    volume0-100
    format"IMA-ADPCM" or "PCM16"
    driver"Intel HD Audio", "AC97", or "" when there is no sound card
    pathThe file that is loaded
    #include "audio.h"

int main(void) {
    if (mos_audio_open("0:/music.adi") != SYS_SUCCESS) return 1;
    syscall_audio_status_t st;
    do {
        mos_sleep(500);
        mos_audio_status(&st);
    } while (st.state == SYSCALL_AUDIO_PLAYING);
    return 0;
}

    Playback runs in the kernel, so it keeps going after the program exits. Call mos_audio_stop() first if it should not.

    Audio streams: sound a program makes

    For games, synthesizers and anything else that makes its own sound. A program opens a stream and keeps writing 16-bit samples into it; the kernel mixes up to 8 streams (from any programs) and the file player together, converting each stream's rate to the sound card's.

    CallDoes
    mos_audio_stream_open(rate, channels)Opens a stream: 8000-96000 Hz, 1 (mono) or 2 (stereo) channels. Returns a handle (1 or more), or SYS_ERR_BUSY when all 8 are taken, SYS_ERR_GENERIC with no sound card, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a bad rate or channel count
    mos_audio_stream_write(h, samples, frames)Queues frames frames (a frame is one sample per channel, stereo interleaved left, right). Returns how many it took: fewer when the queue is full, never blocks
    mos_audio_stream_queued(h)Frames still waiting to be played
    mos_audio_stream_query(h, &info)Fills a syscall_audio_stream_t: queued, capacity (16384 frames), mix_rate (the card's rate), underruns (times the stream ran dry while open)
    mos_audio_stream_set_volume(h, v)0-100, default 100
    mos_audio_stream_close(h)Closes it; what is still queued is dropped

    A stream belongs to the program that opened it and is closed when that program exits. The file player's volume does not affect streams, and opening or stopping a file does not touch them.

    Keep a little queued - 50-100 ms is a good amount - and top it up regularly: too little and the sound breaks up when the program is slow for a moment, too much and it lags behind the picture.

    #include "audio.h"

/* One second of a 440 Hz square wave. */
int main(void) {
    int h = mos_audio_stream_open(22050, 1);
    if (h < 0) return 1;
    static int16_t buf[22050];
    for (int i = 0; i < 22050; i++) buf[i] = (i / 25) % 2 ? 6000 : -6000;
    uint32_t done = 0;
    while (done < 22050) {
        long n = mos_audio_stream_write(h, buf + done, 22050 - done);
        if (n > 0) done += (uint32_t)n;
        else mos_sleep(20);
    }
    while (mos_audio_stream_queued(h) > 0) mos_sleep(20);
    mos_audio_stream_close(h);
    return 0;
}

    Doom's sound effects (programs/doom/sound.c) are a fuller example: up to 16 sounds mixed in the program into one stereo stream.

    Making .adi files

    python3 tools/audioconverter/wavtoadi.py --format IADPCM song.wav song.adi

    Takes 16-bit mono or stereo WAV. Rates from 8 to 48 kHz play as they are; the HD Audio driver resamples when the codec lacks the file's rate.

    PreviousDisks and root commandsNextPictures and icons in your own pixels (mosmedia.h)

    Edit this page on GitHub

    Pictures and icons in your own pixels (mosmedia.h)

    mosmedia.h reads and draws Minimal-OS .img pictures. Besides the raster pictures (RGB or RGBA, lossless) an .img can be a vector picture: paths with solid and gradient paints, fills and strokes. A vector picture is drawn again at the size you ask for, so one small file gives a crisp icon at 16 px and a crisp logo at 1024 px. This page covers the picture half of the header; .vid videos are in the kernel's media documentation.

    Header only, plain C, no libc: it builds in a .run program and on the build PC. Pixels are 0xAARRGGBB (not premultiplied), like windows and easyui.

    Functionsmimg_decodemimg_rendermimg_render_ex
    #include "mosmedia.h"

/* an icon, tinted with the theme's text color, at the size of a button */
static uint32_t pixels[24 * 24];
mimg_render_opts_t o;
mimg_render_opts_init(&o);
o.current_color = 0xFFEAF2F8;                 /* "current color" paints take this */
mimg_render_ex(icon_data, icon_size, pixels, 24, 24, 24, &o);

    Make vector pictures from SVG files with mosmedia vimg icon.svg icon.img on the build PC (see the kernel's media documentation).

    Which kind is it

    mimg_info accepts raster (version 1) and vector (version 2) files:

    typedef struct {
    uint32_t width, height;   /* the size of a raster picture; the natural size of a vector one */
    bool alpha;
    float vb_x, vb_y, vb_w, vb_h;   /* vector: the view box; raster: 0, 0, width, height */
    bool current_color;       /* vector: it has "current color" paints (a tintable icon) */
    bool vector;
} mimg_info_t;
bool mimg_info(const uint8_t* data, size_t size, mimg_info_t* info);

    Returns false for anything that is not an .img this header can read, including damaged headers.

    mimg_decode

    bool mimg_decode(const uint8_t* data, size_t size, uint32_t* out, uint32_t stride);

    Draws the picture at info.width x info.height into out (stride is in pixels). Raster pictures decode exactly as before; a vector picture is drawn at its natural size with black as its "current color". Programs that only know mimg_info and mimg_decode (Photos, Mxplorer, mosWM) show vector files with no change.

    mimg_render

    bool mimg_render(const uint8_t* data, size_t size, uint32_t* out,
                 uint32_t width, uint32_t height, uint32_t stride);

    Draws any .img into width x height pixels of out (1 to 16384 each, stride at least width). The buffer is cleared first. The picture keeps its aspect ratio and is centered in the rectangle; the rest is transparent. A vector picture is rasterized again at that size with anti-aliasing; a raster picture is scaled (bilinear when enlarged, an area average when shrunk). Returns false for a damaged file, a bad size or when it has no memory to work in (below). Use mimg_render_ex for anything else.

    mimg_render_ex

    typedef struct {
    uint32_t current_color;    /* 0xAARRGGBB for "current color" paints (default opaque black) */
    bool clear;                /* true: clear to transparent first; false: draw over the buffer */
    uint8_t fit;               /* MIMG_FIT_CONTAIN (default), MIMG_FIT_STRETCH, MIMG_FIT_COVER */
    void* scratch;             /* memory for the rasterizer ... */
    size_t scratch_size;
    void* (*alloc)(size_t);    /* ... or a way to get it */
    void (*free)(void*);
} mimg_render_opts_t;

void mimg_render_opts_init(mimg_render_opts_t* o);
bool mimg_render_ex(const uint8_t* data, size_t size, uint32_t* out,
                    uint32_t width, uint32_t height, uint32_t stride,
                    const mimg_render_opts_t* opts);   /* opts may be NULL */

    Always start from mimg_render_opts_init; a zeroed struct would draw "current color" paints transparent and composite over the buffer.

    • Tint. "Current color" is what a drawing's currentColor paint becomes: the RGB of current_color colors it and its alpha multiplies the paint's own alpha, so 0x80FFFFFF draws the icon half transparent. Paints with their own colors and gradients are not changed.
    • clear = false composites with source-over onto what is in out (the result stays non-premultiplied), so icons can be drawn straight onto a background or a window.
    • fit matters when width:height is not the picture's shape. CONTAIN shows all of it, STRETCH fills the rectangle and distorts, COVER fills it and crops.

    Memory

    The rasterizer allocates nothing. It needs scratch memory, which you give it in one of three ways, tried in this order:

    1. scratch and scratch_size, when big enough;
    2. alloc/free, called once for the recommended size and freed after;
    3. a built-in 256 KiB buffer (one render at a time; a render that asks for it while another is running returns false).
    size_t mimg_scratch_size(const uint8_t* data, size_t size, uint32_t width, uint32_t height);
size_t mimg_scratch_min(const uint8_t* data, size_t size, uint32_t width, uint32_t height);

    mimg_scratch_size is the recommended size for drawing at width x height (0 for a file that is not an .img); mimg_scratch_min is the least that works. A vector picture is drawn in bands of rows, so less scratch only means more passes: about 72 KiB suffices for a small icon, about 200 KiB for any size, and the minimum is about 15 KiB plus 4 bytes a pixel of width. A raster picture drawn at another size needs room for itself (width x height x 4 of its own size) and cannot use the built-in buffer if it is bigger than 256 KiB.

    Speed

    A 24-unit icon with a few shapes takes about 12 us at 16 px, 18 us at 32, 33 us at 64 and 240 us at 256 (one core of a modern PC, -O2); a detailed logo takes 1.2 ms at 256 px and 16 ms at 1024 px. Render once and keep the pixels when the size does not change.

    Damaged files

    Everything in a file is checked before anything is drawn; truncated, mutated and made-up files make mimg_info/mimg_render return false (or draw something harmless), never read out of bounds. They are fuzzed under AddressSanitizer in the kernel's host tests.

    Spawning and waiting

    Starting other programs with their own arguments, environment, working directory and redirected output, waiting for them, and reading the environment. Include process.h (it includes minimalos.h). The raw calls it builds on (mos_spawn_raw, mos_wait_raw, mos_stat, mos_rename, mos_chdir, mos_clock_*) are in Process and terminal.

    Functionsenvironmos_getenvmos_spawn_exmos_spawnmos_waitpid
    #include "process.h"
#include "stdio.h"

int main(void) {
    const char* const argv[] = { "0:/programs/tool.run", "--fast", NULL };
    mos_spawn_opts_t o = { "0:/programs/tool.run", argv, NULL, "0:/work",
                           "0:/work/out.txt", "0:/work/out.txt",
                           0 /* stack_size: the 8 MiB default */ };
    long pid = mos_spawn_ex(&o);
    if (pid < 0) { printf("spawn failed (%ld)\n", pid); return 1; }

    mos_wait_result_t r;
    mos_waitpid(pid, 0, &r);                       /* sleeps until it ends */
    printf("exit %d%s\n", r.exit_code, r.crashed ? " (crashed)" : "");
    /* 0:/work/out.txt now holds everything it printed */
    return 0;
}

    A program started this way is a *child* of the caller. A child is waited for once; programs started with mos_exec count as children too.

    environ

    extern char** environ;

    The environment the program started with: a NULL-terminated array of "NAME=value" strings. crt0.c sets it from the entry point's third argument (main also receives it as an optional third parameter, int main(int argc, char** argv, char** envp)). It is never NULL; it is an empty array when the program started with no environment, which is the case for programs run from the terminal. A spawned program gets the environment its parent passes (see mos_spawn_ex).

    mos_getenv

    char* mos_getenv(const char* name);

    Returns the value of name (an empty string for NAME=), or NULL when it is not set. name must match whole: OS does not find OSNAME=x. The string belongs to environ; do not modify it.

    mos_spawn_ex

    typedef struct {
    const char* path;                 /* the program (a .run bundle or ELF) */
    const char* const* argv;          /* NULL-terminated; NULL: just { path } */
    const char* const* envp;          /* NULL-terminated "NAME=value"; NULL: inherit */
    const char* cwd;                  /* NULL: the caller's working directory */
    const char* stdout_path;          /* NULL: the caller's output; else a file */
    const char* stderr_path;          /* (replaced) receiving it; may be the same */
    size_t stack_size;                /* main stack in bytes; 0: 8 MiB */
} mos_spawn_opts_t;

long mos_spawn_ex(const mos_spawn_opts_t* o);

    Starts a program as a child of the caller and returns at once.

    FieldDescription
    pathThe program
    argvWhat the child sees as argv[0..argc-1]; argv[0] is normally the path. The array must end with NULL. NULL means { path }. An empty string is a valid argument
    envpThe child's environment. NULL: a copy of the environment the caller started with
    cwdThe child's working directory; it must be an existing directory. NULL: the caller's current one
    stdout_pathNULL: the child writes where the caller's output goes (the terminal, or the caller's own redirection). Otherwise a file that is created, replacing an existing one, and receives everything the child writes to stdout
    stderr_pathThe same for stderr. May name the same file as stdout_path; the two streams are then one, in order
    stack_sizeBytes of main stack for the child. 0: the default, 8 MiB. Values outside 64 KiB..1 GiB are clamped to that range (no error); the size is rounded up to whole pages. Stack pages take memory only once they are used, so a large stack is cheap. Running off the end of it is a page fault: the child crashes with crash_vector == 14

    Returns the child's pid (greater than 0), or SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND (no such program or it is a directory; cwd is not a directory), SYS_ERR_INVAL (a NULL or unreadable pointer, a path that is too long, too many or too long arguments or environment strings), SYS_ERR_GENERIC (an output file could not be created, or the program could not be loaded), SYS_ERR_NOMEM.

    Notes

    • The struct has grown at the end (stack_size). A positional initializer such as { path, argv, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL } leaves it 0, which is the default. If you fill a mos_spawn_opts_t field by field, set stack_size too (or memset the struct first): it is read by the call.
    • Output redirected to a file is buffered by the kernel and written when the buffer fills and when the child ends. The file is complete once mos_waitpid has returned for that child, also after a crash. Read it only after that.
    • Everything the child's own children print without a redirection of their own goes to the same file.

    mos_spawn

    long mos_spawn(const char* path, const char* const* argv);

    mos_spawn_ex with only a path and an argv (NULL-terminated, or NULL). Environment, working directory and output are inherited.

    mos_waitpid

    typedef struct {
    long pid;                 /* the child that ended */
    int exit_code;            /* mos_exit()'s value (0-255); 255 after a crash */
    int crashed;              /* nonzero: it died of a CPU exception */
    int killed;               /* nonzero: it was ended from outside */
    unsigned crash_vector;    /* the exception number when crashed */
} mos_wait_result_t;

long mos_waitpid(long pid, int options, mos_wait_result_t* out);
long mos_wait(mos_wait_result_t* out);               /* any child */

    Waits for a child to end.

    ParameterDescription
    pidA child's pid, or MOS_WAIT_ANY (0) for whichever ends first
    options0 to sleep until it ends, or MOS_WAIT_NOHANG to return at once
    outFilled in on success; may be NULL

    Returns the pid of the child that ended (also in out->pid); SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND when there is no such child: it was never started, was already waited for, or (with MOS_WAIT_ANY) no child is left; SYS_ERR_AGAIN with MOS_WAIT_NOHANG while the child still runs; SYS_ERR_INVAL for other options or an invalid out.

    Notes

    • A child can be waited for once. Waiting again gives SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND.
    • The exit status of a child nobody waits for is kept for a limited time (64 children); after that waiting for an old child gives SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND.
    • A program that ends does not wait for its children.

    Example

    /* run four at once, collect them as they finish */
for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) mos_spawn(worker, args[i]);
mos_wait_result_t r;
while (mos_wait(&r) > 0)
    printf("pid %ld: exit %d\n", r.pid, r.exit_code);

    Clocks and files

    long     mos_file_size(const char* path);
uint64_t mos_monotonic_ms(void);
int64_t  mos_time_unix(void);
    FunctionReturns
    mos_file_sizeSize in bytes of a file; SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND if it does not exist, SYS_ERR_INVAL for a directory (built on mos_stat)
    mos_monotonic_msMilliseconds on the monotonic clock (mos_clock_monotonic_ns() / 1000000)
    mos_time_unixSeconds since 1970-01-01 UTC by the system clock

    System calls

    SYS_SPAWN (53): rdi = a syscall_spawn_t* (size, path, argv, argc, envp, cwd, stdout_path, stderr_path, flags which must be 0). SYS_WAIT (54): rdi = pid (SYS_WAIT_ANY = 0), rsi = flags (SYS_WAIT_NOHANG), rdx = a syscall_wait_t* or NULL (exit_code, flags with SYS_WAIT_CRASHED / SYS_WAIT_KILLED, crash_vector). SYS_CHDIR (52), SYS_STAT (50), SYS_RENAME (51) and SYS_CLOCK (49) are described with their wrappers in Process and terminal.

    PreviousPictures and icons in your own pixels (mosmedia.h)NextThreads

    Edit this page on GitHub

    Threads

    Running several parts of a program at once, and locking what they share. Include thread.h.

    A thread shares everything with the rest of its program: globals, the heap, anything a pointer reaches. Threads of one program run in parallel on different CPUs: N busy threads on N cores do N times the work in the same time, and a thread that waits (on the network, a file, a timer) leaves its CPU to the others. Two threads really do run at the same instant, so everything they share needs a mutex or atomics. A new thread goes to the least loaded CPU, and the scheduler may move it later; see CPUs, affinity and priority. On a single CPU machine, or when the kernel was booted with threads1cpu, all threads share one CPU (mos_threads_multicore() tells).

    Functionsmos_thread_createmos_thread_create_exmos_thread_create_vmmos_thread_joinmos_thread_runningmos_thread_exitmos_thread_yieldmos_mutex_t
    • malloc, calloc, realloc and free are system calls and are safe from any thread.
    • Anything else two threads touch needs a mos_mutex_t.
    • A thread ends when its function returns. mos_exit() from any thread, or main() returning, ends the whole program, threads included.
    • A crash in any thread ends the whole program, like a crash in main.
    • mos_vm_unmap, mos_vm_protect, mos_vm_decommit and free take effect on every CPU before they return: a thread that uses the memory afterwards faults (and ends the program) instead of reading stale data.
    • Windows belong to the thread that created them: keep all window and drawing calls on one thread (usually main's).
    • A network connection or open file belongs to the thread that opened it. Use it from that thread only.

    Example

    #include "thread.h"

static mos_mutex_t lock = MOS_MUTEX_INIT;
static int done;

static void work(void* arg) {
    /* ... a slow download ... */
    mos_mutex_lock(&lock);
    done = 1;
    mos_mutex_unlock(&lock);
}

int main(void) {
    mos_thread_t t;
    if (mos_thread_create(&t, work, NULL, 0) != 0) return 1;
    while (!done) {
        /* handle window events, draw a progress bar ... */
        mos_sleep(16);
    }
    mos_thread_join(&t);
    return 0;
}

    mos_thread_create

    int mos_thread_create(mos_thread_t* t, void (*fn)(void*), void* arg, size_t stack_size);

    Starts fn(arg) on a new thread.

    ParameterDescription
    tFilled in. Must stay valid until mos_thread_join
    fnThe thread's function. The thread ends when it returns
    argPassed to fn
    stack_sizeBytes of stack, taken with malloc. 0 for MOS_THREAD_STACK_DEFAULT (128 KiB)

    Returns 0, or -1 when there is no memory for the stack or the kernel refused.

    Notes

    • main has an 8 MiB stack by default (a spawning program can choose another size with stack_size, see Spawning); a thread gets the stack you ask for, here from malloc. See mos_thread_create_vm for a thread stack that is demand-paged and guarded.

    mos_thread_create_ex

    int mos_thread_create_ex(mos_thread_t* t, void (*fn)(void*), void* arg,
                         size_t stack_size, void* tls);

    mos_thread_create plus two things: the thread starts with FS base tls (see Thread-local storage), and it has an *exit futex*, so mos_thread_join sleeps until the kernel reports the end of the thread instead of polling every millisecond.

    ParameterDescription
    t, fn, arg, stack_sizeAs for mos_thread_create. t must not move until joined
    tlsThe thread's FS base: a block below 0x0000800000000000, or NULL for none

    Returns 0, or -1.

    Notes

    • mos_thread_t has two more fields since this call exists (exit_word, futex_join). Code that declares a mos_thread_t and calls mos_thread_create keeps working unchanged.
    • The kernel sets t->exit_word to 0 and wakes every mos_futex_wait on it when the thread has ended. It is 1 while the thread runs, so you can also wait on it yourself.

    mos_thread_create_vm

    int mos_thread_create_vm(mos_thread_t* t, void (*fn)(void*), void* arg,
                         size_t stack_size, void* tls);

    mos_thread_create_ex with a stack that is a SYS_VM mapping instead of malloc memory. stack_size is rounded up to whole pages (0: MOS_THREAD_STACK_DEFAULT). The stack takes physical memory only as the thread uses it, so a big one is cheap, and it has an unmapped page on each side: running off its low end is a page fault (the whole program ends, as for any crash) rather than corruption of other memory. mos_thread_join unmaps it.

    Returns 0, or -1 (no address space or memory, or the kernel refused).

    Notes mos_thread_t has two more fields for this (stack_size, stack_vm); the other creators set them, so existing code is unaffected.

    mos_thread_join

    void mos_thread_join(mos_thread_t* t);

    Waits until the thread has ended, then frees its stack (free, or unmaps it for a thread made by mos_thread_create_vm). Returns at once for a thread that never started. A thread made by mos_thread_create_ex is waited for with a futex; one made by mos_thread_create by polling every millisecond.

    mos_thread_running

    int mos_thread_running(const mos_thread_t* t);

    Returns nonzero while the thread runs.

    mos_thread_exit

    void mos_thread_exit(void);

    Ends the calling thread (only that thread). Never returns. Returning from the thread's function does the same.

    mos_thread_yield

    void mos_thread_yield(void);

    Lets the program's other threads (and other programs) run.

    mos_mutex_t

    typedef struct { volatile int locked; } mos_mutex_t;
#define MOS_MUTEX_INIT { 0 }

void mos_mutex_lock(mos_mutex_t* m);
int  mos_mutex_trylock(mos_mutex_t* m);    /* 1 when it took the lock */
void mos_mutex_unlock(mos_mutex_t* m);

    A lock. All zero bytes (or MOS_MUTEX_INIT) is unlocked. Not recursive: a thread that locks a mutex it already holds waits forever. Keep what happens under a lock short. A thread waiting for a lock sleeps in 1 ms steps, so the holder can run.

    Futexes

    long mos_futex_wait(volatile uint32_t* addr, uint32_t expected, uint64_t timeout_ns);
long mos_futex_wake(volatile uint32_t* addr, uint32_t count);

    The building block for locks, condition variables and joins: sleep until another thread says a 32-bit word may have changed.

    mos_futex_wait sleeps only while *addr == expected; the check and the sleep are atomic against mos_futex_wake, so a wake-up cannot be lost between them.

    ParameterDescription
    addrA 4-byte-aligned uint32_t in the program's memory (globals, heap, stack)
    expectedSleep only if *addr still has this value
    timeout_ns0 waits without limit; otherwise rounded up to whole milliseconds. A timed wait never returns early
    countWake at most this many sleepers (UINT32_MAX for all)

    Returns (wait) SYS_SUCCESS once woken; SYS_ERR_AGAIN at once when *addr != expected; SYS_ERR_TIMEDOUT when the time ran out; SYS_ERR_INVAL for an unaligned address or one outside the program.

    Returns (wake) how many sleepers it woke (0 when nobody waited), or a negative SYS_ERR_*.

    Notes

    • A wait can return SYS_SUCCESS without a matching wake-up. Always look at the word again and wait again if the condition does not hold.
    • Waiters and wakers are threads of one program; a futex cannot signal another program.

    Example

    static volatile uint32_t ready;

static void producer(void* arg) {
    __atomic_store_n(&ready, 1, __ATOMIC_RELEASE);
    mos_futex_wake(&ready, 1);
}

/* in the consumer */
while (__atomic_load_n(&ready, __ATOMIC_ACQUIRE) == 0)
    mos_futex_wait(&ready, 0, 0);

    Thread-local storage

    long  mos_thread_set_fs(const void* base);
void* mos_thread_get_fs(void);

    Every thread has its own FS base, the register compilers use for thread-local variables (%fs:offset). mos_thread_set_fs sets the calling thread's; mos_thread_get_fs reads it. The kernel keeps it across context switches. A new thread starts with the tls of mos_thread_create_ex, or 0 for mos_thread_create; the main thread starts with 0.

    ParameterDescription
    baseAddress of the thread's TLS block, below 0x0000800000000000; NULL clears it

    Returns (set) SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_INVAL for an address in the upper half (the CPU would fault on it). The value is unchanged then.

    Notes

    • Reading through %fs with a base of 0 faults and ends the program. The convention used by C runtimes is a block whose first word points at the block itself, so %fs:0 yields the thread pointer.

    System call

    SYS_THREAD (47): rdi = SYS_THREAD_CREATE with rsi = a syscall_thread_t* (entry, stack_top, arg), returning the thread's id; or SYS_THREAD_ALIVE with rsi = a thread id, returning SYS_SUCCESS while that thread of the calling program runs and SYS_ERR_NOTFOUND after. entry must be in executable memory of the program (its image, or a SYS_VM mapping with SYS_VM_PROT_EXEC; not malloc memory or a stack) and stack_top in memory it owns. thread.h wraps this; programs should use that.

    More operations of SYS_THREAD: SYS_THREAD_SET_FS (rsi = FS base) and SYS_THREAD_GET_FS (returns it); SYS_THREAD_CREATE_EX with rsi = a syscall_thread_ex_t* (syscall_thread_t plus fs_base and exit_futex, the address of a uint32_t the kernel zeroes and wakes when the thread has ended).

    SYS_FUTEX (48): rdi = SYS_FUTEX_WAIT with rsi = address, rdx = expected value, r10 = timeout in nanoseconds; or SYS_FUTEX_WAKE with rsi = address, rdx = count.

    CPUs, affinity and priority

    unsigned mos_cpu_count(void);
int      mos_threads_multicore(void);
unsigned mos_cpu_current(void);
long     mos_thread_set_affinity(const mos_thread_t* t, uint64_t mask);
long     mos_thread_get_affinity(const mos_thread_t* t);
long     mos_thread_set_priority(const mos_thread_t* t, unsigned priority);
long     mos_thread_get_priority(const mos_thread_t* t);
    FunctionDescription
    mos_cpu_countOnline CPUs (SYS_SYSINFO_CORE_COUNT)
    mos_threads_multicoreNonzero when threads run on different CPUs (the default); 0 with the boot flag threads1cpu
    mos_cpu_currentThe CPU the calling thread runs on now, 0 .. count-1
    mos_thread_set_affinityRestricts a thread to the CPUs in mask (bit n = CPU n; 0 = any). t = NULL is the calling thread. Takes effect before it returns
    mos_thread_get_affinityThe mask (all online CPUs while unrestricted) or a negative error
    mos_thread_set_priorityMOS_PRIO_HIGH (default), MOS_PRIO_NORMAL or MOS_PRIO_LOW
    mos_thread_get_priorityThe priority set

    Priority maps onto the scheduler's three levels. A thread normally starts at the interactive level and drops a level whenever it uses its whole time slice; a blocking call brings it back. The priority is the highest level it may be at: HIGH (default) is unrestricted, NORMAL never sits above the normal level, LOW stays at the background level, so it only runs on its CPU while nothing at a better level there waits (a periodic boost keeps it from starving). It does not change time slices. New threads inherit priority and affinity from the thread that creates them.

    Affinity errors: SYS_ERR_INVAL when the mask names no online CPU or the thread belongs to another program, SYS_ERR_PERM when the kernel pins threads (threads1cpu). Moving between CPUs is the scheduler's job; use affinity only when it matters (cache locality, a dedicated worker).

    What the kernel guarantees across CPUs

    • Memory unmapped, made less accessible (mos_vm_unmap, mos_vm_protect, mos_vm_decommit, free) is flushed from every CPU's TLB before the call returns and before the physical pages are reused.
    • A thread that ends the program (mos_exit, main returning, a crash) stops all other threads, even ones running on other CPUs, before the program's memory is released. If two threads crash at the same time, the first one's crash is the program's exit status.
    • Futex wake-ups reach a waiter on any CPU.

    Virtual memory

    Memory of your own in whole 4 KiB pages: reserve a large range, run generated code, give memory back to the system. Include vm.h (it includes minimalos.h). The raw calls it builds on (mos_vm_map_raw, mos_vm_unmap_raw, mos_vm_protect_raw, mos_vm_decommit_raw) are in minimalos.h; the kernel call is SYS_VM (55).

    Functionsmos_vm_mapmos_vm_unmapmos_vm_protectmos_vm_decommit
    #include "vm.h"
#include "stdio.h"

int main(void) {
    uint8_t* big = mos_vm_map(NULL, (size_t)1 << 30, MOS_VM_PROT_RW, 0);   /* 1 GiB */
    if (!big) { printf("map failed (%ld)\n", mos_vm_last_error()); return 1; }

    big[123456789] = 1;                 /* only this page takes physical memory */
    mos_vm_decommit(big, (size_t)1 << 30);   /* give every page back, keep the range */
    mos_vm_unmap(big, (size_t)1 << 30);      /* remove it */
    return 0;
}

    What you get

    • Demand-zero pages. A page reads as zero until it is written and takes physical memory from its first use. A mapping that is never touched costs nothing, so mapping 1 GiB "just in case" is cheap. If memory has run out when a page is first touched, the program is ended with a page fault; MOS_VM_MAP_POPULATE takes all the memory at once and fails with SYS_ERR_NOMEM instead.
    • Guard pages. A mapping the kernel places (no MOS_VM_MAP_FIXED) has an unmapped page on each side. Reading or writing just before or after it is a page fault (CPU exception 14, reported to a waiting parent as crashed with crash_vector == 14), not silent corruption.
    • No execution by default. Pages are not executable unless you give MOS_VM_PROT_EXEC. Running code from a mapping without it, from the main stack, or from malloc memory is a page fault.
    • Addresses from 2 TiB up (0x20000000000), below the main stack. Your program's image is at 1 TiB, the main stack ends at 0x7FFFF0000000, and malloc memory stays below 4 GiB.

    Addresses given to mos_vm_unmap, mos_vm_protect and mos_vm_decommit must be page aligned; lengths are rounded up to whole pages.

    Constants

    NameValueMeaning
    MOS_VM_PAGE_SIZE4096The page size
    MOS_VM_PROT_NONE0No access (contents are kept)
    MOS_VM_PROT_READ1Readable
    MOS_VM_PROT_WRITE2Writable (implies readable)
    MOS_VM_PROT_EXEC4Executable (implies readable)
    MOS_VM_PROT_RW3Read and write
    MOS_VM_PROT_RX5Read and execute
    MOS_VM_MAP_FIXED1Map exactly at the given address, or fail
    MOS_VM_MAP_POPULATE2Take the physical memory now

    mos_vm_map

    void* mos_vm_map(void* hint, size_t length, int prot, int flags);
void* mos_vm_map_ex(void* hint, size_t length, int prot, int flags, long* error);
long  mos_vm_last_error(void);

    Maps length bytes (rounded up to whole pages) with protection prot.

    ParameterDescription
    hintNULL: anywhere. Otherwise the lowest address you want: the kernel uses the first free place at or above it (the hint itself when it is free). With MOS_VM_MAP_FIXED: the exact address, which must be page aligned and free
    lengthBytes. Must be greater than 0
    protMOS_VM_PROT_* bits
    flags0, or MOS_VM_MAP_FIXED and/or MOS_VM_MAP_POPULATE
    errormos_vm_map_ex only: receives 0 or the error (may be NULL)

    Returns the address, or NULL on failure. The reason is in *error for mos_vm_map_ex, and in mos_vm_last_error() (the last mos_vm_map call, 0 after a success; one value for the whole program) for mos_vm_map. Errors: SYS_ERR_INVAL (zero or too large length, unknown prot or flags bits, a FIXED address that is unaligned, outside user space or already (partly) mapped), SYS_ERR_NOMEM (no room, or POPULATE could not get all its pages; nothing stays mapped then).

    Notes

    • FIXED never replaces anything and adds no guard pages, so two fixed mappings can touch.
    • With POPULATE, a size that cannot be satisfied (for example 64 GiB) fails with SYS_ERR_NOMEM. The attempt briefly uses all free memory, so do not use it to probe how much there is.

    mos_vm_unmap

    long mos_vm_unmap(void* address, size_t length);

    Removes the pages of [address, address + length) and frees their memory. Pages in the range that are not mapped are skipped, so unmapping part of a mapping leaves the two pieces (each keeps its data; the hole faults), and unmapping an unmapped range succeeds.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_INVAL (unaligned address, zero length, outside user space).

    mos_vm_protect

    long mos_vm_protect(void* address, size_t length, int prot);

    Changes the protection of [address, address + length). The whole range must be mapped, otherwise nothing changes. Contents are kept, also while the protection is MOS_VM_PROT_NONE. This is how generated code is made runnable: write it while the pages are read/write, then protect them MOS_VM_PROT_RX.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS, or SYS_ERR_INVAL (part of the range is not mapped, unaligned address, zero length, unknown prot bits), SYS_ERR_NOMEM.

    mos_vm_decommit

    long mos_vm_decommit(void* address, size_t length);

    Gives the physical memory of the range back. The pages stay mapped with their protection and read as zero again. The whole range must be mapped.

    Returns SYS_SUCCESS or SYS_ERR_INVAL.

    mos_vm_reserve and mos_vm_commit

    void* mos_vm_reserve(size_t length);
long  mos_vm_commit(void* address, size_t length);

    mos_vm_reserve maps length bytes with MOS_VM_PROT_NONE: address space that nothing can touch and that costs no memory. mos_vm_commit makes part of it read/write (mos_vm_protect(..., MOS_VM_PROT_RW)); pages still take memory only when first used. A growing buffer can reserve its maximum size once and commit as it grows, and never moves.

    Example: running generated code

    static const uint8_t code[] = { 0xB8, 0x2A, 0, 0, 0, 0xC3 };   /* mov eax,42 ; ret */

uint8_t* p = mos_vm_map(NULL, 4096, MOS_VM_PROT_RW, 0);
for (unsigned i = 0; i < sizeof code; i++) p[i] = code[i];
mos_vm_protect(p, 4096, MOS_VM_PROT_RX);
int v = ((int (*)(void))p)();                  /* 42 */

    Threads on mapped stacks

    thread.h adds int mos_thread_create_vm(mos_thread_t* t, void (*fn)(void*), void* arg, size_t stack_size, void* tls): like mos_thread_create_ex, but the stack is a SYS_VM mapping (0 for 128 KiB, rounded up to pages). It takes memory only as the thread uses it, has an unmapped guard page on both sides, and mos_thread_join unmaps it. A thread's entry point may be in any executable mapping (the image or a MOS_VM_PROT_EXEC mapping) when you call SYS_THREAD yourself; code in a non-executable mapping, in malloc memory or on the stack is refused with SYS_ERR_INVAL.

    The system call

    SYS_VM (55): rdi = operation, SYS_VM_MAP (rsi = syscall_vm_map_t* with size, address, length, prot, flags), SYS_VM_UNMAP (rsi = address, rdx = length), SYS_VM_PROTECT (also r10 = prot) or SYS_VM_DECOMMIT (rsi = address, rdx = length).

    Animation (the Animator module)

    .mof has no animation data yet (the ANIM chunk is reserved, see mof-format.md) and the renderer has no skinning, so the Animator plays transform clips from a plain-text .fanim file: tracks that move, turn and scale the animated object or its children.

    fanim 1
clip spin 2.0                   # name and length in seconds (optional: the last key)
  track . rotation              # "." is the animated object, "arm/hand" a child path
    key 0   0 0 0               # time, then x y z (rotation in degrees)
    key 2   0 360 0
clip lift
  track lid position
    key 0 0 0 0
    key 1 0 0.5 0
    • Values between keys are linear; rotation goes through quaternions (the short way).
    • track channels: position, rotation, scale. Times must not go backwards.
    • The file is source on the module, or the object's model path with .fanim.
    • loop repeats a clip, otherwise it stops on its last key (playing becomes false).
    • speed (negative plays backwards), time (set it to seek), crossfade.
    • animator:play(name, fade) starts a clip, blending from the current one over fade seconds; animator:stop(). Setting clip or playing from Lua works too.
    • A clip file with an error is logged once; the object stays as it is.

    Not done: skeletal animation (needs bones in .mof and GPU skinning), editing clips in the editor.

    Audio (engine/audio)

    Sound for the AudioListener, AudioStream and AudioSampler modules (engine/scene/modules.h). Public header: engine/audio/audio.h (it pulls in no decoder and no OS header). Build: mk/audio.mk.

    AudioDevice -> where the sound goes Mixer -> 32 voices, resampling, saturating mix AudioSystem -> the ECS side: modules, spatialization, pushing to the device

    On this pageFormatsDevicesPushing audioECS behaviourIntegrationTests and numbers

    Formats

    WAV (PCM 8/16/24/32 bit, float, ADPCM: dr_wav), MP3 (dr_mp3), Ogg Vorbis (stb_vorbis). Chosen by the first bytes of the file (RIFF/RF64 = WAV, OggS = Vorbis, anything else = MP3). Mono and stereo play as they are; files with more channels keep their first two. Any sample rate: the mixer resamples linearly to the device rate (and by pitch). Files that cannot be decoded are rejected with a log line (Clip::decode returns nullptr).

    Decoding is from memory (no stdio): the host reads the file (AudioHost:: read_file, so the editor resolves project paths) and the audio system owns the bytes.

    • Sampler clips (AudioSampler) are decoded completely once to int16 and cached by path (stats().clips_cached).
    • Streams (AudioStream) keep the compressed file in memory and decode on the fly into a 4096-frame FIFO per voice; they loop by rewinding the decoder.

    Devices

    AudioDevice::init(Backend, rate):

    Backend
    MinimalOSone stereo int16 stream (mos_audio_stream_open(48000, 2), then 44100 if the rate is refused). Fails when there is no sound card (os_error() is SYS_ERR_GENERIC).
    Nullplays nothing; keeps what it is given and drops what the caller says was "played" (null_advance(frames)), so tests are deterministic. capture() reads back everything written.
    AutoMinimal-OS stream if it can be opened, else the Null device following the clock (real time) - the host build and machines without a sound card.

    Queue model: the OS stream holds 16384 frames; write() never blocks and returns the frames taken. queued(), writable() and underruns() (the kernel's count) are available.

    Pushing audio

    No audio thread. AudioSystem::update() (registered in Phase::Store, or call it yourself) tops the device queue up to about 80 ms every frame: it mixes target - queued frames in chunks of 1024 and writes them. At 60 fps that is ~800 frames per frame. A frame that takes longer than ~80 ms makes the device run dry (an underrun, counted); the next update then refills the full 80 ms at once. If the game calls update less often than every ~80 ms the sound breaks up: call it from the frame loop.

    ECS behaviour

    Each update():

    1. reads the current AudioListener (World::current): its world position, its right axis and volume (the master volume). No listener: master 1, and spatial sources play flat.
    2. finds every entity with an AudioStream or AudioSampler; the first time it sees an AudioStream it starts it if play_on_start (so streams start with the world's first frame; entities created later start when first seen).
    3. syncs live voices with the modules: volume, pitch, loop, spatial.
    4. ends finished one-shot voices, forgets destroyed entities (their voices stop).
    5. mixes and pushes.

    Spatial (spatial = true): distance d from the listener. Gain is 1 up to min_distance, then inverse distance min/d, shifted and scaled so that it reaches exactly 0 at max_distance (silent beyond). Pan = the direction to the source on the listener's right axis (-1 left .. +1 right), faded to 0 within min_distance. Mono sources pan with a constant-power law (centre = -3 dB per side, so a centred mono sound is 0.707 per channel); stereo sources use balance. Gain and pan change smoothly (ramped over a 256-frame block).

    API for scripts and the editor (all on AudioSystem): play_sampler(e) (pitch = pitch * (1 + pitch_variation * random(-1..1)), at most voices overlapping per entity, the oldest is cut), play_stream(e) (restarts), stop_stream(e), pause_stream(e, paused = true), is_playing(e), stop_all(), restart() (forget what started: use it when Play restarts and the world's entities are reused), stats() (voices_active, underruns, mix_ms, mix_ms_max, frames_pushed, clips_cached).

    Missing or undecodable files: one log line per path (audio: cannot read 'x', audio: cannot decode 'x'), play_* returns false, nothing else happens.

    Integration

    mk: add $(AUDIO_SRC) to the editor's source lists (host and OS) together with $(ECS_SRC) $(FLECS_SRC) $(CORE_SRC); mk/audio.mk gives the audio objects their flags. Init order:

    World world;  world.init();
AudioDevice dev;  dev.init();                       // Backend::Auto
AudioHost host;  host.read_file = ...;  host.log = ...;  host.user = ...;
AudioSystem audio;  audio.init(&world, &dev, host); // after the script runtime
// ... world.progress(dt) every frame runs audio.update() in Phase::Store
audio.shutdown();  dev.shutdown();                  // before world.shutdown()

    read_file returns malloc'd bytes (the system frees them) or nullptr. Lua's obj.audio_sampler:play() calls audio.play_sampler(entity).

    Tests and numbers

    tests/host/audio_tests.cpp (131 checks, through the Null device; the MP3 and Ogg files are 2-4 KB tones in tests/data/*.inc, made with ffmpeg). build/os/bin/audio_smoke.run plays 440 Hz for one second through the real device and prints FE AUDIO PASS <frames> <underruns>, FE AUDIO PASS nodevice (no sound card) or FE AUDIO FAIL <why>.

    Mixing 32 voices for 1 s of audio takes ~4 ms on the host (-O2), ~0.4% of real time.
