    The entity system (engine/ecs)

    Runtime objects of the engine live in a flecs v4 world (vendored unmodified in external/flecs, MIT). engine/ecs/ecs.h wraps it: game and editor code include only ecs/ecs.h (it does not include flecs.h); flecs is used inside engine/ecs/*.cpp. Entity ids are fe::Entity (uint64_t, a flecs id, 0 = none/root).

    On this pageWorld APIComponentsThe "current" ruleFrame and phasesHow scripts reach fieldsBuild
    fe::World world;
world.init();
fe::Entity cam = world.create("Camera");               // has Transform + WorldTransform
world.add(cam, fe::ModuleKind::Camera);
world.set_current(cam, fe::ModuleKind::Camera);
world.progress(dt);                                      // runs the frame
world.shutdown();

    World API

    AreaCalls
    entitiescreate(name, parent), destroy (with all descendants), alive, lookup(name) (roots), lookup_child(parent, name), name, set_name
    hierarchyset_parent(child, parent) (0 = root; refuses cycles and sibling name clashes), parent, children(parent, out, max), child_count
    transformtransform(e) (local, writable), world_transform(e) (computed), update_transforms(), add_renderable, renderable, remove_renderable
    moduleshas/add/remove/get/get_mut/set(e, ModuleKind, ...), modified, load(e, ModuleSet), store(e, ModuleSet*)
    fieldsget_field/set_field(e, kind, "name", FieldValue)
    currentset_current, clear_current, current(kind)
    frameprogress(dt), add_system(Phase, fn, user), remove_system

    Names are unique among siblings (a duplicate makes create return 0 and set_name/set_parent return false); . in a name is plain text. The root names fe and flecs belong to the engine.

    Components

    All registered with their size/alignment and with flecs meta (reflection), under the scope fe.:

    • Transform { Vec3 position; Quat rotation; Vec3 scale; }: local, relative to the parent. WorldTransform { Mat4 matrix; }: computed (column-major, as Mat4). Every entity made by create has both. Renderable { uint8_t mesh; char model_path[256]; Vec3 color; bool visible; }: optional; mesh is the editor's MeshKind index.
    • Every ModuleKind of scene/modules.h (fe.rigidbody3d, fe.light, fe.camera, ...), registered from module_info(kind). Components are created with the struct's defaults (a ctor hook copies a default instance). Meta types come from the FieldInfo tables: Float to f32, Int to i32, Bool to bool, Enum to a flecs enum (fe.enums.<module>_<field>, u8, constants named like enum_names), Vec3 and Color to the shared struct fe.Vec3 {x,y,z}, Path to char[256], Bits to u32. Members have the struct's own offsets, so the flecs meta cursor, JSON and the explorer see the same data as the C++ struct. Adding a module or a field in modules.cpp is all that is needed.

    The "current" rule

    Camera, SkyLight, Sky, PostProcess and AudioListener have a current flag (ModuleInfo::has_current). At most one entity per kind has it; whoever turned it on last wins. It is enforced by a flecs OnSet observer per kind, so every way of turning the flag on goes through it: set_current, set_field(..., "current", true), set(), load(), or get_mut() followed by modified(e, kind). (Without modified, flecs cannot know the data changed: that is the one rule for writing through get_mut.) current(kind) is 0 when none is; destroying or removing the current one just leaves none. Other kinds reject it: set_current returns false, they have no current field.

    Frame and phases

    World::progress(dt) runs the flecs pipeline in this order:

    PhaseForNotes
    PreUpdateinput, script start/pre-frame
    Updatescripts, physics: they write Transformthe plug-in place for later systems
    PostUpdatetransform system (first), then callbacksWorldTransform is computed from Transform parents-first (a flecs cascade query over ChildOf)
    Storeaudio, render extraction: read WorldTransform

    add_system(Phase, fn, user) adds a void fn(World&, float dt, void* user) that runs once per frame in that phase. Inside such a callback reads and field writes are immediate, but structural changes (create, destroy, add/remove a module, set_parent) are deferred by flecs to the end of the phase. Engine-internal systems that need queries use world.raw() and component(kind) with flecs.h.

    How scripts reach fields

    The Lua bindings (later) hold an entity id and call get_field(e, kind, "intensity", &v) / set_field(e, kind, "intensity", v) where kind comes from module_by_name("light") (the ModuleInfo::name, the Lua name). Values are validated against the FieldInfo: numbers convert and clamp to the range, enums take an index or the constant's name, strings are cut to 255 chars, a wrong kind of value or an unknown field returns false. Setting current goes through the rule above.

    Build

    mk/ecs.mk defines ECS_SRC (engine/ecs/world.cpp), FLECS_SRC (external/flecs/flecs.c, C, warnings off) and the flags. flecs is built with -DFLECS_NO_OS_API_IMPL -DFLECS_CUSTOM_BUILD -DFLECS_SYSTEM -DFLECS_PIPELINE -DFLECS_META, plus -D__linux__ on Minimal-OS; world.cpp installs the (single-threaded) OS API: libc malloc, clock_gettime, log to stdout. Tests: build/host/bin/ecs_tests (make test); on Minimal-OS build/os/bin/ecs_smoke.run (tools/ci/run_os.sh build/os/bin/ecs_smoke.run 'FE ECS PASS' 'FE ECS FAIL'). Checks shared by both are in tests/common/ecs_checks.h.

    PreviousAudio (engine/audio)NextExporting a game

    Edit this page on GitHub

    Exporting a game

    A game is a project (scenes, scripts, models, textures, sounds) plus the prebuilt player. Exporting packs the project into one .fepak (docs/pak-format.md) and puts a copy of the player next to it. Lua-only games need nothing else: there is no compiler on the OS yet.

    On this pageProject settingsIn the editorCommand lineRunning a gameNotesTesting
    0:/games/MyGame/
  MyGame.run        the player (a copy of feplayer.run; on the PC: MyGame)
  MyGame.fepak      scenes, scripts, models, textures, audio, project.fe
  icon.bmp          the project's icon, when it has one (also inside MyGame.run)

    Project settings

    File > Project settings... edits project.fe in the project folder:

    farcade-project 1
name "My Game"
version "1.0"
entry_scene "scenes/main.fscene"
window_width 1280
window_height 720
icon "icon.bmp"

    graphics true (the default) exports the graphics settings with the game: saving the project settings or exporting writes the editor's current Settings > Graphics to graphics.cfg in the project folder (text, one name value per line, editor/src/graphics_text.h), the export packs it as graphics.cfg, and the player applies it before the first frame (it prints FE PLAYER graphics settings from graphics.cfg). Turn the box "Use these graphics settings for the exported game" off to ship the defaults. The parse/print functions in graphics_text.cpp are the single hook: when engine/gfx/graphics_settings gets to_text / from_text, call them from graphics_settings_to_text / graphics_settings_from_text.

    window_width and window_height are the size of the window when MOSdesk owns the screen (full screen uses the whole screen). The icon is a project relative .bmp; the exporter writes it next to the game and bundles it into the .run as Resources/icon.bmp, where MOSdesk looks for it. A file with no project.fe works too: the folder's name is the game's name and the entry scene is scenes/main.fscene.

    In the editor

    File > Export game... asks for the game's name, the entry scene (the open scene, if you press "Use open scene") and the output folder (default 0:/games/<Name>/). Export saves the scene if it has unsaved changes, writes the settings to project.fe, then:

    1. loads the entry scene and every other .fscene in the project (a few folders deep; build/, export/ and dot folders are skipped),
    2. collects the files they refer to: scripts and their file inputs, models, textures, shaders, and every path field of a module (audio files),
    3. writes <Name>.fepak and copies the player to <Name>.run.

    A referenced file that is missing is reported in the Console (and counted) but does not stop the export. "Run the exported game" starts the result as its own process.

    Command line

    farcade-editor.run --export <project-or-scene> <outdir> [--name N] [--scene S]
                   [--player P] [--entry-only] [--mpkg] [--run [FRAMES]]
build/host/bin/fe-export <project-or-scene> <outdir> ...      # the same on the PC, without the editor

    The first argument is a project folder, or a .fscene file (its project is the folder above scenes/, or its own folder; the scene becomes the entry scene). --entry-only packs only the entry scene and what it uses. --run starts the exported game afterwards (with --frames FRAMES when a number is given). It prints FE EXPORT OK <pak> files=N scenes=N bytes=N missing=N, or FE EXPORT FAIL: ... and exits 1. The editor needs no screen for this.

    The player comes from 0:/programs/feplayer.run on Minimal-OS (so install feplayer.run next to the editor: make os builds both into build/os/bin) and build/host/bin/feplayer on the PC; --player overrides it.

    Running a game

    MyGame.run finds its package next to itself (MyGame.fepak, then game.fepak, then 0:/games/MyGame/MyGame.fepak), or takes it as its argument. Esc or the window's close button quits.

    run 0:/games/MyGame/MyGame.run                      # full screen, or a window under MOSdesk
run 0:/programs/feplayer.run 0:/games/MyGame/MyGame.fepak
feplayer game.fepak --frames 120 --png shot.png     # PC: headless, N frames, last frame as PNG
feplayer path/to/project --frames 60                # run loose project files (no export needed)

    Options: --scene <path> starts at another scene, --scale N renders at 1/N of the screen size and stretches it (slow CPUs), --no-audio, --quiet. The player prints FE PLAYER READY <name> (<w>x<h>, <objects> objects, <n> scripts) after the first frame and FE PLAYER DONE frames=N checksum=XXXXXXXX objects=N scripts=N at the end (the checksum is of the last frame's pixels; with --frames the time step is a fixed 1/60 s, so it is repeatable). Lines that scripts print go to the same output.

    The player runs the scene through the same PlaySession (editor/src/play_session.*) as the editor's Play: Lua scripts, physics, audio, the current camera, sky, sky light and post processing drawn by FarcadeGL. Keyboard and mouse reach scripts as fe.key_down("w"), fe.key_pressed("space"), fe.mouse_x(), fe.mouse_down(0) ... (see docs/scripting.md); in the editor's Play the mouse is in viewport pixels.

    Notes

    • Models (.mof) are packed, found through the VFS and drawn (docs/scenes.md, "Models in scenes").
    • A path in a scene that points outside the project cannot be packed; it is warned about.
    • Packages are not compressed yet (the entry flags have room for zstd).
    • The .run format (MINIRUN1) can carry files under Resources/; the exporter uses that for the icon only, because a running program has no documented way to read its own bundle. The package stays a separate file.
    • --mpkg (or the dialog's "Also make an installable .mpkg") writes <Name>.mpkg next to the game: mos_pkg_unzip(..., "0:/"), the terminal's pkg command and Deliver install it to 0:/programs/<Name>.run and 0:/games/<Name>/<Name>.fepak (+ the icon). The player finds its package there (0:/games/<name>/<name>.fepak). Entries are stored, not LZSS compressed (editor/src/mpkg.h, format of Minimal-OS's pkgformat.h). The icon also sits inside the .run for MOSdesk; no Deliver metadata beyond the archive is written.

    Testing

    make host && make test     # tests/host/export_tests.cpp: pak, VFS, project.fe, export, and the headless player on an exported demo
MINIMAL_OS_DIR=... tools/ci/export_os_test.sh   # QEMU: the editor exports tests/data/export_demo, the exported player runs it

    Graphics: the GPU tier of the FarcadeGL renderer

    On this pageTexture and custom shader assetsCamera screen shadersSupersampling and vsyncFeature levelsPost processing stackGraphics settings in gamesProbe GI (FL0 hybrid GI, CPU side)Anti-aliasing, ambient occlusion and reflections: the choicesCascaded sun shadowsMaterialsWhat the editor callsPipeline (all effects on)Shader compiling and the shader cacheLimits hit (FGSL / FarcadeGL / host JIT)Costs (host CPU backend, 800 x 530, ultra, one core)Tools

    Texture and custom shader assets

    A mesh material can reference an image texture or a combined FGSL shader file. Use the Inspector's Texture and Shader slots, or assign paths from a script through object.material.texture and object.material.shader. Script inputs declared as file (or asset) are path strings and can be dropped on from the Files panel.

    The .fshader format uses the existing FGSL syntax and two comment markers:

    // @vertex
uniform mat4 fgl_ModelViewProjection;
attribute vec3 position;
attribute vec2 texcoord;
varying vec2 uv;
void main() {
    uv = texcoord;
    gl_Position = fgl_ModelViewProjection * vec4(position, 1.0);
}

// @fragment
uniform sampler2D u_texture;
varying vec2 uv;
void main() {
    gl_FragColor = texture2D(u_texture, uv);
}

    u_texture is bound to the material image; without one it is a white texture. Built-in meshes currently get generated planar UVs, and texture alpha is not blended by the XRGB material path. The renderer also supplies the usual FarcadeGL matrix uniforms and u_mat (material color and roughness). A custom shader replaces the built-in material shading. When a visible mesh has a texture or custom shader, the renderer uses its base FarcadeGL path for that frame, so advanced GPU-tier effects (such as shadows, SSAO and fog) are not applied.

    Camera screen shaders

    A Camera module has three screen shader slots (Shader 1-3) and Shader params. While the camera is current, each set shader runs in order as a full screen pass over the finished image (after post processing and particles), on every tier. In Lua they are obj.camera.shader1 .. shader3 and obj.camera.shader_params.

    A screen shader file is the fragment part only (a .fshader without markers; a file with // @vertex and // @fragment sections is used as it is):

    uniform sampler2D u_screen;     // the image so far
uniform vec4 u_res;             // width, height, 1 / width, 1 / height
uniform vec4 u_time;            // seconds, delta, frame, 0
uniform vec4 u_params;          // the camera's Shader params (x, y, z)
varying vec2 uv;                // 0..1, (0, 0) top left
void main() {
    vec3 c = texture2D(u_screen, uv).rgb;
    float g = dot(c, vec3(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722));
    gl_FragColor = vec4(mix(c, vec3(g, g, g), u_params.x), 1.0);
}

    Samples: assets/samples/screen/ (grayscale, invert, pixelate, crt). Each pass uploads the image, draws one triangle and reads it back, so it costs about a readback per shader. A file that cannot be read or compiled is skipped and reported once in the Console; the frame still draws. The editor's CPU preview does not run them (switch the viewport to FarcadeGL).

    Supersampling and vsync

    ssaa (Settings > Graphics > Supersampling): off, 2x (1.41 x the pixels per side) or 4x (2 x 2). The frame is drawn bigger and averaged down with an area filter when read back; it stacks with FXAA / SMAA / TAA and works on every tier (at most 4096 pixels a side). In the editor viewport TAA has no history to work with (a still view is drawn once), so supersampling is the way to smooth stills.

    vsync (games: the player; feplayer --vsync overrides): off (uncapped), double (a frame waits for the next refresh, a late one for the one after), triple (a present thread shows the newest finished frame at each refresh; the game never waits) and adaptive (like double, a late frame is shown at once). refresh_hz (30-240) is the rate it follows: Minimal-OS gives programs no vertical blank signal, so refreshes are paced by the clock (editor/platform/frame_pacer.h).

    fe::gfx::Renderer (engine/gfx) has two tiers, set by GraphicsSettings (engine/gfx/graphics_settings.h).

    • Base tier: forward lighting (Blinn-Phong), sky, tonemap and grade folded into the shaders. Runs everywhere, also on FarcadeGL's CPU backend.
    • GPU tier: shadow maps, SSAO, bloom, FXAA and PBR (GGX) shading. It runs when FarcadeGL runs on a graphics card (FGPU_CAP_HW_3D), or when allow_gpu_effects_on_cpu forces it (slow; tests, screenshots).
    • Fog (Sky.fog) works in both tiers.

    Feature levels

    engine/gfx/feature_level.h is the one place that turns what the device says (fglGetDeviceInfo caps) into the pipeline that runs. Settings > Graphics > Device shows the level and lets you request one (GraphicsSettings::feature_level); Renderer::features().level, Renderer::feature_level() and Renderer::caps() give it to code.

    LevelWhenWhat runs
    FL0today's FGPU on the CPU backendthe base tier: forward lights, ambient, sky, post folded into the shaders, CPU GI
    FL1-readyFL0 plus scissor, mipmaps and 16 texture unitsthe same, with the passes that need those caps taking their cheaper path (below)
    GPU tiera graphics card (FGPU_CAP_HW_3D), or forcedthe multi pass pipeline of the next sections

    Auto picks the highest level the caps allow. Asking for more than the device has is clamped (FL1-ready without the caps gives FL0) except the GPU tier, which can always be forced on the CPU backend (slow; the old allow_gpu_effects_on_cpu switch does the same). The optional hardware features are cap bits (PassCaps: scissor, mipmaps, mrt, tex16); DeviceCaps::from_abi reads them from FGPU_CAP_SCISSOR, FGPU_CAP_MIPMAPS and FGPU_CAP_MRT as soon as the kernel's fgpu_abi.h defines them, and the texture unit count from FGPU_MAX_TEXTURE_UNITS; until then they are off. Nothing branches on the backend name.

    Post processing stack

    Every final-colour shader (base tier and GPU tier) gets the same generated chain (shaders_post.h): exposure and tint, tonemap, contrast, saturation, lift / gamma / gain, vignette, film grain, sRGB. Each choice (operator, grading, grain) is compiled into the shader, not branched on (the host shader machine runs if as predication), so the default look is not slower than before and a neutral grade costs nothing. Changing the operator recompiles the shader once.

    Setting (Post Processing object)Notes
    TonemapNone, Reinhard, ACES, AgX (Sobotka's look: Rec.2020 inset matrix, log2 over -12.47..4.03 EV, a polynomial sigmoid)
    Lift / Gamma / Gainout = pow(max(c * gain + lift * (1 - c), 0), 1 / gamma) after tonemap and saturation
    Film grain0..1, interleaved gradient noise, a new pattern every frame, weaker in the highlights
    Chromatic aberration0..1, GPU tier only (3 taps in the composite pass, linear filtering)
    Bloom radius0..1: the weight of the wide levels in the upsample chain (0.5 = the old look)
    Auto exposuresee below; Exposure becomes a compensation

    Bloom is a chain of up to 5 levels (1/4 to 1/64; a level needs 4 texels on each side, so a small image gets fewer): a bright pass with a soft knee and Karis averaging (no fireflies), a 13 tap downsample at each level, and a tent upsample that adds the wider level scaled by 2 * radius.

    Auto exposure costs no GPU pass. After each frame the renderer meters the image it already read back: 64 x 36 samples with a mild centre weight, each undone through the sRGB curve, the tonemap (inverted from a table) and the exposure that was applied, so the answer is the scene's average luminance (geometric mean) whatever the exposure was. The controller eases the automatic EV towards the value that maps that mean to 0.18, with the rate exposure_speed (1 / s) and the range auto_exposure_min / max; RenderScene::delta_time is the step (negative: wall clock, at most 0.25 s). It works on FL0 and the GPU tier alike. The measurement is a frame late (the first frame is drawn with 0 EV), and contrast / saturation / grading are not undone, so heavy grading shifts the target a little. RendererStats::exposure_ev and meter_log2 show what happened.

    Internal resolution. render_scale (0.25..1) renders every pass at that fraction (sizes rounded to multiples of 8) and upscales bilinearly when the image is read back; the stats report internal_width / internal_height. A 0.5 scale costs about a quarter of the shading. Dynamic resolution (dynamic_resolution, target_frame_ms, min_render_scale) moves the scale between min_render_scale and render_scale to hold the target: the step follows the square root of the time ratio, down by up to 15% a frame, up by at most 3% and only with 15% of the time to spare. It uses the measured frame time (render, readback and upscale). Bands (render_rows) always draw at full size. Screenshots: gfx-agx.png, gfx-graded.png, gfx-autoexposure.png, gfx-post-high.png (fe-gfx-shot --tonemap agx --grade warm --auto-exposure --scale 0.5 ...).

    Graphics settings in games

    The graphics settings are part of the game, not only of the editor. fe::gfx::GraphicsSettings (engine/gfx/graphics_settings.h) is one plain struct, and graphics_settings.cpp stores it as text, by field name, in the style of .fscene:

    farcade-graphics 1
preset high
aa fxaa
shadows cascades
shadow_cascades 3
render_scale 0.75
...
    char text[2048];
size_t n = graphics_settings_to_text(settings, text, sizeof text);      // save: put `text` into project.fe
GraphicsSettings g;
int ignored = graphics_settings_from_text(&g, text, strlen(text));      // load at startup, then
renderer.set_settings(g);                                               // apply (cheap; every frame is fine)

    from_text starts from the defaults, so a missing name keeps its default; unknown names and invalid values are ignored (the return value counts them); a preset line names the preset when nothing differs from it, else the settings read back as custom. A null text returns -1. Every option is an explicit choice and the older, cheaper technique stays selectable next to the newer one; Low is the cheap base tier of before. Names and allowed values:

    NameValues
    presetlow, medium, high, ultra, custom (setting it applies the preset)
    feature_levelauto, fl0, fl1, gpu
    render_scale0.25 to 1; dynamic_resolution bool; target_frame_ms 8 to 100; min_render_scale 0.25 to 1
    shadowsoff, single (one map), cascades; shadow_cascades 2 or 3 (with cascades)
    shadow_resolution512, 1024, 2048, 4096; shadow_distance 1 to 2000 m; soft_shadows, cascade_cache bool
    local_shadowsbool; local_shadow_lights 1 to 4; local_shadow_resolution 512 to 4096
    aooff, ssao, gtao; ao_radius 0.05 to 5; ao_strength 0 to 2; ssr off, on
    aaoff, fxaa, smaa, taa
    bloomoff, simple (4 levels, the first version), chain (5 levels, radius)
    pbrbool (GGX, else Blinn-Phong)
    allow_gpu_effects_on_cpubool (run the GPU tier on the CPU backend, slow)

    Look and style settings (tonemap operator, exposure, grading, bloom strength, grain, fog) belong to the scene's Post Processing and Sky objects, not to this struct. Code can also use the property API (graphics_property_count / graphics_property, graphics_get_text, graphics_set_text, graphics_apply_preset_name), which is what Settings > Graphics and the Lua binding use.

    Scripts read and change them at run time with fe.graphics (engine/script/lua_graphics.h):

    fe.graphics.get("aa")                  -- "fxaa" (strings for choices, numbers, booleans; shadow_resolution is a number)
fe.graphics.set("aa", "off")           -- string, number or boolean; an unknown name or invalid value is a Lua error
fe.graphics.set("render_scale", 0.6)
fe.graphics.preset("low")              -- low | medium | high | ultra
for _, p in ipairs(fe.graphics.list()) do print(p.name, p.type, p.value, p.values and table.concat(p.values, "/")) end
fe.graphics.text()                     -- the settings as text

    A change is written to the host's GraphicsSettings and sets the host's changed flag; the host calls Renderer::set_settings before the next frame. The host connects them with ScriptRuntime::set_graphics_settings(&settings, &changed) (the editor does it for Play and restores the settings at Stop); without it fe.graphics raises "the graphics settings are not available here".

    Probe GI (FL0 hybrid GI, CPU side)

    gi = probes (Settings > Graphics > Global illumination; hemisphere is the old ambient, free, and the default of Low and Medium) replaces the diffuse hemisphere ambient with light the scene itself bounced. It is CPU work, not a pass, so it runs on every feature level (engine/gfx/gi.h):

    1. Voxels. A 48^3 grid of 0.5 m voxels around the camera is built from the draw items by conservative triangle / box voxelization (every voxel a triangle touches; albedo, normal, emissive = unlit items). It is rebuilt when the scene changed (at most every 100 ms, so moving objects re-splat at 10 Hz) or when the camera leaves the middle third of the grid (no toroidal scrolling yet).
    2. Light injection. A quarter of the surface voxels a frame get the sun (with a voxel DDA shadow ray of at most 64 steps), up to 8 local lights (no shadow), emissive, and the irradiance the probes had last frame times SkyLight.gi_bounce: multi-bounce, one frame late.
    3. Probes. A window of 16 x 8 x 16 L1 SH probes at 2 / 1 / 0.5 m (gi_density) around the camera, toroidal (a probe keeps its world cell while the window slides; new cells start from the hemisphere). 1/32, 1/16 or 1/8 of them (gi_update) shoot 32 rays through the voxels each frame, never-seen probes first, blended with hysteresis 0.93. A probe that moved out of geometry (it tries its 6 neighbours) and one whose rays mostly hit back faces is marked invalid and keeps the hemisphere.
    4. Shaders. The probes become a 64 x 128 ARGB8 texture (4 coefficient tiles; the DC term as sqrt(v / 4), the directional terms signed), sampled with 8 linear taps (hardware filtering inside a tile, a manual lerp between two slices) in the base and the GPU tier's lit shader. SkyLight.gi_intensity scales it. Specular ambient (PBR) keeps the hemisphere.

    The probes store diffuse irradiance, so a plain sky reads a little less contrasty than the hemisphere ((s + g) / 2 +- (s - g) / 3 instead of (s + g) / 2 +- (s - g) / 2). Tests (gfx_stack_tests): the voxelizer is deterministic and has no gaps, the probes show colour bleeding next to a red wall, converge from a wrong state, reproduce an open sky, invalidate probes inside a closed box, and both tiers read them; switching back to the hemisphere gives the old pixels. Measured on the host (shared box): a full update of the demo room 60 to 80 ms once (the first frame), then about 1 to 2.5 ms a frame (the update-rate setting scales it); the lit shader costs about 8 extra linear taps a pixel: the demo at 800 x 530 on the CPU backend goes from 175 to 278 ms in the base tier. That is why it is a choice and off at Low. Screenshots: gfx-gi-hemisphere.png, gfx-gi-probes.png (fe-gfx-shot --gi probes). Not done: toroidal voxel scrolling, probe specular / the sky atlas, shadows from local lights in the voxels.

    Anti-aliasing, ambient occlusion and reflections: the choices

    Each technique is a choice next to the older one (Settings > Graphics, graphics_settings.h, text, Lua): aa = off | fxaa | smaa | taa, ao = off | ssao | gtao, ssr = off | on. Low and Medium keep FXAA / SSAO / no SSR (Low is bit-identical to before: the base tier smoke checksum 214c411e and the demo PNG md5 did not change); High takes SMAA, Ultra TAA + GTAO + SSR. All three are GPU tier passes (on the CPU backend they only run when the GPU tier is forced); features().ssr and aa_mode / ao_mode say what runs. FXAA stays selectable after SMAA and TAA exist.

    PassWhat it doesMeasured on the host (800 x 530, High, forced GPU tier)
    FXAAone cheap pass over edge pixels44 ms
    SMAAluma edges (threshold 0.1, contrast adaptation), blend weights from an area texture, neighbourhood blend over the edge pixels only80 ms
    TAAjittered camera (Halton 2,3, 8 frames), full size linear depth, resolve with reprojection + 3x3 neighbourhood clamp104 ms (with its depth pass)
    SSAO12 taps21 ms
    GTAOhalf resolution, 2 slices x 3 steps per side, horizon integral; accumulated over frames while the camera and items stand still; then the same two blurs30 ms
    SSRhalf resolution, 12 step view space march, roughness cutoff 0.55, Fresnel / smoothness weight10 ms (+ a material pass of about 2 ms)

    SMAA is SMAA 1x in structure (edges, weights, blend) but not the reference tables: the area texture (32 x 32, smaa_area_texture, generated at startup, post_stack.h) comes from a small analytic model (the contour as a line between the end heights of the edge run; orthogonal patterns only, no diagonal or corner patterns), and the search is done by the shader with up to 8 nearest taps per side (no search texture, so the weights shader takes more than 16 samples and the host JIT runs it as an interpreter, but only on edge pixels because the others are skipped with a depth mask). The weights go into two targets (one per axis) because the targets have no alpha. Four texture units are enough (weights: edges + area).

    TAA resolves in the HDR encoded space (before bloom and tonemap). The reprojection comes from the depth and the previous view-projection only: no motion vectors, so moving objects are left to the neighbourhood clamp (a little ghosting, history blend 0.1 rising to 0.6 where the history disagrees) and per-object previous transforms are not used. The history is dropped when the size changes, the mode changes, or the pixel was off screen last frame. TAA drives the upscale: with render_scale < 1 the lit pass, depth, AO and SSR run at the internal size, the resolve reads the jittered internal image (bilinear for the colour, nearest 3x3 for the clamp) and writes the full size image, so there is no CPU upscale (RendererStats::taa_upscale). Test: at 0.6 it is closer to the converged full size TAA picture than a plain bilinear upscale.

    GTAO / SSR notes. GTAO needs the normal and depth G-buffer of the AO pass; SSR adds a roughness / metal G-buffer pass (a third geometry pass at half size, only with SSR on). SSR adds the reflected scene colour in the composite pass (it reflects what is on screen; anything that leaves the screen or the depth falls back to the existing hemisphere / probe specular, nothing is subtracted from it). The shaders had to be written around the 32 temporary registers (scalars packed into vec4s, one block per tap) and the host JIT limit of 16 texture samples: GTAO uses 14 samples, SSR 16 + 12 depth taps (it also runs as an interpreter, on the glossy pixels only). Screenshots: gfx-smaa.png, gfx-taa.png, gfx-gtao.png, gfx-ssr.png (fe-gfx-shot --quality high --set aa=smaa --set ao=gtao --set ssr=on).

    Cascaded sun shadows

    shadow_cascades (1..3) splits the sun shadow by view distance (ends at 14% / 38% / 100% of the shadow range for 3, 30% / 100% for 2). All cascades share one map of shadow_resolution: one cascade uses all of it, two or three use an atlas of 2 x 2 tiles of half the size. Each cascade is a texel snapped sphere fit of its slice (the radius in 2^(1/4) steps, the centre on whole texels and the depth in coarse steps, so a rotating or drifting camera does not make shadows swim). A tile is redrawn only when its fit or the casters that reach it changed (a far object moving does not redraw the near cascade). With cascade_cache the far cascades also keep their fit for 2 / 4 frames while the camera stays inside it (moving casters in them lag up to 3 frames). The lit shader picks the finest cascade that contains the pixel (|ndc xy| < 0.97, z < 0.97) and reads that tile with its own bias, PCF radius and normal offset (kCascadeBase in shaders_hq.h lists the frame data layout). GpuTierStats reports cascades, cascades_drawn, cascades_reused and cascade_texel (meters per texel). The point / spot atlas is unchanged. There is no scissor yet, so a tile is cleared by a full screen triangle under its viewport (depth: whole surface, it is scratch).

    Materials

    Each mesh object has a material in the Inspector's Look section: color, Roughness, Metal, Unlit and Shadows. The editor passes these to DrawItem (color, roughness, metallic, unlit, cast_shadows).

    SettingBase tierGPU tier
    Unlit (draws the plain color)yesyes
    Roughnessnoyes
    Metalnoyes
    Shadows (whether the object casts one)noyes

    The defaults (roughness 0.6, metal 0, lit, casts shadows) give the same picture as before materials existed.

    What the editor calls

    • set_settings(s) on change (it is cheap; calling it every frame is fine). Settings set before init() are kept.
    • features() says what actually runs (for the settings UI: grey out what the backend cannot do); backend() is the FarcadeGL backend string.
    • gpu_tier_stats(): milliseconds per stage of the last frame.
    • Output is read back as before (pixels()).

    With the GPU tier off and no fog the old code path runs unchanged (same pixels bit for bit).

    Pipeline (all effects on)

    #passtargetnotes
    1shadowS x S color (packed depth) + own depthcasters from the strongest shadowing directional light; skipped when nothing changed
    2depth, normalhalf size color + depthlinear depth (24 bit packed) and view space normals of all items
    3ssaohalf sizeAlchemy style, 12 spiral samples, ao_radius, ao_strength
    4blur x2half sizedepth aware 5 tap, horizontal then vertical
    5litscene (HDR encoded) or finalitems + sky; PBR, shadow lookup (PCF), AO, fog
    6bloom1/4 .. 1/64bright pass (threshold, Karis average), 13 tap downsamples, tent upsampling chain
    7compositeLDR or finalscene + bloom, then tonemap, grade, vignette, sRGB
    8fxaafinal (context color)FXAA 3.11 style, two draws with a depth mask

    Targets are created lazily and recreated when the size changes; shaders are generated per feature set and cached. Only stages that are on run; without bloom the lit pass writes straight to the final (or FXAA input) target.

    Encodings (targets are 8 bit XRGB)

    • HDR: sqrt(clamp(c, 0, 8) / 8) per channel, with exposure and tint applied when encoding ("pre-exposure"); decode is e * e * 8. Tonemapping happens in the composite pass. Values above 8 clip.
    • Depth (shadow map, SSAO): 24 bit fixed point in r:g:b, cleared to white. Shadow maps are fetched with nearest filtering and filtered by hand (PCF).
    • AO + depth: r = occlusion, g:b = 16 bit depth for the blur.

    Shadows

    Orthographic light camera fitted to the view frustum slice [near, min(shadow_distance, farthest receiver)] (bounding sphere, replaced by the scene sphere when smaller). The radius is quantized in 2^(1/4) steps and the center snapped to whole texels in light space, so the map does not shimmer. Bias: normal offset in the vertex shader, a constant, and receiver plane depth bias per PCF tap (from the normal; FGSL has no derivatives). soft_shadows = 10 Vogel disk taps rotated per pixel. On the CPU backend the map is capped at 1024 (clearing 4096 x 4096 costs about 60 ms).

    PBR

    GGX distribution, Smith-Schlick visibility (k = (r+1)^2/8), Schlick Fresnel with F0 = mix(0.04, albedo, metallic), diffuse scaled by (1 - F) and (1 - metallic). Light intensities keep the base tier's meaning (Lambert without 1/pi), so the specular lobe is multiplied by pi. Ambient: hemisphere light from SkyLight; specular ambient uses the hemisphere color along the reflection vector, blurred towards the average with roughness, times Karis' analytic split-sum approximation. AO multiplies ambient fully and direct light by 40%.

    Fog

    exp(-0.06 * Sky.fog * distance) towards the sky's horizon color (the flat color in SkyMode::Color), applied to lit and unlit items before post.

    Shader compiling and the shader cache

    FarcadeGL keeps every compiled program in 0:/cache/shaders (the SDK's fglcache.h, shared by all programs on the system), so a game's second start, or switching the editor's viewport back to FarcadeGL, skips the compiler. The limit follows the size of the 0: volume: 20 MB under 256 MB, 5 GB under 80 GB, 30 GB under 300 GB and 50 GB above, never more than half the volume; the least recently used programs go first. Settings > Graphics shows its size and has Clear cache and Recompile shaders.

    The renderer compiles at most ~25 ms of shaders a frame (Renderer::set_compile_budget): a frame that needs more stops early, compiling() is true, and the next frame goes on. The editor keeps the last picture with a "Compiling shaders n / m" bar (m is how many the last time needed), the player shows a loading box. Fixed-step player runs (--frames) compile at once, so their frames stay reproducible.

    Limits hit (FGSL / FarcadeGL / host JIT)

    • 32 vec4 temporaries per stage and none are shared between variables of a scope: shaders use blocks and vec4 packing (see comments in shaders_hq.cpp).
    • 64 uniform vec4 registers: the GPU-tier lit shader now keeps camera and per-object values in uniforms and packs light records plus shadow matrices and metadata into a read-only storage buffer. This frees uniform space but does not raise the current 8-light shader-variant limit; lighting loops are still unrolled and bounded by instruction and temporary-register limits.
    • The host JIT takes 16 texture samples per shader at most (else it falls back to the interpreter, 10x slower), turns if into predication (no work is skipped) and takes at most 512 distinct constants. Hence the 12 AO samples, the FXAA split in two passes, and depth masks (the depth test runs before the fragment shader) to skip sky pixels in SSAO and non-edge pixels in FXAA.
    • Linear texture fetches cost about 2.4x nearest on the host.

    Costs (host CPU backend, 800 x 530, ultra, one core)

    Roughly: shadow map 5 to 15 ms when it has to be redrawn (otherwise 0), depth and normal 4, SSAO 15, blur 9, lit 60 (base tier: 30), bloom 10, composite 25, FXAA 28: about 150 to 160 ms per frame. On a card these are small.

    Things that will differ on a real GPU: bilinear/nearest costs, the depth-mask trick (real hardware also rejects early), gl_FragCoord rounding, the exact packing round trip (the host rounds to nearest when storing 8 bit values), and discard handling in the mask passes.

    Tools

    fe-gfx-shot out.png [w h] [--quality low|high|ultra] renders the demo scene (high and ultra force the GPU tier on the CPU backend).

    Modules and scene objects

    The data is defined in engine/scene/modules.h. Each struct there has a field table in modules.cpp, and three parts of the engine read it:

    On this pageModulesEffects and gameplay modulesScene objectsCurrentWhat runs today
    • the Inspector draws its rows from it;
    • the ECS registers it with flecs;
    • the Lua bindings will use the same names.

    Modules

    Modules attach to any object, at most one of each kind. In the Inspector you add one with Add module and remove it with its trash button.

    ModuleLua nameWhat it is for
    Rigidbody 3Drigidbody3dPhysics: dynamic, kinematic or static, mass, damping, gravity, start velocity
    Collider 3Dcollider3dA box, sphere, capsule or mesh shape. *Collision* makes bodies bounce off it; *Trigger* reports objects entering and leaving (on_trigger_enter / on_trigger_exit)
    Character Controller 3Dcharacter_controller3dAn upright capsule with gravity and collision response; scripts steer it with its live velocity and can read whether it is grounded
    Audio ListenerlistenerWhere the game hears from. Has Current
    Audio Streamaudio_streamA long sound streamed from a file (music, ambience), optionally positioned in 3D
    Audio Sampleraudio_samplerShort sounds held in memory and played by scripts, several at once
    LightlightDirectional, point or spot light
    Particle EmitterparticlesCPU particles: rate, bursts, shapes (point, sphere, cone, box), lifetime, speed, gravity, drag, size/color/alpha over life, texture, additive or alpha blend, world or local space, loop or duration, prewarm, seed. Methods play(), stop(), clear(), emit(n)
    Joint 3Djoint3dFixed, hinge (limits, motor), spring or ball-socket joint between this body and another body or the world; break force. Method snap()
    AnimatoranimatorPlays clips of a .fanim file on the object and its children (docs/animation.md). Methods play(name, fade), stop()
    Force Fieldforce_fieldA box or sphere that pushes bodies and particles inside it: directional, radial or vortex, with falloff and turbulence
    SpawnerspawnerMakes copies of another object every so often (or by spawn()), with a random offset, velocity, lifetime and a limit. Methods spawn(), clear()
    Audio Reverb Zonereverb_zoneEcho and muffling for the listener inside a box or sphere
    BillboardbillboardA quad that always faces the camera (icons, foliage cards, glows)
    Text 3Dtext3dA text label in the world, facing the camera

    Scripts steer a character controller by setting its world-space velocity in meters per second. Its capsule collides with the existing physics bodies; grounded reports contacts below the configured slope limit. For example:

    local controller = self.object.character_controller3d
controller.velocity = fe.vec3(3, controller.grounded and 0 or controller.velocity.y, 0)

    Effects and gameplay modules

    All parameters are fields: they are in the Inspector, in the .fscene file, and in Lua as obj.<module>.<field> (obj.particles.emission_rate = 80, obj.joint3d.motor_speed = -90, obj.text3d.text = "Score " .. n); methods are called with a colon (obj.particles:emit(20)). Fields marked *live* are written by the systems while playing (particles.playing, particles.particle_count, joint3d.angle, joint3d.force, joint3d.broken, animator.time, spawner.alive ...) and some are controls too (particles.playing, animator.clip, animator.time). A link field (joint3d.connected, spawner.source) is an object or nil in Lua.

    • Particle Emitter (engine/fx/particles.cpp): a pool of at most 2000 particles per emitter, one seeded random sequence per emitter, so the same seed gives the same particles. Cone and Box particles fly along the object's -Z, Sphere particles away from the center, Point particles anywhere. In the editor the selected emitters preview in the viewport and during Play all of them run; the game renderer draws them over the image (alpha or additive, hidden by meshes, engine/gfx/particles.cpp), the editor draws them with ImGui over the viewport.
    • Joint 3D (engine/physics): rows of the sequential impulse solver. The object needs a Rigidbody 3D. The anchor is a point on this object that the joint keeps on the connected body (or in the world); a Spring hangs from the anchor to this object's origin. Hinge angle, speed and limits count this body turning about its axis. Connected bodies do not collide unless asked.
    • Force Field: a box or sphere (its object's scale sizes it). Directional pushes along the field's direction, Radial away from (negative: towards) the center, Vortex around the object's Y axis. The force is in newtons on rigidbodies (mass 1 for particles); Linear and Quadratic falloff fade it to zero at the edge; Turbulence varies it in space and time. Layers select which collision layers of bodies it pushes.
    • Spawner: copies the template object and its children into the running scene (the template stays: hide or park it). Copies appear at the spawner with the template's scale, get the added velocity (spawner's local space), a share of the spawner's own motion, and are destroyed after lifetime or when more than max_alive exist (the oldest first).
    • Animator: see docs/animation.md. .mof has no animation data and the renderer has no skinning; clips animate transforms.
    • Audio Reverb Zone: inside the zone (fading out over Fade distance outside) the whole mix gets a short reverb (Wet, Room size, Damping) and optionally a low-pass (Muffle). It is one effect on the master bus.
    • Billboard / Text 3D: pictures that face the camera. Text uses a built-in 5x7 bitmap font in the game renderer (ASCII). The editor shows a billboard as a tinted rectangle (textures show in the game).

    Options to make them cheaper or turn them off: Settings > Graphics > Effects (graphics.cfg: particles, particle_density, particle_depth_test, sprites, audio_reverb; fe.graphics too) (particles on/off, density, depth test, sprites, reverb), FxQuality in C++.

    Scene objects

    These are object kinds with their own settings. You add them from Create or the Hierarchy's + menu. They have no mesh: the viewport shows them as an icon you can click, and cameras and lights also get their shape drawn as lines.

    ObjectLua nameWhat it is for
    CameracameraPerspective or orthographic view along the object's −Z axis. Has Current, and up to three screen shaders (Shader 1-3, Shader params; docs/graphics.md)
    SkyskyThe background: a zenith/horizon/ground gradient with a sun disc, or one flat color. Has Current
    Sky LightskylightAmbient light from the sky and the ground. Has Current
    Post Processingpost_processExposure, tonemapping, contrast, saturation, tint, vignette, bloom. Has Current
    Empty—Only a transform: use it as a group, a marker, or a holder for modules

    Lights are Empty objects with a Light module (Create > Light).

    Current

    For cameras, skies, sky lights, post processing and listeners, only one object in a scene is current at a time. That object is the camera the game renders with, the sky that is drawn, or the listener that hears.

    • In the editor: - The Current switch is the first row in the object's settings. - Turning it on takes it from the object that had it, and the console says so. - The Hierarchy marks current objects with a star. - The first object of each kind becomes current when it is created.
    • Duplicates and deletes: - A duplicate is never current. - Deleting the current object leaves none current. The renderer then uses default settings.
    • Play mode: Play/Stop puts the flags back as they were before Play.
    • In C++: Scene::set_current, clear_current, current(kind) and is_current in the editor. The ECS has the same rule (World::set_current), enforced however the flag is set.

    Scripts reach Current like any other field (see scripting.md):

    -- switch to the security camera when the player enters a trigger
-- @prop security object

function on_trigger_enter(self, other)
  if other.name == "Player" then
    self.security.camera.current = true      -- the old camera stops being current
  end
end

function on_update(self, dt)
  local cam = fe.current("camera")           -- the object, or nil
  if cam then cam.camera.fov = 60 + 10 * math.sin(fe.time()) end
  self.object.light.intensity = 2             -- modules by their Lua names
end

    What runs today

    • Done in the editor: the data model, the Inspector, creating objects, the Current rule, and the viewport icons and shapes.
    • Physics: in Play, a built-in physics step runs Rigidbody 3D, Collider 3D and Character Controller 3D (engine/physics). It is a stand-in for Jolt (plan C6), which needs the standard C++ library this engine doesn't use yet. What it does: - Character Controller 3D uses an upright capsule (its default center puts the feet at the object's origin), gravity and the same collision solver. Set character_controller3d.velocity in m/s from a script to move it; grounded is updated by physics, using Slope limit to decide whether a contact counts as ground. A controller is not a Rigidbody: its rotation is fixed. A Collider 3D can provide friction, bounciness and layers; its shape and trigger mode are ignored. - Dynamic bodies fall and are damped (linear and angular) and turn as well as move: inertia comes from the collider shape, freeze_rotation locks the rotation, kinematic bodies move and turn by their velocities, and static bodies and colliders without a body don't move. - Box, sphere, capsule, cylinder and mesh colliders all collide with each other (GJK and EPA on convex shapes, contact manifolds of up to 4 points), so boxes rest flat and stack, spheres and cylinders roll down slopes, and boxes tip over edges. Friction, bounciness (no bounce below 1 m/s) and collision layers apply; the solver is sequential impulses with warm starting. - Mesh colliders use the convex hull of the points given to PhysicsWorld::set_mesh (the editor calls it with the object's mesh vertices when play starts); without points a mesh collider is its size box. Concave triangle meshes are not done. - Triggers report objects entering and leaving them, and first contacts are reported as hits. Scripts get them as on_trigger_enter, on_trigger_exit and on_collision, and the console logs them too. - rigidbody3d.velocity and rigidbody3d.angular_velocity are live. - Joints and Force Fields run in the same step (see Effects and gameplay modules). - Not done: continuous collision (very fast small bodies can tunnel through thin colliders), sleeping, concave meshes. - A new collider starts fitted to the object's mesh: a sphere for spheres, a thin box for planes.
    • Audio: Audio settings are saved, but nothing plays them yet (plan C6: the engine's mixer over SYS_AUDIO_STREAM).
    • Rendering: the editor's CPU preview does not use lights, sky, sky light or post processing. The FarcadeGL renderer (engine/gfx, in progress) does.

    Edit this page on GitHub

    The .mof model format, version 1.0

    .mof ("model file") is Farcade Engine's interchange and import format for 3D models: one self-contained file per model holding meshes, materials, embedded textures, a skeleton and the node hierarchy. Tools write it (the mofconv converter imports glTF 2.0 and OBJ), the editor and the asset cooker read it. It is designed so that an independent reader can be written from this document alone, and so that a reader can trust nothing in the file: every rule below is checkable, and engine/mof/mof_read.cpp checks all of them.

    Reference implementation:

    On this page1. Conventions2. File layout3. Overflow-safe range rule4. Chunks5. Validation summary6. Versioning7. Selective reading8. Relation to cooked, streamable assets9. Writer (reference implementation)10. Importers (mofconv)11. Test coverage
    FileWhat
    engine/mof/mof.hthe structs of this document, reader and writer API
    engine/mof/mof_read.cppvalidating, zero-copy reader (freestanding)
    engine/mof/mof_write.cppwriter (freestanding, allocator hooks)
    engine/mof/mof_import.h, import_*.cppglTF / OBJ importers (host libc)
    tools/mofconvmofconv CLI, mofgen sample generator

    1. Conventions

    • Byte order: little-endian for every integer and float.
    • Types: u8 u16 u32 u64 unsigned, i32 two's complement, f32 IEEE-754 binary32. All fields are naturally aligned inside their records.
    • Alignment: every chunk starts at a file offset that is a multiple of 16, and every offset into a data chunk (vertex streams, index arrays, texture payloads) is a multiple of 16. Readers that map the file at a 16-byte aligned address can therefore use all arrays in place. Padding bytes should be written as zero and must be ignored by readers.
    • "None" index: unsigned index fields use 0xFFFFFFFF (MOF_NONE) for "no reference"; signed parent and mesh fields use -1.
    • Strings: u32 byte offsets into the string table (section 4.1). Offset 0 is the empty string.
    • Coordinate system (same as glTF 2.0): right-handed, +Y up, +Z towards the viewer, units are metres. Front faces are counter-clockwise.
    • Texture coordinates: origin at the top-left of the image, +u right, +v down (glTF convention). The OBJ importer flips v (v' = 1 - v).
    • Matrices: 4x4 f32[16], column-major: element (row r, column c) is m[c * 4 + r]; translation is m[12], m[13], m[14]. Vectors are columns (p' = M p).
    • Rotations: unit quaternions stored x, y, z, w.
    • Local transforms (TRS): M = T * R * S (scale first, then rotation, then translation), as in glTF.
    • Tangents: f32[4], xyz = unit tangent along +u, w = +1 or -1. bitangent = cross(normal, tangent.xyz) * w points towards image-up (decreasing v), i.e. +Y of a tangent-space normal map (glTF convention).
    • Colour spaces: factors are linear. Textures in the base colour and emissive slots are sRGB-encoded; normal, metallic-roughness and occlusion textures are linear. The colour space is a property of the slot, not of the texture.

    2. File layout

    offset 0      header (64 bytes)
table_offset  chunk table: chunk_count entries of 32 bytes
...           chunks, each at a 16-byte aligned offset, in any order
file_size     end of file

    Chunks may appear in any order; the writer puts the bulk data first and the string table last. Gaps between chunks are allowed (and ignored).

    2.1 Header (64 bytes, at offset 0)

    OffsetTypeFieldRule
    0u8[4]magic'M' 'O' 'F' 0x00
    4u16version_majormust be 1
    6u16version_minorany value (section 6)
    8u32flagsreserved, written 0, unknown bits ignored
    12u32chunk_count<= 256
    16u32header_size>= 64, multiple of 16 (64 in 1.0)
    20u32chunk_entry_sizemust be 32 in major version 1
    24u64table_offsetmultiple of 16, >= header_size
    32u64file_sizetotal size of the file in bytes
    40u8[24]reservedwritten 0, ignored

    file_size must be >= header_size and must not exceed the number of bytes the reader has. Bytes after file_size (a file embedded in a larger buffer) are not part of the file and are ignored. The chunk table [table_offset, table_offset + 32 * chunk_count) must lie inside [0, file_size).

    2.2 Chunk table entry (32 bytes)

    OffsetTypeFieldRule
    0u32typefourcc, first character in the low byte ('M' | 'E'<<8 | 'S'<<16 | 'H'<<24)
    4u32flagsbit 0 REQUIRED: a reader that does not know type must reject the file. Other bits reserved
    8u64offsetmultiple of 16, >= end of the chunk table
    16u64sizebytes; offset + size <= file_size (checked without overflow)
    24u32countnumber of records for record chunks, byte size for STRS, 0 for blob chunks
    28u32reservedwritten 0, ignored

    Table rules:

    • Two chunks with non-zero size must not overlap.
    • A known chunk type may appear at most once. Unknown types may repeat.
    • Unknown chunk types without the REQUIRED flag are skipped.
    • For record chunks, size must equal count * record_size exactly.
    • A chunk of a type the model does not need may be absent; an absent record chunk means zero records, an absent blob chunk means zero bytes.

    2.3 Chunk types (version 1.0)

    TypeKindRecord sizeContent
    STRSbytes-string table
    MESHrecords128mof_mesh[]
    SUBMrecords16mof_submesh[] (shared by all meshes)
    VERTblob-vertex streams of all meshes
    INDXblob-index arrays of all meshes
    MATLrecords96mof_material[]
    TEXTrecords64mof_texture[]
    TEXDblob-texture payloads
    SKELrecords128mof_bone[]
    NODErecords64mof_node[]

    ANIM is reserved for a future minor version (keyframed bone animation).

    3. Overflow-safe range rule

    Whenever this document says "[off, off + n * stride) lies inside a chunk of size bytes", a reader must evaluate it as

    off % 16 == 0  &&  off <= size  &&  n * stride <= size - off

    with 64-bit unsigned arithmetic (n is at most 2^32 - 1 and stride at most 16, so the product cannot overflow). off + n * stride must never be computed before these checks.

    4. Chunks

    4.1 STRS: string table

    A byte array of size bytes, count == size, 1 <= size < 2^32. The first byte and the last byte must be 0. A string is referenced by the byte offset of its first character and runs to the next 0 byte; because the table ends in 0, every in-range offset yields a terminated string. A string reference is valid if it is 0 or < size. If STRS is absent, only offset 0 is valid. Strings are UTF-8; names need not be unique. Writers deduplicate identical strings.

    4.2 MESH: meshes (128 bytes each)

    OffsetTypeField
    0u32name (string)
    4u32vertex_count
    8u32index_count (triangle list)
    12u32index_format: 0 = u16, 1 = u32
    16u32stream_mask (below)
    20u32weight_format: 0 = f32[4], 1 = unorm16 u16[4] (value / 65535)
    24u32first_submesh (into SUBM)
    28u32submesh_count
    32u32off_position (VERT)
    36u32off_normal (VERT)
    40u32off_tangent (VERT)
    44u32off_uv0 (VERT)
    48u32off_uv1 (VERT)
    52u32off_color (VERT)
    56u32off_joints (VERT)
    60u32off_weights (VERT)
    64u32off_indices (INDX)
    68f32[3]bounds_min (AABB, mesh space)
    80f32[3]bounds_max
    92f32[3]sphere_center (bounding sphere)
    104f32sphere_radius
    108u32[5]reserved

    stream_mask bits; the position stream is always present:

    BitStreamElementStride
    -positionf32[3]12
    0 NORMALnormalf32[3] unit12
    1 TANGENTtangentf32[4] (section 1)16
    2 UV0texcoord set 0f32[2]8
    3 UV1texcoord set 1f32[2]8
    4 COLORvertex colouru8[4] RGBA unorm, linear (like glTF COLOR_0)4
    5 SKINjoints + weightsu16[4] + weights per weight_format8 + 16 or 8

    Unknown bits are ignored (a later minor version may add streams). The offset of a stream whose bit is clear is meaningless (written 0). Streams are separate arrays (structure of arrays), each vertex_count elements long. Joint indices are indices into the SKEL bone array; a vertex is skinned with sum(weight[i] * bone_matrix[joint[i]]) where bone_matrix = bone_world * inverse_bind. Weights should sum to 1; unused influences have weight 0.

    Validation, for each mesh:

    • name valid; index_format <= 1; weight_format <= 1; index_count % 3 == 0.
    • Every present stream (position always) lies inside VERT (section 3) with its stride.
    • If SKIN is set: the skeleton has at least one bone, and every one of the 4 * vertex_count joint indices is < bone_count.
    • The index array (index_count elements of 2 or 4 bytes at off_indices) lies inside INDX, and every index is < vertex_count.
    • first_submesh <= submesh_total and submesh_count <= submesh_total - first_submesh.
    • All 10 bounds floats are finite, sphere_radius >= 0, and bounds_min[a] <= bounds_max[a] for each axis.

    A mesh may have vertex_count == 0 (an empty mesh keeps mesh indices stable). Index arrays of different meshes are independent: indices are relative to the mesh's own vertex streams.

    4.3 SUBM: submeshes (16 bytes each)

    OffsetTypeField
    0u32first_index (into the owning mesh's index array)
    4u32index_count
    8u32material (material index or MOF_NONE)
    12u32reserved

    Each mesh owns submesh_count consecutive records starting at first_submesh. Validation per referenced submesh: first_index <= mesh.index_count, index_count <= mesh.index_count - first_index, index_count % 3 == 0, material == MOF_NONE || material < material_count. Submeshes normally cover the index array without overlap, but readers must not rely on it. A mesh without submeshes is valid (nothing to draw with a material).

    4.4 VERT, INDX, TEXD: blobs

    Raw bytes referenced by offsets from MESH and TEXT records. count is 0. Data of different meshes or textures may share bytes (the writer stores identical texture payloads once).

    4.5 MATL: materials (96 bytes each)

    PBR metallic-roughness, the glTF 2.0 material model.

    OffsetTypeField
    0u32name
    4u32flags: bit 0 double-sided; bits 1-2 alpha mode (0 opaque, 1 mask, 2 blend; 3 invalid)
    8f32alpha_cutoff (mask mode)
    12f32metallic factor
    16f32roughness factor
    20f32normal_scale
    24f32occlusion_strength
    28f32[4]base_color factor (linear RGBA)
    44f32[3]emissive factor (linear RGB, may exceed 1)
    56texref[5]texture slots

    texref is 8 bytes: u32 texture (index or MOF_NONE), u32 uv_set (0 or 1). Slots in order: 0 base colour (sRGB, multiplied by the factor), 1 normal (tangent space, linear), 2 metallic-roughness (G = roughness, B = metallic, linear), 3 occlusion (R, linear), 4 emissive (sRGB). Unknown flag bits are ignored.

    Validation: name valid; alpha mode <= 2; each slot's texture is MOF_NONE or < texture_count; each uv_set <= 1; all float fields finite.

    4.6 TEXT: textures (64 bytes each)

    OffsetTypeField
    0u32name
    4u32codec: 0 raw RGBA8, 1 PNG, 2 JPEG
    8u32width
    12u32height
    16u32mip_count
    20u32wrap_s: 0 repeat, 1 clamp to edge, 2 mirrored repeat
    24u32wrap_t
    28u32min_filter: 0 nearest, 1 linear
    32u32mag_filter: 0 nearest, 1 linear
    36u32mip_filter: 0 none, 1 nearest, 2 linear
    40u32flags (reserved, 0)
    44u32reserved
    48u64data_offset (into TEXD)
    56u64data_size

    Payload by codec:

    • Raw RGBA8: mip_count levels, largest first, tightly packed, rows top to bottom, 4 bytes per pixel (R, G, B, A). Level i is max(1, width >> i) by max(1, height >> i) pixels. This is where an optional precomputed mip chain lives; mip_count == 1 means only the base level (consumers generate mips if they want them). Rules: 1 <= width, height <= 16384; 1 <= mip_count <= 1 + floor(log2(max(width, height))) (and <= 15); data_size equals the sum of all level sizes exactly (computed in 64 bits).
    • PNG / JPEG: the original file bytes, unmodified. mip_count must be 1. width/height are informational (taken from the image header by the importer; 0 = unknown), each <= 16384. The payload must start with the PNG signature 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A (at least 8 bytes) or with FF D8 FF (JPEG, at least 4 bytes). Decoding is the consumer's job and must itself be robust: the reader does not decode images.

    Validation: name valid; codec, wrap and filter values in range; data_offset % 16 == 0; [data_offset, data_offset + data_size) inside TEXD (both u64, checked as data_offset <= size && data_size <= size - data_offset); the codec rules above.

    4.7 SKEL: skeleton (128 bytes per bone)

    One skeleton per file, shared by all skinned meshes.

    OffsetTypeField
    0u32name
    4i32parent: -1 for a root, otherwise the index of the parent bone
    8u32node: index of the node this bone corresponds to, or MOF_NONE
    12u32reserved
    16f32[3]translation (local bind pose)
    28f32[4]rotation (quaternion x y z w)
    44f32[3]scale
    56f32[16]inverse_bind (column-major)
    120u32[2]reserved

    Bones are ordered parents first: parent == -1 || 0 <= parent < own index. This makes cycles impossible and lets consumers compute world transforms in one forward pass. The local bind transform is relative to the parent bone; for a root bone it is relative to model space (the importer folds the transforms of non-bone ancestors into it). inverse_bind maps model space to the bone's bind space.

    Validation: bone_count <= 65536 (joint indices are u16); name valid; parent rule above; node == MOF_NONE || node < node_count; all 26 floats finite.

    4.8 NODE: node hierarchy (64 bytes each)

    The scene graph of the model, so multi-part models keep their layout.

    OffsetTypeField
    0u32name
    4i32parent: -1 root, else index of the parent node
    8i32mesh: mesh index or -1
    12u32flags: bit 0 skinned (the mesh is deformed by SKEL)
    16f32[3]translation (local, relative to parent)
    28f32[4]rotation
    44f32[3]scale
    56u32[2]reserved

    Validation: name valid; parent == -1 || 0 <= parent < own index; mesh == -1 || 0 <= mesh < mesh_count; if skinned, bone_count > 0; all 10 floats finite. Unknown flag bits are ignored. Several roots are allowed. The skinned flag does not guarantee that the mesh has a SKIN stream (the reader does not cross-check it): consumers skin only meshes whose stream_mask has SKIN and draw others rigidly. A skinned node's own transform does not move the mesh (skinning uses bone matrices), as in glTF.

    5. Validation summary

    A conforming reader rejects the file unless all of these hold, in addition to the per-chunk rules of section 4:

    1. The buffer holds at least 64 bytes; magic, major version, header_size, chunk_entry_size, file_size, chunk_count <= 256 and table_offset are as in section 2.1.
    2. Every chunk entry: aligned offset after the table, range inside the file, no overlap, no duplicate known type, no unknown REQUIRED type.
    3. Record chunk sizes match their counts exactly; STRS starts and ends with 0.
    4. Every string reference, index, parent, joint and range is checked as described, using the overflow-safe rule of section 3.

    The reference reader additionally requires the buffer start to be 16-byte aligned (so the records and streams can be used in place). Checking costs time linear in the file size (each index and joint is visited once); there are no quadratic paths except the chunk overlap test over at most 256 entries.

    Things a reader does not need to check (they cannot cause out-of-bounds access): vertex positions, normals, UVs, colours and weights may hold any bit pattern, quaternions need not be normalised, submeshes may overlap, image payloads are not decoded.

    5.1 Size limits

    Mesh stream and index offsets are u32, so the VERT and INDX chunks are limited to 4 GiB; the reference writer limits whole files to 2 GiB - 1 and refuses larger models. Texture payloads use u64 offsets and sizes, but raw textures are bounded by 16384 x 16384 pixels and imported encoded images by 2 GiB. At most 256 chunks and 65536 bones.

    6. Versioning

    • Major version changes break compatibility; a version 1 reader rejects any other major version.
    • Minor versions only add: new chunk types, new stream_mask bits, new flag bits, or meaning for fields that are reserved (written 0) in 1.0. Record sizes and the meaning of existing fields never change within a major version. A reader therefore accepts any minor version, ignores unknown chunk types, bits and reserved fields, and still reads everything it knows.
    • A new chunk that changes how existing data must be interpreted (so that ignoring it would give wrong results) is written with the REQUIRED flag; older readers then reject the file instead of misreading it.
    • header_size may grow in a later minor version; readers locate the chunk table through table_offset, never by assuming it follows the header.

    7. Selective reading

    Every texture and every mesh can be located and read on its own through the chunk table, without parsing any other chunk:

    1. Read the first 64 bytes. table_offset + 32 * chunk_count is the size of the "head"; read that many bytes from offset 0 and validate the header and table (mof_head_size(), mof_find_chunk() in the reference reader do both).
    2. Texture i: read 64 bytes at TEXT.offset + 64 * i, check i < TEXT.count, check its fields (section 4.6), then read data_size bytes at TEXD.offset + data_offset.
    3. Mesh i: read 128 bytes at MESH.offset + 128 * i, check the stream and index ranges against VERT.size / INDX.size (section 4.2), then read the streams it needs from VERT and its indices from INDX. Its submeshes are submesh_count 16-byte records at SUBM.offset + 16 * first_submesh. Index and joint values must be range-checked after reading, as in 4.2.
    4. Names need the string table (STRS), which is small.

    No chunk contains offsets that only make sense after another record chunk has been parsed, so a tool can extract one texture without touching any mesh data, and vice versa.

    8. Relation to cooked, streamable assets

    .mof is an interchange format. Games do not load .mof files directly: the asset cooker reads them (with the validating reader) and builds the run-time formats that the engine streams for maps, objects and textures. The cooker derives from a .mof:

    • Mesh LOD pages: simplified levels of detail per mesh, split into fixed-size, independently loadable pages (vertex and index data quantised and laid out for the renderer), with per-page bounds taken from or refined beyond the .mof bounds.
    • Mip chains: complete mip chains for every texture, generated from the base level (or taken from a raw RGBA8 texture's precomputed chain when mip_count > 1), with the colour space given by the material slot.
    • Texture tiles: mip levels cut into tiles for virtual/streamed texturing, so only the visible part of a large texture is resident.
    • Skeleton and node data in the engine's run-time layout (bones are already parent-first, so no sorting is needed), and material parameter blocks referencing the cooked textures.

    Because .mof keeps the original PNG/JPEG bytes, full precision floats and the full scene graph, cooking can be redone with new settings without going back to the source files. Section 7 lets the cooker process textures and meshes one at a time with bounded memory.

    9. Writer (reference implementation)

    mof_write(const mof_wdesc*, mof_buffer*, err, errlen) builds a file image from an in-memory description (mof_wmesh, mof_wmaterial, mof_wtexture, mof_wbone, mof_wnode, plus optional opaque extra chunks) into a growable buffer whose memory comes from a caller-supplied realloc-style hook. It computes the mesh bounds (AABB, and a sphere centred on the AABB centre whose radius reaches the farthest vertex), picks 16-bit indices when vertex_count <= 65536 (unless force_index32), interns and deduplicates names, shares identical texture payloads, aligns everything to 16 bytes and writes STRS last. It rejects non-finite positions, out-of-range indices and incomplete skin data, and finally re-validates the result with mof_open (can be switched off with skip_verify), so a successful write is always a valid file. On any failure, including allocation failure, the buffer is released and nothing leaks.

    10. Importers (mofconv)

    mofconv input.(gltf|glb|obj) output.mof [--info] and mofconv --info file.mof. The importer library (engine/mof/mof_import.h) uses libc only (no POSIX calls) so it can later run on Minimal-OS.

    glTF 2.0 (via cgltf, after cgltf_validate):

    • Each glTF mesh becomes one .mof mesh; each triangle primitive becomes a submesh (strips and fans are converted to lists; points, lines, Draco primitives are skipped with a warning). The stream set of a mesh is the union over its primitives; primitives missing a stream get zeros (UVs), white (colour) or generated data (normals, tangents).
    • Attributes: POSITION, NORMAL, TANGENT, TEXCOORD_0/1, COLOR_0 (any component type, converted to RGBA8), JOINTS_0/WEIGHTS_0 (more than 4 influences are dropped with a warning). Normalised and sparse accessors are handled by cgltf.
    • Materials: metallic-roughness factors and all five texture slots, alpha mode/cutoff, double-sided, KHR_materials_emissive_strength (folded into the emissive factor). KHR_materials_pbrSpecularGlossiness is approximated. Texture coordinate sets other than 0 and 1 fall back to 0 with a warning.
    • Images: from buffer views (.glb), base64 data URIs, or external files (relative to the model, percent-decoded). PNG and JPEG bytes are stored unchanged; other formats that stb_image can decode become raw RGBA8. Unreadable images and textures without a PNG/JPEG source (WebP, Basis) are dropped with a warning and the material slots that used them are cleared.
    • Skins: the union of all skins' joints becomes the bone array, sorted parents first. Each mesh's skin-local JOINTS_0 values are remapped to bone indices and the inverse bind matrices are reordered with the bones (first skin wins for a joint used by several skins). A mesh drawn with several different skins uses the first one (warning).
    • Nodes: all glTF nodes, reordered parents first (by depth, then by original index); matrices are decomposed into TRS.

    OBJ + MTL (via fast_obj): one mesh, one submesh per material, one root node. Vertices are unique (position, texcoord, normal) triples; polygons are fan-triangulated; v is flipped. MTL: Kd + d -> base colour (d < 1 selects blend mode), Ke -> emissive, roughness = 1 - sqrt(Ns / 1000) (Blender's convention), metallic 0; map_Kd, map_Ke, map_bump/bump -> base colour, emissive, normal textures. Faces before the first usemtl are assigned to the first MTL material (a fast_obj limitation).

    Generated data:

    • *Normals* (when missing): area weighted, the sum of the unnormalised face cross products of all triangles using the vertex, normalised; degenerate vertices get (0, 1, 0). For OBJ, file normals win where present.
    • *Tangents* (only when the material has a normal map and the file has no TANGENT): a simple per-triangle method (Lengyel), not MikkTSpace. Per triangle, tangent and bitangent directions are derived from the UV gradients (with v flipped to image-up) and summed per vertex; the tangent is Gram-Schmidt orthogonalised against the normal, and w is the sign of dot(cross(n, t), bitangent). Vertices with degenerate UVs get an arbitrary unit vector perpendicular to the normal.

    11. Test coverage

    make test runs mof_tests (round trip of a model using every feature, forward compatibility, selective reading, ~100 targeted corruptions, truncation at every byte, 20000 fixed-seed mutations plus 3000 per sample file with every accepted mutant fully walked, writer error and allocation-failure paths, sample files) and mof_import_tests (generated skinned and textured .gltf and .glb, OBJ + MTL, error cases, 500 mutated .glb files). make test-mof-asan runs both with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. make mof-samples regenerates assets/samples/*.mof; a test fails if the committed samples are stale.

    Game packages: .fepak v1

    A .fepak is the file a game loads its content from: scenes, Lua scripts, models, textures, sounds and shaders in one file, found by *virtual path* (scripts/spin.lua). engine/core/pak.{h,cpp} reads and writes it, engine/core/vfs.{h,cpp} is what the engine's loaders call. Everything is little-endian.

    On this pageHeader (64 bytes)Index entries (40 bytes each, sorted by path)PathsAlignmentReadingThe VFS
    offset 0      header (64 bytes)
              file data, each file aligned (below), in the order of the index
index_offset  index: entry_count entries of 40 bytes, then the string table

    Header (64 bytes)

    OffsetTypeField
    0char[8]magic FEPAK\0\0\0
    8u32version (1)
    12u32header size (64; readers skip to it, so a later version may grow the header)
    16u64index offset
    24u64index size (entries + string table)
    32u32entry count
    36u32header flags (0)
    40u32chunk alignment (65536)
    44u32CRC-32 of the index (entries + string table)
    48u64total file size (a cut-off file is refused)
    56u64reserved (0)

    Index entries (40 bytes each, sorted by path)

    OffsetTypeField
    0u64data offset from the start of the file
    8u64stored size (bytes in the package)
    16u64raw size (bytes after decoding; equal to the stored size in v1)
    24u32name offset in the string table
    28u16name length
    30u16flags: bits 0-3 how the data is stored (0 = raw, 1 = zstd, reserved), other bits 0
    32u32CRC-32 of the raw bytes
    36u32reserved (0)

    Entries are sorted by plain byte order of the path, so a lookup is a binary search. The string table follows the entries; names are not NUL terminated and are at most 255 bytes.

    Paths

    Virtual paths are project relative, use /, have no leading / and no ./ or ... The exporter stores a file under the path the scene uses for it (scenes/main.fscene, scripts/spin.lua, models/ship.mof) and adds project.fe at the root. Paths are case sensitive.

    Alignment

    Data of files of 64 KiB or more starts on a 64 KiB boundary (reads of one chunk never straddle a block, and a later streaming loader can map or prefetch whole chunks, plan C4.8); smaller files start on 16 bytes. The index comes last, so a package can be written in one pass.

    Reading

    PakReader::open takes a PakSource (a read_at callback and a size): a file read with random access (platform::open_read / read_at), or a block of memory. It checks the magic, the version, the total size, the index CRC and that every entry lies inside the file. read returns the entry's bytes in malloc'd memory (plus one zero byte, so text can be used as a C string) after checking the entry's CRC; read_range reads part of an entry for streaming. Entries with a storage kind other than raw are refused in v1.

    Versions: a reader accepts every version up to its own and ignores reserved fields; a change that old readers cannot handle gets a new version number. Compression (zstd, per entry, with the stored size smaller than the raw size) is planned for version 1 files: it only needs the flag and a decoder.

    The VFS

    vfs::read("scripts/spin.lua", &size) looks in the mounted packages (the last mounted first), then, when disk fallback is on, in plain files under the project folder (vfs::set_root). The editor reads plain files; the player turns the fallback off, so a game only sees its package. Full paths that start with the project folder and paths with backslashes are normalized to virtual ones first. vfs::read_cb fits the callbacks the renderer, audio system and play session take (read_asset, read_file).
