    Edit this page on GitHub

    Editor performance on Minimal-OS

    Measure with farcade-editor.run --bench N [--farcadegl] [--profile] (phases idle, mouse, orbit, settle; see editor/bench.h) and, on the host, build/host/bin/fe-editor-bench [--farcadegl] [--adaptive].

    What the editor does:

    • Redraw only what changed. The UI is built every frame (about 5 ms under QEMU TCG), but the ImGui draw lists are hashed; unchanged frames are not rasterized or presented, changed ones redraw only the rectangles of the changed lists (before and after) and present only those (SwRenderer::render_incremental, platform::present_region). The result equals a full redraw (SwRenderer::set_verify, on in editor_tests). An idle editor waits 40 ms between frames.
    • Adaptive viewport resolution (Editor::adaptive_view, on in main_os, --no-adaptive turns it off): while the view changes, the image is rendered at 1/d size (d from the measured ms per pixel, budget 200 ms) and stretched; with FarcadeGL it uses cheap draft shaders. When the view stops, the CPU preview is redrawn sharp; FarcadeGL redraws the full image in bands of about 250 ms, one per UI frame (Renderer::render_rows), so the UI stays usable and a new drag drops the rest.
    • FarcadeGL on QEMU TCG is dominated by fragment shading in the kernel's FGPU (about 6 us per pixel per CPU, linear in pixels, scales with -smp); shader compile, upload and readback are under 30 ms. On KVM/hardware d is 1.

    Not done: multi-core UI rasterization. After the damage tracking the UI raster is 1-5 ms typical and about 20 ms for a viewport repaint, so threads (and their risk) were not worth it.

    PreviousGame packages: .fepak v1NextThe Minimal-OS runtime

    Edit this page on GitHub

    The Minimal-OS runtime

    runtime/minimalos/ is the small C/C++ runtime the engine and the editor link on Minimal-OS. The SDK's own stdlib.h/stdio.h/string.h are tiny inline helpers, and its malloc() is one system call per block on the kernel heap; the runtime replaces them with a libc subset that Dear ImGui, ImGuizmo, stb_image, stb_truetype, cgltf and fast_obj need, while the SDK's other headers (minimalos.h, thread.h, vm.h, window.h, farcadegl.h, process.h, ...) keep working in the same translation unit.

    On this pageUsing itWhy the preludeWhat it providesThe editor on Minimal-OSTests

    Using it

    In a mk/*.mk fragment (any name, any order relative to mk/runtime.mk):

    OS_OBJS_mytool := $(call os_objs,tools/mytool/main.cpp engine/core/math.cpp)
OS_PROGRAMS    += $(BUILD)/os/bin/mytool.run

    make os then builds build/os/bin/mytool.run: the SDK's crt0.c, the objects, build/os/libfe_rt.a and libgcc, linked with the SDK's link.ld (plus .ctors, see below) and bundled with the SDK's mkrun.sh. The ELF stays next to it (mytool.elf). The link rule is a pattern rule with secondary expansion, so OS_OBJS_<name> may be set after or before mk/runtime.mk is read; set it with = if it uses variables of other fragments (as mk/editor_os.mk does with EDITOR_SRC).

    Every Minimal-OS object gets these flags from mk/runtime.mk (prepended to OS_EXTRA_FLAGS):

    -Iruntime/minimalos/include -isystem external/Minimal-OS-SDK/include
-include runtime/minimalos/include/fe_prelude.h

    Write code as on the host: #include <stdio.h>, <math.h>, <new>, ... and the SDK headers by name ("minimalos.h", "thread.h"). If the cross tools are not on PATH, mk/runtime.mk takes them from ~/cross/bin.

    Running a program on Minimal-OS in QEMU:

    tools/ci/run_os.sh build/os/bin/imgui_smoke.run 'FE SMOKE PASS' 'FE SMOKE FAIL' editor/fonts/Inter-Regular.otf
SCREENDUMP=build/os/editor-os.png tools/ci/run_os.sh build/os/bin/farcade-editor.run 'FE EDITOR frames 121'

    It stages the files in $MINIMAL_OS_DIR/src/resources/install2/ (they end up in 0:/programs/), builds the ISO there, boots it headless, types run 0:/programs/<name>.run $ARGS on the serial line and waits for the pass/fail regex. The header of the script lists the options (QEMU_EXTRA, QEMU_SMP, TIMEOUT, SCREENDUMP, MONITOR_CMDS, ...). The serial and monitor logs go to build/os/run_os/.

    Why the prelude

    The SDK headers include "stdlib.h", "string.h" with quotes, and quotes search the including file's directory first, so no -I order can make thread.h or farcadegl.h see the runtime's headers. fe_prelude.h defines the SDK's include guards (MINIMALOS_STDLIB_H, MINIMALOS_STRING_H, MINIMALOS_STDIO_H) before anything else, which turns those three SDK files into empty files, and includes the runtime's versions. What the SDK versions defined besides libc functions is still there: mos_heap_failed, mos_random_bytes, mos_random_u64, mos_vprintf (fe_sdk_compat.h), strlcpy_safe, mos_memcmp, mos_memeq_ct (string.h). tests/os/headers/ compiles thread.h, farcadegl.h, window.h, storage.h, process.h before and after the runtime's headers, in C and C++, and stb_image, stb_image_write, stb_truetype, cgltf and fast_obj against the runtime (every symbol they need is in libfe_rt.a); make os builds them.

    What it provides

    HeaderContents
    string.h, strings.hmem*/str* (SSE2 and rep movsb/stosb for memcpy/memmove/memset), strtok(_r), strdup, strndup, strlcpy, strcasecmp, strerror, ...
    stdlib.h, malloc.h, alloca.hmalloc/calloc/realloc/free/aligned_alloc/posix_memalign/memalign/malloc_usable_size, fe_malloc_stats(); strtod/strtof/strtol/strtoul/strtoll/strtoull/atoi/atol/atof; qsort (stable merge sort), bsearch; abs/div; rand; getenv (the program's environment); exit/atexit/abort/_Exit
    stdio.hsnprintf/vsnprintf/sprintf/vsprintf (stb_sprintf), printf/fprintf/vfprintf, sscanf/vsscanf; FILE: fopen/freopen/fclose/fflush/fread/fwrite/fseek/ftell/rewind/feof/ferror/fgetc/fgets/ungetc/fputc/fputs/puts, remove, rename, perror; stdin/stdout/stderr
    math.hfloat and double: sqrt cbrt sin cos tan asin acos atan atan2 sinh cosh tanh asinh acosh atanh exp exp2 expm1 log log2 log10 log1p logb pow fmod remainder hypot floor ceil round trunc rint nearbyint lrint lround fabs fmin fmax fdim copysign nextafter fma ldexp scalbn frexp modf ilogb nan; isnan/isinf/isfinite/signbit/fpclassify, HUGE_VAL, INFINITY, NAN, M_PI ...
    time.hclock (monotonic µs), time, clock_gettime, nanosleep, usleep, gmtime(_r), localtime(_r) (= UTC), mktime, timegm, strftime
    ctype.h, assert.h, errno.h, limits.h, inttypes.h, sys/types.h, newas usual; limits.h adds PATH_MAX to GCC's
    from GCCstdint.h, stddef.h, stdarg.h, stdbool.h, float.h, intrinsics

    C++ support (fe_cxx.cpp): all forms of operator new/delete (sized, aligned, nothrow; plain new aborts with a message when memory runs out, there are no exceptions), __cxa_pure_virtual, __cxa_atexit (static destructors run in exit()), __dso_handle, __cxa_guard_*. libgcc is linked for 128-bit arithmetic and the like.

    Start and exit

    crt0.c is the SDK's, compiled with -Dmain=fe_crt_main (and its simple memcpy & co. renamed out of the way). fe_crt_main calls main and then exit(), so returning from main runs atexit handlers and static destructors and flushes open FILEs. Static constructors run before main: x86_64-elf-g++ puts them in .ctors, which the SDK's link.ld does not collect, so the link uses build/os/rt/link.ld, the SDK script with .ctors added to .init_array (runtime/minimalos/mklinkld.py). Without this, C++ globals with constructors stay zero; programs built with the SDK's build.sh and g++ have that problem today.

    malloc

    fe_malloc.c: memory comes from SYS_VM in 4 MiB chunks (demand-zero, so an untouched chunk costs no physical memory). Blocks up to 64 KiB are served from 44 size classes (16-byte steps to 128 bytes, then four per doubling), each with its own futex lock, free list and bump span; freed small blocks are reused but not returned to the kernel. Bigger blocks are mappings of their own and are unmapped by free(). Every block has a 16-byte header (16-byte alignment; free() of a bad or already freed pointer aborts with a message). There are no per-thread caches: threads allocating the same size class at the same time take turns on its lock. Pointers are above 2 TiB, which the kernel calls accept (SYS_READ, blits, ...).

    Accuracy and deviations

    • Math (host tests against glibc, make test): sqrt, floor/ceil/round/trunc, fmod, frexp/ldexp/modf exact; sin/cos/exp/log/atan/atan2/exp2/log2/log10/pow within 1 ulp (pow, log2, log10 and exp2 use double-double and are exact for exact cases such as pow(10, 22) and log10(1000)); tan, asin, acos, log1p and the hyperbolics within 2-3 ulp. Trigonometry reduces huge arguments exactly (Payne-Hanek). Float functions evaluate the double function and round. No x87 and no FMA instructions are used.
    • strtod is correctly rounded (19 significant digits are kept; the scaling is done in double-double), including subnormals and hex floats.
    • printf is stb_sprintf: exact to about 16 significant digits (%.17g may differ from glibc in the last digit), ties round half up (%.0f of 2.5 is "3"), %p prints 16 hex digits without 0x. Floats (%.9g) round-trip.
    • sscanf: %d %i %u %o %x %X %c %s %[set] %e %f %g %a %p %n %%, widths, *, hh h l ll j z t L. No fscanf.
    • FILE: one 4 KiB buffer per file; "w" deletes and re-creates the file (MinimaFS writes never shorten a file); data written reaches the disk when the file is closed (or at exit). FILE objects are not locked.
    • errno is one variable for the whole program (no TLS on Minimal-OS); localtime is UTC; no locales, no wide characters, no signals, no setjmp.

    The editor on Minimal-OS

    mk/editor_os.mk builds build/os/bin/farcade-editor.run from mk/editor.mk's IMGUI_SRC, CORE_SRC, EDITOR_SRC, the embedded fonts, editor/platform/platform_minimalos.cpp and editor/main_os.cpp. It prints FE EDITOR READY after the first frame and the average frame time every 60 frames; --frames N quits after N frames (FE EDITOR DONE).

    Tests

    • make test runs build/host/bin/rt_math_test and rt_text_test: the runtime's math, strtod/strtol, sscanf and snprintf sources compiled for the host, every defined symbol renamed to fe_<name> with objcopy, compared with glibc (special values, random arguments over wide ranges, ImGui's own sscanf formats).
    • tests/os/imgui_smoke (build/os/bin/imgui_smoke.run): libm and text checks against values from the PC, FILE I/O, malloc/realloc/aligned_alloc from two threads, a static constructor, ImGui with docking, the default font and Inter loaded from 0:/programs/, five frames of the demo window, one ImGuizmo::Manipulate, the draw data, the ini round trip in memory and on disk. Prints FE SMOKE PASS.

    Scene files

    The editor saves a scene as a .fscene file: plain text, one value per line, written and read by editor/src/scene_io.{h,cpp}. Two objects from the demo scene, as the editor saves them:

    On this pageReading rulesIn the editorUnsaved changes, undo and redoModels in scenes
    farcade-scene 1
next_id 14

object 4
  name "Pillar"
  kind mesh
  position 2.5999999 1 1.60000002
  rotation 0 0 0 1
  scale 0.600000024 2 0.600000024
  mesh cylinder
  color 0.75 0.75999999 0.800000012
  roughness 0.300000012
  metallic 0.899999976
  unlit false
  cast_shadows true
  module collider3d
    shape Cylinder
    mode Collision
    center 0 0 0
    size 1 1 1
    radius 0.600000024
    height 1
    friction 0.5
    bounciness 0
    layer 1
  end
end

object 6
  name "Lamp"
  kind mesh
  parent 4
  position 0 0.649999976 0
  rotation 0 0 0 1
  scale 0.600000024 0.150000006 0.600000024
  mesh sphere
  color 0.980000019 0.850000024 0.449999988
  roughness 0.600000024
  metallic 0
  unlit false
  cast_shadows true
  script "scripts/lamp.lua"
    prop follow object 3
    prop threshold number 6 0 0
  end
end
    • The header farcade-scene <version> comes first. A file from a newer version is refused.
    • Objects keep their ids. Parents (parent) and script inputs that link to objects (prop <name> object <id>) refer to them. next_id makes sure new objects never reuse an id.
    • Modules are written field by field, using the same reflection tables as the Inspector and Lua (engine/scene/modules.h). Enum values are written by name.
    • Script inputs store their value. List inputs store the chosen text and the choices.
    • Floats are written with 9 significant digits, so they read back exactly.
    • Paths inside the project are stored relative to it. This covers textures, models, scripts and audio.

    Reading rules

    • Unknown names are skipped and counted. A name can be unknown at any level: an object line, a module, or a module field. The editor logs how many lines were skipped and the first one.
    • Missing values keep their defaults. A field added later therefore reads back as its default from an older file.
    • These files are refused: - a file without the header; - an object id used twice; - a file that ends inside an object.

    The open scene is left unchanged.

    • Broken links are cleaned up: - a parent or object link to a missing id is cleared; - parent loops are cut.
    • More than one current object of a kind (camera, sky, ...): the first one in the file keeps the flag.

    In the editor

    ActionEffect
    File > Save scene (Ctrl+S)Saves to the open file. If the scene was never saved, it goes to scenes/main.fscene.
    File > Save scene as...Asks for a name and saves to scenes/<name>.fscene.
    Double-click a .fscene in FilesOpens it.
    File > New sceneEmpties the scene.
    • Saving during Play writes the scene as it was before Play.
    • Opening a scene stops Play first.
    • Script inputs after opening: they are read from the script files again, and the saved values are kept.
    • The title bar shows the project and the open scene.

    Unsaved changes, undo and redo

    Unsaved changes. New scene, opening a scene (from Files) and Quit ask first when the scene differs from its last save, open or new. The choices are Save, Don't save and Cancel. Save writes the open file first; if writing fails, nothing else happens.

    Undo and redo:

    ActionKeys
    UndoCtrl+Z, or Edit > Undo
    RedoCtrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z, or Edit > Redo

    How it works:

    • Snapshots. The history keeps whole-scene snapshots: the scene file text, without next_id and the hierarchy's folding.
    • When a snapshot is taken. After a click, key or text input, once no mouse button is down and no field is being edited, and only if the scene changed. So a gizmo drag or a slider drag is one step.
    • Size. Up to 100 steps.
    • What is kept on undo. The selection (where the objects still exist) and the hierarchy's folding. Ids are never reused.
    • Play. There is no undo while playing. Play itself adds no steps, since Stop puts the scene back.

    On Minimal-OS, farcade-editor.run --scene-test saves the demo scene twice, opens it again and prints FE SCENE PASS <objects> <bytes> when it comes back unchanged.

    Models in scenes

    An object with mesh model and a model "<path>.mof" line shows an imported model. .mof files are read through the VFS (engine/core/vfs.h): plain files under the project in the editor, the package in an exported game. A file that cannot be read shows as a cube.

    Importing: Create > Import model... (a path to a .gltf, .glb or .obj), the Files panel's "Import as model" (right click, or double-click the file), and dropping such a file on the viewport or an object all convert it with the engine's importers to a .mof next to the source and use that. The converter is model_convert_file (editor/src/model_import.h).

    What is drawn (editor/src/model_cache.h): every mesh instance of the node tree, one part per submesh, in the bind pose with the node transforms applied. FarcadeGL draws a part with its material's base color factor (the object's color tints it; the default grey is neutral) and its base color texture (PNG, JPEG or raw RGBA8 stored in the .mof, mip 0) with the file's UVs. The CPU preview draws the merged mesh in one color. Bounds, picking, framing and Mesh colliders use the real mesh.

    For other code (an Animator module, say):

    const fe::Model* m = fe::Scene::model_for(object);   // null unless a Model object whose file loaded
m->mesh                  // MeshData: all parts merged (triangle list)
m->parts[i]              // positions, normals, uvs (triangle lists, bind pose), color, texture,
                         //   mesh_index / submesh_index / material / node into m->mof
m->mof                   // the mof_file view: bones (inverse bind matrices), nodes,
                         //   mof_mesh_joints() / mof_mesh_weights() skin streams, materials, textures

    The pointers stay valid until model_cache_clear() (called by Play, Import and when a model file is assigned). To pose a skinned model, compute the bone matrices from m->mof.bones, skin the .mof vertex streams (mof_mesh_positions plus joints and weights of parts[i].mesh_index) and draw the result as your own gfx::DrawItems; the parts are the bind pose. .mof carries no animation clips yet.

    PreviousThe Minimal-OS runtimeNextScripts on objects

    Edit this page on GitHub

    Scripts on objects

    An object can hold several scripts (up to 6), which run in the order the Inspector lists them. A script declares inputs that the Inspector shows and the scene saves for each object, so the same door.lua can sit on two doors with different settings. An object input links to another object, and through that link a script reaches the other object's scripts. That is how scripts on different objects work together.

    Status: scripts run. Press Play and every script on every object starts in the Lua 5.4 runtime (engine/script/runtime.h), with its inputs and object links. Scripts run before the physics step each frame. Trigger and collision events reach them, and print and errors (with file:line) go to the Console. Stop puts the scene back. Tested on the PC (script_tests, the editor tests) and on Minimal-OS (script_smoke).

    On this pageDeclaring inputsWhen the file changesIn the editorAt run time

    Declaring inputs

    Inputs are declared in comments, so the editor reads them without running Lua. One per line, anywhere in the file:

    -- @prop speed   number = 5  range 0 20   -- a slider from 0 to 20
-- @prop gain    number = 1.5             -- a number field (drag to change)
-- @prop label   text   = "Front door"    -- quoted, or the rest of the line
-- @prop mode    list(closed, open, locked) = locked
-- @prop active  toggle = true            -- true/false, on/off, yes/no
-- @prop target  object                   -- a link to another object
-- @prop skin    file                     -- any project file; drag one onto the slot
    TypeInspectorDefaultLua value
    number (float, int)drag field, or a slider with range a b= 5 (0)number
    text (string)text field (63 bytes)= "..." or bare words ("")string
    toggle (bool)switch= true / false (false)boolean
    list(a, b, ...)drop-down, up to 8 choices= b (the first)the chosen string
    objectobject picker; drop a Hierarchy row on itnoneobject handle or nil
    file (asset)file slot; drop a file from the Files panel= "assets/image.png" or emptypath string (project paths save relative)

    Rules:

    • A script can declare up to 12 inputs.
    • A line that does not parse is skipped and the console says so. Examples: an unknown type, an empty list, a default that is not one of the choices, a name used twice.
    • Text after a declaration must be a -- comment.

    When the file changes

    The editor reads the declarations in three cases:

    • when a script is added;
    • when its ⟳ button is pressed;
    • when Play starts.

    Inputs are matched by name:

    • An input still declared with the same type keeps the value set in the editor. A number is clamped into a new range, and a list choice is found again by its text.
    • New inputs get their defaults.
    • Inputs that are gone are dropped.
    • An input whose type changed starts again from its default.
    • If the file cannot be read, the inputs keep their values and the script shows "missing file".

    In the editor

    • Adding a script: drop a script on an object (in the viewport or the Hierarchy) or on Add script in the Inspector. You can also click Add script to pick from the project's scripts (the project folder and scripts/). Each drop adds a script; the same file may be added more than once.
    • Each script's section: open the file in the editor, read the inputs again, move the script earlier, or remove it. Then come its inputs.
    • Object inputs: the picker shows how many scripts each object has. Hovering a linked object lists its scripts, and the arrow button selects it. The Inspector also says how many script inputs link to the selected object.
    • Duplicating: a link that points inside the copied tree goes to the copy. A switch duplicated together with its door gets its own door. Links to objects outside the copied tree stay as they were.
    • Deleting: removing an object clears every link to it.
    • Play and Stop: Stop puts all inputs back as they were before Play.

    At run time

    Each script on each object gets its own instance table self. Its inputs are fields of self, self.object is the object it sits on and self.name is the script's name ("door"). The script file runs once per instance, in an environment of its own: the functions and globals it defines belong to that instance, and self falls back to them, so another script can call door:open().

    -- switch.lua
-- @prop door object
-- @prop mode list(press, hold) = press

function on_event(self, name)
  if name ~= "use" or not self.door then return end
  local d = self.door:script("door")      -- the door's door.lua instance
  if d and not d.locked then
    d:open()                              -- call a function defined in door.lua
  end
  self.door:send("used_by", self.object)  -- every script on the door gets on_used_by
end
    -- door.lua
-- @prop speed number = 2 range 0 5
-- @prop locked toggle = false

function open(self) self.opening = true end
function on_used_by(self, who) print(who.name .. " used me") end

    Callbacks

    All optional, self first. Scripts on one object run in Inspector order each frame, objects in the order their instances were added (Hierarchy order).

    FunctionWhen
    on_start(self)once, before the first on_update; every on_start of a frame runs before any on_update (a script added later starts on the next frame)
    on_update(self, dt)every frame (ECS phase Update)
    on_<name>(self, ...)obj:send("<name>", ...) or fe.broadcast("<name>", ...)
    on_event(self, name, ...)the same events, after on_<name>; an event called event only reaches on_event
    on_trigger_enter(self, other), on_trigger_exit(self, other)an object entered or left a trigger collider on this object
    on_collision(self, other)this object's body hit another one (called on both objects)

    Inputs: Number is a number (an integral value is a Lua integer), Text a string, Toggle a boolean, List the chosen string, Object a handle or nil, and File a path string. Project paths are saved relative to the project. A File input can be used to assign an asset to any object with a mesh:

    -- @prop target object
-- @prop skin file
function on_start(self)
  if self.target then self.target.material.texture = self.skin end
end

    What a script stores in self stays there.

    Input

    Keyboard and mouse, in the editor's Play (over the viewport) and in the player:

    fe.key_down(name)true while the key is held
    fe.key_pressed(name), fe.key_released(name)true during the update after the key went down / up
    fe.mouse_x(), fe.mouse_y()the pointer, in pixels of the game's view
    fe.mouse_down(b), fe.mouse_pressed(b)button 0 left, 1 right, 2 middle
    fe.mouse_wheel()scroll since the last update

    Key names: "a" to "z", "0" to "9", "space", "enter", "escape", "tab", "backspace", "left", "right", "up", "down", "shift", "ctrl", "alt", "f1" to "f12", "pageup", "pagedown", "home", "end", "insert", "delete".

    Objects

    self.object, other in the collision callbacks, fe.find, obj.parent and obj:children() give handles. One handle exists per object, so == and using a handle as a table key work.

    obj.nameread/write; renaming to a sibling's name is an error
    obj.position, obj.rotation, obj.scalelocal, read/write. rotation is Euler degrees (X, then Y, then Z, like the Inspector); scale also takes a number
    obj.world_positionread only, as of the last transform update (the end of the previous frame)
    obj.parenthandle or nil
    obj:children()array of handles (order unspecified)
    obj:script(name)self of the first script on obj called name ("door" or "door.lua"), or nil
    obj:scripts()array of all their self
    obj:send(event, ...)delivers right away, inside the call
    obj:move(dx, dy, dz)adds to position (also obj:move(vec3))
    obj:destroy()a request: the object and its children are destroyed when the outermost callback returns. The handle reads alive == false from then on, and every other access raises "the object no longer exists"
    obj.alivefalse once destroyed
    obj.materialthe look of a mesh object, or nil for objects without a mesh (see below)
    obj.<module>rigidbody3d, collider3d, character_controller3d, listener, audio_stream, audio_sampler, light, particles, joint3d, animator, force_field, spawner, reverb_zone, billboard, text3d, camera, skylight, sky, post_process (see modules.md; methods such as obj.particles:emit(10), obj.animator:play("walk", 0.3), obj.spawner:spawn(), obj.joint3d:snap() — break is a Lua keyword): the module, or nil if the object has none

    A module's fields read and write through the ECS (World::get_field / set_field): numbers are clamped to the field's range, enums are their name strings (light.type == "Spot"), colors and vectors are vec3. Writing an unknown field or a value of the wrong type raises an error that names the module and the field. camera.current = true goes through the one-current rule; inside a frame the world applies that rule at the end of the Update phase, so fe.current("camera") may still return the old camera until then (from trigger_enter & co., called outside a frame, it is immediate).

    obj.material reads and writes the object's look, the same settings as the Inspector's Look section:

    FieldTypeNotes
    colorvec3
    roughnessnumberclamped to 0..1
    metallicnumberclamped to 0..1
    unlittrue / false
    cast_shadowstrue / false
    visibletrue / false
    texturefile path stringImage file path; assign "" to clear
    shaderfile path stringCombined .fshader shader path; assign "" to clear
    local m = self.object.material
m.metallic = 1
m.roughness = 0.2
m.color = fe.vec3(1, 0.8, 0.3)
m.texture = self.skin
    • Roughness, metal and shadows show only with FarcadeGL's GPU tier. Color, unlit and visible show with every renderer. Texture and custom shader assignments are rendered by FarcadeGL's base renderer; while any such material is visible, the advanced GPU-tier effects are not run for that frame.
    • Changes made in Play are visible in the editor while playing and are put back on Stop, like everything else.
    • A wrong type or an unknown field raises an error naming the field.
    • obj.material itself is read only: change its fields instead.

    Positions, rotations and colors come back as new vec3 values: assign the changed vector (obj.position = obj.position + v), changing .x of the copy does nothing.

    vec3

    fe.vec3(x, y, z) (also vec3(...), and fe.vec3(t) from a table) is a table with .x .y .z and a metatable: +, -, * (by a number, or component-wise by another vec3), / (by a number), unary -, ==, tostring, v:length(), v:normalized(), v:dot(w), v:cross(w), fe.dot(a, b), fe.cross(a, b). Wherever a vec3 is assigned you can also give {x=, y=, z=} or {1, 2, 3}.

    The fe library

    fe.find(name)the root object called name, else the match nearest the roots; nil if none
    fe.current(module)the current camera/sky/skylight/post_process/listener object, or nil
    fe.broadcast(event, ...)on_<event> and on_event on every script instance
    fe.time()seconds since the runtime started
    fe.status(text [, progress])shows a line (and a bar when progress, 0..1, is given; without it the bar moves on its own) over the game, in the player and in Play; fe.status() hides it. For loading screens and "waiting for ..." messages; it is drawn together with FarcadeGL's "Compiling shaders" bar
    fe.dtthe dt of the frame being run
    fe.log(...), print(...)to the console (Info), arguments as text separated by tabs
    fe.warn(...), fe.error(...)to the console as Warning / Error

    Scripts see the base functions (pairs, pcall, setmetatable, ...), coroutine, table, string, math and utf8. There is no io, os, package, debug, require, dofile, loadfile or load, and collectgarbage only knows "collect", "count" and "step". Globals a script sets are its instance's own, they are not shared with other scripts.

    Errors

    Errors at load or run time are logged as path:line: message plus a traceback. An instance that fails at run time gets no more callbacks (the others keep running); one that fails to load is not added. A destroyed object's scripts never run again.

    Running scripts from C++

    World world; world.init();
ScriptRuntime scripts; scripts.init(&world, host);       // adds its systems to the world
int id = scripts.add_instance(entity, "scripts/door.lua", text, size, props, nprops, linked_entities);
// each frame: world.progress(dt);  (physics calls scripts.trigger_enter/exit, collision)

    The interpreter is Lua 5.4.7 (external/lua, unmodified) with a generational garbage collector, built for the host and for Minimal-OS (about 200 KB of code); the engine's own setjmp/longjmp shim and a C-locale stub fill the gaps of the Minimal-OS C runtime (engine/script/lua_os_compat.c, engine/script/os_include). mk/script.mk defines LUA_SRC and SCRIPT_SRC.

    Not done: a limit on how long one callback may run (an endless loop in a script hangs the frame).

    Documentation updates

    What's New?

    A guide to recently added and expanded documentation. Follow a link to read the new material in context.

    NewtShooter: walkers, sprinting and grapple kicks

    The guide now documents the walker, a two-legged robot you climb, break into through its roof hatch and destroy from the inside; sprinting on Shift (tap it to dash); the grapple kick; and the larger arena.

    The guide now covers the new tutorial (skip any step with Enter, replay it from the title screen) and the Sky Marathon, a 1.2 km course with 29 checkpoints.

    A new NewtShooter guide covers the physics parkour shooter on this site: the controls, every movement technique with its numbers, slow motion, the weapons and enemies, scoring and style bonuses, the Sky Trial course and how the renderer, physics and soundtrack work.

    New game: Lanternfall

    Lanternfall's guide covers the eight-area platform adventure, trap-dodging, monster battles and keyboard controls.

    The Images and video guide now covers the .vid format, its converter commands and file layout, playback, and decoding. Start with making media files, then read the video layout and hardware decoding sections.

    GPU and 3D graphics

    The GPU and 3D guide explains GPU adapters, the FGPU rendering pipeline and shader support. The SDK references add details for FarcadeGL and the FGSL shading language.

    Storage and installation

    Find the expanded disk and file-system material in Storage and packages, including partitions, MinimaFS and NVMe. The Installing guide covers creating a bootable disk and notes for real hardware.

    NewtShooter

    A first-person shooter where everything obeys F = m·a, including you. It mixes physics, parkour movement and gunplay, and runs from a single HTML file with no libraries: its own WebGL2 renderer, rigid-body physics, movement controller and synthesized sound.

    Play it hereOpen in its own tab
    On this pageGetting startedTutorialControlsMovementSlow motionWeaponsEnemiesArena and scoringThe coursesSettings and savesHow it works

    Getting started

    Open the game, pick a mode and the game captures the mouse. Esc releases it and pauses. It needs a keyboard and mouse and a browser with WebGL2 (current Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari).

    • Tutorial: a guided training hall that teaches one move or weapon per step. The game offers it the first time you pick a mode.
    • Arena: survive waves of drones in Inertia Hall, a 220 m walled test chamber: a central hall with a tower, ramps, pillars and launch pads, ringed by an outer yard where walkers roam, with ramps up to the corner platforms and plenty of loose crates and steel balls.
    • Sky Trial: a short parkour time trial over floating platforms, with a hint for each section.
    • Marathon: the long course, 1.2 km of mixed parkour with 29 checkpoints.

    Tutorial

    The tutorial takes place in the Training Hall, a long walled corridor with one station per move. A beam of light marks the next station and the panel at the bottom says what to do. A step completes when you actually do the move: walk, jump, double jump, slide, wall-run, wall jump, climb and mantle, high jump, dash, grapple, lean, kick, shoot three targets, blast-jump with the shotgun, fire a gravity well, slow time, and finally shoot down a live drone (its orbs don't hurt you here).

    • Skip a step: press Enter. You are moved to the start of the next station, so you can never get stuck behind a wall.
    • Skip the whole tutorial: press Esc and choose Skip tutorial, or answer Skip it when the game offers the tutorial.
    • Replay it: the Tutorial button on the title screen, or Replay tutorial on its results screen.

    The first time you pick Arena, Sky Trial or Marathon, the game asks whether you want the tutorial first. Finishing or skipping it once stops the question.

    Controls

    InputAction
    W A S DRun
    SpaceJump; again in the air to double jump; near a wall to wall jump
    CCrouch; while running, slide; while standing still, charge a high jump
    ShiftHold to sprint; tap to dash in the direction you are moving
    V or middle mouse (hold)Grapple
    FKick
    Q / E (hold)Lean left / right to tilt and peek around cover
    GSlow motion on or off
    Left mouseFire
    Right mouseZoom (rifle); detonate gravity wells early (launcher)
    1 2 3, wheelSwitch weapon; X swaps to the last one
    RReload
    EscPause
    EnterSkip the current tutorial step

    Movement

    You run at 9.6 m/s, or sprint at 13.5 m/s while you hold Shift and move forward. Friction only bites hard at normal speed; above it you keep momentum for a while, and in the air nothing slows you down, so speed you build stays with you. Jumping on the frame you land skips friction entirely (bunny hopping), and air strafing works.

    MoveHowWhat it does
    Double jumpSpace in the air8.6 m/s upward and turns you towards the keys you hold. Landing, a wall-run, a climb or the grapple gives it back.
    SlideC while running faster than 6.2 m/sAdds 4.5 m/s (once every 1.15 s) and glides with little friction. Down a slope gravity speeds you up: the Sky Trial ramp takes you from 11 to about 22 m/s. Land holding C to keep sliding.
    Slide jumpSpace while slidingKeeps the slide's speed and adds a little more.
    Wall-runJump at a wall while moving along it, holding WRuns along any wall at 10 m/s or more for up to 2.2 s, sinking slowly. Space leaps off it, away and upward; C drops off. A new wall resets your double jump.
    Wall jumpSpace next to a wall in the airKicks you off the wall without needing a wall-run.
    ClimbRun straight at a wall, hold W and SpaceRuns up the wall at 7.4 m/s for about 0.6 s, once per jump. Space again turns it into a jump backwards off the wall.
    MantleHold W at a ledgePulls you onto a ledge up to 1.8 m above your feet (2.2 m while climbing) when you would otherwise fall short.
    High jumpHold C standing still, then SpaceCharges for 0.8 s, up to 19.5 m/s: about 8 m straight up.
    SprintHold Shift while moving forwardRaises your running speed from 9.6 to 13.5 m/s.
    DashTap ShiftSets your speed to at least 21.5 m/s in the direction you move (or look). Two charges, 1.45 s each to refill.
    GrappleHold V or middle mouse, aiming at a surface up to 62 m awayReels you in while gravity drops to 40%, with a top speed of 25 m/s, and lets go when you arrive or swing past. Release to fly; Space on the rope launches you upward. Aimed at a drone or warden (it snaps onto one near your crosshair; the dot turns orange), it pulls you to the enemy and holds it in the air. Aimed at a walker it hooks onto the hull and follows it. Aimed at a crate or a roller it yanks that to you.
    Grapple kickGrapple a drone, then F on the rope or within a second of arrivingKills a drone instantly, takes half a warden's health, and briefly slows time.
    KickFLaunches props, hurts and stuns enemies (much harder while sliding) and bats enemy orbs back. Kick a wall in mid-air to push yourself off it.
    LeanHold Q or ETilts your head and moves your eyes up to 0.6 m sideways to peek and shoot around cover, never through walls.
    Launch padsStep on a glowing padThrow you high and forward. Bodies and rolling enemies get thrown too.
    Blast jumpFire the shotgun at your feet in mid-air, or stand near your own gravity wellRecoil and blasts push you; you never take damage from your own weapons.

    Slow motion

    G slows the world to 28% while you move at about 60%, so you are relatively twice as fast as everything else. Orbs, lasers and wrecking balls become easy to read, and your aim stays at full speed. A full meter lasts 6 s. It refills over 15 s after a short pause, and every kill adds 10%. The picture shifts to a cool, desaturated grade and the sound gets muffled while it is on.

    Weapons

    WeaponAmmoDetails
    Newton-9 impulse rifle 132 rounds, 1.25 s reloadAutomatic, about 11 shots a second, 14 damage. Every hit pushes what it hits. Hitting a drone's or warden's glowing core doubles the damage. Right mouse zooms and tightens the spread.
    Momentum scattergun 26 shells, loaded one at a time11 pellets of 9.5 damage with a heavy shove. Firing pushes you backwards at 11.5 m/s (less on the ground unless you aim down), which makes it a movement tool too. Firing interrupts a reload.
    Singularity launcher 33 charges, one back every 4.2 sLobs a shot that falls under gravity and opens a gravity well where it lands. For 1.35 s the well pulls in drones, crates, debris, orbs and (gently) you within 11 m, then bursts for up to 120 damage within 7.5 m and throws everything outward. Right mouse detonates early.

    Physics does damage too. A crate, ball or chunk of debris that hits an enemy faster than 7.5 m/s hurts it in proportion to its mass and speed, and an enemy knocked into a wall hard enough takes damage from the impact.

    Enemies

    EnemyHealthBehaviour
    Drone45Circles you at range and fires slow orange orbs that lead your movement. Its eye flashes red just before it shoots. Shoot orbs down or kick them back.
    Roller35A rolling physics ball that chases you, hops onto ledges, and arms itself when it gets within 2.5 m. It explodes when it dies, however it dies, hurting anything nearby, other enemies included.
    WalkerControl panel: 170A slow, towering two-legged robot (its hull rides about 6 m up on long chicken-walker legs) with a hollow hull, from wave 3 on every other wave. Its armour shrugs off everything from outside; the only weak spot is the control panel inside. Climb the ladder on its back (walk into it holding W or Space; S climbs down, A/D steps off), or grapple up. On the roof, look down at the hatch and kick it in with F, drop inside and shoot the panel, or put a gravity well inside. A second ladder under the hatch gets you back out. The walker holds still while you are on it, climbing it or in the air next to it. You can stand on its roof and ride it. Two side lasers cover the 65° either side of where it faces; they track you slowly for 2 s and do 42 damage each, and get behind it and they can't hit you. A miss sets the ground on fire, and fire spreads and burns for about 15 health a second. It can't aim at you while you are on or inside it. Don't hide underneath, though: it shuffles to put a foot on you, and a stomp does 35 damage. When the panel goes, the walker blows apart into physics wreckage.
    Warden230A heavy flyer that stops, tracks you with a thin red laser for 1.45 s, locks for 0.34 s (the beam flickers) and fires for 26 damage. Move out of the line once it locks. A kick, grapple yank or blast that stuns it cancels the shot.

    From wave 4 on, enemies get 7% more health each wave. Destroyed enemies break into physics debris you can kick around.

    Arena and scoring

    Wave n brings 2 + n drones (up to 13), about 1.2 × n rollers (up to 10) and a warden for every two waves after the first (up to 4), and a walker on wave 3 and every odd wave after it (two from wave 9). Clearing a wave scores 250 × the wave number and restores 25 health. Health also regenerates 4 s after you were last hit, and drones and wardens sometimes drop health orbs worth 15.

    Kills score 100 (drone), 75 (roller), 250 (warden) or 1000 (walker), plus style bonuses for how you got them. Each kill within 4 s of the last raises a chain multiplier by 0.15, up to ×4.

    StyleBonusWhen
    Newton's law150Killed by an impact: a thrown crate, debris, or a wall
    Return to sender150Killed by its own orb, kicked back
    Chain reaction120Killed by an exploding roller
    Boot / Slide kick120Killed by a kick
    Event horizon100Killed by a gravity well
    Grapple kick250Killed by a kick after grappling to it
    Get over here100Killed by a grapple yank
    Wall runner, Swinger, Slide kill, Airborne100, 100, 75, 60You were wall-running, on the rope, sliding, or in the air
    Speed demon80You were moving faster than 20 m/s
    Long shot80A gun kill from more than 45 m
    Close call60You had less than 25 health
    Bullet time40Slow motion was on
    Core hit40The last hit was on the glowing core
    Double, triple, quad, mega kill100 per extra killKills less than 0.7 s apart

    Shooting down an orb scores 25, kicking one back 120 and kicking in a walker's hatch 100. The results screen shows your score, wave, kills, top speed, time survived and the style that earned you the most.

    The courses

    Both courses run in the sky over floating platforms. The clock starts when you first move and keeps real time, so slow motion is no shortcut. Fall off and you reappear at the last checkpoint; targets you already hit stay hit.

    Sky Trial

    The Sky Trial is a line of platforms in the sky, about 450 m long, in twelve sections: gaps, a slide under barriers and down a ramp, a wall-run, a wall-to-wall chain, a climb, a high jump, a grapple swing, a dash gap, a launch pad, a gate that opens when you shoot five targets, a bridge swept by wrecking balls (a good place for slow motion) and a last wall you blast-jump or grapple up. The orange arch at the top is the finish.

    Finish in 70 s for gold, 95 s for silver or 130 s for bronze.

    Marathon

    The Sky Marathon is the long one: 1.2 km in 28 sections, with a checkpoint after each (29 in all). It strings together every kind of section from the Sky Trial plus three new ones: narrow zig-zag beams, rising blocks to jump up, and a 20 m drop where you steer your fall onto the landing. Several kinds come back later in a new order, and the path climbs and falls between about 8 m below and 30 m above the start. A short hint appears the first time you meet each kind of section. The layout is the same every time, so you can learn it. Finish in 3:30 for gold, 4:50 for silver or 6:40 for bronze.

    Settings and saves

    Settings has mouse sensitivity, field of view (75–120°, measured horizontally on a 16:9 screen; it widens a little more at speed), sound and music volume, graphics quality and inverted mouse Y. High renders at up to 1.5× pixel density with a 2048 × 2048 shadow map; Fast renders at 0.75× with a 1024 × 1024 one. Settings together with your best arena score, both best course times and whether you have seen the tutorial, are kept in this browser's local storage under newtshooter-settings and newtshooter-best.

    How it works

    Everything lives in games/newtshooter/index.html, about 200 KB of HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The only thing it loads from elsewhere is its fonts.

    • Rendering: WebGL2. The level is one merged mesh of boxes and ramps with procedural lab-panel, wall-run and tech materials drawn in the fragment shader. Moving objects are instanced cubes and spheres. A directional shadow map follows the camera with 3 × 3 filtered samples, then ACES tone mapping, distance fog, a gradient sky and additive glow effects. The weapon is drawn in a second pass with its own field of view.
    • Physics: rigid boxes and spheres with real rotation and inertia. Box corners and spheres collide with the static world; bodies collide with each other through corner-in-box and sphere tests. Contacts are solved with sequential impulses with friction and restitution, and resting bodies go to sleep. Everything steps at 120 Hz, with the world and the player on separate clocks so slow motion can scale them differently.
    • Player: a box collider moved one axis at a time against boxes and ramps, with step-up, ground snapping on slopes (velocity follows the slope, so running up a ramp and off its end launches you), coyote time and jump buffering.
    • Sound: synthesized with Web Audio and positioned by distance and stereo pan. The soundtrack, Terminal Velocity, is a 140 BPM electro track in A minor generated live: kick, claps, hats, a sidechained rolling bass, a supersaw hook through a dotted-eighth echo, chord stabs, pads, arpeggios, risers and crashes. It is built from 8-bar intro, build, drop and breakdown sections and follows the game: drops while enemies are up, breakdowns between waves, a calmer loop on the title screen. Music is scheduled 0.6 s ahead on its own timer so frame hitches don't interrupt it. Sound effects have a voice budget, so minor sounds such as impacts and footsteps are skipped when the mix is crowded. If the browser or the system suspends audio, the game resumes it.

    The website embeds the game in an iframe that loads only when you press Start and unloads when you leave the page. Pointer lock and fullscreen work inside it.

    Lanternfall

    A platform adventure: cross eight areas, avoid traps and fight monsters. Winning fights levels you up.

    Play it hereOpen in its own tab

    Getting started

    Follow the road to the end. Move through each area, dodge its traps and touch monsters to begin a battle. Win fights to level up and stay alive.

    Operating system · C, x86 Assembly · GPL-3.0

    Minimal-OS

    An operating system for x86_64 written from scratch in C and assembly. It boots through GRUB on BIOS and UEFI, brings up every CPU core, mounts its own file system, starts services, runs user programs in ring 3, and can install itself onto a disk.

    SourceDownload an ISODocumentation

    What is inside

    LayerHighlights
    BootMultiboot2 on BIOS and UEFI, long-mode transition, more than 1 GiB of RAM, a memory tester and a no-disk boot entry in the GRUB menu
    KernelPage and heap allocators, processes and threads, per-CPU run queues with three priority levels, SMP spinlocks
    StorageAHCI and NVMe, MBR and GPT partitions, MinimaFS volumes up to 16 TiB, several mounted drives, .mpkg packages with LZSS compression
    HardwarePCI, framebuffer graphics, UHCI/OHCI and xHCI (USB 3) keyboards and mice, PS/2, AC'97 audio, RTL8139
    GPU and 3DAdapters with VRAM (NVIDIA Pascal/Turing, QEMU/Bochs), write-combining, the FGPU command processor with a 3D pipeline and a shader machine, SYS_GPU; NVIDIA hardware rendering in progress
    InstallThe install command writes a GPT or MBR disk that boots by itself on BIOS and UEFI
    NetworkEthernet, ARP, IPv4, UDP, DHCP, DNS, TCP, and a TLS 1.3 client (TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, X25519)
    User space.run programs, a syscall ABI with a privilege table, .service files, the window and input syscalls mosWM uses

    Try it

    Download an ISO from the releases page, create a disk image, and start QEMU:

    fallocate -l 256M sata256.img
qemu-system-x86_64 -cdrom kernel.iso -m 1024M -boot d -usb -device usb-kbd \
  -device ahci,id=ahci -drive id=disk0,file=sata256.img,if=none,format=raw \
  -device ide-hd,drive=disk0,bus=ahci.0

    At the terminal, format prepares the system disk and help lists every command, a category at a time. The build guide covers compiling from source; make run also attaches an empty disk you can try the installer on.

    Install it on a disk

    disks                      # find the target disk
install sata1              # asks for confirmation, then erases sata1
install nvme0 --mbr --yes  # MBR instead of GPT, no question

    The disk boots on BIOS and UEFI PCs. MOSdesk has an Installer app that does the same with a few clicks; see Installing to a disk.

    Toolchain · C, C++ · v1.1

    Minimal-OS SDK

    Everything needed to write programs for Minimal-OS on a Linux machine: freestanding headers, a tiny C runtime, a linker script, and scripts that build a .run program or a .slib library bundle.

    SourceTry it in Run StudioFunction referenceSyscall reference

    Install

    ./install-toolchain.sh     # compiler and linker (Debian/Ubuntu)
./install.sh               # puts MSDK / msdk on your PATH

    Build a program

    msdk examples/hello.c              # -> hello.run
msdk examples/hello.cpp            # C++ works the same way
msdk programs --main main.cpp      # a project folder
msdk --slib libraries/math         # a shared-library bundle

    Import the .run into MinimaFS and start it from the terminal with run 0:/programs/hello.run.

    A first program

    #include "minimalos.h"
#include "stdio.h"

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    printf("hello from user space, %d argument(s)\n", argc);
    return 0;
}

    Headers

    HeaderProvides
    minimalos.hCore syscalls: write, exit, sleep, uptime, files, directories, packages, mos_exec, cleanup callbacks
    stdio.h / iostreamprintf (%s %c %d %i %u %x %X %ld %lu %%) and std::cout, both header-only
    stdlib.hmalloc, calloc, realloc, free, mos_random_bytes, atoi
    string.hstrlen, strcmp, strstr, … and constant-time mos_memeq_ct
    window.hThe mosWM window API: create, present, events, styles, flags
    easyui.hWidgets in the MOSdesk theme: buttons, sliders, text inputs, toggles, dropdowns, lists
    font.hSmooth Inter text in any pixel buffer, with the bitmap font as fallback
    farcadegl.h / fglsl.hFarcadeGL 3D and its FGSL shader compiler
    net.hTCP, UDP, DNS, status, polling, and TLS handles
    graphics.hFramebuffer drawing: shapes, text, blits
    storage.hDisks and partitions, and root commands for tools like the installer

    The .run format

    A .run is a single file, so copying it into MinimaFS never needs a directory tree. It holds a MINIRUN1 header, an entry table and the payloads:

    FieldLayout
    Headerchar magic[8] = "MINIRUN1", u32 version = 1, u32 count
    Entry × countchar name[64], u32 offset, u32 size
    Payloadsmain.elf, then every file under Resources/

    main.elf must be an x86_64 ELF64 position-independent executable linked at address 0 with no external symbols; the loader applies only R_X86_64_RELATIVE relocations. The SDK's link.ld and crt0.c take care of that.

    .slib bundles

    --slib produces a MINISLIB1 bundle with library.elf, an exports.txt of global symbols, and the public headers. Minimal-OS does not load shared libraries at run time yet; bundles are distribution artifacts, like 0:/etc/minimaSSL.slib.

    Library · C · freestanding

    MinimaSSL

    A deliberately small cryptography library with an OpenSSL-shaped API. It needs no libc on Minimal-OS, so the same sources link into the kernel's TLS 1.3 client and into user programs such as the dlr package manager.

    SourceTLS in Minimal-OS

    What it implements

    HeaderAPI
    openssl/sha.hSHA256_Init, SHA256_Update, SHA256_Final, one-shot SHA256
    openssl/evp.hEVP_aes_256_gcm with the usual EVP_Encrypt* / EVP_Decrypt* calls and the GCM IV and tag controls
    openssl/rand.hRAND_bytes, from the kernel's random source on Minimal-OS (RDRAND where the CPU has it) and getrandom on Linux
    minimaSSL/tls_gcm.hAES-128-GCM with associated data, the record protection TLS 1.3 needs (SDK edition)

    Return values follow OpenSSL's convention: 1 for success, 0 for failure. Contexts are wiped with a cleanse the optimiser cannot remove, and a failed GCM tag check means the plaintext must be thrown away.

    Seal and open with AES-256-GCM

    #include <openssl/evp.h>

EVP_CIPHER_CTX* c = EVP_CIPHER_CTX_new();
int len, total;
EVP_EncryptInit_ex(c, EVP_aes_256_gcm(), NULL, NULL, NULL);
EVP_CIPHER_CTX_ctrl(c, EVP_CTRL_GCM_SET_IVLEN, 12, NULL);
EVP_EncryptInit_ex(c, NULL, NULL, key, iv);
EVP_EncryptUpdate(c, NULL, &len, aad, aad_len);          /* out == NULL: AAD */
EVP_EncryptUpdate(c, ciphertext, &len, plaintext, n);
total = len;
EVP_EncryptFinal_ex(c, ciphertext + total, &len);
EVP_CIPHER_CTX_ctrl(c, EVP_CTRL_GCM_GET_TAG, 16, tag);
EVP_CIPHER_CTX_free(c);                                   /* NULL-safe, zeroizes */

    Where it runs

    • The kernel links the freestanding sources statically for wget https://… (TLS 1.3 with TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256).
    • make minimaSSL-slib builds minimaSSL.slib; formatting a disk installs it as 0:/etc/minimaSSL.slib.
    • The dlr / Deliver package client uses the same SHA-256 and AES-256-GCM code for its transport.

    Testing

    ./test.sh     # builds tests/selftest.c against the library and runs the known-answer tests

    The Minimal-OS tree also carries a TLS GCM known-answer test and an end-to-end HTTPS test against openssl s_server -tls1_3; see Build and debugging.

    3D library · C · header only

    FarcadeGL

    The 3D library of Minimal-OS. Drawing is recorded into a command buffer and submitted in one call, like Vulkan; state is a handful of simple calls and matrices are column-major, like OpenGL. Shaders are written in FGSL, a GLSL-style language compiled inside your program.

    FarcadeGL referenceFGSL languageHow the GPU side works

    How it runs

    FarcadeGL sits on the kernel's FGPU interface, SYS_GPU. The kernel checks every command buffer and runs it through its 3D pipeline: vertex stage, clipping, perspective-correct rasterization, depth test, fragment stage and blending. Shaders become FGPU bytecode in your program; the kernel verifies the bytecode before running it per vertex and per pixel. Surfaces and buffers go into video memory when the GPU driver can hand some out.

    Today the pipeline runs on the CPU. Programs do not depend on that: when a driver can run FGPU work on the card itself, the same programs and the same bytecode run there.

    A first program

    #include "farcadegl.h"
#include "window.h"

static const char* vs =
    "uniform mat4 fgl_ModelViewProjection;\n"
    "attribute vec3 position;\n"
    "attribute vec4 color;\n"
    "varying vec4 v_color;\n"
    "void main() {\n"
    "    v_color = color;\n"
    "    gl_Position = fgl_ModelViewProjection * vec4(position, 1.0);\n"
    "}\n";

static const char* fs =
    "uniform float time;\n"
    "varying vec4 v_color;\n"
    "void main() {\n"
    "    float pulse = 0.75 + 0.25 * sin(time * 4.0);\n"
    "    gl_FragColor = vec4(v_color.rgb * pulse, 1.0);\n"
    "}\n";

int main(void) {
    uint32_t win = mos_window_create(0, 100, 100, 640, 480, "Hello 3D");
    FGLContext* gl = fglCreateContext(&(FGLContextDesc){
        .width = 640, .height = 480, .window_id = win, .depth = 1 });

    FGLVertex cube[36];
    fglMakeCube(cube, 1.0f, NULL);
    FGLBuffer vb = fglCreateBuffer(gl, sizeof cube);
    fglBufferData(gl, vb, 0, cube, sizeof cube);

    FGLShader* sh = fglCreateShader(gl, vs, fs);
    if (!sh) return 1;          /* fglShaderLog(gl) says why */
    /* ... draw frames: see the reference for the full loop */
}

    What it has

    AreaHighlights
    TargetsDraw into a mosWM window or the whole screen (page flipping in VRAM), with an optional depth buffer
    GeometryVertex and index buffers, custom vertex layouts, ready-made plain and textured cubes
    StateDepth test, face culling, wireframe, alpha blending
    ShadersBuilt-in colour, Gouraud and Phong programs, or your own FGSL vertex and fragment shaders with uniforms
    TexturesUpload images and sample them with texture() in FGSL
    MathVectors and column-major 4×4 matrices: perspective, look-at, rotate, translate

    Try it

    Run fglcube in the Minimal-OS terminal (fglcube --shader for the FGSL version), or open Cube on the MOSdesk desktop and press S. Building FarcadeGL needs the 0.4.51 sources; it is not in the 0.4.50 release.

    Desktop environment · C

    MOSdesk

    The Minimal-OS desktop. It renders layered ARGB8888 surfaces with dirty-region updates, keeps your icon layout between boots, and brings themes, wallpapers, settings and smooth text to an OS that started with a text terminal.

    SourcemosWM, its window manager

    Features

    • Six coordinated colour themes and eight photo wallpapers, with fill, crop, stretch and rotation.
    • Smooth OpenType text: ttrend_outline rasterises Inter with exact-area coverage in integer fixed point (no floating point, no libm, no malloc while drawing), with the bitmap font as fallback.
    • A 16-icon, 64×64 pixel-art set compiled into a compact run-length encoded header.
    • Settings for appearance, mouse, cursor packs, sign-in, desktop grid and debug overlays.
    • Optional password sign-in on first launch (a desktop gate, not an OS account).
    • User accounts: each user gets 0:/users/<name> with Documents, Pictures and Desktop folders; anything in Desktop shows on the desktop.
    • Packaged as a Deliver .mpkg, installed by the package manager.

    Built-in apps

    Apps in mosdesk/apps/ are built with MOSdesk and installed to 0:/programs. The desktop and Start menu list them by name.

    InstallerInstalls Minimal-OS on a disk, GPT or MBR, after asking for your password

    Window manager · C

    mosWM

    The user-space window manager behind MOSdesk. It owns the display, draws the desktop and taskbar, and composites the windows applications create through the SDK's window.h. The kernel enforces who may touch which window.

    SourceWrite a mosWM app in Run Studio

    Windows

    • Rounded, themed chrome with per-window colours for the title bar, text, buttons, border and content.
    • Move from the title bar, resize from the lower-right corner; drag to a side, the top or a corner to tile.
    • Minimise, maximise, restore and fullscreen, with an app switcher on the taskbar.
    • Keyboard input goes to the focused window and pointer events to the window under the cursor.
    • A built-in Files window with copy, rename, delete and a right-click menu everywhere.

    Rendering

    mosWM repaints only what changed. The pointer is a small patch over the finished scene, so moving the mouse updates two small rectangles and an idle desktop draws nothing. Window moves, presents, hover highlights and the clock each damage only the rectangle they cover; damage_test.sh checks every partial repaint against a full one. Settings › Debug shows an FPS meter and a per-stage frame profiler — a healthy desktop reads 62.5 fps, mostly asleep.

    The application API

    #include "window.h"
#include "stdlib.h"

int main(void) {
    uint32_t id = mos_window_create(0, 80, 64, 640, 360, "Example");
    uint32_t* pixels = calloc(640 * 360, sizeof(uint32_t));
    for (;;) {
        syscall_window_event_t ev;
        while (mos_window_next_event(id, &ev) == SYS_SUCCESS)
            if (ev.type == SYSCALL_WINDOW_EVENT_CLOSE_REQUEST) { mos_window_close(id); return 0; }
        /* draw ARGB8888 pixels, then */
        mos_window_present(id, pixels, 640 * 4, 0, 0, 640, 360);
        mos_sleep(16);
    }
}

    Events cover resize, close requests, minimise, maximise, focus, keys (USB HID codes), mouse and wheel. mos_window_dispatch_events maps the window events to callbacks, and mos_window_set_style, mos_window_set_resizable and mos_window_set_fullscreen change how a window behaves.

    Security model

    Applications render into their own buffer; the kernel copies those pixels into the window surface, so no app ever holds another app's surface. Only a window's owner (or the process that launched it) can change it, and only the focused window's owner may change the pointer. The window-server role is granted only to the installed mosWM.run launched by the OS, and only after it owns the framebuffer.

    Install and run

    ./mosWM/build.sh                        # -> mosWM/dist/mosWM.run and mosWM.mpkg
run 0:/programs/mosWM/mosWM.run         # by hand, from the Minimal-OS terminal

    The package installs 0:/services/mosWM.service, so the service manager starts the desktop after the boot disk is mounted. Remove that file to boot to the terminal again.

    Web tool · JavaScript

    Run Studio

    A complete little toolchain in a web page: an editor, a C and C++ compiler, a preview of Minimal-OS with mosWM, and a linker that writes real .run and .mpkg files. Source and builds stay in your browser; preview network requests go directly from the browser.

    Open Run Studio

    The compiler

    Studio includes mcc, a C11 and C++ compiler written for it. C++ is lowered to the same syntax tree as C — methods take an explicit this, constructors and destructors become calls at the right places, virtual calls go through a vtable, templates are instantiated per use — so both back ends handle it unchanged. It preprocesses and type-checks your code against the real SDK headers (only the three inline-assembly syscall stubs are swapped for a __syscall builtin) and has two back ends:

    • Preview: JavaScript that runs in a Web Worker against an emulated memory with the same LP64 layout as the device. Every syscall goes to a small emulation of the Minimal-OS kernel that reads the same request structures the real kernel does.
    • Build: x86_64 machine code, linked into a position-independent ELF at base 0 with only R_X86_64_RELATIVE relocations, packed as MINIRUN1, optionally wrapped in an MPKG0001 package.

    Both back ends are checked against GCC and G++ on the same test programs, which print identical output — for C++ that includes the exact order of constructor, copy and destructor calls.

    The preview

    The preview recreates mosWM: window chrome with the kernel's default style or your own, moving, resizing, edge tiling, minimise and maximise, a taskbar, and a terminal for programs that print. Mouse and keyboard input arrive as the same window events mosWM posts, with USB HID key codes. Programs that use graphics.h draw to a full-screen framebuffer with the kernel's 8×8 font.

    3D works too. FarcadeGL programs draw through a JavaScript port of the kernel's GPU pipeline, with the same lighting, texturing, wireframe and FGSL shaders. Its frames are checked against the kernel's own rasterizer and match it pixel for pixel, apart from a few edge pixels. Try the 3D cube sample.

    Networking in the preview

    The preview maps outbound HTTP and HTTPS requests through the browser's fetch API. Use the SDK's DNS, TCP or TLS client calls to send one HTTP/1.x request per connection. Without a proxy, browser same-origin and CORS rules apply. To connect to sites that block browser requests, Studio can use the optional self-hosted HTTP relay; configure it with the httpProxy query parameter. Credentials are omitted and network failures are shown in the Studio output and preview terminal.

    This is not a raw socket implementation: UDP, DHCP, TCP listeners, TLS server sessions, and arbitrary non-HTTP protocols are unavailable. A program built in Studio still uses the full Minimal-OS networking stack when run on the OS.

    Self-hosted relay

    Run studio/proxy/server.mjs on a server with ALLOWED_HOSTS set to exact permitted destination hostnames and ALLOWED_ORIGINS set to the exact Studio origin. For example:

    ALLOWED_HOSTS=google.com,www.google.com \
ALLOWED_ORIGINS=https://fsminecrafter.github.io \
HOST=0.0.0.0 PORT=8787 node studio/proxy/server.mjs

    Put the relay behind HTTPS, then open studio/?httpProxy=https%3A%2F%2Fproxy.example.com%2Fv1%2Ffetch. The relay blocks private/reserved IPv4 addresses, allows 60 requests per client IP per minute, and rejects redirects to non-allowlisted hosts; add every expected redirect hostname explicitly.

    Limits

    • No goto, bit-fields, variable-length arrays, inline assembly or statement expressions; long double is double.
    • C++ without exceptions or RTTI (like the SDK), lambdas, rvalue references, multiple inheritance, member templates or class template specialization.
    • The preview cannot run SYS_EXEC or SYS_PKG. Its GPU cannot page flip, so full-screen FarcadeGL programs present by copying.

    Red Sandbox

    Open in its own tabSource
    3D · WebGL Red Sandbox Loads about 1 MB and uses your GPU.

    Build

    Parts stay loose until you glue them. Pause with Space, place parts, and drop a glue ball where they touch — everything it touches becomes one rigid piece. Turn on Auto glue (T) to stick each new part to the one under it.

    Make it move

    Bearings, axles, gears, belts, clutches and gearboxes make drivetrains. Wire buttons and sensors to motors, solenoids and igniters with the Wire tool (C). Injectors, turbos and igniters make engines whose fuel and air really burn; water, oil and gasoline pour and float things.

    Controls

    Space play or pause · [ ] slower or faster · R rewind · W A S D move · drag to orbit, right-drag to pan · 1–6 tools · ? full help.

    Game · JavaScript, Canvas, Web Audio

    Haul & Wrench

    Open in its own tab
    2D · Canvas · sound on Haul & Wrench Loads about 250 KB. Progress saves in this browser.

    Find the fault

    Click a part to inspect it for free, run a $10 bench test for a real reading, read stored codes with the OBD scan, or start the engine and listen: knocking is oil trouble, a whine is the alternator, stutters are misfires.

    Haul and grow

    Take several loads, deliver them stop by stop and park in the yellow bay. Watch the temperature, refuel, stop at red lights and mind the payload limit. Reputation unlocks better vehicles, cargo and a bank loan. Brave enough? The jungle road leads to Alterax, a military city where jobs pay 75% more, as long as your border pass is real.

    Controls

    →/D gas · ←/A/Space brake, hold to reverse · F refuel · C cruise · H horn · P pause. On the bench: 1–0 tools, R flip the ratchet, I impact wrench. Touch screens get pedals.

    NewtShooter

    Open in its own tabRead the guide
    3D · WebGL2 · sound on NewtShooter One 200 KB file. Needs a keyboard and mouse.

    Move like momentum matters

    Slide to keep speed and gain more on slopes, wall-run along any wall and leap off, climb and mantle ledges, charge a high jump, dash, and grapple across gaps. Nothing slows you down in the air, so the speed you build is yours to keep.

    Physics does the damage

    The Newton-9 rifle pushes whatever it hits, the Momentum shotgun shoves you backwards (aim down to blast-jump), and the Singularity launcher opens gravity wells that pull drones and crates together before they burst. Kick a crate into a drone and the crate does the work, grapple to a drone and kick it out of the sky, or break into a walker and shoot it from the inside. Modes: a guided tutorial, Arena waves, the Sky Trial and the 1.2 km Sky Marathon.

    Controls

    WASD move · Space jump · C slide · Shift sprint, tap to dash · V grapple · F kick · Q/E lean · G slow time · 1–3 weapons · R reload · Esc pause · Enter skip a tutorial step. Full guide.

    Web tool · JavaScript, Canvas, Web Audio

    Media Player

    Drop an .img, .vid or .adi file hereOr use Open a file. Files are decoded in this page and never leave your device.
    0:00.0 0:00.0

    What it opens

    .img pictures (RGB or with transparency), .vid videos with their soundtrack (both the lossless tiles codec and the lossy motion codec), and .adi sound in IMA-ADPCM or PCM16. These are the formats Photos, Video and Player use in MOSdesk.

    Making files

    mosmedia img photo.png out.img and mosmedia vid clip.mp4 out.vid convert pictures and videos (add --codec tiles for lossless video); wavtoadi.py turns a WAV into .adi. See Images and videos in the docs.

    Controls

    Space play or pause · ← → back or forward 5 seconds · , . previous or next frame · click the waveform to jump. Save keeps a picture or frame as PNG, or sound as WAV.
